items.title: llm-anthropic 0.31
items.summary: Release: llm-anthropic 0.31 Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 today. Fable 5.2 is currently ranked first on Artificial Analysis . Anthropic say it "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes", so clearly their internal benchmarks have become more ambitious! I've added the new models to llm-anthropic , so you can now run prompts through Fable 5.2 like this: uv tool install llm llm install llm-anthropic llm keys set anthropic # paste key here llm -m claude-fable-5.2 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" I ran pelicans at all five reasoning levels - low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . You can see them all here - here's the best result I got, from xhigh : max failed to return an image at all, running out of tokens after spending 128,000 thinking about them . That's the same bug that I saw with Opus 5.5 - but it's new for the Fable series, both Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 returned max effort pelicans just fine. It's priced at $8/million input and $40/million output, which is a 20% discount on the previous Fable 5.1 ($10/$50). I also used Fable 5.2 to help identify the source of a mysterious beep . Tags: llm , anthropic , claude , generative-ai , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable
items.summary_html:
Release: llm-anthropic 0.31

Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 today. Fable 5.2 is currently ranked first on Artificial Analysis. Anthropic say it "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes", so clearly their internal benchmarks have become more ambitious!

I've added the new models to llm-anthropic, so you can now run prompts through Fable 5.2 like this:

uv tool install llm
llm install llm-anthropic
llm keys set anthropic
# paste key here
llm -m claude-fable-5.2 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle"

I ran pelicans at all five reasoning levels - low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. You can see them all here - here's the best result I got, from xhigh:

max failed to return an image at all, running out of tokens after spending 128,000 thinking about them. That's the same bug that I saw with Opus 5.5 - but it's new for the Fable series, both Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 returned max effort pelicans just fine.

It's priced at $8/million input and $40/million output, which is a 20% discount on the previous Fable 5.1 ($10/$50).

I also used Fable 5.2 to help identify the source of a mysterious beep.

Tags: llm, anthropic, claude, generative-ai, pelican-riding-a-bicycle, ai, llms, claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.summary: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such. Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. How it works When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. How I built it I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. The research looked good, so I told it: Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces. I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran. This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients. On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn. From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran: I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map. what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...] Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps. each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound. The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for. There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location? I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app. And since I had one spare device, I then said: add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far Giving Claude Code ears I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to give Claude Code ears . Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone. I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket. Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem. I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not. Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun. Tags: projects , ai , generative-ai , llms , claude , coding-agents , claude-code , claude-mythos-fable

Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.

Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.

The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.

Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep!

I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.

Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such.

The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.

How it works

When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract:

We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.

That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!

Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.

When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.

How I built it

I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:

Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve

There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it

I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from

There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app

Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?

That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.

The research looked good, so I told it:

Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else

That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.

I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.

I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.

This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.

On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.

From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:

I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate

This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.

what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]

Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps

That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.

each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp

That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.

The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays

Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for

Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is

At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?

I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.

And since I had one spare device, I then said:

add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far

Giving Claude Code ears

I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to give Claude Code ears.

Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.

I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.

Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.

I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.

Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

items.title: Nvidia's succession dilemma just got real. Here's who could take over if Jensen Huang steps down.
items.summary: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang. ANTHONY WALLACE / AFP via Getty Images Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair and a board investigation are sparking questions about succession. Analysts and former employees point to Colette Kress and Ian Buck as possible successors. Nvidia said Huang is "committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." It's hard to imagine Nvidia without Jensen Huang — and the CEO has repeatedly discussed his intention to work for as long as possible. Now, the question of succession has come into sharp focus this week as Huang admitted to having an affair, and Nvidia's board announced it's investigating whether Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." If Huang steps down from his role, analysts and former employees floated several potential successors, including vice president Ian Buck and chief financial officer Colette Kress. Huang's two children, Madison and Spencer, also work at Nvidia, raising questions about whether leadership could remain in the family. Nvidia told Business Insider in a statement on Sunday that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." Huang would be hard to replace, said Brad Gastwirth, the global head of research at Circular Technology. While Huang doesn't have controlling voting power, he owns about 3.6% of Nvidia and would likely "have considerable input into succession unless the investigation uncovers serious wrongdoing," Gastwirth said. "Jensen's combination of technical expertise, strategic vision, and industry relationships is nearly impossible to replicate," he said. Inside Nvidia's succession dilemma Nvidia has not publicly designated a number two, and Huang is known for keeping an unusually flat leadership structure with as many as 60 direct reports . "That works beautifully while he's in the seat, but it means nobody has been groomed, tested, or publicly positioned as the heir," said Daniel Newman, CEO of The Futurum Group. One former employee said Madison Huang, who works as senior director of product marketing for physical AI, has been asserting greater authority across Nvidia's businesses, which they believe could be an effort to position herself for a larger leadership role. Madison Huang, Jensen Huang's daughter and Nvidia's senior director of product marketing for physical AI. Bloomberg/Getty Images Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson, said Kress is the company's only other highly visible executive and could take over as interim CEO if Huang stepped aside. Kress has worked at Nvidia for 13 years, and prior to that, she held finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft. Colette Kress, chief financial officer of Nvidia. Nvidia Since Kress lacks the engineering background that has been central to Huang's leadership, another possible long-term replacement is Ian Buck , a longtime executive who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia's dominance in AI. Buck heads Nvidia's data center and computing businesses, and he has worked at Nvidia for 22 years. "He's already running the group that is generating virtually all the revenues," the former employee said, referring to Nvidia's data center business. Ian Buck, vice president of accelerated computing at Nvidia. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images A second former employee cited the importance of Nvidia's distinctive culture in promoting a current executive as a successor. "Ideally it has to be someone from the company who's lived the values and the culture," they said. Could Nvidia look to an outsider? Some observers have floated executives from other major technology companies as potential successors, including Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian and Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman. Both oversee enormous cloud computing businesses that invest heavily in AI infrastructure and work closely with Nvidia, giving them firsthand knowledge of the customers and technologies driving its growth. While Huang's departure appears unlikely for now, Gastwirth said losing him under the current circumstances could seriously hurt Nvidia. "I think it would be one of the worst things that could happen to Nvidia," he said. "The company would continue operating, but I would question whether it could maintain the same pace of innovation and execution." Have a tip? Contact this reporter via email at gweiss@businessinsider.com or Signal at @geoffweiss.25. Use a personal email address, a non-work WiFi network, and a non-work device; here's our guide to sharing information securely. Read the original article on Business Insider

Nvidia told Business Insider in a statement on Sunday that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption."

Huang would be hard to replace, said Brad Gastwirth, the global head of research at Circular Technology. While Huang doesn't have controlling voting power, he owns about 3.6% of Nvidia and would likely "have considerable input into succession unless the investigation uncovers serious wrongdoing," Gastwirth said.

"Jensen's combination of technical expertise, strategic vision, and industry relationships is nearly impossible to replicate," he said.

Inside Nvidia's succession dilemma

Nvidia has not publicly designated a number two, and Huang is known for keeping an unusually flat leadership structure with as many as 60 direct reports.

"That works beautifully while he's in the seat, but it means nobody has been groomed, tested, or publicly positioned as the heir," said Daniel Newman, CEO of The Futurum Group.

One former employee said Madison Huang, who works as senior director of product marketing for physical AI, has been asserting greater authority across Nvidia's businesses, which they believe could be an effort to position herself for a larger leadership role.

Madison Huang, Jensen Huang's daughter and Nvidia's senior director of product marketing for physical AI.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson, said Kress is the company's only other highly visible executive and could take over as interim CEO if Huang stepped aside.

Kress has worked at Nvidia for 13 years, and prior to that, she held finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft.

Colette Kress, chief financial officer of Nvidia.

Nvidia

Since Kress lacks the engineering background that has been central to Huang's leadership, another possible long-term replacement is Ian Buck, a longtime executive who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia's dominance in AI.

Buck heads Nvidia's data center and computing businesses, and he has worked at Nvidia for 22 years.

"He's already running the group that is generating virtually all the revenues," the former employee said, referring to Nvidia's data center business.

Ian Buck, vice president of accelerated computing at Nvidia.

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

A second former employee cited the importance of Nvidia's distinctive culture in promoting a current executive as a successor.

"Ideally it has to be someone from the company who's lived the values and the culture," they said.

Could Nvidia look to an outsider?

Some observers have floated executives from other major technology companies as potential successors, including Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian and Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman.

Both oversee enormous cloud computing businesses that invest heavily in AI infrastructure and work closely with Nvidia, giving them firsthand knowledge of the customers and technologies driving its growth.

While Huang's departure appears unlikely for now, Gastwirth said losing him under the current circumstances could seriously hurt Nvidia.

"I think it would be one of the worst things that could happen to Nvidia," he said. "The company would continue operating, but I would question whether it could maintain the same pace of innovation and execution."

items.title: Trump says Jensen Huang told him he didn’t know the person he had an affair with 'was a spy'
items.summary: President Donald Trump said he checked in on Jensen Huang as the Nvidia CEO was caught up in an affair scandal. MANDEL NGAN / AFP via Getty Images President Donald Trump is backing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after an affair scandal. Trump said Huang told him on Monday that he didn't know the person he had an affair with "was a spy." "And I really believe him," Trump said. President Donald Trump is sticking by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. At an impromptu White House press conference on Monday with Dana White , Trump said he had checked in on the exec earlier that day to see how he was doing. On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, and Nvidia's board of directors said it was opening an investigation into whether the CEO was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." Trump said that on a phone call Monday, he asked Huang directly about the allegations that the woman was a spy. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump told reporters at the White House. "I asked him that question. 'Did you have any idea that she was a spy?' Said, 'I had no idea that she was a spy,' and I really believe him." Trump also praised Huang and said he felt "very confident that he'll be in good shape." Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The New York Times has reported that US intelligence officials believe the woman at the center of the scandal, Alice Huang , was recruited to gather information about Nvidia for the Chinese government. The scandal has led to speculation about whether Huang will maintain his role as CEO of Nvidia. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: A $60 billion fintech hired a 14-year-old. Its CEO explains why.
items.summary: Ramp hired a 14-year-old intern after discovering an app he had built for fun that attracted attention from roughly a million people on Twitter. Co-CEO Eric Glyman discussed the hire during a November 5 interview with founder and editor of Upstairs Media, Alex Konrad , explaining how the $60 billion fintech company evaluates engineering talent beyond traditional qualifications, a recalibration playing out across the industry as AI redraws what a junior role even means . A viral app, no assignment “We had an intern who was 14 years old,” Glyman said. “Part of how we found him was he had built his own app for fun that was genuinely useful, and a million people saw it on Twitter and interacted with it. There was no one who was telling him, ‘Hey, go build this project.’ He just was interested in it.” Glyman did not identify the teenager or specify when he worked at Ramp. “Part of how we found him was he had built his own app for fun that was genuinely useful, and a million people saw it on Twitter…” The Minecraft server test Glyman says Ramp looks for developers who have pursued projects on their own, even when that experience doesn’t come from a conventional job, a premium on self-direction that grows sharper as AI erodes the entry-level tasks that once trained new engineers . “A lot of what we’re looking for is strong evidence that someone has built something on their own, created something on their own, and shown their drive where it didn’t come from other people saying, ‘I need you to go do something’.” “A lot of what we’re looking for is strong evidence that someone has built something on their own… and shown their drive where it didn’t come from other people saying, ‘I need you to go do something’.” In a separate November 3 interview with Blackstone , Glyman said Ramp also looks for developers who got their start running Minecraft servers as teenagers. Some teens built their own servers before high school, gaining practical programming experience long before entering the workforce. Glyman acknowledged that the approach has limits, since talented candidates who haven’t had the time, resources, or opportunity to build something independently could be overlooked at precisely the moment the entry-level rungs of the industry are already thinning out . A 28-year-old running engineering In June, Ramp appointed Rahul Sengottuvelu as chief technology officer at 28, replacing co-founder Karim Atiyeh , who became co-CEO alongside Glyman. Sengottuvelu joined Ramp through a 2023 acquisition and later led its applied AI team. He was already building AI products before ChatGPT became a household name. In its leadership announcement , Ramp pointed to Sengottuvelu’s experience building AI products and his ability to make tough technical decisions. He took over as CTO as the company was putting AI to work in more of its products and day-to-day operations. Small teams own the call Glyman also described how Ramp organizes its engineers into small teams of five or six people, giving them responsibility for deciding how to complete their projects. “If you look really deep into Ramp’s organizational design, it’s tons of small teams where we say, ‘Here’s the outcome we want you to drive, but it’s up to you.’ You can make the call on how you want to spend your time. Why hire someone who can surprise you with their creativity and then tell them, ‘Don’t make your own recipe’?” “Why hire someone who can surprise you with their creativity and then tell them, ‘Don’t make your own recipe’?” Glyman says adding more engineers doesn’t always mean getting work done faster since bigger teams often mean more people weighing in on decisions, which can add churn and slow workflow. Ramp instead gives smaller groups ownership of specific projects, with leadership setting the goals rather than prescribing every step. For Glyman, hiring people capable of making their own decisions only makes sense if they’re allowed to do so once they’re on the job.

items.title: Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang
items.summary: The leather-jacketed CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, spurring an investigation by his company and intense discussions worldwide. Recent reporting noted that since last year, US intelligence reports had identified Alice Huang (no relation) as not only the exec for an AI compute company renting access to Nvidia GPUs, but also a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies, including the “neoclouds” like Coreweave who have been some of its biggest customers. So far, Nvidia and Jensen Huang have said that they have “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that hasn’t settled things as the investigation continues. items.title: Hybrid Search Starts with Two Good Candidate Lists
items.summary: Consider a support query containing both an error code and an ordinary description of what went wrong. Exact matching helps find the code. Semantic retrieval helps when the description uses different words from the documentation. Neither signal is sufficient simply because it works well on a different kind of request. The useful question is which evidence each retrieval path contributes. I would resist starting this discussion with a fusion formula. Combining two rankings cannot recover a document that neither path retrieved. It can also make a poor candidate set look more sophisticated without improving its coverage. Before tuning a hybrid result, I want to see the dense and lexical lists separately and understand their failures. Stefan Webb’s Milvus hybrid-search tutorial provides the implementation foundation: a dense field, a server-generated BM25 field, and reciprocal-rank fusion. The walkthrough below uses a small original support corpus to make those relationships inspectable. It builds on the Milvus 2.5 API pattern and should be run against a compatible Standalone or Distributed server, using a client version matched to that server. Give each representation a clear owner The application generates dense embeddings. Milvus generates the BM25 representation from the text field through a schema function. Keeping those responsibilities explicit helps prevent a common category mistake: treating the sparse output as another application-supplied embedding array. The input to the lexical branch is raw text, and the server’s analyzer participates in defining how that text becomes searchable. Install the matching PyMilvus client with its model dependencies, start a test server at the endpoint below, and run the five snippets in order in one Python session. The embedding model may download files on first use. The default endpoint is for a local experiment; supply the authentication and connection settings appropriate to your deployment. These are demonstration documents, not production evaluation data. from pymilvus import (MilvusClient, DataType, Function, FunctionType, AnnSearchRequest, RRFRanker, model) client = MilvusClient(uri="http://localhost:19530") collection = "james_hybrid_support_demo" encoder = model.DefaultEmbeddingFunction() documents = [ "ERR_AUTH_401 means the API credential is missing or expired.", "Rotate an expired API token in account settings before retrying.", "ERR_RATE_429 indicates too many requests; use bounded retry backoff.", "A network timeout does not prove that the server rejected a write.", ] vectors = encoder.encode_documents(documents) dimension = len(vectors[0]) if client.has_collection(collection): raise RuntimeError("Use a fresh demo collection name; existing data is preserved.") Deriving the field dimension from the actual model output avoids copying a number that belongs to a different encoder. I would still record the model identity and revision in a real system. Dimension compatibility is necessary, but it does not establish that document vectors and query vectors inhabit the same semantic space. Both sides must use the intended encoding pipeline. Connect text to BM25 in the schema The schema keeps source text alongside the dense representation. The text field enables analysis, and a BM25 function connects it to the sparse output field. That is the relationship I want visible in code review: which input feeds which derived field, and which system maintains that derivation when the source changes. schema = client.create_schema(auto_id=False, enable_dynamic_field=False) schema.add_field("id", DataType.INT64, is_primary=True) schema.add_field("text", DataType.VARCHAR, max_length=4096, enable_analyzer=True) schema.add_field("dense", DataType.FLOAT_VECTOR, dim=dimension) schema.add_field("sparse", DataType.SPARSE_FLOAT_VECTOR) schema.add_function(Function(name="support_bm25", input_field_names=["text"], output_field_names=["sparse"], function_type=FunctionType.BM25)) An analyzer deserves testing rather than a casual default selection. Error identifiers, punctuation, product names, and multilingual content can expose differences between the text a person sees and the tokens a lexical index uses. A collection that accepts the data successfully can still behave unexpectedly on the precise identifiers that motivated adding full-text search. I would keep small analyzer-focused cases alongside broader relevance judgments. For example, check whether a request for a particular error identifier surfaces the document that explains it. That is a different question from whether a natural-language paraphrase retrieves a useful answer. Separating the cases makes it easier to decide whether a failure belongs to tokenization, dense encoding, or ranking. Build and populate both retrieval paths Each vector field needs an appropriate index and metric. The dense path below uses cosine similarity; the lexical path uses BM25 with a sparse inverted index. These are separate score systems. Their numeric outputs should not be treated as though one unit of cosine similarity means the same thing as one unit of BM25 relevance. indexes = client.prepare_index_params() indexes.add_index(field_name="dense", index_type="AUTOINDEX", metric_type="COSINE") indexes.add_index(field_name="sparse", index_type="SPARSE_INVERTED_INDEX", metric_type="BM25") client.create_collection(collection, schema=schema, index_params=indexes, consistency_level="Strong") client.insert(collection, data=[ {"id": i, "text": text, "dense": vector.tolist()} for i, (text, vector) in enumerate(zip(documents, vectors)) ]) client.flush(collection) client.load_collection(collection) Only the source text and dense vector are supplied during insertion. The schema function produces the sparse representation. The fixed IDs in this demonstration make returned results easy to compare. In a larger system, I would use stable identifiers that let evaluation reports connect a result back to its source document and current version. Changes to source text require careful ingestion behavior. A server-managed BM25 representation does not relieve the application of updating its dense embedding when the text changes. One database can store both fields while those fields still reflect different revisions if the application sends inconsistent updates. I would test that synchronization before trusting a hybrid result as a coherent view of a document. Inspect candidates before judging fusion Choose a query that can exercise both mechanisms, then request more candidates from each branch than the final output needs. Here the corpus contains only four records, so a candidate limit of four is enough to inspect the complete toy result. A production candidate budget needs measurement against corpus size, filtering, and latency constraints rather than being copied from this example. query = "How do I fix ERR_AUTH_401 after my access token expires?" query_vectors = encoder.encode_queries([query]).tolist() dense_candidates = client.search( collection, anns_field="dense", data=query_vectors, limit=4, search_params={"metric_type": "COSINE", "params": {}}, output_fields=["text"]) lexical_candidates = client.search( collection, anns_field="sparse", data=[query], limit=4, search_params={"metric_type": "BM25", "params": {}}, output_fields=["text"]) for label, results in [("dense", dense_candidates), ("BM25", lexical_candidates)]: print(label, [(hit["id"], hit["entity"]["text"]) for hit in results[0]]) The raw query goes to the BM25 field, while the encoded query goes to the dense field. That difference is easy to obscure behind a helper function, but it matters when diagnosing results. I would keep both lists in evaluation artifacts, even if the application ultimately shows only the fused output. No particular ordering is promised by this walkthrough. Model behavior, analyzer settings, and the deployed version can affect it. The useful exercise is to identify which relevant records appear in each candidate set and which are absent from both. If a needed document never becomes a candidate, changing the final ranker’s preference is the wrong place to start repairing the failure. Fuse ranks and preserve the evidence Reciprocal-rank fusion combines positions in ranked lists rather than directly adding their raw similarity scores. That makes it a practical starting point when the branches use different metrics. It still requires judgment about candidate depth and the final result budget. A rank-based method is a baseline to evaluate, not a guarantee that every combined result improves. dense_request = AnnSearchRequest( data=query_vectors, anns_field="dense", param={"metric_type": "COSINE", "params": {}}, limit=4) lexical_request = AnnSearchRequest( data=[query], anns_field="sparse", param={"metric_type": "BM25", "params": {}}, limit=4) combined = client.hybrid_search( collection, reqs=[dense_request, lexical_request], ranker=RRFRanker(), limit=3, output_fields=["text"]) for hit in combined[0]: print(hit["id"], hit["entity"]["text"]) I would compare this output with both standalone baselines on exactly the same requests. Preserve returned IDs and relevance judgments so disagreements can be inspected later. A hybrid system that improves one query class while harming another should make that tradeoff visible. One averaged success figure can conceal a regression in the requests that matter most to the application. Filtering needs the same discipline. If tenant or access restrictions apply, both retrieval branches must operate within the intended authorized scope. The small public toy corpus omits those requirements for clarity. They belong in a production design before relevance tuning, because retrieving an unauthorized candidate is not an acceptable intermediate step simply because a later stage might remove it. Evaluate the retrieval system you intend to ship I would build an evaluation set containing exact identifiers, natural-language paraphrases, ambiguous requests, and queries with no useful answer in the corpus. Measure candidate coverage and final ranking quality, then inspect per-query differences. A small demo proves the API wiring; it cannot establish the business value of hybrid retrieval or justify a general claim about recall improvement. Latency and operational behavior belong beside relevance. The two branches share a request budget, and the service needs a deliberate response when retrieval fails or times out. If an application introduces a fallback, record when that fallback runs. Otherwise a system described as hybrid may often be serving a different retrieval path without its operators noticing. The full-text search documentation and multi-vector search guide explain the relevant API mechanisms. My starting point is narrower: create two understandable candidate lists, preserve their evidence, and test whether fusion helps the actual workload. The additional machinery earns its place when those results support it, not merely when the final call returns successfully. Hybrid Search Starts with Two Good Candidate Lists was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Error identifiers, punctuation, product names, and multilingual content can expose differences between the text a person sees and the tokens a lexical index uses. A collection that accepts the data successfully can still behave unexpectedly on the precise identifiers that motivated adding full-text search.

I would keep small analyzer-focused cases alongside broader relevance judgments. For example, check whether a request for a particular error identifier surfaces the document that explains it. That is a different question from whether a natural-language paraphrase retrieves a useful answer. Separating the cases makes it easier to decide whether a failure belongs to tokenization, dense encoding, or ranking.

Build and populate both retrieval paths

Each vector field needs an appropriate index and metric. The dense path below uses cosine similarity; the lexical path uses BM25 with a sparse inverted index. These are separate score systems. Their numeric outputs should not be treated as though one unit of cosine similarity means the same thing as one unit of BM25 relevance.

indexes = client.prepare_index_params()
indexes.add_index(field_name="dense", index_type="AUTOINDEX",
                  metric_type="COSINE")
indexes.add_index(field_name="sparse", index_type="SPARSE_INVERTED_INDEX",
                  metric_type="BM25")
client.create_collection(collection, schema=schema, index_params=indexes,
                         consistency_level="Strong")
client.insert(collection, data=[
    {"id": i, "text": text, "dense": vector.tolist()}
    for i, (text, vector) in enumerate(zip(documents, vectors))
])
client.flush(collection)
client.load_collection(collection)

Only the source text and dense vector are supplied during insertion. The schema function produces the sparse representation. The fixed IDs in this demonstration make returned results easy to compare. In a larger system, I would use stable identifiers that let evaluation reports connect a result back to its source document and current version.

Changes to source text require careful ingestion behavior. A server-managed BM25 representation does not relieve the application of updating its dense embedding when the text changes. One database can store both fields while those fields still reflect different revisions if the application sends inconsistent updates. I would test that synchronization before trusting a hybrid result as a coherent view of a document.

Inspect candidates before judging fusion

Choose a query that can exercise both mechanisms, then request more candidates from each branch than the final output needs. Here the corpus contains only four records, so a candidate limit of four is enough to inspect the complete toy result. A production candidate budget needs measurement against corpus size, filtering, and latency constraints rather than being copied from this example.

query = "How do I fix ERR_AUTH_401 after my access token expires?"
query_vectors = encoder.encode_queries([query]).tolist()
dense_candidates = client.search(
    collection, anns_field="dense", data=query_vectors, limit=4,
    search_params={"metric_type": "COSINE", "params": {}},
    output_fields=["text"])
lexical_candidates = client.search(
    collection, anns_field="sparse", data=[query], limit=4,
    search_params={"metric_type": "BM25", "params": {}},
    output_fields=["text"])
for label, results in [("dense", dense_candidates), ("BM25", lexical_candidates)]:
    print(label, [(hit["id"], hit["entity"]["text"]) for hit in results[0]])

The raw query goes to the BM25 field, while the encoded query goes to the dense field. That difference is easy to obscure behind a helper function, but it matters when diagnosing results. I would keep both lists in evaluation artifacts, even if the application ultimately shows only the fused output.

No particular ordering is promised by this walkthrough. Model behavior, analyzer settings, and the deployed version can affect it. The useful exercise is to identify which relevant records appear in each candidate set and which are absent from both. If a needed document never becomes a candidate, changing the final ranker’s preference is the wrong place to start repairing the failure.

Fuse ranks and preserve the evidence

Reciprocal-rank fusion combines positions in ranked lists rather than directly adding their raw similarity scores. That makes it a practical starting point when the branches use different metrics. It still requires judgment about candidate depth and the final result budget. A rank-based method is a baseline to evaluate, not a guarantee that every combined result improves.

dense_request = AnnSearchRequest(
    data=query_vectors, anns_field="dense",
    param={"metric_type": "COSINE", "params": {}}, limit=4)
lexical_request = AnnSearchRequest(
    data=[query], anns_field="sparse",
    param={"metric_type": "BM25", "params": {}}, limit=4)
combined = client.hybrid_search(
    collection, reqs=[dense_request, lexical_request],
    ranker=RRFRanker(), limit=3, output_fields=["text"])
for hit in combined[0]:
    print(hit["id"], hit["entity"]["text"])

I would compare this output with both standalone baselines on exactly the same requests. Preserve returned IDs and relevance judgments so disagreements can be inspected later. A hybrid system that improves one query class while harming another should make that tradeoff visible. One averaged success figure can conceal a regression in the requests that matter most to the application.

Filtering needs the same discipline. If tenant or access restrictions apply, both retrieval branches must operate within the intended authorized scope. The small public toy corpus omits those requirements for clarity. They belong in a production design before relevance tuning, because retrieving an unauthorized candidate is not an acceptable intermediate step simply because a later stage might remove it.

Evaluate the retrieval system you intend to ship

I would build an evaluation set containing exact identifiers, natural-language paraphrases, ambiguous requests, and queries with no useful answer in the corpus. Measure candidate coverage and final ranking quality, then inspect per-query differences. A small demo proves the API wiring; it cannot establish the business value of hybrid retrieval or justify a general claim about recall improvement.

Latency and operational behavior belong beside relevance. The two branches share a request budget, and the service needs a deliberate response when retrieval fails or times out. If an application introduces a fallback, record when that fallback runs. Otherwise a system described as hybrid may often be serving a different retrieval path without its operators noticing.

The full-text search documentation and multi-vector search guide explain the relevant API mechanisms. My starting point is narrower: create two understandable candidate lists, preserve their evidence, and test whether fusion helps the actual workload. The additional machinery earns its place when those results support it, not merely when the final call returns successfully.

Hybrid Search Starts with Two Good Candidate Lists was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair is getting the meme treatment.

Jens Kalaene/picture alliance via Getty Images

  • The internet lit up with memes after Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair.
  • Some imagined a payday for Huang's wife. Others spoofed past cheating scandals, like the Coldplay "kiss cam" saga.
  • One meme suggested Huang would be headed back to Denny's, where he worked at age 15.

The internet is making light of Jensen Huang's decidedly dark start to the week.

The Nvidia CEO told staff on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Social media accounts quickly began spoofing Huang's infidelity.

One account turned Huang into the viral Coldplay "kiss cam" moment, when Astronomer's former CEO, Andy Byron, and then head of people, Kristin Cabot, were caught embracing. Another put Huang into the classic "distracted boyfriend" meme, showing a man walking with one woman while looking back at another.

He really did the meme 😭 pic.twitter.com/e0DE7B0AcC

— XHabib (@XHabib) November 8, 2026

Then there's the iPhone Duo, Apple's new foldable that has two screens. One user showed Huang and his wife on the phone's front. When opened, the device also extends to show Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive with whom The New York Times reported Huang had a close relationship.

iPhone Duo简直是phone of meme。要壁纸的评论区👇#jensen #JensenHuang pic.twitter.com/LZ8HKTgdMv

— 在悉尼和稀泥 (@JamesAI) November 9, 2026

Huang's wife, Lori, was a common subject of these memes. One account showed her stacking cash while asking if they would get a divorce. Another showed a video of two people on a boat with the caption: "Me and Jensen Huang's ex wife after she gets half his money in the divorce."

To be sure, Huang in his memo wrote to his wife and kids that he hoped "our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust."

Jensen Huang’s wife divorce lawyers right now pic.twitter.com/QE3EEOtE71

— Not Jerome Powell (@alifarhat79) November 9, 2026

Some X users also memed the subject of Nvidia's investigation: that Huang might have been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." Cue the spy memes, some of which were already bubbling after an OpenAI security incident.

Huang's penchant for leather jackets also came up.

pic.twitter.com/B4VQfD5Mnu

— snootypigeon (@snootypigeon) November 8, 2026

One user made a flowchart titled "How To Tell If Your GF Is A Spy." Many made references to the Austin Powers movie, "The Spy Who Shagged Me."

Don't worry guys, this is the NVIDIA board

the former Taco Bell President is helping to investigate Jensen Huang pic.twitter.com/yVfvnPwQD1

— Jameson Zaballos (@JamesonZaballos) November 9, 2026

Should Huang step down? It's the question tech onlookers (and President Donald Trump) are debating. On social media, that looked like memes predicting Huang's unemployment.

One user joked that he was headed to a new gig at Denny's, where he worked as a dishwasher when he was 15. Another gave him the LinkedIn banner: #OpenToWork.

items.title: A Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle is on the way — and Skydance laid out the timeline for its streamers joining forces
items.summary: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images; Illustration by Omar Marques/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Paramount+ and HBO Max will be available in a bundle early next year. Skydance announced the news in its first earnings report since Paramount bought WBD. David Ellison's company is also combining the Paramount+ and HBO Max tech platforms so it can create a "unified product." The Paramount+ and HBO Max marriage is around the corner. Skydance will bundle the streamers in early 2027, the company said Monday as it shared its third-quarter earnings — its first report since Paramount bought Warner Bros. Discovery in early October. It's unclear how much the HBO Max-Paramount+ bundle will cost. Skydance said it would share more details on the bundle and "its streaming roadmap" in the coming months. HBO Max costs $10.99 a month with ads, or $18.49 for the standard ad-free plan, while Paramount+ is $8.99 a month with ads and $13.99 for the ad-free version. Without a discount, it costs about $20 a month to get HBO Max and Paramount+ with ads separately, and $32.48 to get them without ads. David Ellison's media giant is also planning to combine the Paramount+ and HBO Max tech platforms in the next 11 months so it can create a "unified product." Paramount merged the backend of its namesake streamer with its free service, Pluto TV, over about 18 months in a process known internally as convergence . Skydance said it will lean on AI tools to move faster this time around. "We expect to bring Paramount+ and HBO Max together much faster, aiming to align our backend systems within a year of closing, enabling us to quickly deliver a unified product," Skydance said in its third-quarter shareholder letter. Skydance posted solid Q3 earnings Skydance largely met Wall Street's expectations in its third-quarter report. The new media company met its revenue projections and exceeded adjusted earnings estimates. Revenue climbed 5% year-over-year to $7 billion, within the $6.95 billion to $7.15 billion range that Paramount had told investors to expect. Adjusted EBITDA, a measure of profitability excluding certain items, was $1 billion, above the company's $875 million to $975 million range. Shares were volatile in early after-hours trading, following a surge of over 8.5% on Monday. Skydance's stock entered earnings down more than 11% since the October 6 merger. items.title: How agentic AI raises the bar for law firms
items.summary: The legal world is looking to scale AI beyond chatbots, bringing in agents to automate parts of lawyers’ workflows. While adoption is growing rapidly, some firms are moving slower than others. Laura Mandaro, managing editor at The Information, talked to three legal experts about how firms can overcome pushback, encourage adoption and measure AI’s returns. Isabel Parker, Chief Innovation Officer, White & Case Jillian Burnett, VP Engagement, Legora Sunita Verma, CTO, Ironclad The agent advantage At many law firms, drafting non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) are a time sink. Sunita Verma of Ironclad, an AI-driven contract management company, said this is a workflow that can easily be outsourced to an agent. “One of the themes we hear consistently from our customers is that they want their lawyers spending less time on NDAs and more time on strategic deals,” she said. For some clients that have outsourced NDAs to AI, the time saved has made it possible to bring work previously handled by external legal providers in-house. But not every law firm has embraced AI. Isabel Parker said that while lawyers at White & Case were comfortable using AI for basics like summarizing documents, most remained resistant to a wider rollout of agents. The firm does use agents to improve client experiences, mostly through client-specific skills that capture preferences, from tone of voice to who needs to be included on contracts and communications. The skills make institutional knowledge easier to share. “In the past, a lawyer might say, ‘I’m about to submit this to X client, how do they like to see it again? Has anyone written this down?’ And emails would be flying around and everyone’s hair on fire,” Parker said. “This makes it much more streamlined.” Getting lawyers on board Jillian Burnett acknowledges that skepticism from lawyers can be a barrier to adopting agentic tools like Legora, the agentic operating system for legal work. A bigger obstacle, she said, is AI fatigue, and an understandable unwillingness to sacrifice time for training with vendors to learn new tools. “If you just released a new functionality and they just went through training on our assistant, lawyers aren’t necessarily going to want to give you more of their billable time to learn something new,” she said. She stressed the importance of showing lawyers what the platform and its agents can deliver through individual training sessions and small focus groups, noting that lawyers will give you their time when it’s clearly worth it. “By the time Legora walks into a meeting with a customer, we already understand their workflows and can present use cases directly relevant to the matters on their desk,” she said. Another challenge is deciding which skills to operationalize. “When you have a lot of people creating skills, it can get super noisy,” she said. One way to reduce that noise is to set up knowledge teams or steering committees made up of innovation leads, senior partners and other decision-makers to help set the criteria for which skills should become firm-wide standards. Legora can then help users find skills through tags, such as practice areas, and give firms control over how broadly those skills are shared. Factoring in the costs As vendors move to consumption-based pricing, law firms face costs that are far harder to predict. “Accounting for technology spend is entirely new for law firms. It’s utterly unpredictable and we’re just not set up for it yet,” Parker said. Legora uses customer data to help clients forecast consumption and track spending. “We’re working with our clients day in and day out to provide them with visibility into their consumption patterns, and to offer suggestions on how to optimize their credit consumption,” Burnett said. Burnett said the baseline metrics are efficiency, speed and reduced risk. For some clients, that means keeping headcount flat while absorbing more work; for others, faster client turnarounds. Parker urged firms to take a longer-term view, ensuring that developing talent doesn’t become a casualty of chasing efficiency. White & Case is preserving opportunities for junior lawyers to learn rather than automating every task. Verma said Ironclad takes a similar approach with developers. “We made a very conscious decision to pair our senior developers with junior developers so they can learn that art of judgment, which is something that AI will never be able to replace,” she said.

The legal world is looking to scale AI beyond chatbots, bringing in agents to automate parts of lawyers’ workflows. While adoption is growing rapidly, some firms are moving slower than others. Laura Mandaro, managing editor at The Information, talked to three legal experts about how firms can overcome pushback, encourage adoption and measure AI’s returns.

  • Isabel Parker, Chief Innovation Officer, White & Case
  • Jillian Burnett, VP Engagement, Legora
  • Sunita Verma, CTO, Ironclad

The agent advantage

At many law firms, drafting non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) are a time sink. Sunita Verma of Ironclad, an AI-driven contract management company, said this is a workflow that can easily be outsourced to an agent.

“One of the themes we hear consistently from our customers is that they want their lawyers spending less time on NDAs and more time on strategic deals,” she said. For some clients that have outsourced NDAs to AI, the time saved has made it possible to bring work previously handled by external legal providers in-house.

But not every law firm has embraced AI. Isabel Parker said that while lawyers at White & Case were comfortable using AI for basics like summarizing documents, most remained resistant to a wider rollout of agents.

The firm does use agents to improve client experiences, mostly through client-specific skills that capture preferences, from tone of voice to who needs to be included on contracts and communications. The skills make institutional knowledge easier to share.

“In the past, a lawyer might say, ‘I’m about to submit this to X client, how do they like to see it again? Has anyone written this down?’ And emails would be flying around and everyone’s hair on fire,” Parker said. “This makes it much more streamlined.”

Getting lawyers on board

Jillian Burnett acknowledges that skepticism from lawyers can be a barrier to adopting agentic tools like Legora, the agentic operating system for legal work. A bigger obstacle, she said, is AI fatigue, and an understandable unwillingness to sacrifice time for training with vendors to learn new tools.

“If you just released a new functionality and they just went through training on our assistant, lawyers aren’t necessarily going to want to give you more of their billable time to learn something new,” she said. She stressed the importance of showing lawyers what the platform and its agents can deliver through individual training sessions and small focus groups, noting that lawyers will give you their time when it’s clearly worth it.

“By the time Legora walks into a meeting with a customer, we already understand their workflows and can present use cases directly relevant to the matters on their desk,” she said.

Another challenge is deciding which skills to operationalize.

“When you have a lot of people creating skills, it can get super noisy,” she said. One way to reduce that noise is to set up knowledge teams or steering committees made up of innovation leads, senior partners and other decision-makers to help set the criteria for which skills should become firm-wide standards. Legora can then help users find skills through tags, such as practice areas, and give firms control over how broadly those skills are shared.

Factoring in the costs

As vendors move to consumption-based pricing, law firms face costs that are far harder to predict.

“Accounting for technology spend is entirely new for law firms. It’s utterly unpredictable and we’re just not set up for it yet,” Parker said.

Legora uses customer data to help clients forecast consumption and track spending.

“We’re working with our clients day in and day out to provide them with visibility into their consumption patterns, and to offer suggestions on how to optimize their credit consumption,” Burnett said.

Burnett said the baseline metrics are efficiency, speed and reduced risk. For some clients, that means keeping headcount flat while absorbing more work; for others, faster client turnarounds.

Parker urged firms to take a longer-term view, ensuring that developing talent doesn’t become a casualty of chasing efficiency. White & Case is preserving opportunities for junior lawyers to learn rather than automating every task. Verma said Ironclad takes a similar approach with developers.

“We made a very conscious decision to pair our senior developers with junior developers so they can learn that art of judgment, which is something that AI will never be able to replace,” she said.

items.title: Why Jensen-Gate may actually help the AI boom
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaking at the Fireworks AI conference in San Francisco on Nov. 3, 2026. Alistair Barr/Business Insider Jensen Huang's affair and China spy claims rattle Nvidia, but global AI demand isn't impacted. The scandal could shift AI chip supply from China to US firms as Megaspeed faces scrutiny. US cloud giants could gain access to more AI chips as China gets cut off more severely. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affair and the allegations of Chinese espionage surrounding it have rocked Silicon Valley. Amid all the drama, there's an important question: What does this mean for the AI boom? Probably very little, according to Wall Street's reaction on Monday. This extraordinary episode could end up being a storm in a honeypot when it comes to America's massive AI buildout. It might even help. First, some important context. Huang has admitted to being unfaithful to his wife, and Nvidia's board is investigating whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, was recruited to spy for China, according to The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal. That's a serious allegation, but it's not an established fact. Business Insider has not independently verified the US government's assessment. And intelligence agencies can be wrong. Their confident claims about weapons of mass destruction in Iraq turned out to be very wrong. (Talk about "artificial" intelligence). Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. Now, back to the AI boom. Will software developers stop using Claude Code and Codex because Jensen Huang cheated on his wife and his lover might be a Chinese spy? No. Will the 1.2 billion people using ChatGPT every week suddenly stop asking it questions? Of course not. And will businesses abandon their efforts to use AI to save time and money, and increase productivity? Highly unlikely. In fact, Western companies might drop Chinese open-weight models over this scandal, helping US AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI. Anyway, the main point is that rampant demand for AI isn't going anywhere because of one CEO's private life. "We still foresee significant upside for AI chipmakers and anticipate technological advancements and the need for significantly more computing power in the years ahead," Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello wrote on Monday. "We still anticipate that Nvidia's forecast of $3 trillion to $4 trillion of annual AI infrastructure spending by 2030 will come to fruition, regardless of this news." Nvidia could continue to dominate The more interesting question is what happens to the supply of the powerful chips needed to run AI. Nvidia dominates this market, and Huang has been instrumental in building that position. His departure could disrupt the company's strategy, relationships, and financing arrangements. Eventual lawmaker probes could be another headache for Nvidia. That uncertainty manifested itself in a 4% drop in Nvidia shares. But the rest of the tech market jumped on Monday, with rival AI chipmaker AMD surging 13%. That's a sign that demand is still strong, but might shift away from Nvidia if Jensen Huang is forced to step down. Beyond that, there's another possibility worth considering. Megaspeed has faced scrutiny over whether its overseas data centers helped Chinese customers access Nvidia chips despite US export restrictions. The scandal could make such arrangements harder, potentially ending Nvidia's ability to sell GPUs in China. That would keep more of Nvidia's supply available for American customers — welcome news for Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and other companies spending enormous sums building AI data centers. There's no guarantee this happens, or that additional supply would lower prices. But with demand for Nvidia's products still enormous, it's a plausible upside for the US. Meanwhile, Huang has spent years lobbying Washington to loosen restrictions on chip sales to China, with limited success. Bernstein chip analyst Stacy Rasgon questioned whether any alleged Chinese influence was necessary, given Huang's longstanding position (as the CEO of a for-profit company) of wanting to sell his products as far and wide as possible. "A key worry seems to be that Ms. Huang might have influenced Jensen to lobby the US to allow more sales of Nvidia's products into China," Rasgon wrote in a note to investors on Monday. "This seems superfluous to us as he has been doing that for years anyway and hardly needs encouragement (though not terribly successfully as China sales remain low)." The scandal could also pass. Huang could remain Nvidia's CEO, and there's no indication customers are canceling orders (outside of China where the government is actually blocking GPU sales). Morningstar's Colello expects Nvidia's business to remain strong. He maintained his $310 fair value estimate for the stock, almost double its Monday trading price. "We also must consider the possibility of the entire episode fading away for Nvidia," he wrote. "Jensen Huang's position as Nvidia's co-founder and only CEO likely gives him more support with the board than most other executives. US President Donald Trump announced his support when the allegations first arose." The future of AI depends on whether people and businesses keep finding the technology useful, and whether companies can build enough infrastructure to meet demand. Jensen Huang's romantic life changes neither equation. If anything, this affair might leave America with more chips to power its AI ambitions. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Nvidia stock and CEO Jensen Huang's net worth tumble after bombshell affair revelations
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a message to staff that he was unfaithful to his wife. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Nvidia shares dropped sharply on Monday after revelations about CEO Jensen Huang's personal life. The chipmaker is investigating whether Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." Nvidia stock fell as much as 9% before paring the loss to end 4% lower at $178.67. Nvidia stock dropped sharply on Monday as markets reacted to news of CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital relationship. The stock fell as much as 9%, before paring the loss to end the day about 4% lower at $178.67. The stock is down 22% in the last month, and down 5% year to date. Tech stocks have faced a broader sell-off amid investor concerns that AI infrastructure won't be built as quickly as hoped, sparked by neocloud firms' high debt levels and the Democrats' big gains in the midterm elections, which could slow data center construction. Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has overseen a meteoric rise, with the company worth trillions since the AI boom supercharged demand for its chips. As its founder and longtime CEO, Huang is pivotal to Nvidia's ongoing success, and Monday's share price decline likely reflects concerns the scandal could lead to his departure from the chipmaker. "The so-called 'key-man risk' looms large here, and it's doubtful markets have adequately priced it in," Mohamed El-Erian, the legendary bond investor, wrote in an X post. "This will not be easy for the board to navigate." As one of its founders, Huang has a substantial financial stake in Nvidia, which has ballooned in value as the company has grown. As of Friday's market close, he has a net worth of $155 billion, making him the 10th richest person on earth, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Huang's Nvidia stake fell in value by as much as $13 billion to around $138 billion on Monday morning, Business Insider calculated based on his most recent ownership disclosure. Revelations about Huang's personal life In late October, The New York Times reported that American intelligence agencies discovered that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang , a Chinese citizen and former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. US officials suspected her company was steering Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, and concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset, the report said. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told the Times, "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected." On Sunday, Jensen Huang sent a note to staff acknowledging he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, Lori Huang , to whom he's been married for over 40 years. Nvidia's board of directors opened an investigation into whether its CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." "My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully." Read the original article on Business Insider
