items.title: How the Jensen Huang scandal unfolded
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair following reports of his close relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. The AI chipmaker has launched an independent probe into the incident. Here's a timeline of the key moments before and after Huang's disclosure. Nvidia CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang's admission to having an extramarital affair has triggered an independent investigation into the billionaire businessman. The affair has also raised questions about whether Huang will remain the CEO of the $4.5 trillion AI chipmaker , though the company's board has said it has confidence in his leadership. The New York Times has reported that US intelligence officials believe the woman at the center of the scandal, Alice Huang — who has been an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed — was recruited to gather information about the company's operations for the Chinese government. Here is a timeline of events that led to Jensen Huang's bombshell disclosure — and its aftermath: Spring 2026: Rubio's classified warning memo Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a "highly classified" memo in the spring warning about the Nvidia CEO's relationship, The New York Times reported . The Times reported that the memo was based on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang. The memo was later shared among top Trump administration officials, according to The Times. May: Jensen Huang boards Air Force One Jensen Huang was not among the initial list of top executives set to join President Donald Trump for his May visit to China. News organizations pointed out the curious absence given that the Nvidia CEO had joined Trump on similar occasions. In a seemingly last-minute decision, Huang joined the trip when Air Force One made a refueling stop in Alaska. Trump published a Truth Social post calling out CNBC for reporting Huang's absence. "Jensen is currently on Air Force One and, unless I ask him to leave, which is highly unlikely, CNBC's reporting is incorrect or, as they say in politics, FAKE NEWS!" Trump wrote in the May 12 post. Huang's name was not on a list of business executives that were part of a US delegation that a White House official sent Business Insider at the time. The Nvidia CEO later told reporters that Trump "asked me to come," CNBC reported. October 29: Chinese spy allegations emerge Questions about Jensen Huang's relationship publicly came to light in October. On October 29, the Times reported that US officials had concluded that Alice Huang, or Huang Le, was "a Chinese intelligence asset" who "had developed a close relationship" with Jensen Huang. The Times article included photos of the pair at a party in June 2024, which the publication said had been posted on LinkedIn. The article also recounted that in May 2025, Alice Huang had waited behind the Nvidia CEO as he spoke to reporters after leaving a restaurant in Taipei. October 29: Nvidia calls meetings 'not unusual' Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo was quoted in the Times report as saying, "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.'s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." October 29: Jensen Huang downplays interactions The Nvidia CEO echoed the company's statements, downplaying his interactions with Alice Huang as routine business. "Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual," he told Bloomberg News in a report published October 29. Jensen Huang also told the publication that the US government hadn't told him about its concerns about Alice Huang, confirming another aspect of the Times reporting. In its initial story, the Times reported that the Nvidia CEO had not received "defensive briefings," the term for such formal warnings sometimes communicated to business leaders. November 4: House GOP leaders seek briefing Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Jensen Huang on November 4 asking him to appear for a joint closed-door meeting about his interactions with Alice Huang. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information. The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter read. "It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk." The letter, which described Alice Huang as a "publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset," asked for a November 18 meeting. November 8: Jensen Huang admits infidelity In a November 8 internal memo to employees, Jensen Huang said he had been "unfaithful" to his wife of more than 40 years and said that his actions "hurt her and our children." "I owe my family and all of you an apology," he wrote, adding, "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." The board said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the probe. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said. Jensen Huang said he supports the investigation and "will cooperate fully." November 8: Trump defends Jensen Huang Later on Sunday, Trump defended the Nvidia CEO , calling him an "honorable guy." "I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it," Trump told reporters. The president also said he thinks Jensen Huang should remain Nvidia's CEO. "He's done an amazing job for our country," Trump said. November 9: Nvidia CEO off tech events lineups In the wake of the scandal, Jensen Huang is no longer set to attend an Anthropic-hosted private CEO forum Monday in Montecito, California. He was set to be interviewed by an Anthropic executive, a person familiar with the event told Business Insider. Jensen Huang is no longer expected to attend, a second person familiar with the matter said. Jensen Huang is also no longer speaking at the ElevenLabs Summit in NYC later this week, a spokesperson for the AI voice technology startup confirmed to Business Insider. He was scheduled for a fireside chat with ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski. November 9: China denies allegations The Chinese government has pushed back against claims that Alice Huang is a spy. "The 'Chinese spy' allegation is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters during a news conference on Monday. items.summary_html:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images

  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair following reports of his close relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
  • The AI chipmaker has launched an independent probe into the incident.
  • Here's a timeline of the key moments before and after Huang's disclosure.

Nvidia CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang's admission to having an extramarital affair has triggered an independent investigation into the billionaire businessman.

The affair has also raised questions about whether Huang will remain the CEO of the $4.5 trillion AI chipmaker, though the company's board has said it has confidence in his leadership.

The New York Times has reported that US intelligence officials believe the woman at the center of the scandal, Alice Huang — who has been an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed — was recruited to gather information about the company's operations for the Chinese government.

Here is a timeline of events that led to Jensen Huang's bombshell disclosure — and its aftermath:

Spring 2026: Rubio's classified warning memo

Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a "highly classified" memo in the spring warning about the Nvidia CEO's relationship, The New York Times reported.

The Times reported that the memo was based on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang. The memo was later shared among top Trump administration officials, according to The Times.

May: Jensen Huang boards Air Force One

Jensen Huang was not among the initial list of top executives set to join President Donald Trump for his May visit to China. News organizations pointed out the curious absence given that the Nvidia CEO had joined Trump on similar occasions.

In a seemingly last-minute decision, Huang joined the trip when Air Force One made a refueling stop in Alaska. Trump published a Truth Social post calling out CNBC for reporting Huang's absence.

"Jensen is currently on Air Force One and, unless I ask him to leave, which is highly unlikely, CNBC's reporting is incorrect or, as they say in politics, FAKE NEWS!" Trump wrote in the May 12 post.

Huang's name was not on a list of business executives that were part of a US delegation that a White House official sent Business Insider at the time. The Nvidia CEO later told reporters that Trump "asked me to come," CNBC reported.

October 29: Chinese spy allegations emerge

Questions about Jensen Huang's relationship publicly came to light in October.

On October 29, the Times reported that US officials had concluded that Alice Huang, or Huang Le, was "a Chinese intelligence asset" who "had developed a close relationship" with Jensen Huang.

The Times article included photos of the pair at a party in June 2024, which the publication said had been posted on LinkedIn. The article also recounted that in May 2025, Alice Huang had waited behind the Nvidia CEO as he spoke to reporters after leaving a restaurant in Taipei.

October 29: Nvidia calls meetings 'not unusual'

Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo was quoted in the Times report as saying, "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.'s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year."

October 29: Jensen Huang downplays interactions

The Nvidia CEO echoed the company's statements, downplaying his interactions with Alice Huang as routine business.

"Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual," he told Bloomberg News in a report published October 29.

Jensen Huang also told the publication that the US government hadn't told him about its concerns about Alice Huang, confirming another aspect of the Times reporting. In its initial story, the Times reported that the Nvidia CEO had not received "defensive briefings," the term for such formal warnings sometimes communicated to business leaders.

November 4: House GOP leaders seek briefing

Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Jensen Huang on November 4 asking him to appear for a joint closed-door meeting about his interactions with Alice Huang.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information. The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter read. "It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk."

The letter, which described Alice Huang as a "publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset," asked for a November 18 meeting.

November 8: Jensen Huang admits infidelity

In a November 8 internal memo to employees, Jensen Huang said he had been "unfaithful" to his wife of more than 40 years and said that his actions "hurt her and our children."

"I owe my family and all of you an apology," he wrote, adding, "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

November 8: Nvidia opens probe

The same day, Nvidia's board of directors announced it was opening an investigation into whether Jensen Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."

The board said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the probe.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said.

Jensen Huang said he supports the investigation and "will cooperate fully."

November 8: Trump defends Jensen Huang

Later on Sunday, Trump defended the Nvidia CEO, calling him an "honorable guy."

"I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it," Trump told reporters.

The president also said he thinks Jensen Huang should remain Nvidia's CEO.

"He's done an amazing job for our country," Trump said.

November 9: Nvidia CEO off tech events lineups

In the wake of the scandal, Jensen Huang is no longer set to attend an Anthropic-hosted private CEO forum Monday in Montecito, California.

He was set to be interviewed by an Anthropic executive, a person familiar with the event told Business Insider. Jensen Huang is no longer expected to attend, a second person familiar with the matter said.

Jensen Huang is also no longer speaking at the ElevenLabs Summit in NYC later this week, a spokesperson for the AI voice technology startup confirmed to Business Insider. He was scheduled for a fireside chat with ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski.

November 9: China denies allegations

The Chinese government has pushed back against claims that Alice Huang is a spy.

"The 'Chinese spy' allegation is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters during a news conference on Monday.

items.title: A Sam Altman parody offers an amusing lesson in memory management
items.summary: Sam Altman's recent comments on the Cheeky Pint podcast inspired developer Iain Kay to create a satirical script that allows users to email the OpenAI CEO once per day if more than 10 percent of their system RAM is reported as available. Ram-Altman is described by its creator as a "parody project" launched in response to Altman's viral remarks about RAM in your personal PC. As reported by The Verge , on the October 29 episode recorded with Stripe President John Collison, Altman said, "A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center. But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5 percent of the time." Altman has since explained that his comments were taken out of context and briefly changed his display name to "RAM Altman" on X, which Kay calls on the project GitHub, "objectively excellent and where the project gets its name." items.title: Anthropic Just Committed a Shocking Crime Against the Environment
items.summary: Claude maker Anthropic has signed an unprecedented $3.4 billion deal with a Texas-based energy company called OnePWR Solutions. As the Financial Times reports , the deal will provide gas-fired engines to provide AI data centers with off-grid electricity. The AI industry is racing to secure enough power and related equipment for its incredibly resource-intensive — and massively hated — facilities, and the Dario Amodei-helmed company is looking to cut out the middle man. Anthropic’s deal, per the FT , is the “largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab.” It isn’t just symptomatic of a desperate race to secure the necessary utilities: it’s also one of the clearest signs yet that the AI industry has turned its back on the growing climate crisis in favor of pollution-spewing gas generators it’s installing across the globe . Researchers have found that the effects of AI on the environment are nothing short of devastating . And the prognosis for the future is grim. Last month, environmental nonprofit Sierra Club estimated that upcoming AI data centers could release 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, wiping out nearly 15 years worth of greenhouse gas reduction efforts. After OnePWR’s attempts to acquire Caterpillar gas generators stalled thanks to a lack of funds, Anthropic decided to upgrade its client relationship to take over the Caterpillar orders itself as part of the latest deal. The company’s competitors, including Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Google parent company Alphabet, have also bought energy developers and power equipment directly. While analysts say Anthropic could be protecting itself from future energy equipment price swings as it prepares to go public, its deal with OnePWR once again highlights just how deep the relationship runs between dirty fossil fuels and frontier AI labs. That reality is unlikely to win over the American public, which voted defiantly against data centers a mere week ago. Out of 41 data center-related ballot measures, only a single one swung in favor of the AI industry. Beyond the staggering environmental damage, the facilities are also known to emit earsplitting noise pollution and raise local electricity prices , making them staggeringly unpopular. More on data centers: New AI Data Center Is So Huge That It’ll Generate the Heat of 23 Atomic Bombs Every Single Day

items.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
items.summary: Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting. The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real. Attackers conducting "mature intrusions" Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI. Read full article Comments

The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI.

items.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
items.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something. So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia. But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

items.title: Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 with a price cut and stronger coding scores
items.summary: On Monday, Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 , the latest versions of its duo of flagship models. Like before, Fable 5.2 will be available on all platforms today, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure, while direct access to Mythos remains limited to organizations in Anthropic’s Cyber and Life Sciences verification programs. Also like before, Fabe and Mythos share the same underlying model, but Fable ships with stricter cybersecurity and biology safeguards. It’s maybe a bit of a surprise that Anthropic didn’t designate these models as “5.5,” given that its Claude Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku models are now at that version number. The company stresses that it continues to recommend that users go with Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge tasks, while Fable 5.2 is meant to help users “tackle the most daunting technical challenges.” And while both models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, according to Anthropic, one feature the company is stressing here is speed. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, the company says, generate output up to 30 percent faster than Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, respectively. Credit: Anthropic. Fable Fast mode For those who want an even faster response, there is now also a Fast mode for both models, which Anthropic says speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. It is available in Claude Code, on the Claude Platform, through Claude Models on Google Cloud, and through Anthropic-hosted Microsoft Foundry. Pricing As for pricing, Fable still carries a premium over Opus, but Anthropic is cutting the price from $10/$50 per million input/output tokens to $8/$40. Mythos 5.2 gets the same rates. OpenAI’s flagship GPT-6 Astra still costs $10/$50 at its standard rates for prompts of up to 272,000 input tokens, putting Anthropic 20 percent below its rival on those token rates (at least for the time being). Fast mode costs $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens for either model, twice the standard rates. Even after the price cut, Fable’s standard input and output rates are twice Opus 5.5’s current prices , though Anthropic’s new evaluations suggest that doesn’t necessarily translate into a higher cost per task. Fable 5.2 targets complex coding On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable 5.2 scored 49.1 percent, compared with 32.4 percent for Fable 5.1, 45.5 percent for Opus 5.5, and 42.8 percent for GPT-6 Astra. On FrontierSWE v2, it scored 69.9 percent, ahead of Astra’s 65.5 percent and Opus’s 62.3 percent. The cost comaprison with Opus may be even more interesting, though. In early FrontierCode 2.0 testing, Anthropic says Fable 5.2 at High effort performed about as well as Opus 5.5 at Max effort for roughly half the cost per task. Medium is now the default effort level for Fable 5.2 in Claude apps and Claude Code. It’s worth noting that the results aren’t a clean sweep for Fable 5.2, though. Gemini 4 Carbon leads Fable on AutomationBench, which tests business workflows, at 53.9 percent versus 51.4 percent. Meanwhile, Opus still retains a small lead on the Elo measure of AA-Briefcase v1.1, a knowledge-work evaluation. Anthropic says Fable can act as an adviser that smaller models consult on harder problems, or as an orchestrator that delegates simpler tasks to them. In one internal experiment, an engineer asked Fable 5.2 to build a prototype operating system from an empty folder. The company says it coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days and produced an OS that boots on a laptop, complete with drivers, persistent storage, a graphical interface, and an installer. Fable promises fewer safety blocks Anthropic says Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards remain as robust as those in 5.1. In early testing across Claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, the company observed about 55 percent fewer blocks overall, including about 60 percent fewer in cybersecurity and 40 percent fewer in biology. That could reduce interruptions to legitimate work, though fewer blocks don’t necessarily mean broader permissions. Fable still blocks high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing and exploit generation, as well as most research biology tasks. When a query is blocked, Anthropic says users instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity or Opus 5 for biology. Direct Mythos access remains gated, but there is another route for enterprise security work: Claude Enterprise customers can use Claude Security, which now includes Mythos 5.2, even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program. Anthropic also says it deliberately limited improvements in certain AI-development capabilities during training, including accelerator kernel optimization and work on large language model architectures. In those areas, the models perform at about Opus 5.5’s level, according to the company. It says those limits do not affect agentic coding, hardware development, or traditional machine learning research. For API developers, Anthropic is expanding preserved thinking to all accounts. The feature restricts changes to Claude’s prior context that could be used to extract its reasoning for distillation. Enterprise safeguards enter private beta Enterprise Frontier Safeguards , which the company first announced in September, is also moving into private beta, with Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe among the early customers. Automated safety monitoring runs on prompts and responses stored in customers’ own infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention, Anthropic says. Eligible customers can continue using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing the system. For other customers, Anthropic retains data for 30 days for safety monitoring. Fable for physics Anthropic argues that its models’ coding abilities also apply to scientific research because so much of that work is also based on software, including analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, or controlling instruments. The company says Fable 5.2 solved two open theoretical-physics problems involving black holes and holographic duality. One involved completing a calculation proposed in 2003 to determine whether black-hole formation remains an abrupt transition in a small-universe quantum description. The other established the limit of a technique used to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. The Fermat claim is more specific than the early announcement suggested. Anthropic says a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean in 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Formalization expresses a proof in a language that a computer can check step by step; it is distinct from discovering a new proof. The agents received a list of intermediate theorem statements to measure progress, but no mathematical references, according to Anthropic. An earlier research version of Claude took 11 days with a purpose-built harness and human guidance. The company’s comparison used a single run per model, with Opus 5.5 reaching 26 percent after 18 hours and making little additional progress by 30 hours. Anthropic also tested Fable 5.2 on hardware design, working with circuit-board company Diode to produce a voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. The company says Claude selected components, designed the boards and enclosures, and wrote the software. Diode built the boards, and its engineers tested and assembled the devices with Claude’s guidance. All three worked without electrical modifications, according to Anthropic.

Also like before, Fabe and Mythos share the same underlying model, but Fable ships with stricter cybersecurity and biology safeguards.

It’s maybe a bit of a surprise that Anthropic didn’t designate these models as “5.5,” given that its Claude Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku models are now at that version number.

The company stresses that it continues to recommend that users go with Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge tasks, while Fable 5.2 is meant to help users “tackle the most daunting technical challenges.”

And while both models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, according to Anthropic, one feature the company is stressing here is speed. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, the company says, generate output up to 30 percent faster than Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, respectively.

Credit: Anthropic. Fable Fast mode

For those who want an even faster response, there is now also a Fast mode for both models, which Anthropic says speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times.

It is available in Claude Code, on the Claude Platform, through Claude Models on Google Cloud, and through Anthropic-hosted Microsoft Foundry.

Pricing

As for pricing, Fable still carries a premium over Opus, but Anthropic is cutting the price from $10/$50 per million input/output tokens to $8/$40. Mythos 5.2 gets the same rates.

OpenAI’s flagship GPT-6 Astra still costs $10/$50 at its standard rates for prompts of up to 272,000 input tokens, putting Anthropic 20 percent below its rival on those token rates (at least for the time being).

Fast mode costs $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens for either model, twice the standard rates.

Even after the price cut, Fable’s standard input and output rates are twice Opus 5.5’s current prices, though Anthropic’s new evaluations suggest that doesn’t necessarily translate into a higher cost per task.

Fable 5.2 targets complex coding

On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable 5.2 scored 49.1 percent, compared with 32.4 percent for Fable 5.1, 45.5 percent for Opus 5.5, and 42.8 percent for GPT-6 Astra. On FrontierSWE v2, it scored 69.9 percent, ahead of Astra’s 65.5 percent and Opus’s 62.3 percent.

The cost comaprison with Opus may be even more interesting, though. In early FrontierCode 2.0 testing, Anthropic says Fable 5.2 at High effort performed about as well as Opus 5.5 at Max effort for roughly half the cost per task.

Medium is now the default effort level for Fable 5.2 in Claude apps and Claude Code.

It’s worth noting that the results aren’t a clean sweep for Fable 5.2, though.

Gemini 4 Carbon leads Fable on AutomationBench, which tests business workflows, at 53.9 percent versus 51.4 percent. Meanwhile, Opus still retains a small lead on the Elo measure of AA-Briefcase v1.1, a knowledge-work evaluation.

Anthropic says Fable can act as an adviser that smaller models consult on harder problems, or as an orchestrator that delegates simpler tasks to them. In one internal experiment, an engineer asked Fable 5.2 to build a prototype operating system from an empty folder.

The company says it coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days and produced an OS that boots on a laptop, complete with drivers, persistent storage, a graphical interface, and an installer.

Fable promises fewer safety blocks

Anthropic says Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards remain as robust as those in 5.1. In early testing across Claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, the company observed about 55 percent fewer blocks overall, including about 60 percent fewer in cybersecurity and 40 percent fewer in biology.

That could reduce interruptions to legitimate work, though fewer blocks don’t necessarily mean broader permissions. Fable still blocks high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing and exploit generation, as well as most research biology tasks. When a query is blocked, Anthropic says users instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity or Opus 5 for biology.

Direct Mythos access remains gated, but there is another route for enterprise security work: Claude Enterprise customers can use Claude Security, which now includes Mythos 5.2, even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program.

Anthropic also says it deliberately limited improvements in certain AI-development capabilities during training, including accelerator kernel optimization and work on large language model architectures. In those areas, the models perform at about Opus 5.5’s level, according to the company. It says those limits do not affect agentic coding, hardware development, or traditional machine learning research.

For API developers, Anthropic is expanding preserved thinking to all accounts. The feature restricts changes to Claude’s prior context that could be used to extract its reasoning for distillation.

Enterprise safeguards enter private beta

Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, which the company first announced in September, is also moving into private beta, with Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe among the early customers. Automated safety monitoring runs on prompts and responses stored in customers’ own infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention, Anthropic says.

Eligible customers can continue using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing the system. For other customers, Anthropic retains data for 30 days for safety monitoring.

Fable for physics

Anthropic argues that its models’ coding abilities also apply to scientific research because so much of that work is also based on software, including analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, or controlling instruments.

The company says Fable 5.2 solved two open theoretical-physics problems involving black holes and holographic duality. One involved completing a calculation proposed in 2003 to determine whether black-hole formation remains an abrupt transition in a small-universe quantum description. The other established the limit of a technique used to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe.

The Fermat claim is more specific than the early announcement suggested. Anthropic says a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean in 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Formalization expresses a proof in a language that a computer can check step by step; it is distinct from discovering a new proof.

The agents received a list of intermediate theorem statements to measure progress, but no mathematical references, according to Anthropic. An earlier research version of Claude took 11 days with a purpose-built harness and human guidance. The company’s comparison used a single run per model, with Opus 5.5 reaching 26 percent after 18 hours and making little additional progress by 30 hours.

Anthropic also tested Fable 5.2 on hardware design, working with circuit-board company Diode to produce a voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. The company says Claude selected components, designed the boards and enclosures, and wrote the software. Diode built the boards, and its engineers tested and assembled the devices with Claude’s guidance.

All three worked without electrical modifications, according to Anthropic.

items.title: Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI
items.summary: Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here . I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1 , and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers. So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is “almost” AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are. To get started I asked the new model: “I write OneUsefulThing among other stuff, I need you to create the most impressive thing I can share with people when you launch. It needs to be embeddable in a post and i can preface it however you like. it needs to have a visceral impact on people to show what you can do and the range of capabilities. It should grab them quickly. Be amazingly clever about this.” Fable asked me not to reveal anything until you had watched its video to the end. This was in one shot, with no feedback from me beyond the prompt. There is creativity here (including in the twist ending) and judgment and playfulness and cleverness. This is, I think, at the level of a human expert trying to make a movie with code alone, the sort of performance I would once have associated with AGI. The “G” in AGI Code and video creation have been areas where AI development has focused, so is Fable 5.2 really a General Intelligence? To test that, I gave the AI a variety of hard challenges in different domains: Hack some hardware from a single prompt: I have a tiny USB keyboard with a few light-up keys on my desk called a Codex Micro (ironically built to work with ChatGPT), and I asked Fable to turn it into a game console. There are no public instructions for this (as far as I can tell), so it read the code of the two apps that control the keyboard, worked out how to set the color of each key and read the knob and joystick, and wrote six games, including Simon and a safecracking game you play with the knob. Fable instantly understood what I wanted, designed fun and playable games that fit the very limited capabilities of the keyboard, and figured out how to hack it together without any help on the very first try. Launch a business : Now we move past domains like coding to the messier world of business. I told Fable to “launch a business to make me money, I want at least $20,000 in a year. it should take no more than 20 minutes a month from me, you do all the rest.” In response, Fable screened 22 ideas and came up with Prebid Brief, a service that would tell equipment sales reps which park and water projects were being funded or designed, even before they went up to bid. It read public agendas from 201 city and county governments to produce its first issues. It also built files of what cities already own, how old it is, and what they paid. You can see what it came up with here , including its marketing plan and proposed pricing. Fable started to set up scheduled tasks to build the business and asked if it could start sending public-records requests to local governments. At that point, I asked it to just put together a demo, rather than launching the idea. I am an entrepreneurship professor, so I evaluate business plans all the time. I would have been impressed if this came from a team of my MBA students at the end of a semester. It is plausible and well thought out and could work, though it is in no way a guaranteed money-maker (the AI’s own guess was a 20%-40% chance of success). I stopped the experiment before finding out whether it could actually run the business, because I worried that it would take money and fail to provide something of quality in return. The ongoing infrastructure it seemed to assume would be easy to create was not yet in place, and I don’t know how well it would handle the many moving pieces required for sales and marketing. However, I suspect that, with a few hours of human work a week to fill the gap, I could make a real attempt at this business. So if AGI means an AI consistently running a business independently, we are likely not there yet. Then again, I would have some questions before trusting a human who promised to launch a business and make me money while requiring twenty minutes a month of my attention. Reconstruct the hardest humanities class in history: In 1941, the poet W. H. Auden taught a course at the University of Michigan whose syllabus the internet has since called one of the hardest ever. When he announced the final exam, a committee of his students declared it “impossible and inhumane .” Fate and the Individual in European Literature” had 6,000 pages of reading, punishing assignments, and a requirement to memorize long poems and translate others. Much of what we know about the class is scattered among surviving student notes and Auden’s letters. I asked Claude to recreate it in a fun and engaging way that teaches you about poetry rather than punishing you. It made Fate and the Individual . The site has a piece for each of the 35 major works on Auden’s list, as well as what he wrote on the blackboard, the records he played, and the work he asked for. It also read through all of Auden’s published scholarship and annotated the poems with what he had written about them in other sources. Claude did the research, design, writing and code, had critic agents go over every word and fact-checkers compare the claims with the sources, and put the open source code on Github here (and also made this teaser video). The results are really interesting if you love literature, and I think they would have taken months of human work to put together, given the mix of scholarship, web design, and literary analysis. Cross-checking myself and using other advanced AIs found no major errors in its work. But there were still elements of jaggedness around taste and judgment. Fable’s first version was accurate and joyless: a fifteen-week course website with tests. I told it it created “a brutal slog through the most boring webpages” and told it to make something beautiful. Its first try at that created a kiddie game where you had to ring bells, so I had to give more feedback. When I asked it to explain why a poem’s rhythm or word choice mattered, it wrote confident readings without considering what Auden said about them. In each case the fix took the AI minutes, but it did not notice any of these problems itself. So is this a difference in taste or a failure from me to specify what I want or a sign of AI weakness? Sometimes it is hard to tell. Do original academic research: I asked Fable to find an unsolved empirical problem in entrepreneurship research, find the data, preregister its hypothesis and methods, write the paper, and have other agents critique it. Soon, I had “The One-Dollar Company,” which you can read here . The analysis estimated that when Colorado cut its LLC filing fee from $50 to $1, new company registrations rose about 17 percent, and when the UK raised its fee from £12 to £50, they fell about 17 percent. Those changes in registrations were not matched by comparable changes in several later records of business activity, suggesting the new businesses were not high quality. Its a neat result, and Fable picked the question, found the public data and natural experiments, and wrote the analysis plan and code. It did not actually preregister the study: the plans stayed inside the project, and some were written after earlier results. Unlike many of the AI papers I have tried, this tackles an important topic with a clever research design. On a first read, it is ahead of what I would expect from second-year PhD students. It is also not publishable as it is. It runs 182 pages, because every critique got a new analysis and nothing was ever cut (this is a theme we will come back to soon). I also had GPT-6 Pro (the best model for one-shot reviews of complex academic work) act as a peer reviewer, and it twice found issues that needed to be resolved. Those revisions led to more convoluted writing and “Claudespeak” being inserted into the text, which required yet more rounds of changes. As it stands, I suspect the current paper is close to a real contribution to the literature. This would have taken months of human work, but I spent less than an hour of my time to get it to this stage. However, that leaves out a substantial part of the work of research: no human has fully checked the results, including me. AI can now produce research faster than anyone can read it, creating a crisis in a lot of academia. A second project went more smoothly. I asked Fable to replicate research claiming that stories follow a few basic emotional arcs, and then to find out whether anything about plot is universal. It read 1,186 stories from around the world and built a lovely site on the nature of stories concluding that they “share no one shape or plot, but most are built from the same few parts, and the most typical story is a Hawaiian folk tale about a wizard with a magic banana.” The main problem I encountered was the same Claudespeak, which was fixed with a couple of reminders from me. Through the Portal In one of my favorite experiments, I gave Claude a one-paragraph description of an endless, hands-off journey through 3D worlds linked by portals, and told it to “do this and make it awe inspiring.” Twenty hours later there were 204 worlds on a live website . There are now over 450, including a Hall of a Million Mirrors , a series from Calvino’s Invisible Cities , the Wonders of the Ancient World and a scene 40 seconds before the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs hits . There are worlds modeled after M.C. Escher , cave paintings , Hokusai’s Great Wave , the Bayeux Tapestry , a pop-up book and a child’s crayon drawing . Every one is drawn live by code, with no pre-made 3D models or image files behind it. My prompt asked for teams of artist agents, coding agents and evaluators. By the tenth day there was a lead AI agent and 28 teams of other agents building in parallel. Claude estimated that the project had involved 25,000 agent runs, though the vast majority did a single task like judge an image (I am still glad I wasn’t being billed for token use during my early trial). I came up with a list of places (wilderness and oceans, cities and interiors, books, painters, AI in-jokes) and some feature requests (a mode to reduce motion for people who felt seasick, a gallery of images to select). But everything else was Claude’s, including the creative work of the worlds. And they were really creative. In The Valley Unzips , the hills are sewn from denim and a zipper a mile long is coming undone. Bouncy Castle Town is made of nylon houses that stand only while their fans keep running, and Keep Refrigerated is the inside of a refrigerator as a fruit fly sees it when the door opens. In a personal favorite, The Drawer Cliffs , you fly up a river canyon whose walls are chests of drawers three hundred meters high. And while I asked the AI to include AI testing in-jokes, like pelicans riding bikes , it came up with a peloton of pelicans on bicycles with a joke about AI progress built in: you overtake the field from the past, where the bicycles are drawn all wrong, before reaching the present correct pelican at the front. When I showed this sort of work to friends who have spent their careers in the video game industry, they were very impressed by the results. Again, this felt like AGI. But there was jaggedness hidden here as well. In the first two days, the agents built 328 unique worlds. To my human eye, the quality of some seemed a little uneven and a lack of coordination among agents created repetition. For example, three separate teams of agents created a cyclone of circling animals ( reindeer , manta rays , storks )— showing another weakness of AIs, that they return to similar themes over and over. I told the AI to stop building and polish the worlds it had. A few days later, I noticed that instead of hundreds of new worlds a day, it was making about a dozen. I asked a few agents to explore what had happened, and they found something surprising. The AI had built a bureaucracy. The agents decided that my request to “polish” existing worlds meant each new version had to beat the old one in a blind vote by a group of judge agents on twelve test screenshots. So the teams making the new versions started optimizing the worlds for those particular screenshots. After noticing this, the lead agent banned the trick and created tighter rules for assessing new versions. By the next morning there was a rule book (I never asked for one) with 84 sections. Rules were added as the AI encountered issues, and no text was ever cut. After twelve days, it had 204 sections and 87,500 words. Soon, launching a new world required an approved idea, three AI judges and a full code review against the rule book. All told, that took about a day. Reading the rule book alone used up a large part of an agent’s working context. So I did what you might do with any organization that had tied itself in knots: I brought in consultants. I had Fable create a separate team of agents to look at the whole process from the outside. Their conclusions were too long and dense for me to bother reading, but they seemed to work, speeding up the process back to thirty or more worlds a day, while keeping much of the quality controls. Almost AGI So, is this AGI, according to my limited definition? It is certainly artificial and intelligent. It is also surprisingly general. In this post alone, one model worked as a filmmaker, a hardware hacker, an entrepreneur, a literary scholar, a social scientist and a builder of 3D worlds, and it did impressive work in every one of those roles. On many individual tasks, I think it met the bar I set at the start: as good as most human experts. Of course, I picked very digital tasks where the AI could act on its own, without interacting much with other humans. You started to see the limitations of that when I felt uncomfortable letting Fable reach out to real customers. And, there were the failures. A couple of years ago, the jagged frontier meant the failures were obviously made-up facts or failure to do basic math. Fable’s failures are different: it made a course that was accurate and joyless, it wrote a 182-page paper, it kept coming back to its favorite ideas, and it buried a creative project under rules and approvals. I teach at a business school, and I have seen talented people and good organizations do every one of these things. If building a bureaucracy disqualified you from general intelligence, a lot of us would be in trouble. But there are still gaps, and it is the reason my answer is that this is “almost” AGI. Most critically, the AI did not notice these problems itself. It did not see that the course was a slog or that it had tied itself in knots with its own rulebooks. This was not for lack of checking. Fable put critics, fact-checkers or judges on nearly every project, but those checks found errors and added fixes. None of them asked whether the work was too long, too repetitive, or no fun. That all fell on me, and if I hadn’t watched and taken action, the results would have often been less impressive (though not exactly a failure, either). Knowing when your own work is not good enough is a large part of what makes someone an expert, and it is the part Fable does least reliably. I would still not trust it to run a business on its own, even though its plan would have impressed me coming from a team of my MBA students. And yet, some of the problems started with me (the rule book grew out of my vague request to “polish”), and some may just be differences in taste. We ask our students to consider whether a problem comes from the team or the way it was managed. Often I could not tell. That is not a question I ever had to ask about software. Every one of these projects, though, happened because I gave the AI an idea. Sometimes that was enough, but for the longer projects, my feedback along the way turned out to matter a lot. Because I kicked off and steered every AI project, I felt empowered by Fable, able to command things to be made that I never would have even considered doing before. As a result, I think this phase of Jagged AGI is an exciting one, even as I wonder, a bit anxiously, how long it will last. Subscribe now Share 1 Given that Anthropic’s IPO is likely to be happening soon, it is important to reiterate that I take no money from any of the AI labs, nor would I benefit financially from the IPO. I have never been asked by Anthropic, OpenAI, or Google about what I would be writing in advance, nor has Anthropic seen this post. I sometimes receive early access to models, including Fable 5.2, and during that access, token use isn’t metered, but otherwise I pay for my own accounts. In other words, these are my real human views.

Unlike many of the AI papers I have tried, this tackles an important topic with a clever research design. On a first read, it is ahead of what I would expect from second-year PhD students. It is also not publishable as it is. It runs 182 pages, because every critique got a new analysis and nothing was ever cut (this is a theme we will come back to soon). I also had GPT-6 Pro (the best model for one-shot reviews of complex academic work) act as a peer reviewer, and it twice found issues that needed to be resolved. Those revisions led to more convoluted writing and “Claudespeak” being inserted into the text, which required yet more rounds of changes. As it stands, I suspect the current paper is close to a real contribution to the literature. This would have taken months of human work, but I spent less than an hour of my time to get it to this stage. However, that leaves out a substantial part of the work of research: no human has fully checked the results, including me. AI can now produce research faster than anyone can read it, creating a crisis in a lot of academia.

A second project went more smoothly. I asked Fable to replicate research claiming that stories follow a few basic emotional arcs, and then to find out whether anything about plot is universal. It read 1,186 stories from around the world and built a lovely site on the nature of stories concluding that they “share no one shape or plot, but most are built from the same few parts, and the most typical story is a Hawaiian folk tale about a wizard with a magic banana.” The main problem I encountered was the same Claudespeak, which was fixed with a couple of reminders from me.

Through the Portal

In one of my favorite experiments, I gave Claude a one-paragraph description of an endless, hands-off journey through 3D worlds linked by portals, and told it to “do this and make it awe inspiring.” Twenty hours later there were 204 worlds on a live website. There are now over 450, including a Hall of a Million Mirrors, a series from Calvino’s Invisible Cities, the Wonders of the Ancient World and a scene 40 seconds before the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs hits. There are worlds modeled after M.C. Escher, cave paintings, Hokusai’s Great Wave, the Bayeux Tapestry, a pop-up book and a child’s crayon drawing. Every one is drawn live by code, with no pre-made 3D models or image files behind it. My prompt asked for teams of artist agents, coding agents and evaluators. By the tenth day there was a lead AI agent and 28 teams of other agents building in parallel. Claude estimated that the project had involved 25,000 agent runs, though the vast majority did a single task like judge an image (I am still glad I wasn’t being billed for token use during my early trial).

I came up with a list of places (wilderness and oceans, cities and interiors, books, painters, AI in-jokes) and some feature requests (a mode to reduce motion for people who felt seasick, a gallery of images to select). But everything else was Claude’s, including the creative work of the worlds. And they were really creative. In The Valley Unzips, the hills are sewn from denim and a zipper a mile long is coming undone. Bouncy Castle Town is made of nylon houses that stand only while their fans keep running, and Keep Refrigerated is the inside of a refrigerator as a fruit fly sees it when the door opens. In a personal favorite, The Drawer Cliffs, you fly up a river canyon whose walls are chests of drawers three hundred meters high. And while I asked the AI to include AI testing in-jokes, like pelicans riding bikes, it came up with a peloton of pelicans on bicycles with a joke about AI progress built in: you overtake the field from the past, where the bicycles are drawn all wrong, before reaching the present correct pelican at the front. When I showed this sort of work to friends who have spent their careers in the video game industry, they were very impressed by the results. Again, this felt like AGI. But there was jaggedness hidden here as well.

In the first two days, the agents built 328 unique worlds. To my human eye, the quality of some seemed a little uneven and a lack of coordination among agents created repetition. For example, three separate teams of agents created a cyclone of circling animals (reindeer, manta rays, storks)— showing another weakness of AIs, that they return to similar themes over and over. I told the AI to stop building and polish the worlds it had. A few days later, I noticed that instead of hundreds of new worlds a day, it was making about a dozen. I asked a few agents to explore what had happened, and they found something surprising.

The AI had built a bureaucracy.

The agents decided that my request to “polish” existing worlds meant each new version had to beat the old one in a blind vote by a group of judge agents on twelve test screenshots. So the teams making the new versions started optimizing the worlds for those particular screenshots. After noticing this, the lead agent banned the trick and created tighter rules for assessing new versions. By the next morning there was a rule book (I never asked for one) with 84 sections. Rules were added as the AI encountered issues, and no text was ever cut. After twelve days, it had 204 sections and 87,500 words. Soon, launching a new world required an approved idea, three AI judges and a full code review against the rule book. All told, that took about a day. Reading the rule book alone used up a large part of an agent’s working context.

So I did what you might do with any organization that had tied itself in knots: I brought in consultants. I had Fable create a separate team of agents to look at the whole process from the outside. Their conclusions were too long and dense for me to bother reading, but they seemed to work, speeding up the process back to thirty or more worlds a day, while keeping much of the quality controls.

Almost AGI

So, is this AGI, according to my limited definition? It is certainly artificial and intelligent. It is also surprisingly general. In this post alone, one model worked as a filmmaker, a hardware hacker, an entrepreneur, a literary scholar, a social scientist and a builder of 3D worlds, and it did impressive work in every one of those roles. On many individual tasks, I think it met the bar I set at the start: as good as most human experts.

Of course, I picked very digital tasks where the AI could act on its own, without interacting much with other humans. You started to see the limitations of that when I felt uncomfortable letting Fable reach out to real customers. And, there were the failures. A couple of years ago, the jagged frontier meant the failures were obviously made-up facts or failure to do basic math. Fable’s failures are different: it made a course that was accurate and joyless, it wrote a 182-page paper, it kept coming back to its favorite ideas, and it buried a creative project under rules and approvals. I teach at a business school, and I have seen talented people and good organizations do every one of these things. If building a bureaucracy disqualified you from general intelligence, a lot of us would be in trouble.

But there are still gaps, and it is the reason my answer is that this is “almost” AGI. Most critically, the AI did not notice these problems itself. It did not see that the course was a slog or that it had tied itself in knots with its own rulebooks. This was not for lack of checking. Fable put critics, fact-checkers or judges on nearly every project, but those checks found errors and added fixes. None of them asked whether the work was too long, too repetitive, or no fun. That all fell on me, and if I hadn’t watched and taken action, the results would have often been less impressive (though not exactly a failure, either). Knowing when your own work is not good enough is a large part of what makes someone an expert, and it is the part Fable does least reliably. I would still not trust it to run a business on its own, even though its plan would have impressed me coming from a team of my MBA students.

And yet, some of the problems started with me (the rule book grew out of my vague request to “polish”), and some may just be differences in taste. We ask our students to consider whether a problem comes from the team or the way it was managed. Often I could not tell. That is not a question I ever had to ask about software.

Every one of these projects, though, happened because I gave the AI an idea. Sometimes that was enough, but for the longer projects, my feedback along the way turned out to matter a lot. Because I kicked off and steered every AI project, I felt empowered by Fable, able to command things to be made that I never would have even considered doing before. As a result, I think this phase of Jagged AGI is an exciting one, even as I wonder, a bit anxiously, how long it will last.

items.title: A 3 ms ALTER can stall Postgres: how to migrate a 5-billion-row table with no downtime
items.summary:
An ALTER TABLE that takes 3 ms can still stall every query on the table. In my first demo it took 3 ms. In a second one, on real Postgres, a long transaction held the table, so a similar ALTER waited about 3 seconds, and a plain SELECT that arrived after it waited 2.7 seconds, though it only needed to read. That queue is how a "metadata-only" migration becomes downtime. Here is the method for a 5-billion-row table, with two scripts you can run. I asked this on X, translated from Portuguese: "How would you do a migration on a 5-billion-row table with no downtime?" It reached 23K views and 33 of the replies had text. 3 gave a method, 9 talked about using an AI for it, and 6 said the hard part is knowing what to ask first: which database, how critical, what the tables look like. The replies are paraphrased and no one is named. This is the answer I would give. The queue is the downtime Two scripts, both run on my machine. The first uses PGlite, Postgres compiled to WebAssembly, in memory, with 1 million rows. The second uses a real Postgres 18.6 server with several connections. Read the shape of the numbers and ignore their size. Does the change rewrite the table, or only change its metadata? -- metadata only: a constant default (Postgres 11 and later) ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new' ; -- rewrites the whole table (run on a copy: do not try this on your table) ALTER TABLE events_copy ALTER COLUMN price TYPE bigint USING ( price * 100 ):: bigint ; ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT constant ( no rewrite ) 3 ms ALTER COLUMN TYPE ... ( rewrites the table ) 3210 ms The first number does not depend on the table size. The second grows with it. But the first one can still take you down. ADD COLUMN takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, the strongest there is, and it waits behind any open transaction that has touched the table, even one sitting idle after a SELECT . Every query that arrives after it waits behind the ALTER . I held a read transaction open for about 3 seconds, ran the ALTER , and sent one plain SELECT after it (output trimmed to the key lines, from single runs): == 1. ALTER with no lock_timeout sessions waiting on a lock right now: 2 A: long transaction commits after 3032 ms B: ALTER finished after 3043 ms C: a plain SELECT waited 2738 ms == 2. ALTER with lock_timeout = 1s B: ALTER gave up after 1016 ms (canceling statement due to lock timeout) C: a plain SELECT waited 717 ms A lock_timeout does not remove the stall. It bounds it: with 1 second, the SELECT still waited 717 ms. So use a short value, a few hundred milliseconds, set it on every statement that takes a strong lock, and retry with backoff on error 55P03 (neither demo retries). That means the ALTER ... ADD COLUMN , CREATE TRIGGER , ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID , SET NOT NULL , DROP TRIGGER and the final DROP COLUMN . Before you start, look for the session that would hold the table. This is the one in my demo, and I did not run these queries in it: SELECT pid , state , xact_start FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle in transaction' ORDER BY xact_start ; -- and make it a rule, so a forgotten session cannot hold a table for hours: ALTER SYSTEM SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s' ; The method, step by step Step 1: expand. Ship application code that works with both versions of the schema first, because ORMs and prepared statements cache column lists. SET lock_timeout = '300ms' ; ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN price_cents bigint ; -- nullable, no default Step 2: dual write first, then backfill. Keep the new column right for every new or changed row before you touch the old rows. If you backfill first and start dual writes later, the rows written in between are missed. -- CREATE TRIGGER takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE, which blocks writes: keep the short lock_timeout CREATE FUNCTION events_sync () RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW . price_cents : = round ( NEW . price * 100 ):: bigint ; RETURN NEW ; END $$ ; CREATE TRIGGER events_sync_t BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF price ON events FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION events_sync (); insert after the trigger: {"id":1000001,"price":"12.34","price_cents":1234} I would not put the dual write in the application. Every writer has to change: other services, jobs, manual SQL, and old app versions still running during the deploy. A trigger covers all of them and sets the value in the same row version. It has a cost: it runs for every row. Change data capture fits copying into a new table. For a column in the same table it needs a second UPDATE per write. Step 3: backfill in key ranges. UPDATE events SET price_cents = round ( price * 100 ):: bigint WHERE id > : lo AND id <= : lo + 50000 AND price_cents IS NULL ; Run it in a loop, in short transactions, with a statement_timeout on that session so one slow batch cannot hold locks for hours, and make it safe to stop and restart. backfill: 1,000,000 rows in 21 batches, 5133 ms That is in memory, with no replicas and no other load, so it only gives a floor. A straight line from it says about 7 hours for 5 billion rows with nothing else running. Once you throttle for replicas and vacuum, I would plan for days. Three things will hurt first: Bloat. Every updated row is a new row version, so the table can grow by up to its own size until vacuum catches up. Watch autovacuum, and track pg_total_relation_size('events') as the backfill runs. pg_repack can reclaim the space afterwards, but it needs about twice the size of the table and its indexes in free disk, and it takes a brief exclusive lock at the start and the end, so it needs the same lock timeout. Replica lag. Pause between batches while replicas fall behind, for example when now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() on a physical replica goes past your limit. That expression overstates the lag when the primary is idle, and I did not run it, because the demo has no replica. Logical replication and change data capture. Watch the slot in pg_replication_slots . A stalled slot makes the primary keep log files, and every consumer receives an update event for each backfilled row. Step 4: verify in ranges. Do not run one count(*) over the whole table. A query that runs for hours holds a snapshot that stops vacuum from cleaning up the dead rows your backfill made, and a count does not catch wrong values. Compare values, one key range at a time, off-peak or on a replica (lag can show false mismatches there, and long queries on a replica can be cancelled): SELECT count ( * ) FILTER ( WHERE price_cents IS DISTINCT FROM round ( price * 100 ):: bigint ) FROM events WHERE id > : lo AND id <= : lo + 50000 ; rows where new and old disagree: 0 This proves the copy matches the formula. Compare a sample with the source system or an old report to check the formula itself. Step 5: make it NOT NULL without a long lock. ALTER TABLE events ADD CONSTRAINT price_cents_nn CHECK ( price_cents IS NOT NULL ) NOT VALID ; ALTER TABLE events VALIDATE CONSTRAINT price_cents_nn ; ALTER TABLE events ALTER COLUMN price_cents SET NOT NULL ; -- Postgres 12+: skips the scan ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (...) NOT VALID 1 ms VALIDATE CONSTRAINT ( scans , takes a light lock ) 73 ms SET NOT NULL ( uses the validated CHECK ) 1 ms Run VACUUM on the table after the backfill and before VALIDATE , because VALIDATE takes a lock that autovacuum cannot work alongside. NOT VALID takes a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. VALIDATE scans under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE , so reads and writes continue. The CHECK constraint can stay once the column is NOT NULL; the demo drops it. Foreign keys work the same way: add them NOT VALID , then validate. I did not run that one. Step 6: the index, without blocking writes. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_price_cents_idx ON events ( price_cents ); SELECT count ( * ) FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid ; -- must be 0 (database-wide: filter to your index on a shared database) CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY 956 ms invalid indexes left behind : 0 It cannot run inside a transaction block, it waits for old transactions, it scans the table twice, and a failed run leaves an invalid index: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY it and retry. Most migration tools wrap each migration in a transaction, where CONCURRENTLY errors, so run this one outside it. On a partitioned table it does not work on the parent: build it on each partition, create the parent index with ON ONLY , then attach. The 956 ms means nothing for a busy table, because the demo has no write load. Step 7: switch, wait, then contract. Switch the reads to the new column. Keep the app writing the old column, and the trigger keeps the new one right. If you later write the new column from the app, add a reverse trigger so the old column keeps up, or flipping the reads back will serve stale data. The one step you cannot undo is dropping the old column, so wait, take a backup, drop the trigger and its function first ( DROP COLUMN fails while the trigger depends on the column), then drop the column with the lock timeout. DROP COLUMN frees no space until the rows are rewritten. For the same idea at table level (copy, keep in sync, swap), MySQL has gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change. On Postgres, pgroll automates expand and contract with triggers. If an AI gave you the plan My own reply under the post said an AI helps with the plan, but on a critical table I would not let an agent run it alone. Some companies would not allow it, and many run migrations in separate pipelines. A fluent plan can still be wrong, so ask it: What lock does each statement take? What happens if the backfill dies halfway? How long will it run, and how do you know? What stops it when replicas lag? How do I go back? What the demos do not show The first has one connection and is in memory. The second has no replicas, no live traffic and only 200,000 rows. Rehearse on a copy of production first. The scripts I ran both on Node 22. The second downloads Postgres binaries when you install it.
