items.summary_html:
An ALTER TABLE that takes 3 ms can still stall every query on the table. In my first demo it took 3 ms. In a second one, on real Postgres, a long transaction held the table, so a similar ALTER waited about 3 seconds, and a plain SELECT that arrived after it waited 2.7 seconds, though it only needed to read. That queue is how a "metadata-only" migration becomes downtime. Here is the method for a 5-billion-row table, with two scripts you can run.

I asked this on X, translated from Portuguese: "How would you do a migration on a 5-billion-row table with no downtime?" It reached 23K views and 33 of the replies had text. 3 gave a method, 9 talked about using an AI for it, and 6 said the hard part is knowing what to ask first: which database, how critical, what the tables look like. The replies are paraphrased and no one is named. This is the answer I would give.

The queue is the downtime

Two scripts, both run on my machine. The first uses PGlite, Postgres compiled to WebAssembly, in memory, with 1 million rows. The second uses a real Postgres 18.6 server with several connections. Read the shape of the numbers and ignore their size.

Does the change rewrite the table, or only change its metadata?

-- metadata only: a constant default (Postgres 11 and later)
ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new';
-- rewrites the whole table (run on a copy: do not try this on your table)
ALTER TABLE events_copy ALTER COLUMN price TYPE bigint USING (price*100)::bigint;

ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT constant (no rewrite)   3 ms
ALTER COLUMN TYPE ... (rewrites the table)     3210 ms

The first number does not depend on the table size. The second grows with it. But the first one can still take you down. ADD COLUMN takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, the strongest there is, and it waits behind any open transaction that has touched the table, even one sitting idle after a SELECT. Every query that arrives after it waits behind the ALTER. I held a read transaction open for about 3 seconds, ran the ALTER, and sent one plain SELECT after it (output trimmed to the key lines, from single runs):

== 1. ALTER with no lock_timeout
sessions waiting on a lock right now: 2
A: long transaction commits after 3032 ms
B: ALTER finished after 3043 ms
C: a plain SELECT waited 2738 ms

== 2. ALTER with lock_timeout = 1s
B: ALTER gave up after 1016 ms (canceling statement due to lock timeout)
C: a plain SELECT waited 717 ms

A lock_timeout does not remove the stall. It bounds it: with 1 second, the SELECT still waited 717 ms. So use a short value, a few hundred milliseconds, set it on every statement that takes a strong lock, and retry with backoff on error 55P03 (neither demo retries). That means the ALTER ... ADD COLUMN, CREATE TRIGGER, ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID, SET NOT NULL, DROP TRIGGER and the final DROP COLUMN.

Before you start, look for the session that would hold the table. This is the one in my demo, and I did not run these queries in it:

SELECT pid, state, xact_start FROM pg_stat_activity
 WHERE state = 'idle in transaction' ORDER BY xact_start;
-- and make it a rule, so a forgotten session cannot hold a table for hours:
ALTER SYSTEM SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';
The method, step by step

Step 1: expand. Ship application code that works with both versions of the schema first, because ORMs and prepared statements cache column lists.

SET lock_timeout = '300ms';
ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN price_cents bigint;  -- nullable, no default

Step 2: dual write first, then backfill. Keep the new column right for every new or changed row before you touch the old rows. If you backfill first and start dual writes later, the rows written in between are missed.

-- CREATE TRIGGER takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE, which blocks writes: keep the short lock_timeout
CREATE FUNCTION events_sync() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN NEW.price_cents := round(NEW.price * 100)::bigint; RETURN NEW; END $$;

CREATE TRIGGER events_sync_t BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF price ON events
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION events_sync();

insert after the trigger: {"id":1000001,"price":"12.34","price_cents":1234}

I would not put the dual write in the application. Every writer has to change: other services, jobs, manual SQL, and old app versions still running during the deploy. A trigger covers all of them and sets the value in the same row version. It has a cost: it runs for every row. Change data capture fits copying into a new table. For a column in the same table it needs a second UPDATE per write.

Step 3: backfill in key ranges.

UPDATE events SET price_cents = round(price * 100)::bigint
 WHERE id > :lo AND id <= :lo + 50000 AND price_cents IS NULL;

Run it in a loop, in short transactions, with a statement_timeout on that session so one slow batch cannot hold locks for hours, and make it safe to stop and restart.

backfill: 1,000,000 rows in 21 batches, 5133 ms

That is in memory, with no replicas and no other load, so it only gives a floor. A straight line from it says about 7 hours for 5 billion rows with nothing else running. Once you throttle for replicas and vacuum, I would plan for days. Three things will hurt first:

  • Bloat. Every updated row is a new row version, so the table can grow by up to its own size until vacuum catches up. Watch autovacuum, and track pg_total_relation_size('events') as the backfill runs. pg_repack can reclaim the space afterwards, but it needs about twice the size of the table and its indexes in free disk, and it takes a brief exclusive lock at the start and the end, so it needs the same lock timeout.
  • Replica lag. Pause between batches while replicas fall behind, for example when now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() on a physical replica goes past your limit. That expression overstates the lag when the primary is idle, and I did not run it, because the demo has no replica.
  • Logical replication and change data capture. Watch the slot in pg_replication_slots. A stalled slot makes the primary keep log files, and every consumer receives an update event for each backfilled row.

Step 4: verify in ranges. Do not run one count(*) over the whole table. A query that runs for hours holds a snapshot that stops vacuum from cleaning up the dead rows your backfill made, and a count does not catch wrong values. Compare values, one key range at a time, off-peak or on a replica (lag can show false mismatches there, and long queries on a replica can be cancelled):

SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE price_cents IS DISTINCT FROM round(price*100)::bigint)
  FROM events WHERE id > :lo AND id <= :lo + 50000;

rows where new and old disagree: 0

This proves the copy matches the formula. Compare a sample with the source system or an old report to check the formula itself.

Step 5: make it NOT NULL without a long lock.

ALTER TABLE events ADD CONSTRAINT price_cents_nn CHECK (price_cents IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE events VALIDATE CONSTRAINT price_cents_nn;
ALTER TABLE events ALTER COLUMN price_cents SET NOT NULL;  -- Postgres 12+: skips the scan

ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (...) NOT VALID       1 ms
VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (scans, takes a light lock) 73 ms
SET NOT NULL (uses the validated CHECK)        1 ms

Run VACUUM on the table after the backfill and before VALIDATE, because VALIDATE takes a lock that autovacuum cannot work alongside. NOT VALID takes a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. VALIDATE scans under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, so reads and writes continue. The CHECK constraint can stay once the column is NOT NULL; the demo drops it. Foreign keys work the same way: add them NOT VALID, then validate. I did not run that one.

Step 6: the index, without blocking writes.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_price_cents_idx ON events (price_cents);
SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;  -- must be 0 (database-wide: filter to your index on a shared database)

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY                      956 ms
invalid indexes left behind: 0

It cannot run inside a transaction block, it waits for old transactions, it scans the table twice, and a failed run leaves an invalid index: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY it and retry. Most migration tools wrap each migration in a transaction, where CONCURRENTLY errors, so run this one outside it. On a partitioned table it does not work on the parent: build it on each partition, create the parent index with ON ONLY, then attach. The 956 ms means nothing for a busy table, because the demo has no write load.

Step 7: switch, wait, then contract. Switch the reads to the new column. Keep the app writing the old column, and the trigger keeps the new one right. If you later write the new column from the app, add a reverse trigger so the old column keeps up, or flipping the reads back will serve stale data. The one step you cannot undo is dropping the old column, so wait, take a backup, drop the trigger and its function first (DROP COLUMN fails while the trigger depends on the column), then drop the column with the lock timeout. DROP COLUMN frees no space until the rows are rewritten.

For the same idea at table level (copy, keep in sync, swap), MySQL has gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change. On Postgres, pgroll automates expand and contract with triggers.

If an AI gave you the plan

My own reply under the post said an AI helps with the plan, but on a critical table I would not let an agent run it alone. Some companies would not allow it, and many run migrations in separate pipelines. A fluent plan can still be wrong, so ask it:

  • What lock does each statement take?
  • What happens if the backfill dies halfway?
  • How long will it run, and how do you know?
  • What stops it when replicas lag?
  • How do I go back?
What the demos do not show

The first has one connection and is in memory. The second has no replicas, no live traffic and only 200,000 rows. Rehearse on a copy of production first.

The scripts

I ran both on Node 22. The second downloads Postgres binaries when you install it.

Script 1: the migration steps (PGlite).

// demo.mjs: run with `npm install @electric-sql/pglite` then `node demo.mjs`
import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite';

const db = new PGlite();
const rows = Number(process.env.ROWS || 1_000_000);
const BATCH = 50_000;

async function timed(label, sql) {
  const s = performance.now();
  const r = await db.query(sql);
  console.log(label.padEnd(46), `${(performance.now() - s).toFixed(0)} ms`);
  return r;
}

console.log((await db.query('select version()')).rows[0].version.split(',')[0]);
await db.exec(`
  create table events (
    id bigint generated always as identity primary key,
    price numeric(12,2) not null,
    created_at timestamptz not null default now()
  );
`);
await timed(`load ${rows.toLocaleString('en-US')} rows`, `insert into events(price) select (random()*1000)::numeric(12,2) from generate_series(1, ${rows})`);
await db.exec('analyze events');

console.log('\n-- 0. The fork: metadata-only or table rewrite?');
await timed('ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT constant (no rewrite)', `alter table events add column status text not null default 'new'`);
await db.exec('create table events_copy as select * from events');
await timed('ALTER COLUMN TYPE ... (rewrites the table)', 'alter table events_copy alter column price type bigint using (price*100)::bigint');
await db.exec('drop table events_copy');

console.log('\n-- 1. Expand: add the new column, nullable, with a lock timeout');
await db.exec(`set lock_timeout = '300ms'`);
console.log('lock_timeout =', (await db.query('show lock_timeout')).rows[0].lock_timeout);
await timed('ADD COLUMN price_cents bigint (nullable)', 'alter table events add column price_cents bigint');

console.log('\n-- 2. Dual write FIRST: a trigger keeps the new column right for every new or changed row');
await db.exec(`
  create function events_sync() returns trigger language plpgsql as $$
  begin new.price_cents := round(new.price * 100)::bigint; return new; end $$;
  create trigger events_sync_t before insert or update of price on events
    for each row execute function events_sync();
`);
const ins = await db.query(`insert into events(price) values (12.34) returning id, price, price_cents`);
console.log('insert after the trigger:', JSON.stringify(ins.rows[0]));

console.log('\n-- 3. Backfill in key-range batches (short transactions)');
const maxId = Number((await db.query('select max(id)::bigint as m from events')).rows[0].m);
let done = 0, batches = 0;
const t0 = performance.now();
for (let lo = 0; lo < maxId; lo += BATCH) {
  const r = await db.query(
    `update events set price_cents = round(price * 100)::bigint
       where id > $1 and id <= $2 and price_cents is null`, [lo, lo + BATCH]);
  done += r.affectedRows; batches++;
  if (batches % 5 === 0) console.log(`  batch ${batches}: ${done.toLocaleString('en-US')} rows filled`);
  // in production, pause here while replica lag is above your limit, then continue
}
console.log(`backfill: ${done.toLocaleString('en-US')} rows in ${batches} batches, ${(performance.now() - t0).toFixed(0)} ms`);

console.log('\n-- 4. Verify in key ranges, not with one count(*) over the whole table');
let bad = 0;
for (let lo = 0; lo < maxId; lo += BATCH) {
  const r = await db.query(
    `select count(*) filter (where price_cents is distinct from round(price*100)::bigint) as bad
       from events where id > $1 and id <= $2`, [lo, lo + BATCH]);
  bad += Number(r.rows[0].bad);
}
console.log('rows where new and old disagree:', bad);

console.log('\n-- 5. Make it NOT NULL without a long lock: validated CHECK first');
await timed('ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (...) NOT VALID', 'alter table events add constraint price_cents_nn check (price_cents is not null) not valid');
await timed('VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (scans, takes a light lock)', 'alter table events validate constraint price_cents_nn');
await timed('SET NOT NULL (uses the validated CHECK)', 'alter table events alter column price_cents set not null');
await db.exec('alter table events drop constraint price_cents_nn');

console.log('\n-- 6. Index without blocking writes');
await timed('CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY', 'create index concurrently events_price_cents_idx on events (price_cents)');
const inv = await db.query(`select count(*) as invalid from pg_index where not indisvalid`);
console.log('invalid indexes left behind:', inv.rows[0].invalid);

console.log('\n-- 7. Later, once reads are switched and you have waited: contract');
await db.exec('drop trigger events_sync_t on events');
console.log('trigger dropped; the old column stays until you are sure');

Script 2: the lock queue (real Postgres).

// lock.mjs: run with `npm install embedded-postgres pg` then `node lock.mjs`
// A short ALTER can still stall every query behind it. Real Postgres, several connections.
import EmbeddedPostgres from 'embedded-postgres';
import pg from 'pg';
import { mkdtempSync } from 'node:fs';
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os';
import { join } from 'node:path';

const port = 54329;
const server = new EmbeddedPostgres({
  databaseDir: mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'lockdemo-')),
  user: 'postgres', password: 'pw', port, persistent: false,
  onLog: () => {}, onError: () => {},
});
await server.initialise();
await server.start();
await server.createDatabase('demo');

const connect = async (name) => {
  const c = new pg.Client({ host: 'localhost', port, user: 'postgres', password: 'pw', database: 'demo' });
  await c.connect();
  c.name = name;
  return c;
};
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
const now = () => performance.now();

const admin = await connect('admin');
console.log((await admin.query('select version()')).rows[0].version.split(' on ')[0]);
await admin.query('create table events (id bigint generated always as identity primary key, price numeric(12,2) not null)');
await admin.query('insert into events(price) select (random()*1000)::numeric(12,2) from generate_series(1, 200000)');

async function scenario(label, lockTimeout) {
  console.log(`\n== ${label}`);
  const A = await connect('A'); // a long transaction that has read the table
  const B = await connect('B'); // the migration
  const C = await connect('C'); // an ordinary read that arrives after the migration
  await A.query('begin');
  await A.query('select count(*) from events');
  console.log('A: long transaction is open (it only read the table)');

  const t0 = now();
  const bDone = (async () => {
    if (lockTimeout) await B.query(`set lock_timeout = '${lockTimeout}'`);
    const s = now();
    try {
      await B.query(`alter table events add column status_${lockTimeout ? 'b' : 'a'} text not null default 'new'`);
      return `B: ALTER finished after ${(now() - s).toFixed(0)} ms`;
    } catch (e) {
      return `B: ALTER gave up after ${(now() - s).toFixed(0)} ms (${e.message})`;
    }
  })();
  await sleep(300);

  const cDone = (async () => {
    const s = now();
    await C.query('select 1 from events limit 1');
    return `C: a plain SELECT waited ${(now() - s).toFixed(0)} ms`;
  })();
  await sleep(200);
  const waiting = await admin.query(
    `select count(*) as n from pg_stat_activity where datname='demo' and wait_event_type='Lock'`);
  console.log(`sessions waiting on a lock right now: ${waiting.rows[0].n}`);

  await sleep(2500);
  await A.query('commit');
  console.log(`A: long transaction commits after ${(now() - t0).toFixed(0)} ms`);
  console.log(await bDone);
  console.log(await cDone);
  await Promise.all([A.end(), B.end(), C.end()]);
}

await scenario('1. ALTER with no lock_timeout', null);
await admin.query('alter table events drop column if exists status_a');
await scenario('2. ALTER with lock_timeout = 1s', '1s');

await admin.end();
await server.stop();

items.title: OnBlink: Communicate with minimal movement
items.summary: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge What I Built OnBlink lets someone speak a phrase or open an app using only their eyes and a regular webcam. A blink signal opens a menu. The highlight steps through phrases like "Yes", "I need help" or "I'm thirsty", and a second signal picks one. The Mac says it out loud, or opens an app. It's built for people who can't easily speak or type, and for the people around them. Highlights: Two ways to select. Double blink (SmartSpectra's built-in blink detection) or long blink (close your eyes for about a second), so people can use whichever signal is easiest for them. Your own phrases and apps. Add, edit, reorder and test menu items. Each one speaks a sentence or opens an app. Heart rate check-ins (optional). If someone's heart rate stays well above their own baseline level from earlier in the session, OnBlink offers a short check-in: "I am fine", "I need a break" or "I need help". Private option prompts (optional). Options can be read softly, or sent to headphones or a single earbud, while the chosen phrase is spoken out loud for everyone. Guided setup. A 10-step tutorial, a framing guide that waits until your face is in position, and a practice run. Demo Check out OnBlink Code Repository: https://github.com/gavin-rose/onblink Setup takes three commands ( npm install , npm start , then paste a free Presage API key in the tutorial). The README covers requirements, usage, settings, data handling and how the detector was tuned. OnBlink runs on macOS. How It Responds to Human Signals OnBlink uses five live SmartSpectra signals: Signal How OnBlink uses it Blinking Double blink input: blink, wait for "Blink again", blink once more Face landmarks Long blink input, measured from how open each eye is Pulse rate Live heart rate display and optional check-ins, using only readings the SDK marks stable Talking Ignores eye closures while the person is speaking Validation status Drives the framing guide, pauses input when the person moves out of view, and pauses check-ins during motion Integrating the SDK. OnBlink is an Electron app built on the SmartSpectra Node SDK. The renderer requests faceMetrics and cardioMetrics , decodes each metrics message, and feeds blinks, landmarks, talking and pulse into small, separate modules: the menu, the long blink detector and the check-in logic. The main process handles settings, speech and opening apps, and the page can only ask it to run a saved action by its id. Long blink. SmartSpectra's blink signal is a short detection pulse, which is perfect for quick double blinks. For hold-based input, I measured eye openness directly from the face landmarks: Each eye is compared to its own recent level, so it works for people whose eyes naturally open different amounts. A closure that lasts 0.7 to 2.5 seconds counts as a long blink. It's ignored if the head moves or the person is talking. Some people find a deliberate one-second close easier than a quick double blink, and in my own testing setup it was the more dependable option. It's also very hard to trigger by accident, which matters when a false trigger means the computer speaks for you. I tuned the thresholds with labeled recordings: I pressed a key after each blink, long blink and wink, then replayed the recordings through the detector. It caught all 5 deliberate long blinks and didn't fire on the 15 other labeled actions. The analysis scripts are in the repo's research folder. Check-ins. During the first minute of steady readings, OnBlink learns the person's usual heart rate. If stable readings stay well above that level (15 bpm or 20% for 45 seconds on the default setting), it offers a check-in through the same menu. It only reacts to rises, waits until the person is in position and not using the menu, and appears at most once every 10 minutes. It's an offer to talk, never a health judgment. Prize Categories Best Thoughtful Real-World Use The need. People with limited speech or movement often have the hardest time asking for the simplest things: a drink, help, or a break. Dedicated eye-tracking devices exist, but they're expensive and need special hardware. OnBlink only needs a laptop webcam. Designed for the people using it: A choice of signal and pace. Double blink with relaxed or quick spacing, or long blink, plus an adjustable menu speed. Hard to trigger by accident. Single blinks are ignored, input pauses when the person is out of view, and the menu closes on its own if nothing is picked. Quick phrases first. Yes and No come first, then urgent needs, so common answers take the fewest steps. Speaking up without the effort of starting. The check-in gives someone an easy way to speak up when their body suggests something might be wrong. Considerate of the room. Option prompts can stay quiet or go to an earbud, so only the chosen phrase is spoken out loud. Doesn't stop on its own. The screen stays awake during a session, and auto stop is off by default, so nobody has to restart it. Easy for a caregiver to set up. A tutorial with a practice run, plus a settings screen with a Test button for every phrase. Consent and Data Handling Consent first. Before the first session, OnBlink shows a plain-language consent screen, also part of the tutorial, explaining what the camera is used for. Nothing starts until the person accepts. Camera. On only after pressing Start, and off when pressing Stop or at an optional time limit. SDK telemetry. Turned off ( enableTelemetry: false ). Presage's telemetry and privacy document says the SDK transmits no telemetry when it's off. Storage. OnBlink saves only the menu items, settings and the API key (encrypted with the macOS Keychain), locally on the user's computer. Deleting the app's settings folder removes everything. Never stored or sent. Video, eye or face data, and heart rate. The heart rate level used for check-ins is kept in memory only and discarded when the session stops. Sharing and AI services. OnBlink shares nothing and uses no AI services. Phrases are spoken locally by macOS, and only when the person picks them. Optional features. Check-ins are off until the person turns them on. Not a medical device. OnBlink is a communication aid. It does not diagnose, treat or monitor any condition, and it should not be relied on in an emergency. Check-ins are only an offer to talk. Agent Session I built OnBlink with Claude Code: exploring what the SDK could measure, recording and analyzing my own blink data, and building and refining the app. The SDK was pretty easy to understand and use but I definitely leaned hard into Claude for the visuals as that isn't normally my wheelhouse.

What I Built

A blink signal opens a menu. The highlight steps through phrases like "Yes", "I need help" or "I'm thirsty", and a second signal picks one. The Mac says it out loud, or opens an app. It's built for people who can't easily speak or type, and for the people around them.

Highlights:

  • Two ways to select. Double blink (SmartSpectra's built-in blink detection) or long blink (close your eyes for about a second), so people can use whichever signal is easiest for them.
  • Your own phrases and apps. Add, edit, reorder and test menu items. Each one speaks a sentence or opens an app.
  • Heart rate check-ins (optional). If someone's heart rate stays well above their own baseline level from earlier in the session, OnBlink offers a short check-in: "I am fine", "I need a break" or "I need help".
  • Private option prompts (optional). Options can be read softly, or sent to headphones or a single earbud, while the chosen phrase is spoken out loud for everyone.
  • Guided setup. A 10-step tutorial, a framing guide that waits until your face is in position, and a practice run.
Demo

Check out OnBlink

Code

Repository: https://github.com/gavin-rose/onblink

Setup takes three commands (npm install, npm start, then paste a free Presage API key in the tutorial). The README covers requirements, usage, settings, data handling and how the detector was tuned. OnBlink runs on macOS.

How It Responds to Human Signals

OnBlink uses five live SmartSpectra signals:

Signal How OnBlink uses it Blinking Double blink input: blink, wait for "Blink again", blink once more Face landmarks Long blink input, measured from how open each eye is Pulse rate Live heart rate display and optional check-ins, using only readings the SDK marks stable Talking Ignores eye closures while the person is speaking Validation status Drives the framing guide, pauses input when the person moves out of view, and pauses check-ins during motion

Integrating the SDK. OnBlink is an Electron app built on the SmartSpectra Node SDK. The renderer requests faceMetrics and cardioMetrics, decodes each metrics message, and feeds blinks, landmarks, talking and pulse into small, separate modules: the menu, the long blink detector and the check-in logic. The main process handles settings, speech and opening apps, and the page can only ask it to run a saved action by its id.

Long blink. SmartSpectra's blink signal is a short detection pulse, which is perfect for quick double blinks. For hold-based input, I measured eye openness directly from the face landmarks:

  • Each eye is compared to its own recent level, so it works for people whose eyes naturally open different amounts.
  • A closure that lasts 0.7 to 2.5 seconds counts as a long blink. It's ignored if the head moves or the person is talking.
  • Some people find a deliberate one-second close easier than a quick double blink, and in my own testing setup it was the more dependable option. It's also very hard to trigger by accident, which matters when a false trigger means the computer speaks for you.

I tuned the thresholds with labeled recordings: I pressed a key after each blink, long blink and wink, then replayed the recordings through the detector. It caught all 5 deliberate long blinks and didn't fire on the 15 other labeled actions. The analysis scripts are in the repo's research folder.

Check-ins. During the first minute of steady readings, OnBlink learns the person's usual heart rate. If stable readings stay well above that level (15 bpm or 20% for 45 seconds on the default setting), it offers a check-in through the same menu. It only reacts to rises, waits until the person is in position and not using the menu, and appears at most once every 10 minutes. It's an offer to talk, never a health judgment.

Prize Categories

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use

The need. People with limited speech or movement often have the hardest time asking for the simplest things: a drink, help, or a break. Dedicated eye-tracking devices exist, but they're expensive and need special hardware. OnBlink only needs a laptop webcam.

Designed for the people using it:

  • A choice of signal and pace. Double blink with relaxed or quick spacing, or long blink, plus an adjustable menu speed.
  • Hard to trigger by accident. Single blinks are ignored, input pauses when the person is out of view, and the menu closes on its own if nothing is picked.
  • Quick phrases first. Yes and No come first, then urgent needs, so common answers take the fewest steps.
  • Speaking up without the effort of starting. The check-in gives someone an easy way to speak up when their body suggests something might be wrong.
  • Considerate of the room. Option prompts can stay quiet or go to an earbud, so only the chosen phrase is spoken out loud.
  • Doesn't stop on its own. The screen stays awake during a session, and auto stop is off by default, so nobody has to restart it.
  • Easy for a caregiver to set up. A tutorial with a practice run, plus a settings screen with a Test button for every phrase.
Consent and Data Handling
  • Consent first. Before the first session, OnBlink shows a plain-language consent screen, also part of the tutorial, explaining what the camera is used for. Nothing starts until the person accepts.
  • Camera. On only after pressing Start, and off when pressing Stop or at an optional time limit.
  • SDK telemetry. Turned off (enableTelemetry: false). Presage's telemetry and privacy document says the SDK transmits no telemetry when it's off.
  • Storage. OnBlink saves only the menu items, settings and the API key (encrypted with the macOS Keychain), locally on the user's computer. Deleting the app's settings folder removes everything.
  • Never stored or sent. Video, eye or face data, and heart rate. The heart rate level used for check-ins is kept in memory only and discarded when the session stops.
  • Sharing and AI services. OnBlink shares nothing and uses no AI services. Phrases are spoken locally by macOS, and only when the person picks them.
  • Optional features. Check-ins are off until the person turns them on.
  • Not a medical device. OnBlink is a communication aid. It does not diagnose, treat or monitor any condition, and it should not be relied on in an emergency. Check-ins are only an offer to talk.
Agent Session

I built OnBlink with Claude Code: exploring what the SDK could measure, recording and analyzing my own blink data, and building and refining the app. The SDK was pretty easy to understand and use but I definitely leaned hard into Claude for the visuals as that isn't normally my wheelhouse.

items.title: The 5 latest developments in the Jensen Huang scandal
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images The fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's scandal continues. On Monday, Nvidia shares and Huang's net worth took a dive. More questions about Huang's relationship with a Chinese business executive are arising. The fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's admission of an affair continues. On Monday, shares of Nvidia fell roughly 5% a day after Nvidia's board said it was investigating reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy campaign. The woman at the center of the allegations is Alice Huang, who has been an executive for Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. The New York Times reported in late October that US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, who developed a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO, was passing information to Beijing. Several news outlets, including Business Insider, have since reported on other major developments. Here are the highlights: • The Commerce Department stopped an investigation into Megaspeed after receiving an email from Nvidia's general counsel asking about the monthslong probe, The New York Times reported . The case was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department, the outlet reported. • In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner were pitching China-based investors on a Southeast Asia data center project "worth several hundred million dollars," The Financial Times reported . The pair told investors they would have "no problem securing GPUs," one investor who was present for the pitch told the publication. • The Nvidia CEO started working with Heller, a PR firm known for guiding leaders through sex scandals, as early as October 2025, Wired reported . Risa Heller, the crisis communications specialist who founded the firm, has previously worked with the likes of former Rep. Anthony Weiner and chef Mario Batali. Wired noted that Heller also handles corporate communications that are unrelated to scandals. • Jensen Huang is no longer expected to appear at Anthropic's CEO forum on Monday, and his name disappeared — and then reappeared — from the speaker lineup for ElevenLabs' conference on Wednesday, Business Insider's Henry Chandonnet and Geoff Weiss reported . • Similarly, Madison Huang, Jensen's daughter and a senior Nvidia executive, abruptly dropped out of an AI-focused event in Seoul, Bloomberg reported . Read the original article on Business Insider

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images

  • The fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's scandal continues.
  • On Monday, Nvidia shares and Huang's net worth took a dive.
  • More questions about Huang's relationship with a Chinese business executive are arising.

The fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admission of an affair continues.

On Monday, shares of Nvidia fell roughly 5% a day after Nvidia's board said it was investigating reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy campaign.

The woman at the center of the allegations is Alice Huang, who has been an executive for Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. The New York Times reported in late October that US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, who developed a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO, was passing information to Beijing.

Several news outlets, including Business Insider, have since reported on other major developments.

Here are the highlights:

• The Commerce Department stopped an investigation into Megaspeed after receiving an email from Nvidia's general counsel asking about the monthslong probe, The New York Times reported. The case was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department, the outlet reported.

• In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner were pitching China-based investors on a Southeast Asia data center project "worth several hundred million dollars," The Financial Times reported. The pair told investors they would have "no problem securing GPUs," one investor who was present for the pitch told the publication.

• The Nvidia CEO started working with Heller, a PR firm known for guiding leaders through sex scandals, as early as October 2025, Wired reported. Risa Heller, the crisis communications specialist who founded the firm, has previously worked with the likes of former Rep. Anthony Weiner and chef Mario Batali. Wired noted that Heller also handles corporate communications that are unrelated to scandals.

• Jensen Huang is no longer expected to appear at Anthropic's CEO forum on Monday, and his name disappeared — and then reappeared — from the speaker lineup for ElevenLabs' conference on Wednesday, Business Insider's Henry Chandonnet and Geoff Weiss reported.

• Similarly, Madison Huang, Jensen's daughter and a senior Nvidia executive, abruptly dropped out of an AI-focused event in Seoul, Bloomberg reported.

items.title: The Guardian view on Jensen Huang’s affair: why did Trump ignore the warnings? | Editorial
items.summary: The AI chip boss’s actions raise urgent questions about corporate influence, national security and the US president’s willingness to listen to intelligence warnings It could be the plot of a spy thriller. One of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution admitted to having an affair with a Chinese businesswomen said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. When Donald Trump was briefed about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s liaisons with Alice Huang, he took no action. Perhaps he thought only marriage vows had been broken. Or perhaps Mr Trump was willing to overlook the conduct of a friend who championed his unpopular datacentre expansion, whose company donated to his White House ballroom and who echoed his opposition to AI safeguards against expert advice. Nvidia became the cornerstone of AI by supplying brute computing power. As tech giants scrambled for the firm’s graphics processing units (GPUs), Mr Huang sold the picks and shovels for the AI gold rush – and amassed a $160bn fortune. When China joined the race for tech supremacy, Nvidia’s microchips became a national security issue. In October 2022, the US slapped export controls on GPU sales to China. Thirty months later, Nvidia was effectively banned from selling to Beijing. Mr Huang lobbied for looser controls. Such was his sway with Mr Trump that the White House scrapped Biden-era global AI chip restrictions and then permitted sales of Nvidia’s prized H200 processors to Chinese customers. items.title: Will Jensen Huang resign? Trump and tech leaders sound off on whether Nvidia's CEO can keep his job.
items.summary: President Donald Trump presented the National Medal of Science to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in October. Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images Jensen Huang's affair raises the question of whether a star CEO can be too important for a company to lose. Trump and tech insiders defended Huang, saying his leadership is crucial to Nvidia and US interests. Others warned the scandal raises national security concerns and said it should cost Huang his job. Jensen Huang helped make Nvidia indispensable to the AI boom. Now, amid an investigation into his personal conduct, the company must confront the question of whether he is indispensable to Nvidia, too. The cofounder and CEO has long been credited with steering the chipmaker's extraordinary rise, helping to turn it into the world's most valuable company and himself into one of the most powerful figures in tech. Yet on Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair . The woman at the center of the controversy is Alice Huang , who has been an executive for Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials believe she was passing information to Beijing. Nvidia's board said it is looking into whether he was a target of a foreign-intelligence effort. The company now faces an awkward dilemma: Is its star CEO too important to step down? Some tech leaders, investors, and other executives say Huang's track record and importance to Nvidia make him impossible to replace. Others say that no CEO should be indispensable, particularly when a board is examining whether his or her personal conduct created risks for the company. Here's what they're saying: President Donald Trump Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump praised Huang's work and said he hopes "everything's fine." "He's done such an incredible job," said Trump. "He's a fine person, in my opinion." Asked whether he wished he had acted on intelligence alleging the woman Huang had an affair with was a spy, the president said he did not. "No, I don't think so," Trump said, adding that he thinks Huang is "an honorable guy." "I think he probably has an excuse for it," said Trump. "You have to hear it." Gavin Baker, managing partner and CIO of Atreides Management Baker is in the "stay" camp. He said on X on Sunday that he has known Huang for nearly 30 years and does not believe Huang would knowingly disadvantage the US or Nvidia. "The only thing he has ever said to me about China is the absolute importance of keeping the American hardware ecosystem, led by Nvidia, ahead of China. That's it," wrote Baker. "I have never known him to be anything other than patriotic and deeply pro-American." Baker said that Huang should remain CEO because he sees Nvidia's China strategy as advancing US national security interests rather than undermining them. He said on X that Huang has consistently advocated for giving China less powerful versions of the company's chips, and Baker warned that removing Huang could benefit China. "I'm not sure what China hoped to gain from this espionage operation given they are restricting sales of Nvidia GPUs inside of China but it is worth considering that having Jensen removed as the CEO of Nvidia might serve China's own national security goals," Baker wrote. Ben Thompson, founder of Stratechery The founder of Stratechery, a subscription-based newsletter and podcast, is also in favor of keeping Huang put and urged Nvidia leaders' detractors "to do some reflecting of their own." In a post on Stratechery, Thompson said that Huang is essential to Nvidia's success. He said AI is the most important industry to the US, and that Nvidia is one of the most important companies supporting it. "I do not subscribe to the idea that anyone could do his job; there are great men, and Huang is one of them. That he is flawed does not change this reality; indeed, great men always are," Thompson wrote. He added that he hopes Huang can keep his job amid the turmoil. "Yes, conduct the investigations; yes, demand better controls. At the end of this, however, absent evidence of any sort of clear betrayal of U.S. interests, it is in the interests of the U.S. that Huang continue to be CEO of Nvidia," wrote Thompson. "I very much hope that is where this ends up." Gary Black, managing partner of The Future Fund Black doesn't expect Huang to stick around. "I doubt Jensen Huang will be able to remain as $NVDA CEO," he wrote on X on Sunday. "While Huang has not committed any crime or tort, his code of conduct and judgment will be called into question which will likely result in his removal by the NVDA Board." Still, Black said he thinks Huang lacks a natural successor within the company. He told Business Insider Nvidia will likely bring in someone from the outside or pick a board member to be interim CEO. Ryan Fedasiuk, senior fellow at The Foundation for American Innovation Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at The Foundation for American Innovation, a technology think tank, anticipates broader fallout. "I don't believe this personal affair will remain an isolated event," he wrote on X on Monday. "I also don't believe it can be separated from the company's broader PR crisis in DC: selling advanced chips to China, including through unscrupulous measures." Fedasiuk said the affair could invite congressional scrutiny in part because it involved one of Nvidia's customers. "I don't see how it's possible for him to survive," Fedasiuk told Business Insider. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives In an X post on Sunday, Ives called the saga a stain on Huang's reputation. "This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang," Ives wrote. Ives later said in a follow-up post that investors largely expect Huang to remain CEO but are factoring in a small chance that the board investigation could lead to his removal or departure. Ives added that Huang was not replaceable in investors' eyes, which he said was a worry for Wall Street. Read the original article on Business Insider

President Donald Trump presented the National Medal of Science to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in October.

Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images

  • Jensen Huang's affair raises the question of whether a star CEO can be too important for a company to lose.
  • Trump and tech insiders defended Huang, saying his leadership is crucial to Nvidia and US interests.
  • Others warned the scandal raises national security concerns and said it should cost Huang his job.

Jensen Huang helped make Nvidia indispensable to the AI boom. Now, amid an investigation into his personal conduct, the company must confront the question of whether he is indispensable to Nvidia, too.

The cofounder and CEO has long been credited with steering the chipmaker's extraordinary rise, helping to turn it into the world's most valuable company and himself into one of the most powerful figures in tech.

Yet on Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair. The woman at the center of the controversy is Alice Huang, who has been an executive for Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials believe she was passing information to Beijing. Nvidia's board said it is looking into whether he was a target of a foreign-intelligence effort.

The company now faces an awkward dilemma: Is its star CEO too important to step down?

Some tech leaders, investors, and other executives say Huang's track record and importance to Nvidia make him impossible to replace. Others say that no CEO should be indispensable, particularly when a board is examining whether his or her personal conduct created risks for the company.

Here's what they're saying:

President Donald Trump

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump praised Huang's work and said he hopes "everything's fine."

"He's done such an incredible job," said Trump. "He's a fine person, in my opinion."

Asked whether he wished he had acted on intelligence alleging the woman Huang had an affair with was a spy, the president said he did not.

"No, I don't think so," Trump said, adding that he thinks Huang is "an honorable guy."

"I think he probably has an excuse for it," said Trump. "You have to hear it."

Gavin Baker, managing partner and CIO of Atreides Management

Baker is in the "stay" camp. He said on X on Sunday that he has known Huang for nearly 30 years and does not believe Huang would knowingly disadvantage the US or Nvidia.

"The only thing he has ever said to me about China is the absolute importance of keeping the American hardware ecosystem, led by Nvidia, ahead of China. That's it," wrote Baker. "I have never known him to be anything other than patriotic and deeply pro-American."

Baker said that Huang should remain CEO because he sees Nvidia's China strategy as advancing US national security interests rather than undermining them. He said on X that Huang has consistently advocated for giving China less powerful versions of the company's chips, and Baker warned that removing Huang could benefit China.

"I'm not sure what China hoped to gain from this espionage operation given they are restricting sales of Nvidia GPUs inside of China but it is worth considering that having Jensen removed as the CEO of Nvidia might serve China's own national security goals," Baker wrote.

Ben Thompson, founder of Stratechery

The founder of Stratechery, a subscription-based newsletter and podcast, is also in favor of keeping Huang put and urged Nvidia leaders' detractors "to do some reflecting of their own."

In a post on Stratechery, Thompson said that Huang is essential to Nvidia's success. He said AI is the most important industry to the US, and that Nvidia is one of the most important companies supporting it.

"I do not subscribe to the idea that anyone could do his job; there are great men, and Huang is one of them. That he is flawed does not change this reality; indeed, great men always are," Thompson wrote.

He added that he hopes Huang can keep his job amid the turmoil.

"Yes, conduct the investigations; yes, demand better controls. At the end of this, however, absent evidence of any sort of clear betrayal of U.S. interests, it is in the interests of the U.S. that Huang continue to be CEO of Nvidia," wrote Thompson. "I very much hope that is where this ends up."

Gary Black, managing partner of The Future Fund

Black doesn't expect Huang to stick around.

"I doubt Jensen Huang will be able to remain as $NVDA CEO," he wrote on X on Sunday. "While Huang has not committed any crime or tort, his code of conduct and judgment will be called into question which will likely result in his removal by the NVDA Board."

Still, Black said he thinks Huang lacks a natural successor within the company. He told Business Insider Nvidia will likely bring in someone from the outside or pick a board member to be interim CEO.

Ryan Fedasiuk, senior fellow at The Foundation for American Innovation

Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at The Foundation for American Innovation, a technology think tank, anticipates broader fallout.

"I don't believe this personal affair will remain an isolated event," he wrote on X on Monday. "I also don't believe it can be separated from the company's broader PR crisis in DC: selling advanced chips to China, including through unscrupulous measures."

Fedasiuk said the affair could invite congressional scrutiny in part because it involved one of Nvidia's customers.

"I don't see how it's possible for him to survive," Fedasiuk told Business Insider.

Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives

In an X post on Sunday, Ives called the saga a stain on Huang's reputation. "This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang," Ives wrote.

Ives later said in a follow-up post that investors largely expect Huang to remain CEO but are factoring in a small chance that the board investigation could lead to his removal or departure. Ives added that Huang was not replaceable in investors' eyes, which he said was a worry for Wall Street.

items.title: Le Steam Frame entre dans le top 5 Steam : et si la VR servait enfin à comprendre les protéines ?
items.summary: Le Steam Frame entre dans le top 5 Steam : et si la VR servait enfin à comprendre les protéines ? Le Steam Frame vient d'entrer directement à la 5e place des casques les plus utilisés sur Steam, un mois seulement après sa sortie et malgré des ruptures de stock persistantes (Steam Hardware Survey). Autrement dit : le parc de casques VR grandit vite, et la question n'est plus « la VR va-t-elle s'installer ? » mais « qu'allons-nous y faire d'utile ? ». Je fais de la biologie structurale depuis dix ans, et je tourne des protéines à la souris. Un site de liaison, une poche druggable, un changement de conformation : ce sont des objets tridimensionnels, mais je les empile en 2D et je perds le sens de l'échelle. Le mois dernier, un ami m'a prêté son casque. J'ai lancé NexoPeek, un laboratoire moléculaire VR pour Meta Quest développé par Seven Sportz. Je suis entré dans l'hémoglobine à l'échelle humaine, j'ai vu l'oxygène se fixer — et quelque chose s'est débloqué. NexoPeek propose 12 visites guidées narrées sur 6 piliers (bases de la biotechnologie, fondements de la vie, voies et interactions, médicaments en action, technologies génétiques, biotechnologies vertes) : glycolyse, aspirine bloquant les COX, CRISPR-Cas9 en action. À côté, un visualiseur PDB professionnel : recherche intelligente qui résout un nom de gène sur RCSB PDB, UniProtKB, AlphaFold DB, SWISS-MODEL et PDBe ; presets Mol* en un geste (cartoon, ball-and-stick, spacefill CPK, surface moléculaire, carte de facteurs B, trace en tube) ; chargement de fichiers locaux (.pdb, .cif, .mol2) avec cartes de champ électrostatique et volumes de densité électronique. Le banc d'analyse : prédiction de poches par IA (PrankWeb / P2Rank, cloud ou moteur hors ligne), superposition d'homologues avec Foldseek, inspection des liaisons hydrogène, import 3D d'un ligand depuis PubChem, mesure de distance interatomique en ångströms, pastilles de résidus projetant un halo 3D. Le mode Room View fait flotter la molécule dans la pièce réelle. Un point de méthode : NexoPeek est un logiciel d'éducation et de visualisation scientifique. Il ne fournit ni avis médical, ni diagnostic, ni traitement, et ses aides à l'analyse complètent les pipelines validés — elles ne les remplacent pas. Un parc VR qui se démocratise, c'est une opportunité pédagogique rare. La structure de la matière vivante mérite mieux qu'un écran plat. https://www.meta.com/experiences/nexopeek/1453797551140347/

Le Steam Frame entre dans le top 5 Steam : et si la VR servait enfin à comprendre les protéines ?

Le Steam Frame vient d'entrer directement à la 5e place des casques les plus utilisés sur Steam, un mois seulement après sa sortie et malgré des ruptures de stock persistantes (Steam Hardware Survey). Autrement dit : le parc de casques VR grandit vite, et la question n'est plus « la VR va-t-elle s'installer ? » mais « qu'allons-nous y faire d'utile ? ».

Je fais de la biologie structurale depuis dix ans, et je tourne des protéines à la souris. Un site de liaison, une poche druggable, un changement de conformation : ce sont des objets tridimensionnels, mais je les empile en 2D et je perds le sens de l'échelle. Le mois dernier, un ami m'a prêté son casque. J'ai lancé NexoPeek, un laboratoire moléculaire VR pour Meta Quest développé par Seven Sportz. Je suis entré dans l'hémoglobine à l'échelle humaine, j'ai vu l'oxygène se fixer — et quelque chose s'est débloqué.

NexoPeek propose 12 visites guidées narrées sur 6 piliers (bases de la biotechnologie, fondements de la vie, voies et interactions, médicaments en action, technologies génétiques, biotechnologies vertes) : glycolyse, aspirine bloquant les COX, CRISPR-Cas9 en action.

À côté, un visualiseur PDB professionnel : recherche intelligente qui résout un nom de gène sur RCSB PDB, UniProtKB, AlphaFold DB, SWISS-MODEL et PDBe ; presets Mol* en un geste (cartoon, ball-and-stick, spacefill CPK, surface moléculaire, carte de facteurs B, trace en tube) ; chargement de fichiers locaux (.pdb, .cif, .mol2) avec cartes de champ électrostatique et volumes de densité électronique.

Le banc d'analyse : prédiction de poches par IA (PrankWeb / P2Rank, cloud ou moteur hors ligne), superposition d'homologues avec Foldseek, inspection des liaisons hydrogène, import 3D d'un ligand depuis PubChem, mesure de distance interatomique en ångströms, pastilles de résidus projetant un halo 3D. Le mode Room View fait flotter la molécule dans la pièce réelle.

Un point de méthode : NexoPeek est un logiciel d'éducation et de visualisation scientifique. Il ne fournit ni avis médical, ni diagnostic, ni traitement, et ses aides à l'analyse complètent les pipelines validés — elles ne les remplacent pas.

Un parc VR qui se démocratise, c'est une opportunité pédagogique rare. La structure de la matière vivante mérite mieux qu'un écran plat.

items.title: Nobody tells the implementer why
items.summary: I dictate a lot of what I ask my agents, and the transcriber has a weakness for names. "Siobhán" comes out as something else, and nothing in the rest of the message lets anyone recover it. When that request then goes to a lead agent, which passes it to a product manager, which passes it to an architect, which passes it to whoever writes the code, I wanted to know two things: what reaches the end of the chain, and whether the agents add noise of their own along the way. It is the children's game of telephone, played with agents. But I did not want the artificial version, with ten agents in a row whispering to each other. In real setups a message rarely crosses more than three or four agents, and when it does it is because there is a hierarchy: a lead and roles under it. So that is what I measured. The setup Six client requests, three for software and three for an event agency. The software ones ask for a small Python module (appointment reminders for an optician, seat proration for a SaaS bill, a GDPR purge job). The event ones ask for a plan: a company away-day, a Spanish–Finnish wedding, a scientific conference. Each request is written the way a client talks, and each contains facts of several kinds, tagged in advance: names, numbers, prohibitions, conditions, priorities, details easy to overlook, and reasons ("because the old field went stale after the March CRM migration"). Two team shapes, both realistic: In the chain, the implementer's message has been rewritten three times. In the relay it is also hop 4, but its author has the original request in front of it. That difference is what separates distance from audience. The event teams have three roles (account manager, logistics, vendor liaison) instead of four, so their chain is one hop shorter. Each message between agents went out in one of three formats: free prose, a numbered requirement list, or a short note with the client's original request attached verbatim. The original request came in four versions: clean, or with one transcription error of a different type (a mangled name, a homophone, or punctuation that changes the meaning: "No, do it this way" against "No do it this way"). The models were Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, running as real nested subagents in Claude Code, and GPT-6 Luna in my own harness, which passes the same messages from role to role. Three repetitions per cell: 853 valid Claude runs and 432 Luna runs. Every message was scored fact by fact as preserved, lost, distorted or inverted: names and numbers by deterministic checks, the rest by a judge from a different family from the agents: GPT-6.1 Sol (through Codex) for the Claude runs, and Claude Opus 5.5 for the Luna runs. The final artifact, the code or the plan, went through hidden tests that check each requirement. Almost everything arrives Most of the request survives the trip. At hop 4, in the Claude runs, prohibitions arrive intact 98% of the time, details that are easy to miss 96%, numbers 92%, names and conditions 90%, priorities 85%. Luna lands in the same range: 91–99% for everything except one type. That type is the reasons. The why is not worn away. It is cut In the Claude chain, the reason behind a decision travels well for two hops: 88–99% in the lead's message to the PM, 83–97% from the PM to the architect. Then the architect writes to the implementer, and it falls to 8–31%. The obvious reading would be distance: four hops, four chances to lose something. The relay rules that out. There, the lead writes hop 4 itself, with the client's request in front of it, and only keeps the reason in 24% of its messages to the implementer, with Haiku and with Sonnet alike. It has the information; it chooses not to pass it on. Share of messages that keep the reason behind a decision (software teams, prose and list formats). The drop is in the message to the implementer, and it happens just the same when the writer has the full request at hand. So it is not a telephone effect in the sense of something wearing away from mouth to mouth. It is a decision about the audience: whoever writes to the person who builds writes instructions, and instructions do not carry reasons. Luna does the same, only earlier: it drops the reason from the very first message (it keeps it in 30% of its messages to the PM) and stays low all the way down. In the event teams the cut is milder. The vendor, who books the caterer and writes the plan, still gets the reason 75–84% of the time in the Claude chain, and 40–64% when the lead writes to it directly in the relay. The executor writing code is the one who hears it least. Does losing it matter? That was my next question, and the answer is less tidy than I expected. Within each rule, format and model, I compared runs where the reason reached the implementer with runs where it did not, and looked at whether the final artifact obeyed the rule. With Claude, keeping the reason did not help: rules were obeyed slightly less often when their reason arrived (10 points less, 95% interval −15 to −5). With Luna the difference goes the other way, +9 points, but the interval crosses zero. The negative effect in Claude is concentrated in Haiku and in rules whose reason names the old thing. "Inactivity is measured on last_seen_at , not last_login , because the mobile app stopped updating last_login ": with that reason in the message, Haiku used the right field 59% of the time; without it, 97%. My hypothesis is that the reason puts the wrong name back into the message and acts as a distractor. This analysis was not planned before the runs, so I take it as a hypothesis, not a conclusion. But it is enough to stop me from claiming that the why is always worth carrying. What does matter, clearly, is losing the requirement itself. In the Claude runs, a fact that arrived intact at the implementer was satisfied in the final artifact 95% of the time; one that was lost on the way, 40%. Losses are rare, but each one shows up in the result. Names freeze; punctuation gets repaired The transcription errors behave very differently depending on the type. A mangled name cannot be repaired from the text: nothing in the request says how "Siobhán" should be spelled. But it can be questioned, the way a person would ask "is that name right?". Almost nobody did. In the Claude hand-offs, under 2% of the messages that carried a mangled name marked it as doubtful; Luna, never. The name froze and reached the artifact as transcribed: every final plan or module that used it used the wrong version. Punctuation errors that change the meaning, on the other hand, were repaired about two thirds of the time in the hand-offs (Claude 66%, Luna 73%), probably because the rest of the request makes the intended reading obvious. Claude repeated the wrong reading as given in about one message in seven; Luna, in one in twenty. The format matters, depending on the model For Claude, the hand-off format barely changes anything: a numbered list keeps a little more at hop 4 than prose (88% against 85% of facts), and the final code scores about the same in all three formats. For Luna it changes everything. Final software module, mean share of hidden tests passed. Luna's code is not worse in itself: with a list or with the original attached it lands next to Claude. In prose, its summary drops the input fields, and the implementer invents them. When I first saw Luna's numbers I assumed its code was simply worse. It is not. The client lists the fields of the input data ("each appointment has id , customer_name , email …"), and Luna, summarising in prose, dropped that list from the message to the implementer in 54 of 72 runs. The implementer then invented the names ( appointment["appointment_id"] instead of appointment["id"] ), and the module crashed on the first test. With a numbered list the contract arrived 89% of the time; with the original attached, always. Its code then scored 0.76 and 0.86, next to Sonnet. Claude kept that contract in practically every run, in all three formats. Its failures came from somewhere else: in 29 of its 216 software runs, Haiku's implementer did not deliver code at all, but a specification, because that was the shape of the message the architect had sent it. The type of deliverable had drifted down the chain too. What I am taking from this If the reason matters to the person executing, it has to be in their message, and nobody will put it there for you. The intermediate roles carry it; the one writing to the executor removes it. If you want the implementer to know why , say so in the delegation or attach the original. Attach the original request to the last hop. It was the most robust format across the three models and the only one where Luna did not lose the data contract. It costs tokens, but the alternative is the implementer guessing field names. Contracts travel verbatim, not summarised. Field names, signatures and output shapes are exactly the kind of thing a summary in prose drops because it looks like detail. Ask your agents to flag names they cannot verify. A mangled name cannot be fixed downstream, but it can be questioned, and in these runs nobody did. This fits with what I found when comparing ways of making coding agents collaborate : what helped was the shape of the team and its hand-offs, not a better conversation protocol. Here too, the biggest effect was not in the models' intelligence but in what each message is asked to carry. Limits Six hand-written requests, three per domain. The transcription errors are synthetic: written to look like what a transcriber does, not produced by running one. Claude ran in Claude Code with real subagents; Luna ran in my own harness. Comparisons between them mix model and harness. The judge was validated on a pilot sample of 150 labels against a second model as annotator (Claude Opus 5.5) and a third as adjudicator (Claude Fable 5.1), not against human labels. Both are from the same family as the Claude agents. On the pilot, its agreement was good on losses and weaker on distortions (κ 0.79 overall), so distortion rates are probably underestimated. Its agreement with itself on a second pass was 0.93 (GPT) and 0.97 (Claude). Two checks on the event plans were corrected after seeing the data: they counted "not Coachline" as a booking of Coachline. With the correction, only 3 plans across both grids book the vendor the client excluded. Sonnet delegated twice in the same step in 7% of its first attempts, mostly in event runs (25 of 30). Those runs were repeated; excluding them moves no figure by more than about two points. The analysis of whether the reason helps obey the rule was not planned in advance. Claude Code adds the account's name and email to the main session's context even when the system prompt is replaced. In 17 of the 853 Claude runs the lead used them, treating my email as the client's or naming me as the go-between. No scored fact depends on it; the published data has them replaced. The code, the six requests, every message between agents, the final artifacts and the scores are in experiments/agent-telephone . The design, with its hypotheses fixed before the runs and every later change dated, is in DESIGN.md ; scripts/article_numbers.py recomputes every figure in this article from the published data. It is the children's game of telephone, played with agents. But I did not want the artificial version, with ten agents in a row whispering to each other. In real setups a message rarely crosses more than three or four agents, and when it does it is because there is a hierarchy: a lead and roles under it. So that is what I measured.

The software ones ask for a small Python module (appointment reminders for an optician, seat proration for a SaaS bill, a GDPR purge job). Each request is written the way a client talks, and each contains facts of several kinds, tagged in advance: names, numbers, prohibitions, conditions, priorities, details easy to overlook, and reasons ("because the old field went stale after the March CRM migration").

In the chain, the implementer's message has been rewritten three times. In the relay it is also hop 4, but its author has the original request in front of it. That difference is what separates distance from audience.

The event teams have three roles (account manager, logistics, vendor liaison) instead of four, so their chain is one hop shorter.

Most of the request survives the trip. At hop 4, in the Claude runs, prohibitions arrive intact 98% of the time, details that are easy to miss 96%, numbers 92%, names and conditions 90%, priorities 85%. Luna lands in the same range: 91–99% for everything except one type.

That type is the reasons.

The why is not worn away. It is cut

In the Claude chain, the reason behind a decision travels well for two hops: 88–99% in the lead's message to the PM, 83–97% from the PM to the architect. Then the architect writes to the implementer, and it falls to 8–31%.

The obvious reading would be distance: four hops, four chances to lose something. The relay rules that out. There, the lead writes hop 4 itself, with the client's request in front of it, and only keeps the reason in 24% of its messages to the implementer, with Haiku and with Sonnet alike. It has the information; it chooses not to pass it on.

Share of messages that keep the reason behind a decision (software teams, prose and list formats). The drop is in the message to the implementer, and it happens just the same when the writer has the full request at hand.

So it is not a telephone effect in the sense of something wearing away from mouth to mouth. It is a decision about the audience: whoever writes to the person who builds writes instructions, and instructions do not carry reasons. Luna does the same, only earlier: it drops the reason from the very first message (it keeps it in 30% of its messages to the PM) and stays low all the way down.

In the event teams the cut is milder. The vendor, who books the caterer and writes the plan, still gets the reason 75–84% of the time in the Claude chain, and 40–64% when the lead writes to it directly in the relay. The executor writing code is the one who hears it least.

Does losing it matter?

That was my next question, and the answer is less tidy than I expected. Within each rule, format and model, I compared runs where the reason reached the implementer with runs where it did not, and looked at whether the final artifact obeyed the rule. With Claude, keeping the reason did not help: rules were obeyed slightly less often when their reason arrived (10 points less, 95% interval −15 to −5). With Luna the difference goes the other way, +9 points, but the interval crosses zero.

The negative effect in Claude is concentrated in Haiku and in rules whose reason names the old thing. "Inactivity is measured on last_seen_at, not last_login, because the mobile app stopped updating last_login": with that reason in the message, Haiku used the right field 59% of the time; without it, 97%. My hypothesis is that the reason puts the wrong name back into the message and acts as a distractor. This analysis was not planned before the runs, so I take it as a hypothesis, not a conclusion. But it is enough to stop me from claiming that the why is always worth carrying.

What does matter, clearly, is losing the requirement itself. In the Claude runs, a fact that arrived intact at the implementer was satisfied in the final artifact 95% of the time; one that was lost on the way, 40%. Losses are rare, but each one shows up in the result.

Names freeze; punctuation gets repaired

The transcription errors behave very differently depending on the type.

A mangled name cannot be repaired from the text: nothing in the request says how "Siobhán" should be spelled. But it can be questioned, the way a person would ask "is that name right?". Almost nobody did. In the Claude hand-offs, under 2% of the messages that carried a mangled name marked it as doubtful; Luna, never. The name froze and reached the artifact as transcribed: every final plan or module that used it used the wrong version.

Punctuation errors that change the meaning, on the other hand, were repaired about two thirds of the time in the hand-offs (Claude 66%, Luna 73%), probably because the rest of the request makes the intended reading obvious. Claude repeated the wrong reading as given in about one message in seven; Luna, in one in twenty.

The format matters, depending on the model

For Claude, the hand-off format barely changes anything: a numbered list keeps a little more at hop 4 than prose (88% against 85% of facts), and the final code scores about the same in all three formats.

For Luna it changes everything.

Final software module, mean share of hidden tests passed. Luna's code is not worse in itself: with a list or with the original attached it lands next to Claude. In prose, its summary drops the input fields, and the implementer invents them.

When I first saw Luna's numbers I assumed its code was simply worse. It is not. The client lists the fields of the input data ("each appointment has id, customer_name, email…"), and Luna, summarising in prose, dropped that list from the message to the implementer in 54 of 72 runs. The type of deliverable had drifted down the chain too.

What I am taking from this
  • If the reason matters to the person executing, it has to be in their message, and nobody will put it there for you. The intermediate roles carry it; the one writing to the executor removes it. If you want the implementer to know why, say so in the delegation or attach the original.

  • Contracts travel verbatim, not summarised. Field names, signatures and output shapes are exactly the kind of thing a summary in prose drops because it looks like detail.
  • Ask your agents to flag names they cannot verify. A mangled name cannot be fixed downstream, but it can be questioned, and in these runs nobody did.

items.title: How do you budget by paycheck when bills do not line up with paydays?
items.summary: Assign every bill to the paycheck that arrives on or before its due date, then subtract those bills from that paycheck. What remains is the money you can plan with. A monthly budget hides this, because rent and your paycheck rarely share a date. The rest of this article shows the method on paper, where it breaks, and how I built it into a one-file app. Why does a monthly budget fail when pay is uneven? A monthly budget assumes money arrives once and bills leave once. Real pay does not work that way. You may be paid every two weeks, twice a month, or on irregular dates. Bills ignore all of that. Rent is due on the 1st. The phone bill lands on the 12th. Insurance is due on the 20th. The monthly total can look healthy while one paycheck carries almost every large bill. You open the account on the 19th and the balance is gone. Discipline is rarely the issue. The monthly view hides which paycheck is responsible for which bill. How common is living close to the edge? Common enough that timing matters. The Federal Reserve's 2025 household survey asked adults about a hypothetical $400 emergency expense. 63 percent said they would cover it using only cash, savings, or a credit card paid off at the next statement. That means more than a third would need another route. The survey measures emergency cushions, not paycheck-to-paycheck living, so treat it as context and not as a count of that group. The figure was unchanged from the previous three years. Source: Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025, Executive Summary , Federal Reserve Board. When the cushion is thin, a bill landing one paycheck early or late decides whether the month works. How do you assign bills to paychecks? Use one rule: a bill belongs to the latest paycheck that arrives on or before its due date. Three steps apply it. List your paydays for the next month, with the amount of each. List every bill with its due date, including the ones that come every few months. Place each bill under the latest payday that falls on or before it. Here is an example with made-up numbers. You are paid $1,500 on the 5th and on the 19th. Paycheck Bills it covers Bills total Left over 5th, $1,500 Electricity (8th) $140, phone (12th) $45 $185 $1,315 19th, $1,500 Insurance (20th) $120, internet (25th) $60, rent (1st) $1,100 $1,280 $220 Rent is due on the 1st, which is before the 5th payday. So the paycheck from the 19th covers it, a bill that belongs to next month's calendar. The monthly total here is $3,000 in and $1,465 out. That looks comfortable. By paycheck, the 19th leaves only $220 for two weeks of living. What do you do with the leftover? Read the leftover as a spending limit for that period, not as a bonus. Divide it by the days until the next payday. On the 19th, $220 over 17 days is about $12.90 a day. On the 5th, $1,315 over 14 days is about $94 a day. Those two numbers are very different, and the monthly view would have shown you one average. Knowing this in advance lets you act. You can move a bill's due date with the provider, shift a savings transfer to the lighter paycheck, or plan the tight stretch. Why does this fall apart in a spreadsheet? The method is simple. Keeping it current is the work. Each new bill needs a row, a due date and a paycheck. Each payday shift needs a fix to a formula. Quarterly and yearly bills are the worst case. They vanish from view for months, then land in one paycheck with no warning. A spreadsheet can do this. In my experience the upkeep stops after a few weeks, and a broken formula gives a wrong number with total confidence. How does Paycheck Budget handle it? I built the same rule into one HTML file that opens in your browser. It has three short screens for setup. Your pay and next payday. The bills that repeat. A choice between plan mode and plan and track. You enter a bill once. The app places it in the right paycheck every time it comes round: monthly, every two weeks, every few months, or once. Plan mode needs only your pay and your bills. It never asks you to log a coffee. Plan and track adds a + Spend button. You type an amount, tap a category, and the Today screen shows one number: safe to spend today, counted line by line. The Paychecks screen lists the next six paychecks, each with its bills, debt minimums and savings. A calendar shows paydays, bills and spending by day. What about debt and savings? Debt sits in the same plan. You enter your debts. The app shows a payoff date under two strategies. Avalanche pays the highest interest rate first. It usually costs the least interest. Snowball pays the smallest balance first. It gives earlier wins. The app shows the total interest under each, so you compare the cost instead of guessing. Savings goals sit beside them, and each paycheck shows its savings. Where is my data stored? In your browser, on that computer, and nowhere else. It runs without an account or subscription, works offline, and never connects to your bank. There is a trade-off. Clearing your browsing data erases your numbers. So the app has a Download a backup button and reminds you once a week. A backup file restores everything, in the same browser or another one. Chrome or Edge is recommended. Nothing to install: you download the file and double-click it. Which approach should you pick? If your pay is steady and your bills are few, a monthly budget works. Keep it. If your paydays are uneven, or one paycheck always feels tighter than the others, budget by paycheck. Start on paper with the three steps above. Use a tool when the upkeep becomes the obstacle. This is a planning method, not financial advice. The numbers above are examples, so replace them with your own. Written with AI assistance. Every claim about the app comes from the version shipped on 2026-10-30. Paycheck Budget is the one-file budget app this article describes. Try the free demo first; the full version is on Gumroad .
