How do you assign bills to paychecks?

Use one rule: a bill belongs to the latest paycheck that arrives on or before its due date. Three steps apply it.

  1. List your paydays for the next month, with the amount of each.
  2. List every bill with its due date, including the ones that come every few months.
  3. Place each bill under the latest payday that falls on or before it.

Here is an example with made-up numbers. You are paid $1,500 on the 5th and on the 19th.

Paycheck Bills it covers Bills total Left over 5th, $1,500 Electricity (8th) $140, phone (12th) $45 $185 $1,315 19th, $1,500 Insurance (20th) $120, internet (25th) $60, rent (1st) $1,100 $1,280 $220

Rent is due on the 1st, which is before the 5th payday. So the paycheck from the 19th covers it, a bill that belongs to next month's calendar.

The monthly total here is $3,000 in and $1,465 out. That looks comfortable. By paycheck, the 19th leaves only $220 for two weeks of living.

What do you do with the leftover?

Read the leftover as a spending limit for that period, not as a bonus. Divide it by the days until the next payday.

On the 19th, $220 over 17 days is about $12.90 a day. On the 5th, $1,315 over 14 days is about $94 a day.

Those two numbers are very different, and the monthly view would have shown you one average. Knowing this in advance lets you act. You can move a bill's due date with the provider, shift a savings transfer to the lighter paycheck, or plan the tight stretch.

Why does this fall apart in a spreadsheet?

The method is simple. Keeping it current is the work. Each new bill needs a row, a due date and a paycheck. Each payday shift needs a fix to a formula.

Quarterly and yearly bills are the worst case. They vanish from view for months, then land in one paycheck with no warning.

A spreadsheet can do this. In my experience the upkeep stops after a few weeks, and a broken formula gives a wrong number with total confidence.

How does Paycheck Budget handle it?

I built the same rule into one HTML file that opens in your browser. It has three short screens for setup.

  1. Your pay and next payday.
  2. The bills that repeat.
  3. A choice between plan mode and plan and track.

You enter a bill once. The app places it in the right paycheck every time it comes round: monthly, every two weeks, every few months, or once.

Plan mode needs only your pay and your bills. It never asks you to log a coffee. Plan and track adds a + Spend button. You type an amount, tap a category, and the Today screen shows one number: safe to spend today, counted line by line.

The Paychecks screen lists the next six paychecks, each with its bills, debt minimums and savings. A calendar shows paydays, bills and spending by day.

What about debt and savings?

Debt sits in the same plan. You enter your debts. The app shows a payoff date under two strategies.

  • Avalanche pays the highest interest rate first. It usually costs the least interest.
  • Snowball pays the smallest balance first. It gives earlier wins.

The app shows the total interest under each, so you compare the cost instead of guessing. Savings goals sit beside them, and each paycheck shows its savings.

Where is my data stored?

In your browser, on that computer, and nowhere else. It runs without an account or subscription, works offline, and never connects to your bank.

There is a trade-off. Clearing your browsing data erases your numbers. So the app has a Download a backup button and reminds you once a week. A backup file restores everything, in the same browser or another one.

Chrome or Edge is recommended. Nothing to install: you download the file and double-click it.

Which approach should you pick?

If your pay is steady and your bills are few, a monthly budget works. Keep it.

If your paydays are uneven, or one paycheck always feels tighter than the others, budget by paycheck. Start on paper with the three steps above. Use a tool when the upkeep becomes the obstacle.

This is a planning method, not financial advice. The numbers above are examples, so replace them with your own.

Written with AI assistance. Every claim about the app comes from the version shipped on 2026-10-30.

Paycheck Budget is the one-file budget app this article describes. Try the free demo first; the full version is on Gumroad.

items.title: Most uni students now use AI, but that doesn’t mean they like it
items.summary: Xavier Arnau/Getty via Canva, Wikimedia, The Conversation , CC BY-NC The university experience has changed drastically since artificial intelligence (AI) became widely available four years ago. Students are increasingly using AI for around-the-clock feedback , and most are required to use it as part of new assessment redesigns. But as AI is used more in courses and changes how university works, how do students feel about it? Our research In 2024, we began a research project across four Australian unis – Monash University, the University of Queensland, Deakin University and the University of Technology Sydney – asking students about AI. Undergraduate and postgraduate students were asked how frequently they use AI for study, their most common uses of AI, why they choose to use it and their concerns around the tech. This year, we repeated the survey at the same unis, hearing from more than 10,000 students. The survey included responses from neurodivergent students, students with disability, those who spoke languages other than English at home and students who were the first in their family to attend uni. Students were recruited via email, posts on online university platforms, and signs with QR codes. We also ran 20 focus groups with 79 students online in 2024. What we found A published snapshot of our 2026 survey data shows the most common reason students use AI is to edit or improve their writing, with nearly 70% selecting this option. About 64% of students use it to generate ideas or examples, and 60% said they use AI to teach them how to do something. Around half of students seek out information through AI and also ask it for feedback on their work. We also know more students are using AI. When comparing the data to 2024 responses, the proportion of students who reported never using AI for their studies fell slightly, from 17% to 15%. It mirrors findings from this year’s Australian Student Wellbeing Report , which found 84% of students have used AI tools for assignments and study, increasing 10% from the previous year. Why students use AI Students reported using AI for a range of different reasons. About 55% use it to speed up their working process and also to help themselves overcome mental blocks. Nearly half of students said they use AI to make study easier in general. Participants also reported using AI to help improve their personal wellbeing during study sessions. About 41% said the tech helps reduce stress and around 32% said they feel more confident when using AI in their work. There are concerns But using AI does not necessarily mean students are comfortable with it. We found many are limiting their AI use, some are trying to avoid using it, and 15-17% are avoiding it altogether in their studies. The reasons for limiting AI use vary, but the most common explanation, selected by 67% of participants who use AI, related to concerns around AI’s accuracy. About 62% of students said they limited or avoided AI use as it conflicts with their personal learning values and around 57% said they preferred to do the work themselves. Just under half of students expressed ethical concerns in using AI. These concerns might relate to AI presenting biased information, privacy issues, threats to academic integrity, and the environmental impacts of AI technologies. Over the last two years, students have become less worried about breaking uni rules too. This year, 56% of participants said they avoided using AI out of a fear of being caught – decreasing 7% when compared with 2024 data. Unis can help Over the last four years, unis have been navigating complex changes. But their guidance on AI hasn’t always been clear to students. Research shows students have learned more about AI on their own than they have from their unis. Our 2024 survey and focus groups also showed widespread anxiety and confusion among students about using AI for study, partly due to confusing university academic integrity policies around AI rules. One participant at the time asked for clearer rules: just have some kind of concrete policy in place that you can look at and go like, ‘right, this is okay. This isn’t. Thank you.’ And even if it’s something I would personally disagree with, at least it’s set in stone. Another student recognised the complexity of AI regulation too: we’re in this very grey area where nobody knows what’s really happening. Guidance around AI has improved Our findings show there has been some progress over the last two years. Students who reported receiving sufficient guidance from unis rose from 36% in 2024 to 47% in 2026. This might be because unis are setting more consistent AI guidelines across their institutions, rather than putting the responsibility on educators to set rules around AI use for each subject. This is happening alongside changes to assessment that incorporate use of AI. But our recent survey suggests there is more to do to help students feel confident they will not break rules. Students’ perspectives matter Of all the concerns about AI in higher education, perhaps one of the most important questions is whether unis are doing enough to listen to students about their feelings towards AI and how they use it. When unis don’t engage students in these conversations, they miss opportunities to understand how AI is influencing learning. More importantly, they miss the opportunity to involve students in shaping how AI is used in education. items.summary_html:
Xavier Arnau/Getty via Canva, Wikimedia, The Conversation, CC BY-NC

The university experience has changed drastically since artificial intelligence (AI) became widely available four years ago.

Students are increasingly using AI for around-the-clock feedback, and most are required to use it as part of new assessment redesigns.

But as AI is used more in courses and changes how university works, how do students feel about it?

Our research

In 2024, we began a research project across four Australian unis – Monash University, the University of Queensland, Deakin University and the University of Technology Sydney – asking students about AI. Undergraduate and postgraduate students were asked how frequently they use AI for study, their most common uses of AI, why they choose to use it and their concerns around the tech.

This year, we repeated the survey at the same unis, hearing from more than 10,000 students.

The survey included responses from neurodivergent students, students with disability, those who spoke languages other than English at home and students who were the first in their family to attend uni.

Students were recruited via email, posts on online university platforms, and signs with QR codes. We also ran 20 focus groups with 79 students online in 2024.

What we found

A published snapshot of our 2026 survey data shows the most common reason students use AI is to edit or improve their writing, with nearly 70% selecting this option. About 64% of students use it to generate ideas or examples, and 60% said they use AI to teach them how to do something.

Around half of students seek out information through AI and also ask it for feedback on their work.

We also know more students are using AI. When comparing the data to 2024 responses, the proportion of students who reported never using AI for their studies fell slightly, from 17% to 15%.

It mirrors findings from this year’s Australian Student Wellbeing Report, which found 84% of students have used AI tools for assignments and study, increasing 10% from the previous year.

Why students use AI

Students reported using AI for a range of different reasons.

About 55% use it to speed up their working process and also to help themselves overcome mental blocks. Nearly half of students said they use AI to make study easier in general.

Participants also reported using AI to help improve their personal wellbeing during study sessions. About 41% said the tech helps reduce stress and around 32% said they feel more confident when using AI in their work.

There are concerns

But using AI does not necessarily mean students are comfortable with it. We found many are limiting their AI use, some are trying to avoid using it, and 15-17% are avoiding it altogether in their studies.

The reasons for limiting AI use vary, but the most common explanation, selected by 67% of participants who use AI, related to concerns around AI’s accuracy.

About 62% of students said they limited or avoided AI use as it conflicts with their personal learning values and around 57% said they preferred to do the work themselves. Just under half of students expressed ethical concerns in using AI. These concerns might relate to AI presenting biased information, privacy issues, threats to academic integrity, and the environmental impacts of AI technologies.

Over the last two years, students have become less worried about breaking uni rules too. This year, 56% of participants said they avoided using AI out of a fear of being caught – decreasing 7% when compared with 2024 data.

Unis can help

Over the last four years, unis have been navigating complex changes. But their guidance on AI hasn’t always been clear to students.

Research shows students have learned more about AI on their own than they have from their unis.

Our 2024 survey and focus groups also showed widespread anxiety and confusion among students about using AI for study, partly due to confusing university academic integrity policies around AI rules.

One participant at the time asked for clearer rules:

just have some kind of concrete policy in place that you can look at and go like, ‘right, this is okay. This isn’t. Thank you.’ And even if it’s something I would personally disagree with, at least it’s set in stone.

Another student recognised the complexity of AI regulation too:

 we’re in this very grey area where nobody knows what’s really happening.

Guidance around AI has improved

Our findings show there has been some progress over the last two years. Students who reported receiving sufficient guidance from unis rose from 36% in 2024 to 47% in 2026.

This might be because unis are setting more consistent AI guidelines across their institutions, rather than putting the responsibility on educators to set rules around AI use for each subject. This is happening alongside changes to assessment that incorporate use of AI.

But our recent survey suggests there is more to do to help students feel confident they will not break rules.

Students’ perspectives matter

Of all the concerns about AI in higher education, perhaps one of the most important questions is whether unis are doing enough to listen to students about their feelings towards AI and how they use it.

When unis don’t engage students in these conversations, they miss opportunities to understand how AI is influencing learning. More importantly, they miss the opportunity to involve students in shaping how AI is used in education.

The research mentioned in this article has been funded by the Deputy Vice-Chancellor Education Portfolios at Monash University, University of Queensland, Deakin University and University Technology Sydney

items.title: AI use is now universal in higher education. Why are universities failing to adapt?
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) use among university students is now near-universal in many countries . Yet, as of a year ago, fewer than one in five universities in a 90-country UNESCO survey had a formal AI policy. Since ChatGPT arrived in late 2022, the threat to academic integrity has loomed large. Unis must now ensure students earn degrees by showing what they can do, not what AI can do. This requires policies that drive structural change to assessment and curriculum, not just rules about when AI can be used. But it’s not so straightforward. The challenge for universities Universities, in particular, have struggled to adapt to generative AI more than primary and high schools. This is because university classes are often large and contact time between students and teachers is limited. Together, this makes it hard for teachers to get to know students personally and to ensure they learn what is required for their degrees. UNESCO has published an AI competency framework , but it focuses primarily on schools and stops short of providing specific guidance for higher education. University AI policies are often vague A study published in July examined the public AI policies and guidelines of 39 Australian universities that teach information and communications technology. This is a subject area where AI can readily complete coding tasks. The analysis found wide variation among the universities’ AI policies. Often, AI rules were buried in institutions’ misconduct policies rather than assessment design procedures. Out of the 39 unis, only one had published specific guidance around AI. The universities’ general guidance on AI use was often vague, too. One simply required AI use to be “ethical, pedagogically sound, transparent and purposeful” but did not provide any further detail. The researchers argued that AI was disrupting assessments faster than universities could build the structures to govern it. Only seven of the 39 universities had documented a body, such as a task force, to coordinate their response. Many have also left it to individual unit coordinators to spell out what AI use is allowed. This means the rules can differ between units. The risks also go well beyond cheating. Global discussion among leading researchers and policymakers this year has shifted to a deeper issue: using AI to avoid learning altogether . This is when students’ offload their work to AI entirely and, as a result, learn nothing themselves . It is difficult to gauge how much of this offloading is already occurring. Universities’ current policies aren’t sufficient in addressing student offloading to AI. Students cannot be forced to learn through a policy. Teachers have also been using AI tools to detect whether students have included AI-generated text in their submissions. But universities are now moving away from this as the technology is not always accurate. Experts have warned that relying solely on AI detectors can lead to false accusations of student academic misconduct. Assessment reform Instead of focusing on more systemic responses, universities have mainly responded to AI by changing how assessments work. This has usually meant: a greater emphasis on in-person exams and oral presentations where AI cannot be easily accessed permitting the use of AI in some assessments , such as take-home essays, where students have cited their use of the technology. But while redesigned assessments can show whether learning has occurred, it is still not enough. It also matters what students are assessed on. What are other countries doing? In other parts of the world, such as the European Union , attention is turning to explicitly developing students’ capabilities to adapt to constant change . These include teaching students to: make sound judgements about how much they know about a subject critically evaluate information, both with and without AI make decisions about their learning processes and goals independently of AI or an educator. However, these capabilities are hard to develop and mostly don’t transfer between subjects. Instead, they must be taught explicitly to students, in the context of their subject area or discipline. One way of doing this would be to incorporate specific modules into courses that teach this. So, what’s the right approach? In 2023, a number of academics, including myself, wrote evidence-based assessment principles for the Australian higher education regulator. The principles were formed to guide unis on how to adapt assessments to account for students’ AI use. One principle focuses on assuring students are actually learning content and not offloading work to AI, which institutions have attempted to address through assessment redesign. These attempts at redesign are having an effect. The second principle is about preparing students for a world where AI is ubiquitous. Students need to learn how to effectively use AI for when they enter the workforce. This principle has proven much harder for unis to adapt to, as skills tied to today’s AI tools quickly become outdated as the technology rapidly advances. This means simple “AI literacy” is not enough for students alone. While there is no one-size-fits-all approach, unis would also benefit from collaborating with each other to tackle the problem. However, institutions tend to compete rather than share resources. Only one of the 39 in the study I previously cited mentioned learning from other institutions. A national strategy would help In 2024, the higher education regulator required every uni to submit AI action plans outlining what they are doing to adapt to AI. The regulator has also since published guides outlining strategies. But a regulator can only set expectations. It cannot fund the long-term work of enabling changes to policy and practice across the country. That was the job of the Office for Learning and Teaching, which funded teaching innovation and helped universities share what worked . It closed in 2016, and a promised replacement never materialised. A national approach would mean an enabling body – independent of any single university – sharing evidence and guidance across the sector. This might look similar to Ireland’s Higher Education Authority , which has published a national framework on AI in teaching and learning. However, there are challenges in setting this up in Australia, given how protective universities are about their autonomy. There would be questions around who funds such a body. And it would be difficult for a national authority to keep pace with technology that changes faster than policy. Still, unis must engage deeply and collaboratively with this debate about how to adapt to AI. Otherwise they risk becoming redundant in the age of intelligent machines. Jason M. Lodge receives funding from the Medical Research Future Fund and Studiosity. He has received funding from the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency, the Australian Department of Education, Queensland Department of Education, the Office for Learning and Teaching, the Higher Education Research and Development Society of Australasia, Australasian Society for Computers in Learning in Tertiary Education, and Echo360. He is one of the convenors of the Castlereagh Statement: A cross-sector call to action on Australian education and training in the age of AI.
items.summary_html:
Artificial intelligence (AI) use among university students is now near-universal in many countries. Yet, as of a year ago, fewer than one in five universities in a 90-country UNESCO survey had a formal AI policy.

Since ChatGPT arrived in late 2022, the threat to academic integrity has loomed large. Unis must now ensure students earn degrees by showing what they can do, not what AI can do.

This requires policies that drive structural change to assessment and curriculum, not just rules about when AI can be used. But it’s not so straightforward.

The challenge for universities

Universities, in particular, have struggled to adapt to generative AI more than primary and high schools.

This is because university classes are often large and contact time between students and teachers is limited. Together, this makes it hard for teachers to get to know students personally and to ensure they learn what is required for their degrees.

UNESCO has published an AI competency framework, but it focuses primarily on schools and stops short of providing specific guidance for higher education.

University AI policies are often vague

A study published in July examined the public AI policies and guidelines of 39 Australian universities that teach information and communications technology. This is a subject area where AI can readily complete coding tasks.

The analysis found wide variation among the universities’ AI policies. Often, AI rules were buried in institutions’ misconduct policies rather than assessment design procedures. Out of the 39 unis, only one had published specific guidance around AI.

The universities’ general guidance on AI use was often vague, too. One simply required AI use to be “ethical, pedagogically sound, transparent and purposeful” but did not provide any further detail.

The researchers argued that AI was disrupting assessments faster than universities could build the structures to govern it. Only seven of the 39 universities had documented a body, such as a task force, to coordinate their response.

Many have also left it to individual unit coordinators to spell out what AI use is allowed. This means the rules can differ between units.

The risks also go well beyond cheating. Global discussion among leading researchers and policymakers this year has shifted to a deeper issue: using AI to avoid learning altogether. This is when students’ offload their work to AI entirely and, as a result, learn nothing themselves. It is difficult to gauge how much of this offloading is already occurring.

Universities’ current policies aren’t sufficient in addressing student offloading to AI. Students cannot be forced to learn through a policy.

Teachers have also been using AI tools to detect whether students have included AI-generated text in their submissions. But universities are now moving away from this as the technology is not always accurate.

Experts have warned that relying solely on AI detectors can lead to false accusations of student academic misconduct.

Assessment reform

Instead of focusing on more systemic responses, universities have mainly responded to AI by changing how assessments work. This has usually meant:

  • a greater emphasis on in-person exams and oral presentations where AI cannot be easily accessed

  • permitting the use of AI in some assessments, such as take-home essays, where students have cited their use of the technology.

But while redesigned assessments can show whether learning has occurred, it is still not enough. It also matters what students are assessed on.

What are other countries doing?

In other parts of the world, such as the European Union, attention is turning to explicitly developing students’ capabilities to adapt to constant change. These include teaching students to:

  • make sound judgements about how much they know about a subject

  • critically evaluate information, both with and without AI

  • make decisions about their learning processes and goals independently of AI or an educator.

However, these capabilities are hard to develop and mostly don’t transfer between subjects. Instead, they must be taught explicitly to students, in the context of their subject area or discipline.

One way of doing this would be to incorporate specific modules into courses that teach this.

So, what’s the right approach?

In 2023, a number of academics, including myself, wrote evidence-based assessment principles for the Australian higher education regulator. The principles were formed to guide unis on how to adapt assessments to account for students’ AI use.

One principle focuses on assuring students are actually learning content and not offloading work to AI, which institutions have attempted to address through assessment redesign. These attempts at redesign are having an effect.

The second principle is about preparing students for a world where AI is ubiquitous. Students need to learn how to effectively use AI for when they enter the workforce.

This principle has proven much harder for unis to adapt to, as skills tied to today’s AI tools quickly become outdated as the technology rapidly advances. This means simple “AI literacy” is not enough for students alone.

While there is no one-size-fits-all approach, unis would also benefit from collaborating with each other to tackle the problem.

However, institutions tend to compete rather than share resources. Only one of the 39 in the study I previously cited mentioned learning from other institutions.

A national strategy would help

In 2024, the higher education regulator required every uni to submit AI action plans outlining what they are doing to adapt to AI. The regulator has also since published guides outlining strategies.

But a regulator can only set expectations. It cannot fund the long-term work of enabling changes to policy and practice across the country.

That was the job of the Office for Learning and Teaching, which funded teaching innovation and helped universities share what worked. It closed in 2016, and a promised replacement never materialised.

A national approach would mean an enabling body – independent of any single university – sharing evidence and guidance across the sector. This might look similar to Ireland’s Higher Education Authority, which has published a national framework on AI in teaching and learning.

However, there are challenges in setting this up in Australia, given how protective universities are about their autonomy. There would be questions around who funds such a body. And it would be difficult for a national authority to keep pace with technology that changes faster than policy.

Still, unis must engage deeply and collaboratively with this debate about how to adapt to AI. Otherwise they risk becoming redundant in the age of intelligent machines.

items.title: Google claims its new AI software cuts inference latency by over 90% — but there’s a catch
items.summary: Google’s eighth-generation TPU announcement on Monday included more than new chips, introducing TPU Sync , an open-source system designed to speed up AI inference by tackling a problem that worsens as context windows grow: moving data between different types of memory. The software is made for developers running large models, particularly ones handling million-token contexts and reinforcement-learning workloads. The company claims it can cut KV-cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90% in some tests. The company claims it can cut KV-cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90% in some tests. Inside the memory hierarchy Written in C++, the framework moves data between accelerator memory, host DRAM, storage, and the network. It uses zero-copy transfers and native PjRtBuffer hardware descriptors to avoid unnecessary copies. Combined host-to-device and device-to-host throughput reached 223 GB/s per Ironwood TPU host, approaching the theoretical 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 limit. Google’s numbers, with caveats In Google’s benchmarks , moving KV caches for the 235-billion-parameter Qwen3 model went from taking several seconds to about 230 milliseconds. That cut the average time to first token (TTFT) by 60% when relatively few requests were running at once. With a larger 480-billion-parameter model, the reduction reached 90%. Google saw similar gains when testing prefix caching with 64,000-token contexts. TTFT dropped by as much as 90%, throughput increased by more than 50%, and P99 inter-token latency fell 30%. Developers may see different results depending on what they’re running, how much cached data they can reuse, and how much network bandwidth they have available. The software is made for developers running large models, particularly ones handling million-token contexts and reinforcement-learning workloads. The company claims it can cut KV-cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90% in some tests.

Inside the memory hierarchy

Written in C++, the framework moves data between accelerator memory, host DRAM, storage, and the network. It uses zero-copy transfers and native PjRtBuffer hardware descriptors to avoid unnecessary copies.

items.title: Jensen Huang disappears from lineup at Anthropic and ElevenLabs events
items.summary: Jensen Huang's name and image disappeared from ElevenLabs' Wednesday conference lineup. Screenshot/Business Insider Jensen Huang is no longer set to attend a Monday Anthropic CEO forum, according to a person familiar with the matter. Huang's name also disappeared from the speaker lineup for an ElevenLabs conference set for Wednesday. Nvidia's board opened an investigation into whether Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." Jensen Huang was scheduled for two tech events this week. Then the CEO disclosed he had an affair, and Nvidia's board opened an investigation. Ahead of its expected IPO next week, Anthropic is hosting a private CEO forum this week in Montecito. Huang was set to be interviewed by an Anthropic executive on Monday evening, a person familiar with the event told Business Insider. He is no longer expected to attend, according to a second person familiar with the matter. Anthropic declined to comment. Huang's name and image have also disappeared from the speaker list for the ElevenLabs Summit in New York. The Nvidia CEO was scheduled for a fireside chat with ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski on Wednesday, where the two would have a "conversation on the future of AI." The slot previously held for Huang now shows a "closing keynote" from Staniszewski alone. ElevenLabs, an AI startup that specializes in voice technology, and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The speaker lineup on the conference's site now begins with CEOs from ElevenLabs and Ramp. Screenshot via ElevenLabs In a Sunday note to staff, Huang said that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife. He apologized to his wife and kids, and said that his Nvidia colleagues deserved better. "I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence," Huang wrote. That same day, Nvidia said that its board of directors opened an investigation into whether Huang had been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." The investigation followed an October report by The New York Times, which said that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang had developed a close relationship with Nvidia's CEO. US officials believed Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, the Times reported. In his memo to staff, Huang said that he intended to cooperate fully with the investigation. Other speakers at ElevanLabs' Wednesday conference include several of the AI company's other executives, as well as leaders from Ramp , McKinsey, and AWS. items.title: Cursor and Google join OpenAI in giving coding agents a voice. Claude Code stays silent.
items.summary: Two of the biggest players in the AI coding space are betting that developers want to talk to their agents while they work, with both announcing a two-way voice feature that lets users ask questions and give follow-up instructions without returning to the keyboard. On Friday , Cursor announced Voice Chat with Agents , a Grok Voice -powered feature that lets developers call an agent and talk through a change. On the very same day, Google announced Voice mode in Antigravity , which uses Gemini Live to bring spoken conversations to its desktop app and command-line tool. In a blog post announcing the feature, Nick Van der Auwermeulen , developer relations engineer at Google, contrasts the back-and-forth dynamic of human colleagues with the “rhythm” of working with coding agents. “Some of the best engineering happens out loud,” Van der Auwermeulen writes. “You talk a bug through with a teammate, think out loud in front of a whiteboard, or say ‘ wait, try it the other way ’ halfway through a pairing session. Working with an agent has mostly had a different rhythm: you type a prompt, the agent works, you read what it did, and you type again.” “Some of the best engineering happens out loud.” The longer a job runs, he adds, the more often developers need to check in. A command might be waiting for approval, or a developer might spot a requirement the original instructions missed. “Each of those moments pulls you back to the keyboard and away from whatever you were looking at,” he continues. And so Antigravity’s voice mode keeps a live call open while the coding agent works, so the developer can hear an update or approve a command without reaching for the keyboard. Cursor, for its part, makes a similar pitch for keeping the conversation going. “Describe a change out loud, ask what an agent is working on, and hear updates as the work moves forward,” the company writes. “Describe a change out loud, ask what an agent is working on, and hear updates as the work moves forward.” Look who’s talking Antigravity , for the uninitiated, is Google’s agentic software development platform. It debuted alongside Gemini 3 last November , with version 2.0 landing in May replete with a separate desktop app. There’s also a terminal client, Antigravity CLI , and extensions for developers who want to work from editors such as VS Code, JetBrains IDEs and Xcode. Antigravity is now where Google is consolidating its various coding tools, having moved individual Gemini CLI users to Antigravity in June, while it’s also in the midst of sunsetting Jules , a previously launched background coding agent. It’s worth noting that Antigravity’s existing dictation feature already turns speech into a written prompt. Now, to start a two-way call in the desktop app, the user clicks the waveform button beside it and tells the agent what they want it to do. Starting a voice call Antigravity replies aloud and keeps the call open while the coding agent works, with the user able to ask how it’s going or give it further instructions. You can also interrupt the agent mid-sentence to ask a question or give it another instruction. Antigravity responds out loud When the agent finishes, its written summary and a button to review the code changes appear in the same chat. Reviewing the fix mid-call Additionally, voice mode also works in the Antigravity CLI. Users run the /voice live command to start a call, and hear the agent reply while it works away in the terminal. Starting a terminal voice call Coding agents talk back Cursor, which was acquired by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in August for $60 billion, has followed a similar path toward embracing voice. It added dictation in October 2025 , and in release notes last month, the company said it had updated existing voice calls to let agents give short spoken progress updates. One difference with Cursor’s rollout is where you can call from. Cursor supports voice chat on the web and iOS as well as on desktop, while Google offers it in the Antigravity desktop app and CLI. Cursor’s calls run on Grok Voice , which xAI launched through its API back in April . “The push now, it seems, is to keep the conversation going after the agent starts work.” However, Google and Cursor aren’t the first AI companies to bring two-way voice to coding agents. OpenAI launched a Codex desktop app in February with a built-in dictation feature . And as The New Stack reported in July , the company added two-way voice to Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app, letting developers give instructions and check on tasks by speaking. The Codex CLI has offered live voice conversations since the spring , with OpenAI enabling them by default in September . Anthropic, for what it’s worth, has a voice mode which offers two-way voice functionality inside the Claude app only. In Claude Code, specifically, voice still only goes one way via dictation — the /voice command turns developers’ vocal instructions into prompt text , and the agent replies in writing. Dictation itself is useful for describing a bug or sketching out a feature aloud, and it’s showing up across the AI coding landscape, from the major AI labs to well-funded startups such as Replit . The push now, it seems, is to keep the conversation going after the agent starts work, so developers can follow up about a decision, clarify a requirement, or change direction before the work is finished.

items.title: Google Cloud's new TPUs were designed for context and security
items.summary: Google Cloud released two new versions of its TPU AI processors Monday, rounding out the eighth generation of its homegrown challenger to Nvidia's control of the AI chip market. The new TPUs complement the 8t and 8i chips launched earlier this year; the "t" stands for model training, and the "i" targets inference workloads. The new 8tx includes one of AMD's Epyc CPUs to create a secure hardware processing enclave, and the 8iMax was designed to expand the amount of memory that the chip can handle to reduce a key AI bottleneck. "This is the first time we have introduced four TPU systems in a single year," Google Cloud's Amin Vahdat said in a blog post . "With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads." Package deal

items.title: Meta launches Muse Ember to take on Claude Haiku and GPT-6 Luna
items.summary: Meta on Monday debuted Muse Ember , a smaller, more efficient multimodal member of its Muse model family. The company is clearly taking a similar approach to the other frontier labs, with a family of models that cover everything from focused, high-volume tasks (think OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna and Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 ) to frontier intelligence like OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1, and, most recently, Meta’s Muse Wonder Full . And just like its competitors, Meta is pitching the smaller model for agentic subtasks like reading files, running tests, and making targeted fixes, with a larger model like Muse Wonder doing the planning. Muse Ember is available in Muse Code and through the Meta Model API under the model ID muse-ember-1.0 . It will likely soon be available on services like OpenRouter and on the neoclouds, too, given that Meta has done the same for its other Muse models in the past. Like with previous Muse model releases, Meta is keeping Ember’s model weights private. Ember is Meta’s take on a small, price-efficient model, and at least when it comes to the benchmarks, it’s a strong entry. Credit: Meta. At max reasoning, Meta puts Ember at about $0.14 per task on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , compared with $0.41 for Haiku and $0.15 for Luna. Ember matches Haiku’s rounded score at about a third of the cost and scores higher than Luna for about a cent less per task. At xhigh, the other Ember setting shown in Meta’s chart, the model scores about 34 at roughly $0.12 per task. Muse Ember pricing Ember, which has a 1M-token context window and supports up to 512K output tokens, is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens, and $0.50 per million output tokens. Those input and output rates match GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at their standard short-context prices. Both charge $0.01 per million cached input tokens at those rates, with higher prices for longer prompts. Ember is available in Muse Code and through the Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0 , with support for the Responses API. How Chinese rivals compare And while Meta doesn’t directly compare the new model to Chinese competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 , Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 Flash, and MiniMax M3.1 Flash in the chart, Ember undercuts the listed uncached input rates for all three. It also undercuts DeepSeek’s direct off-peak and MiniMax’s listed output prices and matches GLM’s. DeepSeek has a slightly lower off-peak cache-hit rate of $0.003 per million tokens. On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, for example, Ember scores 36 at max reasoning, while DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is at 33, MiniMax at 29, and GLM at 28. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, meanwhile, scores 28 on this same benchmark, while Haiku gets to 36, both at max reasoning. Muse Ember vs. Muse Spark Meta’s own Muse Spark 1.3 scores 37 at max reasoning and costs $2.39 per task at the standard API rates used in the comparison. Meta also offers a Spark Contributor tier, where it uses requests to improve its products. That tier matches Ember’s uncached input price and charges $0.20 per million output tokens. Credit: Meta. Meta reports a lead over Haiku and Luna on its own Personal Superintelligence Index, a measure of personal and knowledge work. One benchmark where Ember doesn’t fare as well is FrontierCode 2.0, which evaluates whether a repository maintainer would merge an agent’s changes. Ember scores 27.2 percent, compared with 34.9 percent for Haiku and 28.5 percent for DeepSeek. Spark 1.3 scores 23.1 percent. Meta Muse Ember benchmarks. Credit: Meta. Computer use on OSWorld Ember can take text, images, audio, and video as inputs, and Meta says it can operate desktop apps from screenshots. On OSWorld 2.1 , it got nearly the same partial-credit score as Haiku, 69.5 percent versus 68.9 percent, but finished more tasks outright, 33.8 percent versus 27.8 percent for Haiku and 17 percent for Luna. In a separate OSWorld 2.1 run, Spark 1.3 earned nearly identical partial credit to Ember and completed 39.25 percent of tasks. Meta says the new model is the first it trained using the larger Muse Wonder Full model. That’s similar to what the company did with Muse Wonder to train the specialized models it began rolling out to its Muse personal agent and Meta AI .

items.title: An internal Disney presentation reveals its top streaming priorities, from creator content to a free tier
items.summary: Disney told tech employees how it's planning to improve its streaming service in the coming year. Bernd Weißbrod/picture alliance via Getty Images; Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images Disney tech execs unveiled a list of streaming priorities for the year ahead in a town hall. The Mouse House is planning to add creator content to Disney+ and is working on a free offering. A leaked presentation gives a clear view into CEO Josh D'Amaro's streaming vision. Disney has plans to make big changes to its namesake streamer, Business Insider has learned. Disney+'s priorities for the next year include uploading more vertical video clips , adding creator content, and working on a free tier, according to screenshots of an internal presentation viewed by Business Insider. Tech leaders told employees how they're planning to boost engagement on Disney+ in a town hall late last week. In the meeting, execs, including VP of product management Dave Lindsay, unveiled Disney's streaming strategy and priorities for the 2027 fiscal year, which began in October. In the town hall, some tech employees also pressed management for details on a possible next round of layoffs. The leaked slide deck gives one of the clearest views yet into CEO Josh D'Amaro's plan to have Disney+ be the "digital centerpiece" of the company, while making its flagship service more competitive with paid streamers, YouTube, and social media. According to Nielsen, Disney's streamers accounted for 4.8% of US TV viewership in August — well behind YouTube at 15.8% and Netflix at 7.7%, but more than twice the share of rivals Paramount+ and Peacock. Here's what's in the works for Disney+ in the next year, according to the presentation: Ramping up to adding 500 new vertical clips per day, and introducing creator content in early 2027 A free tier with always-on FAST channels and content sampling 4K livestreaming for the Super Bowl Fully unifying Disney+ and Hulu into one app Inside Disney's streaming priorities Like other Hollywood giants, Disney is betting on short videos to boost engagement and attract younger viewers hooked on YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok. The Mouse House plans to ramp up to adding 500 vertical clips per day on its streamer by the end of next quarter, which concludes in early April. The effort is starting this quarter with a goal of about 150 clips a day, the slide deck said. Disney is planning to add "new content types every quarter," the presentation said. These include clips of sports, news, and short-form "micro series" (including micro dramas ). It's aiming to integrate creator content starting next quarter, the presentation said. The company announced a deal with TikTok in early August that would put a curated feed of user-generated content on its streamer. Disney's forthcoming free offering , which Business Insider first reported on in July, was referenced several times in the streaming presentation. The deck mentioned a "Free Plan" and "the free experience," which it said would include "FAST channel creation" and "content sampling." FAST channels are free, always-on streaming feeds — supported by advertising — popularized by services like Pluto TV and The Roku Channel. Disney+ already has a few always-on channels for paid subscribers, including ones for Disney princesses and Pixar films. Viewers join in the middle of a show or movie instead of starting on-demand from the beginning. As for "sampling," Disney has discussed making some Disney+ content available without a subscription, Business Insider previously reported. Other media giants, including Paramount+ , are considering free streaming tiers to reach new viewers. Audiences have flocked to free services like Tubi and YouTube as streamers have raised prices. Disney+ will livestream the Super Bowl in the US for the first time in mid-February, which the presentation called a major "tentpole" moment. Peacock, Paramount+, and Tubi have streamed Super Bowl coverage from NBC, CBS, and Fox, respectively. The company's livestreaming priorities include "live 4K HDR, lower latency, scale, live event monitoring and live content security" to deliver the Big Game to millions of viewers in high-quality, lag-free picture, while protecting against piracy. Disney+ and Hulu are joining forces Disney is still working toward merging Hulu with Disney+, as part of a multi-phased plan known internally as "Project Gemini." The yearslong project of adding Hulu's content and features to Disney+ will "deepen engagement" and "increase lifetime fan value," D'Amaro said in August. While the presentation didn't give a target date for the complete Hulu integration, its road map said "One App Milestones" are scheduled through Disney's fiscal fourth quarter, which runs from early July to early October. It's unclear what those milestones are, or what finishing them would mean. (Project Gemini had been scheduled to conclude by the end of 2026, Business Insider reported in May .) Putting Hulu and Disney+ under one roof is part of Disney's plan to build a super app , where users can play games and buy merchandise without leaving the streamer. The company hopes that an interactive experience will increase time spent and make customers less likely to cancel, D'Amaro told employees in August, while shopping features could drive revenue to other parts of its business. D'Amaro told employees in August that Disney planned to "introduce elements of this expanded ecosystem" in the spring. Read the original article on Business Insider

Tech leaders told employees how they're planning to boost engagement on Disney+ in a town hall late last week. Here's what's in the works for Disney+ in the next year, according to the presentation:

  • Ramping up to adding 500 new vertical clips per day, and introducing creator content in early 2027
  • A free tier with always-on FAST channels and content sampling
  • 4K livestreaming for the Super Bowl
  • Fully unifying Disney+ and Hulu into one app

The Mouse House plans to ramp up to adding 500 vertical clips per day on its streamer by the end of next quarter, which concludes in early April. The effort is starting this quarter with a goal of about 150 clips a day, the slide deck said.

Disney is planning to add "new content types every quarter," the presentation said. These include clips of sports, news, and short-form "micro series" (including micro dramas). It's aiming to integrate creator content starting next quarter, the presentation said. The company announced a deal with TikTok in early August that would put a curated feed of user-generated content on its streamer.

Disney's forthcoming free offering, which Business Insider first reported on in July, was referenced several times in the streaming presentation. The deck mentioned a "Free Plan" and "the free experience," which it said would include "FAST channel creation" and "content sampling."

FAST channels are free, always-on streaming feeds — supported by advertising — popularized by services like Pluto TV and The Roku Channel. Disney+ already has a few always-on channels for paid subscribers, including ones for Disney princesses and Pixar films. Viewers join in the middle of a show or movie instead of starting on-demand from the beginning.

As for "sampling," Disney has discussed making some Disney+ content available without a subscription, Business Insider previously reported.

Other media giants, including Paramount+, are considering free streaming tiers to reach new viewers. Audiences have flocked to free services like Tubi and YouTube as streamers have raised prices.

Disney+ will livestream the Super Bowl in the US for the first time in mid-February, which the presentation called a major "tentpole" moment. Peacock, Paramount+, and Tubi have streamed Super Bowl coverage from NBC, CBS, and Fox, respectively.

The company's livestreaming priorities include "live 4K HDR, lower latency, scale, live event monitoring and live content security" to deliver the Big Game to millions of viewers in high-quality, lag-free picture, while protecting against piracy.

Disney+ and Hulu are joining forces

Disney is still working toward merging Hulu with Disney+, as part of a multi-phased plan known internally as "Project Gemini." The yearslong project of adding Hulu's content and features to Disney+ will "deepen engagement" and "increase lifetime fan value," D'Amaro said in August.

While the presentation didn't give a target date for the complete Hulu integration, its road map said "One App Milestones" are scheduled through Disney's fiscal fourth quarter, which runs from early July to early October. It's unclear what those milestones are, or what finishing them would mean. (Project Gemini had been scheduled to conclude by the end of 2026, Business Insider reported in May.)

Putting Hulu and Disney+ under one roof is part of Disney's plan to build a super app, where users can play games and buy merchandise without leaving the streamer. The company hopes that an interactive experience will increase time spent and make customers less likely to cancel, D'Amaro told employees in August, while shopping features could drive revenue to other parts of its business.

D'Amaro told employees in August that Disney planned to "introduce elements of this expanded ecosystem" in the spring.

items.title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
items.summary: Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That's the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets , including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories. The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the "Yes, and don't ask again" option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local ".claude/settings.local.json" file on the user's computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it. This isn't really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user's local machine (assuming that machine doesn't become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer's global .gitignore list , which usually prevents it from being shared publicly. items.title: Google Unveils TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx: A Dual-Chip TPU and a Confidential TPU
items.summary: Google has added two new systems to its eighth-generation TPU lineup. TPU 8i Max targets massive context windows and rack density. TPU 8tx targets secure, confidential inference. Google TPU 8i Max is a dual-chip package built from 2 TPU 8i chips. Both arrive alongside TPU 8t and TPU 8i, announced in April . TL;DR Size: TPU 8i Max = 2 TPU 8i chips in 1 package. TPU 8tx = TPU 8t silicon plus 5th Gen AMD EPYC hosts. Runs on: Google Cloud TPU systems. Performance: 8i Max doubles TPU 8i compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth. 8tx cuts latency up to 2x versus TPU 8t. Best: 2x the silicon in the existing rack footprint (TPU 8i Max). Worst: No absolute specs, benchmarks, prices or regions published for either system. What did Google announce? Google announced both systems today. These are new system configurations, not new chips. Google reuses its existing eighth-generation silicon and changes packaging, hosts, memory and networking around it. How does TPU 8i Max work? TPU 8i Max attacks the memory wall. Google team combines 2 low-latency TPU 8i chips onto 1 package. The result doubles compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth compared with TPU 8i. Each TPU 8i chip is rated at 10.1 PFLOPS of FP4, 288 GB of HBM and 8,601 GB/s . It also carries 384 MB of on-chip SRAM. Doubling those figures implies about 20.2 PFLOPS FP4, 768 MB SRAM and 17.2 TB/s per package. Google did not publish these absolute figures. It also did not state HBM capacity for TPU 8i Max. TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon in the existing rack footprint. Google positions it for agents working across whole codebases or hours of video. What makes TPU 8tx different? TPU 8tx is built for regulated enterprises and governments. It keeps data and model weights protected even while in active use. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory during processing. TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as TPU 8t . It pairs that silicon with 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU hosts. It also adopts the Boardfly network from TPU 8i. Google claims up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t, with a near-zero security penalty. Teams can fine-tune, distill and run reinforcement learning on 1 system. That avoids moving sensitive data between separate clusters. What changed in the TPU software stack? TorchTPU: Open-sourced last month , it runs PyTorch and Hugging Face models natively. vLLM and SGLang get TPU backends. TPU agent suite (preview): Plugs into Claude Code, Cursor and Antigravity for onboarding and kernel tuning. TPU Sync: An open-source C++ library that tiers KV cache across HBM, host DRAM and storage. Agent Compute Engine: Suspends idle agent sessions and moves working memory off-chip. Preview is targeted for the coming months. Cloud Pathways and GKE dynamic slicing: Both are now GA. Dynamic slicing cuts job startup up to 5x and speeds fault recovery up to 4.5x. On Qwen3 235B, TPU Sync dropped median KV transfer latency from several seconds to about 230 ms. TTFT fell 60% on average for 235B and 90% for 480B under low concurrency. These tests ran on Ironwood (TPU v7x), not the new systems. How do the numbers compare? Spec Google TPU 8i Max Google TPU 8tx NVIDIA Rubin GPU Microsoft Maia 200 AWS Trainium3 Role Long-context inference Confidential inference, small-scale training Training and inference Inference Training and inference Silicon 2x TPU 8i chips TPU 8t silicon Dual-die GPU TSMC 3nm TSMC 3nm Peak FP4 ~20.2 PFLOPS (derived) Not disclosed (TPU 8t: 12.6) 50 PFLOPS NVFP4 >10 PFLOPS Not disclosed (2.52 PFLOPS FP8) HBM capacity Not disclosed Not disclosed (TPU 8t: 216 GB) 288 GB HBM4 216 GB HBM3e 144 GB HBM3e HBM bandwidth ~17.2 TB/s (derived) Not disclosed (TPU 8t: 6.5 TB/s) 22 TB/s 7 TB/s 4.9 TB/s On-chip SRAM ~768 MB (derived) Not disclosed (TPU 8t: 128 MB) Not disclosed 272 MB Not disclosed Host CPU Not disclosed 5th Gen AMD EPYC NVIDIA Vera Not disclosed Not disclosed Availability 2027 ( Bloomberg via Quartz ) 2027 ( Bloomberg via Quartz ) H2 2026 volume production Announced Jan 2026 Trn3 announced Dec 2025 Derived = 2x Google’s published TPU 8i per-chip figures. TPU 8t values come from Google’s technical deep dive . & Key Takeaways TPU 8i Max puts 2 TPU 8i chips in 1 package. It doubles TPU 8i compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth. TPU 8tx brings confidential inference to TPU 8t silicon. TPU Sync cut KV transfer latency over 90% on Ironwood. Google has added two new systems to its eighth-generation TPU lineup. TPU 8i Max targets massive context windows and rack density. TPU 8tx targets secure, confidential inference. Google TPU 8i Max is a dual-chip package built from 2 TPU 8i chips. Both arrive alongside TPU 8t and TPU 8i, announced in April.

TL;DR
  • Size: TPU 8i Max = 2 TPU 8i chips in 1 package. TPU 8tx = TPU 8t silicon plus 5th Gen AMD EPYC hosts.
  • Runs on: Google Cloud TPU systems.
  • Performance: 8i Max doubles TPU 8i compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth. 8tx cuts latency up to 2x versus TPU 8t.
  • Best: 2x the silicon in the existing rack footprint (TPU 8i Max).
  • Worst: No absolute specs, benchmarks, prices or regions published for either system.
What did Google announce?

Google announced both systems today. These are new system configurations, not new chips. Google reuses its existing eighth-generation silicon and changes packaging, hosts, memory and networking around it.

How does TPU 8i Max work?

TPU 8i Max attacks the memory wall. Google team combines 2 low-latency TPU 8i chips onto 1 package. The result doubles compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth compared with TPU 8i.

Each TPU 8i chip is rated at 10.1 PFLOPS of FP4, 288 GB of HBM and 8,601 GB/s. It also carries 384 MB of on-chip SRAM. Doubling those figures implies about 20.2 PFLOPS FP4, 768 MB SRAM and 17.2 TB/s per package. Google did not publish these absolute figures. It also did not state HBM capacity for TPU 8i Max.

TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon in the existing rack footprint. Google positions it for agents working across whole codebases or hours of video.

What makes TPU 8tx different?

TPU 8tx is built for regulated enterprises and governments. It keeps data and model weights protected even while in active use. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory during processing.

TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as TPU 8t. It pairs that silicon with 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU hosts. It also adopts the Boardfly network from TPU 8i. Google claims up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t, with a near-zero security penalty.

Teams can fine-tune, distill and run reinforcement learning on 1 system. That avoids moving sensitive data between separate clusters.

What changed in the TPU software stack?
  • TorchTPU: Open-sourced last month, it runs PyTorch and Hugging Face models natively. vLLM and SGLang get TPU backends.
  • TPU agent suite (preview): Plugs into Claude Code, Cursor and Antigravity for onboarding and kernel tuning.
  • TPU Sync: An open-source C++ library that tiers KV cache across HBM, host DRAM and storage.
  • Agent Compute Engine: Suspends idle agent sessions and moves working memory off-chip. Preview is targeted for the coming months.
  • Cloud Pathways and GKE dynamic slicing: Both are now GA. Dynamic slicing cuts job startup up to 5x and speeds fault recovery up to 4.5x.

On Qwen3 235B, TPU Sync dropped median KV transfer latency from several seconds to about 230 ms. TTFT fell 60% on average for 235B and 90% for 480B under low concurrency. These tests ran on Ironwood (TPU v7x), not the new systems.

items.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
items.summary: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI. But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”

Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. 

Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. 

“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”

Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. 

He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says.

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says, laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”

Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides  some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”
