items.title: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
items.summary: By Shreya S Ramanujam , Yongce Li , Afshine Amidi , Sina Ghiassian , Benjamin Klein . Introduction Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen: If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode. A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything . “In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.” Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual . At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not. Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize: High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants. Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis. Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail ( “Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?” ) rises from 0.77 to 0.86 , and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~ 82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~ 69% ). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses. So, what exactly does factuality mean? Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Say you see this synopsis about Bridgerton Season 1: Synopsis A: “Bridgerton follows Daphne Bridgerton, the eldest daughter of the powerful Bridgerton family as she makes her debut onto Regency London’s competitive marriage market.” It’s easy to judge that this synopsis is factually correct — no wrong facts, and it gives the reader a clear, accurate glimpse of what to expect from the show. Let’s take another example: Synopsis B: “Set in modern-day London, this gritty crime drama follows Detective Daphne Bridgerton as she hunts a serial killer while hiding her own criminal past.” Another easy one — the plot is so blatantly off the mark that it is definitely not factual. But what about this? Synopsis C: “Bridgerton follows the mysterious, sharp-tongued Lady Whistledown as she exposes the secrets of London’s high society through her scandalous gossip sheet.” Technically, every statement here is true — Lady Whistledown does indeed publish a gossip sheet, and if there’s one thing she is known for, it’s her scathing exposés. So then, is this a factual synopsis? Not quite! While technically true, it paints a misleading picture of the show. A new viewer might reasonably expect it to revolve around Lady Whistledown, rather than Daphne navigating the marriage market. This, too, is a type of non-factuality we want to catch. Lastly, here’s the trickiest of all: Synopsis D: “When Daphne Bridgerton makes her society debut, she catches the eye of the aloof Duke of Hastings, and the two begin a passionate love affair that sets the whole ton abuzz.” Again, every statement is true, but the phrasing is misleading. A new viewer might assume they fall in love immediately, missing the fact that their relationship begins as a fake, mutually beneficial arrangement. This is another type of nuanced error our system should flag. So now that we have an idea of the kinds of errors we care about, the real question is: how do we build a system that is able to catch both glaring as well as subtle factuality violations? Current Service and Its Limitations Our current factuality pipeline is a straightforward, holistic LLM call. We feed a reasoning model everything we know about a title (text assets, metadata, and a detailed factuality rubric) and ask it to judge the factuality of a synopsis. We repeat the call several times to reduce output randomness, and if any run flags the synopsis as non-factual, it fails. This approach has two main limitations: High cost: Each judgment requires multiple (five, to be exact) calls to a large reasoning model over extremely long contexts (100k+ tokens), which does not scale well. Misaligned reasoning: The model can fail synopses for nitpicky reasons (e.g., “This is a show about wonderful magic” gets failed because the characters never literally call the magic “wonderful”) while overlooking nuanced errors by convincing itself they “don’t really make the synopsis false.” This misalignment makes verdicts less reliable and rationales less useful for downstream correction. Optimizing the Holistic Pipeline To understand exactly where we should optimize the current holistic pipeline, we study the current pipeline both qualitatively and quantitatively on a custom factuality benchmark that we built. This benchmark comprises synopses hand-labeled by human annotators as factual or non-factual, along with their rationales. This analysis reveals several key insights: Insight 1: Do we really need five holistic calls? Let’s think back to why we added multiple holistic calls in the first place: to reduce sampling noise. In practice, though, we see an interesting dichotomy: Blatantly true / false synopses (Bridgerton A, B): All runs agree on the verdict with near-identical reasoning. Nuanced errors (Bridgerton C, D): The model is much more likely to disagree with itself — some runs catch the error, some don’t. This is exactly where additional sampling helps. This suggests a simple optimization: A and B don’t really need all 5 calls. If we can somehow identify these “easy” synopses upfront, we can cut down on the number of calls for them, while still giving harder cases like C and D the extra calls they need. The easiest way to do this is to ask the model to output its confidence alongside its verdict and rationale. We can then separate “easy” (high confidence) synopses from “hard” (low confidence) ones and only send the hard cases through additional checks. Think of it like airport security: most bags go straight through, but those that trigger the alarm (low confidence) get extra screening. Implementing this easy fix makes our pipeline go from the current holistic model to a new “confidence gated” holistic model: Insight 2: Five identical judges calls give us no new information With confidence gating, our pipeline only escalates harder synopses to the full five holistic calls. But extra calls only help with sampling noise , not systematic reasoning errors: if every run follows the same flawed rationale, they’ll all reach the same wrong verdict, rendering the extra calls useless. How can we ensure that each call counts? Idea: Diversify the judges and make them specialized Instead of running five holistic judges with the same generic factuality prompt, we introduce two specialized judges that individually target the two aspects of factuality we care about: Literal Judge: Is the synopsis literally true? Implicature Judge: Does this synopsis give a false picture to a new reader who has not watched this show? Explicitly searching for specific types of errors helps us better flag both literal and subtler implicature errors. In practice, we observe that this works better than repeatedly querying a single holistic judge, hoping that sampling stochasticity will surface nuanced errors. Insight 3: The rationale reveals mistakes the verdict hid At this point, we have a pretty good pipeline, but we’re still underusing one of the richest signals available to us: the model’s rationale behind its verdict. For nuanced errors, we often see the model identify a point of contention, then brush it aside based on a faulty assumption or because it deems the issue too minor to affect the verdict. Can we use these shaky spots in the rationale to catch (and correct) errors the verdict misses? Idea: Secondary atomic-claim checking via a router : Since our literal and implicature judges are already strong reasoning models, we ask them to additionally critically analyse their own reasoning and surface shaky spots — any doubts, concessions, or assumptions that might need rechecking. These include cases where the model: Makes an assumption. Raises a doubt that the available evidence can’t resolve (e.g., an external critic quote). Notices a contradiction but dismisses it as insufficient to change the verdict. We pass all concessions from both judges to a router model, which: Reframes them as self-contained, verifiable atomic claims, each with a materiality field specifying the evidence needed to support or refute it. Routes each claim to the appropriate secondary Stage-2 judge: a web judge for external facts (e.g., citations, media quotes, or prior work), or a source-material recheck focused on the reframed atomic claim. By pinpointing the exact point of contention, the recheck is more targeted, making it easier to mark the claim as true or false. Putting It All Together: Proposed Cascade Factuality Service Our findings lead to three key improvements: specialized judges, confidence-gated escalation, and targeted rechecking of shaky reasoning using a secondary stage when escalated. We implement these improvements as a tiered system shown in the figure below: every synopsis first passes through both the literal and the implicature judges. High-confidence verdicts are retained, while low-confidence cases escalate to the router and Stage-2 judges for further checking. Stage 2 can overturn the initial verdict in two cases: FAIL → PASS: All concessions, including the original failure reasons, are supported by the secondary check. PASS → FAIL: At least one concession is contradicted. Results Based on our discussions from above, we evaluate three different pipelines: Evaluation: Datasets and Metrics We evaluate these systems on two datasets: show-level and episode-level synopses. Each datapoint includes a synopsis, a human gold label (factual / not factual), and the annotator’s rationale. For episode-level synopses, we additionally require that the synopsis be specific to that particular episode, not just a generic synopsis of the overall show. We focus on two main axes: Quality and Cost. The quality metrics are listed below: Recall-FAIL is our primary metric: higher recall means fewer Gold FAILs are missed. We also track Precision-PASS, which measures how reliably PASS verdicts identify Gold PASSes, and alignment with human rationales. On the cost side, we want to reduce both the average number of LLM calls per synopsis and the end-to-end cost of producing a final verdict. Latency is not our primary optimization target, but we do want to ensure the median (P50) latency does not blow up to impractical judgement times. Evaluation Results The best numbers per metric per dataset are shown in bold. Note: We compared the cascade against two holistic ablations — increased reasoning effort and a smaller, cheaper model — to test if simple ablations could achieve better performance. For episode-level synopses, we also added a full-show summary to the prompt to provide context from previous episodes; we observe summaries substantially improve performance when compared to non-summary context variants, so we report only summary-based variants. Our takeaways from this experiment are: Cascade improves quality. Our primary metric, Recall-FAIL improves on both show and episode level synopses, with a limited impact on Recall-PASS. In other words, we now catch more Gold FAIL synopses without sacrificing the reliability of our PASS verdicts. Cascade is cheaper. Cascade cuts total cost by 52.4% on the show-level dataset. Cascade (with summary) is also 15% cheaper than the current (no summary) holistic pipeline on episodic dataset. Cascade’s P50 latency increases with respect to the holistic baseline. Even so, this remains within what we consider a reasonable range for factuality judgment. Simple tweaks aren’t enough. Increasing reasoning effort makes the factuality checker too lenient, while using a smaller model makes it too strict — neither addresses the underlying problems of the holistic baseline. Summary context matters for episodic tasks. Without a full-show summary, the model tends to over-fail because it lacks the context to determine whether a detail from the episode summary fits the broader storyline. Alignment with Human Rationale So far, we’ve established that the cascade produces better verdicts: it catches more non-factual synopses and produces more reliable PASS decisions. But are these verdicts correct for the right reasons ? To measure this, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge to compare each pipeline’s reasoning against the human rationale on Gold-FAIL (GF) synopses. The judge assigns a Reasoning Similarity Score (RSS) of 0 (dissimilar), 0.5 (partially similar), or 1 (very similar) based on rationale overlap. We observe that cascade is significantly better aligned with human rationale in all cases. This is a big gain — not only is the cascade giving us more accurate factuality verdicts, but it also identifies the same points of contention in the synopsis as a specialized human annotator. Conclusion + Future Work Overall, our proposed cascade pipeline improves both cost and quality of the existing factuality service: On the cost side, confidence gating lets us avoid unnecessary calls, reducing the average cost of factuality evaluation. On the quality side, two diverse judges allow us to collect complementary informative verdicts, while the Stage-2 judges recheck and correct the assumptions behind uncertain decisions. This results in higher verdict accuracy and substantially better alignment between model and expert annotator reasoning. The cascade gives us a path toward a factuality system that is not just more accurate, but also more interpretable and self-correcting . Some future directions to consider would be: Adding multimodal inputs to help verify claims that text assets alone cannot confirm. Use the rationale from factuality checking to correct the faulty synopsis. Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Lastly, here’s the trickiest of all:

Synopsis D: “When Daphne Bridgerton makes her society debut, she catches the eye of the aloof Duke of Hastings, and the two begin a passionate love affair that sets the whole ton abuzz.”

Again, every statement is true, but the phrasing is misleading. A new viewer might assume they fall in love immediately, missing the fact that their relationship begins as a fake, mutually beneficial arrangement. This is another type of nuanced error our system should flag.

So now that we have an idea of the kinds of errors we care about, the real question is: how do we build a system that is able to catch both glaring as well as subtle factuality violations?

Current Service and Its Limitations

Our current factuality pipeline is a straightforward, holistic LLM call. We feed a reasoning model everything we know about a title (text assets, metadata, and a detailed factuality rubric) and ask it to judge the factuality of a synopsis. We repeat the call several times to reduce output randomness, and if any run flags the synopsis as non-factual, it fails. This approach has two main limitations:

  1. High cost: Each judgment requires multiple (five, to be exact) calls to a large reasoning model over extremely long contexts (100k+ tokens), which does not scale well.
  2. Misaligned reasoning: The model can fail synopses for nitpicky reasons (e.g., “This is a show about wonderful magic” gets failed because the characters never literally call the magic “wonderful”) while overlooking nuanced errors by convincing itself they “don’t really make the synopsis false.” This misalignment makes verdicts less reliable and rationales less useful for downstream correction.
Optimizing the Holistic Pipeline

To understand exactly where we should optimize the current holistic pipeline, we study the current pipeline both qualitatively and quantitatively on a custom factuality benchmark that we built. This benchmark comprises synopses hand-labeled by human annotators as factual or non-factual, along with their rationales. This analysis reveals several key insights:

Insight 1: Do we really need five holistic calls?

Let’s think back to why we added multiple holistic calls in the first place: to reduce sampling noise. In practice, though, we see an interesting dichotomy:

  • Blatantly true / false synopses (Bridgerton A, B): All runs agree on the verdict with near-identical reasoning.
  • Nuanced errors (Bridgerton C, D): The model is much more likely to disagree with itself — some runs catch the error, some don’t. This is exactly where additional sampling helps.

This suggests a simple optimization: A and B don’t really need all 5 calls. If we can somehow identify these “easy” synopses upfront, we can cut down on the number of calls for them, while still giving harder cases like C and D the extra calls they need.

The easiest way to do this is to ask the model to output its confidence alongside its verdict and rationale. We can then separate “easy” (high confidence) synopses from “hard” (low confidence) ones and only send the hard cases through additional checks. Think of it like airport security: most bags go straight through, but those that trigger the alarm (low confidence) get extra screening.

Implementing this easy fix makes our pipeline go from the current holistic model to a new “confidence gated” holistic model:

Insight 2: Five identical judges calls give us no new information

With confidence gating, our pipeline only escalates harder synopses to the full five holistic calls. But extra calls only help with sampling noise, not systematic reasoning errors: if every run follows the same flawed rationale, they’ll all reach the same wrong verdict, rendering the extra calls useless. How can we ensure that each call counts?

Idea: Diversify the judges and make them specialized

Instead of running five holistic judges with the same generic factuality prompt, we introduce two specialized judges that individually target the two aspects of factuality we care about:

  • Literal Judge: Is the synopsis literally true?
  • Implicature Judge: Does this synopsis give a false picture to a new reader who has not watched this show?

Explicitly searching for specific types of errors helps us better flag both literal and subtler implicature errors. In practice, we observe that this works better than repeatedly querying a single holistic judge, hoping that sampling stochasticity will surface nuanced errors.

Insight 3: The rationale reveals mistakes the verdict hid

At this point, we have a pretty good pipeline, but we’re still underusing one of the richest signals available to us: the model’s rationale behind its verdict. For nuanced errors, we often see the model identify a point of contention, then brush it aside based on a faulty assumption or because it deems the issue too minor to affect the verdict. Can we use these shaky spots in the rationale to catch (and correct) errors the verdict misses?

Idea: Secondary atomic-claim checking via a router:

Since our literal and implicature judges are already strong reasoning models, we ask them to additionally critically analyse their own reasoning and surface shaky spots — any doubts, concessions, or assumptions that might need rechecking. These include cases where the model:

  • Makes an assumption.
  • Raises a doubt that the available evidence can’t resolve (e.g., an external critic quote).
  • Notices a contradiction but dismisses it as insufficient to change the verdict.

We pass all concessions from both judges to a router model, which:

  1. Reframes them as self-contained, verifiable atomic claims, each with a materiality field specifying the evidence needed to support or refute it.
  2. Routes each claim to the appropriate secondary Stage-2 judge: a web judge for external facts (e.g., citations, media quotes, or prior work), or a source-material recheck focused on the reframed atomic claim. By pinpointing the exact point of contention, the recheck is more targeted, making it easier to mark the claim as true or false.
Putting It All Together: Proposed Cascade Factuality Service

Our findings lead to three key improvements: specialized judges, confidence-gated escalation, and targeted rechecking of shaky reasoning using a secondary stage when escalated.

We implement these improvements as a tiered system shown in the figure below: every synopsis first passes through both the literal and the implicature judges. High-confidence verdicts are retained, while low-confidence cases escalate to the router and Stage-2 judges for further checking. Stage 2 can overturn the initial verdict in two cases:

  • FAIL → PASS: All concessions, including the original failure reasons, are supported by the secondary check.
  • PASS → FAIL: At least one concession is contradicted.
Results

Based on our discussions from above, we evaluate three different pipelines:

Evaluation: Datasets and Metrics

We evaluate these systems on two datasets: show-level and episode-level synopses. Each datapoint includes a synopsis, a human gold label (factual / not factual), and the annotator’s rationale. For episode-level synopses, we additionally require that the synopsis be specific to that particular episode, not just a generic synopsis of the overall show.

We focus on two main axes: Quality and Cost. The quality metrics are listed below:

Recall-FAIL is our primary metric: higher recall means fewer Gold FAILs are missed. We also track Precision-PASS, which measures how reliably PASS verdicts identify Gold PASSes, and alignment with human rationales.

On the cost side, we want to reduce both the average number of LLM calls per synopsis and the end-to-end cost of producing a final verdict. Latency is not our primary optimization target, but we do want to ensure the median (P50) latency does not blow up to impractical judgement times.

Evaluation Results

The best numbers per metric per dataset are shown in bold.

Note: We compared the cascade against two holistic ablations — increased reasoning effort and a smaller, cheaper model — to test if simple ablations could achieve better performance. For episode-level synopses, we also added a full-show summary to the prompt to provide context from previous episodes; we observe summaries substantially improve performance when compared to non-summary context variants, so we report only summary-based variants.

Our takeaways from this experiment are:

  • Cascade improves quality. Our primary metric, Recall-FAIL improves on both show and episode level synopses, with a limited impact on Recall-PASS. In other words, we now catch more Gold FAIL synopses without sacrificing the reliability of our PASS verdicts.
  • Cascade is cheaper. Cascade cuts total cost by 52.4% on the show-level dataset. Cascade (with summary) is also 15% cheaper than the current (no summary) holistic pipeline on episodic dataset.
  • Cascade’s P50 latency increases with respect to the holistic baseline. Even so, this remains within what we consider a reasonable range for factuality judgment.
  • Simple tweaks aren’t enough. Increasing reasoning effort makes the factuality checker too lenient, while using a smaller model makes it too strict — neither addresses the underlying problems of the holistic baseline.
  • Summary context matters for episodic tasks. Without a full-show summary, the model tends to over-fail because it lacks the context to determine whether a detail from the episode summary fits the broader storyline.
Alignment with Human Rationale

So far, we’ve established that the cascade produces better verdicts: it catches more non-factual synopses and produces more reliable PASS decisions. But are these verdicts correct for the right reasons?

To measure this, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge to compare each pipeline’s reasoning against the human rationale on Gold-FAIL (GF) synopses. The judge assigns a Reasoning Similarity Score (RSS) of 0 (dissimilar), 0.5 (partially similar), or 1 (very similar) based on rationale overlap.

We observe that cascade is significantly better aligned with human rationale in all cases. This is a big gain — not only is the cascade giving us more accurate factuality verdicts, but it also identifies the same points of contention in the synopsis as a specialized human annotator.

Conclusion + Future Work

Overall, our proposed cascade pipeline improves both cost and quality of the existing factuality service:

  • On the cost side, confidence gating lets us avoid unnecessary calls, reducing the average cost of factuality evaluation.
  • On the quality side, two diverse judges allow us to collect complementary informative verdicts, while the Stage-2 judges recheck and correct the assumptions behind uncertain decisions. This results in higher verdict accuracy and substantially better alignment between model and expert annotator reasoning.

The cascade gives us a path toward a factuality system that is not just more accurate, but also more interpretable and self-correcting. Some future directions to consider would be:

  • Adding multimodal inputs to help verify claims that text assets alone cannot confirm.
  • Use the rationale from factuality checking to correct the faulty synopsis.

Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Elon Musk predicts a future of abundance where, if you 'wish for a castle,' AI will build it for you
items.summary: Elon Musk says AI will be able to build a castle for anyone who wants one. Mark Schiefelbein/AP Elon Musk envisions a world where anyone can "wish for a castle," and AI will make it for them. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO also predicted "extremely high income" and amazing healthcare for all. Musk spoke about productivity gains from AI and robots, and responded to data center backlash. A world where everyone gets a castle sounds like Oprah wrote a fairy tale. Elon Musk says that's what the future holds thanks to AI. "Super intelligence will saturate all human needs by far," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO said by webcast at Baron Capital's annual conference on Friday. "You could wish for a castle, or whatever you want basically, and the digital superintelligence can make it for you as a side project," he added. There will also be "universal extremely high income," and " universal medical care that is better than the best medical care available on Earth today," Musk said. The world's richest man has repeatedly predicted that advances in AI, robotics, and energy will slash costs, supercharge productivity, and boost economic growth. He's suggested that could usher in an age of abundance where goods and services are no longer scarce, money ceases to matter , and "everyone can have a penthouse if they want." Actually, AI/Robotics will mean everyone can have a penthouse if they want. The output of goods & services will be several orders of magnitude higher than today’s economy. Read the Iain Banks Culture books for the best imagining of how it will be. That said, what is the future you want? Amazing abundance seems the best to me. — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) April 18, 2026 Speaking to Ron Baron, one of his biggest shareholders and most steadfast supporters, Musk said tech advances will enable humans to harness so much energy that it will "completely saturate anything anyone could ever wish for on Earth." Describing the superintelligence era, he said: "Our economy will seem quaint, and our money system will seem like exchanging seashells for currency ." Musk predicted that digital superintelligence will rapidly expand the global economy by 20% to 30% as it promises to "double the productivity of white-collar work." He also envisioned humanoid robots being five times as productive as people. They'll work faster, he said, and can be on the job 24/7 as they don't "take vacation, or bathroom breaks, or need to eat food, or anything like that." He estimated that 20 million to 30 million robots could match the current output of working Americans. During the conversation, Musk addressed the public backlash to the data centers powering the AI boom, which has centered on the water and power they consume and the noise they make. He said that Memphis is " booming " because of SpaceX's presence there. "The restaurants are full, the hotels are full. We're paying at times twice the prevailing wage that people were earning before," Musk said. "We've also helped out with local schools, and the tax revenue that the county and the city are earning is tremendous." Musk has faced intense skepticism over his past claims of future abundance, particularly his recommendation that people stop saving for retirement because their wealth will be "irrelevant," and his proposal of government checks for all as the best response to job losses from AI. Several of his peers have made similar projections. Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates recently said AI will usher in " true abundance ," and robots will be able to "build houses, grow food, do surgery." But Gates also warned the 20-year transition to get there will be hugely "tumultuous," as people won't be needed to make most goods and services. Similarly, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said AI promises to "raise the quality of life for everyone," but there will be "unprecedented" disruption before it does. Read the original article on Business Insider

A world where everyone gets a castle sounds like Oprah wrote a fairy tale. Elon Musk says that's what the future holds thanks to AI.

"Super intelligence will saturate all human needs by far," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO said by webcast at Baron Capital's annual conference on Friday.

"You could wish for a castle, or whatever you want basically, and the digital superintelligence can make it for you as a side project," he added.

There will also be "universal extremely high income," and "universal medical care that is better than the best medical care available on Earth today," Musk said.

The world's richest man has repeatedly predicted that advances in AI, robotics, and energy will slash costs, supercharge productivity, and boost economic growth.

He's suggested that could usher in an age of abundance where goods and services are no longer scarce, money ceases to matter, and "everyone can have a penthouse if they want."

Actually, AI/Robotics will mean everyone can have a penthouse if they want. The output of goods & services will be several orders of magnitude higher than today’s economy. Read the Iain Banks Culture books for the best imagining of how it will be. That said, what is the future you want? Amazing abundance seems the best to me.

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) April 18, 2026

Speaking to Ron Baron, one of his biggest shareholders and most steadfast supporters, Musk said tech advances will enable humans to harness so much energy that it will "completely saturate anything anyone could ever wish for on Earth."

Describing the superintelligence era, he said: "Our economy will seem quaint, and our money system will seem like exchanging seashells for currency."

Musk predicted that digital superintelligence will rapidly expand the global economy by 20% to 30% as it promises to "double the productivity of white-collar work."

He also envisioned humanoid robots being five times as productive as people. They'll work faster, he said, and can be on the job 24/7 as they don't "take vacation, or bathroom breaks, or need to eat food, or anything like that." He estimated that 20 million to 30 million robots could match the current output of working Americans.

During the conversation, Musk addressed the public backlash to the data centers powering the AI boom, which has centered on the water and power they consume and the noise they make. He said that Memphis is "booming" because of SpaceX's presence there.

"The restaurants are full, the hotels are full. We're paying at times twice the prevailing wage that people were earning before," Musk said. "We've also helped out with local schools, and the tax revenue that the county and the city are earning is tremendous."

Musk has faced intense skepticism over his past claims of future abundance, particularly his recommendation that people stop saving for retirement because their wealth will be "irrelevant," and his proposal of government checks for all as the best response to job losses from AI.

Several of his peers have made similar projections. Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates recently said AI will usher in "true abundance," and robots will be able to "build houses, grow food, do surgery."

But Gates also warned the 20-year transition to get there will be hugely "tumultuous," as people won't be needed to make most goods and services.

Similarly, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said AI promises to "raise the quality of life for everyone," but there will be "unprecedented" disruption before it does.

items.title: Baidu’s ERNIE Evolve Automated Research System Beats NanoChat and NanoGPT Records
items.summary: Baidu has just released ERNIE Evolve , an automated research system that improves AI training and inference code. Given a repository, an objective and evaluation criteria, it picks research directions, edits code and runs experiments. Only changes that pass a hidden evaluator and a separate reviewer are kept. Baidu team tested the ERNIE Evolve automated research system on three public benchmarks. It then optimized inference for ERNIE-5.5-Flash, still in development. TL;DR Size: It is an agent system; Baidu has not disclosed which LLMs power its agents. Runs on: Benchmarks used 1 NVIDIA B200 (NanoChat, SOL-ExecBench) and 8×H100 (Speedrun Track 1). Production tests ran on Kunlunxin P800 and GPUs (GPU model not disclosed). Performance: Beat the best public result on 3 of 4 public metrics, and cleared production checks on ERNIE-5.5-Flash. Best: Generation speed on Kunlunxin P800 reached 623.6% of baseline after 4 research rounds. Worst: SOL-ExecBench mean SOL of 0.819, behind the 0.827 leaderboard best. Bottom line (best): Real production inference gains: +33.7% deterministic throughput, +14.9% decode speed. Bottom line (worst): Self-reported, system not released, and public-benchmark margins are small. What is ERNIE Evolve? ERNIE Evolve is an automated research system from Baidu that optimizes code against a fixed, measurable objective. Baidu announced it on X as a practical step toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). In RSI, AI systems improve the software that builds and serves AI. How does ERNIE Evolve work? The system runs 2 nested loops. The outer loop decides what to investigate. The inner loop develops and tests improvements inside each direction. Director: picks the next research direction and a starting code version. It reads an Experience Bank of past results and a Knowledge Base of papers and code. Selector: chooses a candidate from a lane’s tree and names the next hypothesis to test. Executor: implements that plan in an isolated environment. Evaluator: a fixed program kept outside the repository. No agent can see it. Gains must exceed the noise threshold. Reviewer: checks whether a change follows the intended direction or exploits an evaluation loophole. Several research lanes run in parallel, each with its own tree of code versions. Failed experiments are recorded, so later rounds can avoid repeating them. How did ERNIE Evolve score on public benchmarks? Baidu ran the same loop on NanoChat AutoResearch , NanoGPT Speedrun and SOL-ExecBench . NanoChat AutoResearch: 0.8763 validation BPB within a 5-minute, single-GPU budget. It added an n-gram branch and a document-retrieval branch beside the network, mixed by a learned gate. NanoGPT Speedrun Track 1: 38.9 s to target loss on 8×H100, versus the 39.9 s record. The results repo reports 38.92 s over 18 runs. NanoGPT Speedrun Track 3: 2,590 steps, versus 2,690. It decomposed weights into direction and magnitude, then added EMA-Nesterov extrapolation. SOL-ExecBench: 0.819 mean SOL across 235 kernel problems on B200, short of the 0.827 leader. ERNIE Evolve vs other automated research systems Metrics ERNIE Evolve (Baidu) Recursive Hyra-1.0 (Tencent Hunyuan) (auto)²-research (rekursiv.ai) NanoChat val BPB ↓ 0.8763 0.9109 0.9015 0.8878 Speedrun Track 1 ↓ 38.9 s 77.5 s 76.4 s Not reported Speedrun Track 3 ↓ 2,590 steps Not reported Not reported Not reported SOL-ExecBench, self-reported ↑ 0.819 0.754 0.771 Not reported SOL-ExecBench, per Baidu (Eval Stack v1.1) ↑ 0.819 0.676 0.736 Not reported Production use reported ERNIE-5.5-Flash inference Not disclosed Science tasks (math, molecules) Not disclosed What is released Final code + logs Run artifacts Results repo Recipe + harness tools Recursive and Hyra-1.0 Speedrun times were set against the older ~79.7 s record, so they are not like-for-like. Hyra SOL self-report via Tencent coverage . && What did ERNIE Evolve do for ERNIE-5.5-Flash inference? Baidu team then pointed the system at 3 live engineering tasks on ERNIE-5.5-Flash. Baselines had already been tuned by engineers. Low latency on Kunlunxin P800: generation speed rose to 623.6% of baseline over 4 rounds. Round 1 enabled fused mHC and speculative decoding via the model’s multi-token prediction layer (282.9%). Round 2 cut host-side overhead (588.8%). Round 4 fixed dispatch so DeepEP’s low-latency path engaged. Deterministic inference for RL: under SGLang’s deterministic mode, throughput rose 33.7% in about 3 days. Time per output token fell 26% and time to first token fell 12%. A Triton kernel for deterministic sampling, which used about 14% of GPU time, gave the largest single gain. Single-request decoding on GPUs: speed rose 14.9% with accuracy unchanged. 3 of 7 research directions produced gains. Key changes: FP16 instructions for tiny FP8 matmuls and a 2-level MoE expert scheduler. Key Takeaways Two nested loops: a Director picks directions, lanes evolve code trees. A hidden Evaluator plus a Reviewer guards against reward hacking. Public wins on NanoChat (0.8763 BPB) and Speedrun (38.9 s, 2,590 steps). ERNIE-5.5-Flash: 623.6% speed on Kunlunxin P800, +33.7% deterministic throughput. System stays closed; only results and logs are on GitHub. Check out the ERNIE Evolve research post and the results repo on GitHub . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. Need to partner with us for promoting your GitHub Repo OR Hugging Face Page OR Product Release OR Webinar etc.? Connect with us

  • Best: Generation speed on Kunlunxin P800 reached 623.6% of baseline after 4 research rounds.
  • Worst: SOL-ExecBench mean SOL of 0.819, behind the 0.827 leaderboard best.
  • Bottom line (best): Real production inference gains: +33.7% deterministic throughput, +14.9% decode speed.
  • Bottom line (worst): Self-reported, system not released, and public-benchmark margins are small.
What is ERNIE Evolve?

ERNIE Evolve is an automated research system from Baidu that optimizes code against a fixed, measurable objective. Baidu announced it on X as a practical step toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). In RSI, AI systems improve the software that builds and serves AI.

How does ERNIE Evolve work?

The system runs 2 nested loops. The outer loop decides what to investigate. The inner loop develops and tests improvements inside each direction.

  • Director: picks the next research direction and a starting code version. It reads an Experience Bank of past results and a Knowledge Base of papers and code.
  • Selector: chooses a candidate from a lane’s tree and names the next hypothesis to test.
  • Executor: implements that plan in an isolated environment.
  • Evaluator: a fixed program kept outside the repository. No agent can see it. Gains must exceed the noise threshold.
  • Reviewer: checks whether a change follows the intended direction or exploits an evaluation loophole.

Several research lanes run in parallel, each with its own tree of code versions. Failed experiments are recorded, so later rounds can avoid repeating them.

How did ERNIE Evolve score on public benchmarks?

Baidu ran the same loop on NanoChat AutoResearch, NanoGPT Speedrun and SOL-ExecBench.

  • NanoChat AutoResearch: 0.8763 validation BPB within a 5-minute, single-GPU budget. It added an n-gram branch and a document-retrieval branch beside the network, mixed by a learned gate.
  • NanoGPT Speedrun Track 1: 38.9 s to target loss on 8×H100, versus the 39.9 s record. The results repo reports 38.92 s over 18 runs.
  • NanoGPT Speedrun Track 3: 2,590 steps, versus 2,690. It decomposed weights into direction and magnitude, then added EMA-Nesterov extrapolation.
  • SOL-ExecBench: 0.819 mean SOL across 235 kernel problems on B200, short of the 0.827 leader.
ERNIE Evolve vs other automated research systems MetricsERNIE Evolve (Baidu)RecursiveHyra-1.0 (Tencent Hunyuan)(auto)²-research (rekursiv.ai)NanoChat val BPB ↓0.87630.91090.90150.8878Speedrun Track 1 ↓38.9 s77.5 s76.4 sNot reportedSpeedrun Track 3 ↓2,590 stepsNot reportedNot reportedNot reportedSOL-ExecBench, self-reported ↑0.8190.7540.771Not reportedSOL-ExecBench, per Baidu (Eval Stack v1.1) ↑0.8190.6760.736Not reportedProduction use reportedERNIE-5.5-Flash inferenceNot disclosedScience tasks (math, molecules)Not disclosedWhat is releasedFinal code + logsRun artifactsResults repoRecipe + harness tools

Recursive and Hyra-1.0 Speedrun times were set against the older ~79.7 s record, so they are not like-for-like. Hyra SOL self-report via Tencent coverage.

&&

What did ERNIE Evolve do for ERNIE-5.5-Flash inference?

Baidu team then pointed the system at 3 live engineering tasks on ERNIE-5.5-Flash. Baselines had already been tuned by engineers.

  • Low latency on Kunlunxin P800: generation speed rose to 623.6% of baseline over 4 rounds. Round 1 enabled fused mHC and speculative decoding via the model’s multi-token prediction layer (282.9%). Round 2 cut host-side overhead (588.8%). Round 4 fixed dispatch so DeepEP’s low-latency path engaged.
  • Deterministic inference for RL: under SGLang’s deterministic mode, throughput rose 33.7% in about 3 days. Time per output token fell 26% and time to first token fell 12%. A Triton kernel for deterministic sampling, which used about 14% of GPU time, gave the largest single gain.
  • Single-request decoding on GPUs: speed rose 14.9% with accuracy unchanged. 3 of 7 research directions produced gains. Key changes: FP16 instructions for tiny FP8 matmuls and a 2-level MoE expert scheduler.
Key Takeaways
  • Two nested loops: a Director picks directions, lanes evolve code trees.
  • A hidden Evaluator plus a Reviewer guards against reward hacking.
  • Public wins on NanoChat (0.8763 BPB) and Speedrun (38.9 s, 2,590 steps).
  • ERNIE-5.5-Flash: 623.6% speed on Kunlunxin P800, +33.7% deterministic throughput.
  • System stays closed; only results and logs are on GitHub.

items.title: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
items.summary: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust. How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur? An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system. There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals? Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform. Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration. The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents. Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability. Does true zero-trust architecture exist? The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist? Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub , we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system. We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted. But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component? References Wickremasinghe G, Sandjaja FR, Rafferty K, Sharma V. State-verification in asynchronous blockchain-driven agentic AI systems. 40th International Conference on Information Networking (ICOIN) 2026 Jan 14 (pp. 139-144). IEEE. Sandjaja, F. R., Abdul Majeed, A., Abdullah, A., Wickremasinghe, G., Rafferty, K., & Sharma, V. (Accepted/In press). Policy design in zero-trust distributed networks: challenges and solutions. In Industrial Networks and Intelligent Systems: 12th EAI International Conference, INISCOM 2026: (to appear in proceedings). Melis M, Del Rincon JM, Sharma V. Improving Certified Robustness via Adversarial Distillation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2606.31653. 2026 Jun 30 (Accepted to appear in BMVC’26).

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur?

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

Does true zero-trust architecture exist?

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

items.summary_html:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Kent Nishimura/Reuters

  • An internal list shows Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's 36 direct reports.
  • Huang is known for having many direct reports and said he had 55 last year.
  • Huang has previously said that having more direct reports helps with information flow.

Editor's note: In November 2026, Nvidia's board announced it was initiating an investigation after recent reporting that CEO Jensen Huang had been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." He also admitted to having an affair. A spokesperson said that Huang is "committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption."

It's unclear what will happen to his role as a result of this investigation. Huang is known for having more direct reports compared to other tech leaders. Here's what Business Insider previously reported in October 2025 about his org chart.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had 36 direct reports as of October 2025, according to an internal list obtained by Business Insider. Nvidia's top leadership team has seen some executive departures, including Jay Puri and Laura Fay, since then, though this list offers a glimpse into the inner circle at the top of the world's most valuable company.

Huang is known for having more direct reports compared to other tech leaders. Previously, in an interview at Stanford in March 2024, Huang said he had 55 direct reports, adding that many were paid the same amount.

Huang has 36 direct reports as of October 2025, according to an internal list obtained by Business Insider. Nvidia's top leadership team may have seen some executive changes since then, though this list offers a glimpse into the inner circle at the top of the world's most valuable company.

Some of the executives reporting to Huang, according to the list, include Ian Buck, the architect behind Nvidia's breakthrough software Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA), as well as CTO Michael Kagan and chief scientist Bill Dally.

"The more direct reports the CEO has, the less layers are in the company," Huang said at The New York Times DealBook Summit in 2023. "It allows us to keep information fluid, allows us to make sure that everyone is empowered by information."

Nvidia's workforce has grown massively in recent years thanks to the AI boom, and Huang's notoriously fierce work ethic has helped shape its hardcore culture.

It's unknown whether Huang's smaller fleet of direct reports signals a shift away from the horizontal structure.

Tech leaders have varying views on direct reports. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said he prefers not to have too many and instead runs the social media giant with a "core army" of 30 lieutenants —not all of whom he manages directly. CEO Elon Musk has 19 direct reports at Tesla as of August, and five at xAI.

A Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment.

Huang also said at Stanford that he doesn't schedule one-on-one meetings with direct reports so that information can spread more easily throughout the organization — unless a meeting is requested, in which case he'll "drop everything."

items.title: SpaceX now fundamentally an "infrastructure company," senior official says
items.summary: For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with the development of newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence. At last week's UP.Summit conference in Florida, the vice president of launch at SpaceX, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company's changing focus, how it is embracing AI, and why the Falcon 9 rocket—which has dominated global launch for a decade and remains the world's preeminent launch vehicle—is firmly on the road to retirement. "In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point," Dontchev said. "We're building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars." Read full article Comments
