“I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote in a memo. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.”

While infidelity among the obscenely rich isn’t in itself surprising, his affair could have major ripple effects on the entire economy — which has become massively dependent on the fate of the AI industry.

Shares of the chipmaker fell a stunning eight percent when trading resumed Monday morning — but then greed kicked in, with the stock rebounding to a loss of around four percent. Nvidia’s investigation into the affair clearly has investors rattled, though, and likely worried that Huang could lose control of one of the most valuable companies in the world, so expect a wild ride as the market grapples with exactly how bad the scandal actually is.

The woman Huang was involved with is Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang — no relation; it’s common last name — who has been accused of passing sensitive information to Beijing, Reuters reports. (The Chinese government has since described the narrative as “purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear.”)

Huang holds a roughly 3.6 percent stake in Nvidia, making him the fifth-largest shareholder. Nonetheless, he has ruled the chipmaker with an iron first, with dozens of executives reporting directly to him, per Reuters.

The timing of the revelation couldn’t have been worse. As last week’s midterm elections proved, the AI industry has an enormous PR problem and is struggling to convince voters of the tech’s benefits.

“The market’s probably telling you now this does no favors to the stock whatsoever in a time when there’s a lot of conjecture as to the buildout of data centres,” Pepperstone head of research Chris Weston told Reuters.

Fellow billionaires have since come to Huang’s defense, with Tesla CEO Elon Musk agreeing with a post on his social media platform that his actions were “dumb” but that he was “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”

President Donald Trump, who himself has a lengthy history of facing infidelity and sexual assault accusations, tried to downplay the severity of Huang’s actions, a revelation that would’ve once buried any executive’s chances of saving face.

“I hope everything’s fine,” Trump told reporters on Sunday. “He’s done such an incredible job.”

items.title: The Ninety Percent Problem: Unlocking Value in Unstructured Data for Enterprises
items.summary: Enterprises spent two decades perfecting their structured data. AI just made the other eighty to ninety percent – the messy, noisy, uncatalogued majority – the biggest prize in the building. Most companies cannot even tell you what they own. For twenty years, the corporate data story has been a story about tables. Rows, columns, schemas, warehouses. Chief data officers built careers, and vendors built empires, on the disciplined organization of structured data: transactions, ledgers, customer records. It was expensive, it was precise, and it was, broadly, the right call. It was also only ever a fraction of the story. The uncomfortable truth, familiar to anyone who has run a data audit at a large financial institution, is that somewhere between 80 and 90 percent of enterprise data is unstructured: contracts, emails, call recordings, loan files, PDFs scanned in 2004 and never opened since. Until recently, this did not matter much, because no economically viable technology could read it at scale. Compliance said keep it; economics said ignore it. So enterprises did both, for decades, at petabyte scale. Generative AI has just inverted that equation, and the market has been slow to price in what that means. Speaking at LangChain’s Interrupt conference in June 2026 [1] , Andrew Ng, who has advised Fortune 50 boards through his firm and has seen more enterprise AI programs up close than almost anyone, put it plainly: (Shutterstock/paper-cut-design) “Now that AI can process unstructured data: text, images, PDF files, audio, maybe video – organizing that to get it to AI or agents at the right time and right place for it to create value is suddenly much more valuable than it used to be.” He went further, forecasting that many businesses will undertake data re-architecture programs measured in the tens, perhaps hundreds, of millions of dollars to make their estates “AI ready.” Notably, Ng admitted he has yet to find a single vendor solution in this space that satisfies him. His own teams are running experiments internally instead. When the most connected figure in applied AI says the market has no good answer, that is not a gap. That is a canyon. Here is what the strategy decks do not say, but what enterprise clients admit to me privately, with striking consistency, when talking about their unstructured data: “We have no idea what we have.” Not “our data is siloed.” Not “our governance needs maturing.” No idea. What we have. A global bank retaining thirty years of documents for regulatory reasons cannot tell you how many customer contracts sit in its archives, in what languages, with what clauses, under which permissions. An insurer cannot say which of its forty million stored PDFs are duplicates, which are drafts, which are the legally binding versions. The data was kept because it had to be kept, and because storage was cheap enough that deleting it was riskier than hoarding it. Nobody was ever going to read it, so nobody ever counted it. The numbers bear the confessions out. IDC [2] projects the global datasphere will nearly quadruple between 2024 and 2028, approaching 400 zettabytes, roughly 80 to 90 percent of it unstructured, and only a tiny fraction of that unstructured mass is ever analyzed at all. Veritas famously found that over half of stored enterprise data is “dark” – its contents and value entirely unknown to its owner – with another third redundant, obsolete, or trivial (ROT) [3] . Enterprise structured and unstructured data growth through 2028. (Source: IDC, Worldwide Global DataSphere Structured and Unstructured Data Forecast, 2024–2028, September 2024. Graphic recreated with AI to improve resolution and readability.) Look at that chart: the red mass is growing exponentially. The structured data is accelerating, but not nearly as fast. Every quarter, the gap between what enterprises hold and what enterprises know gets wider. That gap is now, thanks to AI, a gap between book value and extractable value. It is the largest unexploited asset class inside the modern corporation. Our own research says the same thing. In September, we analyzed 16PB of live production data across 856 file-share scans in enterprise NAS environments, including regulated industries [4] . Just 4.4% of stored capacity had been modified in the previous 90 days, and only 9.9% was accessed in any given 90-day period. More than 83% of capacity, and 97.5% of individual files, had not been modified in over a year; 88% of files had not even been accessed. Apparently, enterprises are using their most expensive storage tier for a cold archive. Noisy, duplicated, and permissioned for a world that no longer exists Why can’t firms simply “point the AI at the archive”? Because unstructured data is not merely unread – it is noisy . It is nine drafts of the same agreement with no marker of which one was executed. It is email threads where the critical decision lives in a forwarded attachment. It is call transcripts riddled with transcription errors, spreadsheets exported to PDF and back, folder structures that encode the org chart of 2009. Feed that noise to a language model or an agent and you do not get insight; you get confidently articulated garbage, drawn from a draft that was never signed. And the plumbing is worse than the content. As Ng noted at Interrupt, enterprise permissions were designed for humans, not agents. It’s everywhere and nowhere. Fragmentation, no consistent schema, critical files “sitting on someone’s laptop.” An AI agent that inherits the wrong permissions is a compliance incident waiting for a timestamp. Cataloging is the first dollar of value This points to a conclusion that is unfashionable in a market intoxicated by agents: the first step is not building the agent. It is the unglamorous, urgent work of cataloging – using AI itself to rapidly inventory the estate. What exists, where it lives, what it is, which version is authoritative, who may see it, what is duplicate, what is toxic, what is gold. The economics of this have transformed: classification that would have taken an army of analysts a decade can now be done in months, cheaply, by the same models that will later consume the data. Fast, AI-driven cataloging is not a prerequisite to value; it is value – it de-risks the compliance exposure of dark data on day one and builds the map every subsequent agent will navigate. Aron Brand is the Chief Technology Officer at CTERA. (Photo: CTERA) Ng’s broader argument at Interrupt was that AI’s real returns come not from incremental automation but from redesigning workflows end to end; his example being banks moving from week-long loan approvals to ten-minute loan products. Every one of those redesigned workflows runs on documents: applications, statements, appraisals, correspondence. Unstructured, almost entirely. The firms that treat their document mountains as a liability to be warehoused will keep paying primary-storage prices for data nobody has changed in over a year [4] . The firms that catalog first – that spend this year finding out, finally, what they have – will be the only ones whose agents have something true to say. The ninety percent problem is about to mint its first winners. They will be the ones who counted. About the Author: Aron Brand has more than 22 years of experience in designing and implementing distributed software systems. Prior to joining the founding team of CTERA, Aron acted as Chief Architect of SofaWare Technologies, a Check Point company, where he led the design of security software and appliances for the service provider and enterprise markets. items.summary_html:
Enterprises spent two decades perfecting their structured data. AI just made the other eighty to ninety percent – the messy, noisy, uncatalogued majority – the biggest prize in the building. Most companies cannot even tell you what they own.

For twenty years, the corporate data story has been a story about tables. Rows, columns, schemas, warehouses. Chief data officers built careers, and vendors built empires, on the disciplined organization of structured data: transactions, ledgers, customer records. It was expensive, it was precise, and it was, broadly, the right call. It was also only ever a fraction of the story.

The uncomfortable truth, familiar to anyone who has run a data audit at a large financial institution, is that somewhere between 80 and 90 percent of enterprise data is unstructured: contracts, emails, call recordings, loan files, PDFs scanned in 2004 and never opened since. Until recently, this did not matter much, because no economically viable technology could read it at scale. Compliance said keep it; economics said ignore it. So enterprises did both, for decades, at petabyte scale.

Generative AI has just inverted that equation, and the market has been slow to price in what that means.

Speaking at LangChain’s Interrupt conference in June 2026 [1], Andrew Ng, who has advised Fortune 50 boards through his firm and has seen more enterprise AI programs up close than almost anyone, put it plainly:

(Shutterstock/paper-cut-design)

“Now that AI can process unstructured data: text, images, PDF files, audio, maybe video – organizing that to get it to AI or agents at the right time and right place for it to create value is suddenly much more valuable than it used to be.”

He went further, forecasting that many businesses will undertake data re-architecture programs measured in the tens, perhaps hundreds, of millions of dollars to make their estates “AI ready.” Notably, Ng admitted he has yet to find a single vendor solution in this space that satisfies him. His own teams are running experiments internally instead. When the most connected figure in applied AI says the market has no good answer, that is not a gap. That is a canyon.

Here is what the strategy decks do not say, but what enterprise clients admit to me privately, with striking consistency, when talking about their unstructured data: “We have no idea what we have.”

Not “our data is siloed.” Not “our governance needs maturing.” No idea. What we have. A global bank retaining thirty years of documents for regulatory reasons cannot tell you how many customer contracts sit in its archives, in what languages, with what clauses, under which permissions. 

An insurer cannot say which of its forty million stored PDFs are duplicates, which are drafts, which are the legally binding versions. The data was kept because it had to be kept, and because storage was cheap enough that deleting it was riskier than hoarding it. Nobody was ever going to read it, so nobody ever counted it.

The numbers bear the confessions out. IDC [2] projects the global datasphere will nearly quadruple between 2024 and 2028, approaching 400 zettabytes, roughly 80 to 90 percent of it unstructured, and only a tiny fraction of that unstructured mass is ever analyzed at all. Veritas famously found that over half of stored enterprise data is “dark” – its contents and value entirely unknown to its owner – with another third redundant, obsolete, or trivial (ROT) [3].

Enterprise structured and unstructured data growth through 2028. (Source: IDC, Worldwide Global DataSphere Structured and Unstructured Data Forecast, 2024–2028, September 2024. Graphic recreated with AI to improve resolution and readability.)

Look at that chart: the red mass is growing exponentially. The structured data is accelerating, but not nearly as fast. Every quarter, the gap between what enterprises hold and what enterprises know gets wider. That gap is now, thanks to AI, a gap between book value and extractable value. It is the largest unexploited asset class inside the modern corporation.

Our own research says the same thing. In September, we analyzed 16PB of live production data across 856 file-share scans in enterprise NAS environments, including regulated industries [4]. Just 4.4% of stored capacity had been modified in the previous 90 days, and only 9.9% was accessed in any given 90-day period. More than 83% of capacity, and 97.5% of individual files, had not been modified in over a year; 88% of files had not even been accessed. Apparently, enterprises are using their most expensive storage tier for a cold archive.

Noisy, duplicated, and permissioned for a world that no longer exists

Why can’t firms simply “point the AI at the archive”? Because unstructured data is not merely unread – it is noisy. It is nine drafts of the same agreement with no marker of which one was executed. It is email threads where the critical decision lives in a forwarded attachment. It is call transcripts riddled with transcription errors, spreadsheets exported to PDF and back, folder structures that encode the org chart of 2009. Feed that noise to a language model or an agent and you do not get insight; you get confidently articulated garbage, drawn from a draft that was never signed.

And the plumbing is worse than the content. As Ng noted at Interrupt, enterprise permissions were designed for humans, not agents. It’s everywhere and nowhere. Fragmentation, no consistent schema, critical files “sitting on someone’s laptop.” An AI agent that inherits the wrong permissions is a compliance incident waiting for a timestamp.

Cataloging is the first dollar of value

This points to a conclusion that is unfashionable in a market intoxicated by agents: the first step is not building the agent. It is the unglamorous, urgent work of cataloging – using AI itself to rapidly inventory the estate. What exists, where it lives, what it is, which version is authoritative, who may see it, what is duplicate, what is toxic, what is gold. The economics of this have transformed: classification that would have taken an army of analysts a decade can now be done in months, cheaply, by the same models that will later consume the data. Fast, AI-driven cataloging is not a prerequisite to value; it is value – it de-risks the compliance exposure of dark data on day one and builds the map every subsequent agent will navigate.

Aron Brand is the Chief Technology Officer at CTERA. (Photo: CTERA)

Ng’s broader argument at Interrupt was that AI’s real returns come not from incremental automation but from redesigning workflows end to end; his example being banks moving from week-long loan approvals to ten-minute loan products. Every one of those redesigned workflows runs on documents: applications, statements, appraisals, correspondence. Unstructured, almost entirely.

The firms that treat their document mountains as a liability to be warehoused will keep paying primary-storage prices for data nobody has changed in over a year [4]. The firms that catalog first – that spend this year finding out, finally, what they have – will be the only ones whose agents have something true to say.

The ninety percent problem is about to mint its first winners. They will be the ones who counted.

items.title: Nvidia Drama Explodes; The Startup Tricking Scammers by Using AI Agents
items.summary: Shares of Nvidia were trading down 5% early Monday morning, a sign of the huge uncertainty now hanging over the AI chip giant in the wake of the company’s disclosure Sunday that it would investigate recent reporting that CEO Jensen Huang “had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Adding to the drama, Huang acknowledged having had an affair, saying he was “deeply sorry.” The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a “close relationship” with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly shared intelligence with Beijing authorities. We don’t know where this will lead. But given Huang’s position as one of AI’s biggest advocates, the ripples could be felt everywhere in the sector. Meanwhile, an Australian startup has come up with a new way to fight AI-enabled cybercrimes: sending an army of AI agents to pose as gullible grandmas and unsuspecting job seekers so as to lure the bad guys. Apate.ai is going up against a multibillion-dollar scam industry powered by thousands of workers in scam compounds, mostly in Southeast Asia. These scammers have gotten more sophisticated with the help of technology. Investigators have struggled to keep pace with ever-evolving tactics, and often only begin the chase after victims report their losses. Apate.ai, founded in 2024, thinks it’s found a way to help tip the scales. By posing as potential victims, its army of AI agents are able to engage scammers in lengthy conversations designed partly to waste time and divert attention from real victims.

items.title: Does the Harness Move the Result or Only the Cost? An Ablation on a Local Model in .NET
items.summary: I wrote two pieces arguing the harness is the bottleneck. This month the counter-evidence arrived, so I built a rig to test my own claim. A few weeks ago I published “Harness Engineering Is the New Bottleneck, Not the Model.” A week later I followed it with a piece about running a harness eval loop on my own .NET agent. Both pieces leaned the same way: stop obsessing over which model is in the loop, look at what is wrapped around it. I still think that was a useful correction at the time. But I wrote both pieces before reading the evidence I am going to walk through below, and some of it cuts against me. Not against “the harness matters” as a slogan, but against the way I let that slogan blur two different things together. The two things are these. A harness piece can move the result : more tasks actually solved. Or it can move the cost : more tokens, more minutes, more money, for the same tasks solved. When I wrote “the harness is the bottleneck,” I was mostly thinking about the first. A lot of the new evidence says the second is far more common. So this article does three things. It goes through the counter-evidence, carefully, with every number labeled by where it came from. It re-reads my own two pieces through that lens. And it builds an ablation rig in .NET, against a local model through Ollama or llama.cpp, where I can switch individual harness pieces off and see which ones move the result and which ones only move the bill. The counter-evidence, as Jaroslaw Wasowski put it together The piece that made me stop and re-read my own work was Jaroslaw Wasowski’s “Harness Engineering: When Agent Harness Moves the Result and When It Only Moves the Cost” on Level Up Coding. It is member-only, and I could read only the opening, so I went to his primary sources directly. Where my reading of a primary source differs from how his intro frames it, I say so. His core move is simple and, I think, right: judge a harness on two axes, result and cost, and never infer one from the other. He also openly revises his own earlier view that the harness is a moat worth hiding behind. I appreciated that. It is easier to write the next article than to say the last one was partly wrong. The METR note METR published a research note in February 2026, “Measuring Time Horizon Using Claude Code and Codex.” The question was whether vendor harnesses beat METR’s own default scaffolds when measuring how long a task a model can complete. METR’s defaults are ReAct (a plain act and observe loop) and Triframe (advisor, actor and rater subagents choosing each action). What the note reports, as I read it on METR’s site: Opus 4.5 with Claude Code beat Opus 4.5 with ReAct in 50.7% of bootstrap samples. That is a coin flip. GPT-5 with Codex beat GPT-5 with Triframe in only 14.5% of bootstrap samples. Not statistically significant either way. Raising the Opus 4.5 token budget from 8M to 32M for the Claude Code runs barely moved the preliminary time horizon. METR is careful to call it a research note, not a vetted publication. It covers two models. The vendor harnesses are built for interactive use with a human, and the evaluation was fully autonomous, which METR flags itself. One discrepancy I want to be upfront about. Wasowski’s intro puts a token gap of up to 40x next to the METR finding. When I read the METR note, I could not find a 40x figure in it. The 40x I could trace comes from the next paper. His full text may attribute it precisely and I only saw the opening, so I am not calling it an error. I am telling you where I found the number. The Scaffold Effect “The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents: Harness Choice as a Hidden Variable in Coding-Agent Evaluation” by Naman Vats and Oleg Golev (Sentient Labs), arXiv 2607.22585, preliminary work under review at the DL4C workshop at ICML 2026. This one I read in full, and it is the cleanest experiment in this whole debate. Setup: three harnesses (Goose, OpenCode, OpenHands-SDK), two models (Qwen 3.6 Plus and MiniMax M2.5, through OpenRouter), 50 tasks sampled from Terminal-Bench Pro across eight categories, 300 trials in total. Same sandbox, a 900 second wall-time cap. Findings, from the paper: Pass rates sat between 38% and 50%. Within one model, the spread across harnesses was 2 points for Qwen and 8 points for MiniMax. Most pairwise differences were not distinguishable from zero. Tokens per solved task differed by roughly 40x between harnesses. Goose used around 28K (Qwen) and 37K (MiniMax) tokens per solve. OpenCode used around 1.15M and 1.55M. Upgrading the model changed token cost by only 1.0x to 1.3x. The harness moved the bill far more than the model did. That is the “0 to 8 point band” and the “40x” in one table. Same tasks, nearly the same outcomes, wildly different bills. Two details in the paper matter more to me than the headline, though. First, the failure fingerprints were properties of the harness, consistent across both models: Goose tends to stop when stuck, OpenHands-SDK pushes toward closure and sometimes submits plausible wrong answers, OpenCode tends to run into the time cap. Second, on the IMPL category, OpenHands-SDK solved 69% against 38% for the other two. So the averaged band hides at least one place where the harness did move the result, on one kind of work. The authors are honest about scale: with 50 tasks, every task is worth 2 points, and they read their pass-rate differences as descriptive. Keep that sentence in mind. It is going to come back to bite my own rig. DeepSWE and the fixed harness DeepSWE (Datacurve, arXiv 2607.07946) is a benchmark of 113 long-horizon tasks across 91 open-source repositories. The design choice relevant here: every model is evaluated inside the same mini-swe-agent harness, with the same bash tool and the same prompt, explicitly so the leaderboard reflects model capability rather than scaffolding. They acknowledge the trade: real developers use Codex CLI or Claude Code, not mini-swe-agent. I find that choice telling. People who build benchmarks for a living decided the harness is enough of a confounder that it has to be pinned to a deliberately minimal one. That is not the same as “the harness does not matter.” It is “the harness matters enough that we have to hold it still to see anything else.” Model-harness fit Wasowski’s companion piece, “Harness Engineering: Model-Harness Fit: Why a Better Teacher Makes a Worse Agent,” summarizes a Salesforce preprint he cites as arXiv 2609.09134. I could not locate that preprint myself, so treat every number in this paragraph as secondhand, through his summary. As he describes it: a harness built around a weaker model lifted its success on seven agentic tasks from 29.2% to 78.0% without touching the weights. Fine-tuning the same model on a stronger expert’s full trajectories dropped it to 63.1%. Correcting single bad turns instead, one per failed rollout, brought it to 79.7%. A separate ICML 2026 paper I could read, “The Interplay of Harness Design and Post-Training in LLM Agents” by Kyungmin Kim and co-authors, reaches a compatible conclusion on an ALFWorld-based benchmark: harness and post-training cannot be separated, a harness bolted on after training recovers little, and for the smaller model the harness was a prerequisite for post-training to help at all. Put those two next to the Scaffold Effect and a picture forms that is more interesting than either camp. Swapping one reasonable harness for another, on a capable model, mostly moves cost. Building a harness that fits a specific, weaker model can move the result enormously. Those are different claims, and I had been making the second while citing evidence for the first. Two practitioners who measured instead of arguing Two pieces from the same weeks did something I respect more than any thread: they measured their own setup and reported where it disappointed them. Both are member-only, I could read only their introductions, and every figure below is author-reported from their own runs. Fareed Khan, “Fixing Over-Engineering in LLM Coding Agents.” He built what he calls a proportional-code system around Qwen3.8–27B, aimed at agents that write far more code than a ticket needs. His opening example is a request that needed one database constraint and got 56 new lines, including a DELETE that silently removes members. His numbers: across 34 trap tickets, an unguided agent's passing answers added a median of 1.5x the reference code (the intro calls it "typical"). With his full system, on 25 held-out tickets, that dropped to 0.88x. The part I keep thinking about: of the 11 pieces he designed, only 4 shipped, and his first hypothesis, H1, missed. Seven of eleven pieces did not earn their place. That is not a failure of his project. That is what an honest ablation looks like when you run one. Pasquale Molinaro, “I Had a Free Qwen3.8–27B Agent Copy 10 Web Pages. It Spent 64% of Its Time Measuring Pixels.” Qwen3.8–27B at Q4_K_M on two free Kaggle T4s, rebuilding ten pages from the Design2Code benchmark under three conditions: a one-shot copy, a one-shot copy plus one revision, and an agent that starts from the one-shot page with a renderer and 20 minutes per page. He expected the agent, the only condition that could look at its own output, to win clearly. His numbers: the agent issued 237 measuring commands, and 64% of its 169 minutes went to measuring pixels. Most of the score gain traced back to a single page, through a change you cannot even see in a browser. That second point is the one that scared me. An aggregate score went up, and the honest explanation was “one task, invisible change.” If he had stopped at the aggregate, he would have published a harness win. Re-reading my own two pieces So, what does this do to what I wrote? In “Harness Engineering Is the New Bottleneck,” my strongest piece of evidence was LangChain moving a fixed model from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 by rebuilding the harness. I did flag that it was one receipt, not two. What I did not do was ask what kind of harness change it was. In light of the fit papers, that result reads less like “harnesses beat models” and more like “one team fitted a harness to one model and one benchmark.” Real, but narrower than the headline I hung on it. In the eval loop piece, I actually had both axes in my own data and did not name them. The semantic search tool kept the pass rate flat and cut tokens by 41%. That was a pure cost move, and I kept it for exactly that reason. The self-review step moved the pass rate by 13 points and held at 68% on a rerun. That looked like a result move. But I scored 12 issues, I did not pair the comparison by issue, and with 12 issues each one is worth about 8 points. I would still bet the review step is real, because it gives the model information it did not have before (test output plus a fresh look at the diff). I would no longer state it as confidently as I did. My revised position, before any new data: harness pieces reliably move cost and only conditionally move the result. My working guess about the condition is that a piece moves the result when it feeds the model a signal it could not get otherwise (a compiler error, a failing check, a rendered page), and mostly moves cost when it adds ceremony (a plan, another loop, more room to wander). That guess is testable, so I built something to test it. The rig I wanted the smallest thing that could tell the two axes apart. Here is what I settled on and why. A local model. The fit evidence says harnesses matter most for weaker models, and both practitioners above ran a 27B local model. If harness pieces only move cost on a small local model, the strongest version of my original claim is in real trouble. Local also means I can run a few hundred configurations without watching a bill. No SDK. The rig talks to any OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint with a plain HttpClient. Ollama exposes one at http://localhost:11434/v1, llama.cpp's llama-server at http://localhost:8080/v1. No NuGet packages at all, so between configurations the only thing that changes is the harness, not a library version. Eight small tasks with traps. Each task is a C# function or class to implement. Each has visible checks the agent can run and hidden checks used only for scoring. The hidden checks target the edge cases a quick implementation misses: overflow, culture-sensitive lowercasing, SemVer pre-release ordering, a Turkish dotted capital I. A selftest command proves every reference solution passes all hidden checks and every starter fails them. Four switchable pieces. A planner, a verifier tool, a harness-driven retry loop, and a tool budget. Ten configurations. “Add one piece to bare” and “remove one piece from full.” I need both directions, because pieces overlap. If the verifier and the retry loop both feed check output back to the model, removing either one from the full harness might show nothing, while adding either one to the bare harness shows a lot. Only one direction would mislead me about which pieces are redundant. Two cost metrics, not one. Tokens per run and tokens per solve, the metric the Scaffold Effect paper uses. Plus wall time, and the share of wall time spent in builds and checks, because Molinaro’s 64% made me want to know where the minutes go, not just how many there are. Explicit outcomes. Dragos Bilaniuc’s “Reliability at the Core: Five Ground Rules for Building an Agent Loop” shaped the loop: every way a run can end is a named terminal (completed, budget_exhausted, turn_limit, model_error), the tool budget is checked before a tool fires rather than after, and a failed model call never leaves a half-written turn in the history. +-----------------+---------+----------+-------+--------+---------------------------------+ | Config | Planner | Verifier | Retry | Budget | Question it answers | +-----------------+---------+----------+-------+--------+---------------------------------+ | bare | off | off | 0 | 6 | Baseline | | +plan | on | off | 0 | 6 | Does a plan alone help? | | +verify | off | on | 0 | 6 | Does the agent use checks well? | | +retry | off | off | 2 | 6 | Does harness feedback help? | | +budget | off | off | 0 | 20 | Does more room help? | | full | on | on | 2 | 20 | Everything | | full-no-plan | off | on | 2 | 20 | Is the plan carrying weight? | | full-no-verify | on | off | 2 | 20 | Is the verifier redundant? | | full-no-retry | on | on | 0 | 20 | Is the retry redundant? | | full-tight | on | on | 2 | 6 | Do checks eat the budget? | +-----------------+---------+----------+-------+--------+---------------------------------+ And the tasks, with what the hidden checks go after: +--------------+------------------------------+------------------------------------------+ | Task | What the agent implements | What the hidden checks target | +--------------+------------------------------+------------------------------------------+ | 01-duration | ParseDuration("1h30m") | Case, whitespace, repeated/out-of-order | | | | units, unit without a number | | 02-slugify | Slugify(text) | Diacritics, "İstanbul", only separators | | 03-intervals | Merge(intervals) | Touching intervals, unsorted, empty | | 04-semver | Compare(a, b) | Pre-release precedence, build metadata | | 05-csv | SplitLine(line) | Escaped quotes, trailing comma, no trim | | 06-lru | LruCache | Get and update refresh recency, cap 1 | | 07-backoff | Delays(attempts, base, max) | Cap, zero, negative, overflow at 100 | | 08-roman | ToRoman(value) | 3999, 944, out-of-range throws | +--------------+------------------------------+------------------------------------------+ Setting it up You need the .NET 10 SDK and a local model server. On my Mac: brew install --cask dotnet-sdk brew install ollama # The default context window has been small in the Ollama versions I have used. # A long agent history gets truncated silently, and that hits "full" harder than "bare". OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=16384 ollama serve In a second terminal: ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b If you prefer containers, the Docker route works too. On a Mac, Docker cannot use the GPU, so expect it to be much slower than native Ollama: docker run -d --name ollama -p 11434:11434 -e OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=16384 \ -v ollama:/root/.ollama ollama/ollama docker exec ollama ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b And the llama.cpp route, which is what I would use to match the GGUF and quantization exactly: brew install llama.cpp llama-server -hf Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-GGUF:Q4_K_M --jinja -c 16384 --port 8080 --jinja matters: without the chat template, tool calls come back as plain text and the rig counts them as fallback writes instead of tool calls. Any model with tool calling works. A model without it makes Ollama reject the request, and those runs end as model_error, which the report excludes and lists. The project layout: harness-ablation/ Ablation.csproj checklib/Check.cs src/HarnessConfig.cs src/TaskSpec.cs src/ChatClient.cs src/AgentRunner.cs src/Report.cs src/Program.cs tasks/01-duration.task ... tasks/08-roman.task The code Ablation.csproj Exe net10.0 enable enable Ablation true HarnessConfig.cs: the switches namespace Ablation; /// /// One harness configuration. Every switch is one piece I can remove on its own. /// /// Extra model call that writes a plan before the agent acts. /// The agent may call run_checks (build + visible checks) itself. /// After the agent stops, the harness runs the visible checks and, if they fail, /// feeds the output back for up to this many more attempts. /// Hard cap on tool calls for the whole run, checked before each call. public sealed record HarnessConfig(string Name, bool Planner, bool VerifierTool, int Retries, int ToolBudget) { public const int TightBudget = 6; public const int LooseBudget = 20; // "Add one piece to bare" and "remove one piece from full". Same tasks, same model, same seed. public static readonly IReadOnlyList All = [ new("bare", Planner: false, VerifierTool: false, Retries: 0, ToolBudget: TightBudget), new("+plan", Planner: true, VerifierTool: false, Retries: 0, ToolBudget: TightBudget), new("+verify", Planner: false, VerifierTool: true, Retries: 0, ToolBudget: TightBudget), new("+retry", Planner: false, VerifierTool: false, Retries: 2, ToolBudget: TightBudget), new("+budget", Planner: false, VerifierTool: false, Retries: 0, ToolBudget: LooseBudget), new("full", Planner: true, VerifierTool: true, Retries: 2, ToolBudget: LooseBudget), new("full-no-plan", Planner: false, VerifierTool: true, Retries: 2, ToolBudget: LooseBudget), new("full-no-verify", Planner: true, VerifierTool: false, Retries: 2, ToolBudget: LooseBudget), new("full-no-retry", Planner: true, VerifierTool: true, Retries: 0, ToolBudget: LooseBudget), new("full-tight", Planner: true, VerifierTool: true, Retries: 2, ToolBudget: TightBudget), ]; public static HarnessConfig Get(string name) => All.FirstOrDefault(c => c.Name.Equals(name, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)) ?? throw new ArgumentException($"Unknown config '{name}'. Known: {string.Join(", ", All.Select(c => c.Name))}"); } The difference between the verifier and the retry is deliberate. With the verifier, the model decides when to look at the checks. With the retry, the harness decides, after the model says it is done. Those are different bets about who should own verification, and I wanted to price them separately. A task file Each task is one text file with five sections. Here is the one with my favorite trap. A naive baseDelay * Math.Pow(2, i) overflows TimeSpan well before attempt 100. == prompt == Implement `Backoff.Delays(int attempts, TimeSpan baseDelay, TimeSpan max)` in Solution.cs. Return one delay per retry attempt: attempt i (starting at 0) waits baseDelay * 2^i, but never more than max. attempts == 0 returns an empty list. A negative attempts value throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. Anything in between is unclear, and I would rather read unclear ten times than have the table tell me a confident story it has not earned. Read them. The table tells you where to look, the transcripts tell you why. What building the rig taught me before any model touched it Before pointing the rig at a real model, I tested the plumbing against a tiny scripted fake server: a Python script that speaks the OpenAI format and behaves badly on purpose. One task always answers with a code block instead of a tool call, one re-reads the same file forever, a couple write a wrong first draft. It was meant to be a five-minute sanity check. It found four bugs, and every one of them would have quietly bent a real ablation. Every request failed on the first try. HttpClient.PostAsJsonAsync streams the JSON body chunked, without a Content-Length header, and the fake server could not read it. Ollama and llama.cpp handle chunked bodies as far as I know, but a proxy in between might not. One StringContent later, it was fine. A configuration where every run crashed was labeled “cost only.” With zero tokens recorded everywhere, my token ratio fell below 0.8 and the verdict logic happily called it a cost move. Infrastructure failures now get excluded from the statistics and listed loudly at the bottom of the report, instead of being scored as harness failures. Dropped connections were scored as harness failures. The fake server closed every connection, and as far as I can tell .NET now and then reused one that was already dead. Real model servers do this under load too. Because a turn is only added to the history after a successful response, a transport retry cannot duplicate a message, which is exactly the property Bilaniuc’s rules ask for. Before that fix, those runs would have counted against whichever configuration made more calls, which is the full one. A harness with more model calls would have looked worse purely because it rolled the network dice more often. Two configurations with identical results got different verdicts. Same pass counts, same tasks, one labeled result, the other one task short of it. The bootstrap shared one random stream across configurations, and with eight tasks the lower bound of the interval sat right on zero, so the resampler's luck decided the label. Each configuration now gets its own seeded resampler. But I want to say the uncomfortable part out loud: the fix made the verdict reproducible, not robust. At eight tasks, a verdict at the boundary is still a coin flip with a fixed seed. None of this is about models or harnesses. All of it is about the measurement, and all of it would have shown up in a results table looking like a finding. What I am betting on I prefer to write down my expectations before looking at the table, for the same reason I set my noise threshold before looking in the eval loop piece: afterward, I will find a story for whatever comes out. These are my bets for a 7B coding model on these eight tasks, with the reasoning, so I can be wrong in public. +-----------------+-------------------+-----------------+-------------------+----------------+ | Config | Pass rate | Tokens | Wall time | Expected label | +-----------------+-------------------+-----------------+-------------------+----------------+ | bare | baseline | baseline | baseline | baseline | | +plan | flat | up, modest | up, modest | cost only | | +verify | up | up | up, a lot | result | | +retry | up | up on failures | up | result | | +budget | flat | up | flat to up | cost only | | full | up, like +verify | up the most | up the most | result | | full-no-plan | same as full | below full | below full | (vs full) cost | | full-no-verify | close to full | below full | below full | (vs full) ? | | full-no-retry | close to full | below full | below full | (vs full) ? | | full-tight | below full | below full | below full | unclear | +-----------------+-------------------+-----------------+-------------------+----------------+ The reasoning, piece by piece: The planner moves cost. These tasks are small enough that the prompt already is the plan. My guess is that a separate planning call costs one extra round trip and some prompt tokens and changes very little. If the planner earns a result verdict on a 7B model, that is the most interesting thing the rig could tell me, because it would mean smaller models need structure that larger ones do not, which is the fit papers' claim in miniature. The verifier and the retry move the result. They are the only pieces that give the model information it cannot produce itself: the compiler’s opinion and the checks’ opinion. That matches the self-review result from my own eval loop and the one place the Scaffold Effect paper showed a harness moving outcomes. If either one comes back cost only, my revised position from earlier in this article is wrong too, not just the original one. The verifier and the retry overlap. Removing one from the full harness should show much less than adding it to bare, because the other one covers for it. That is the reason for having both ablation directions. More budget mostly buys more reading. With a looser budget, I expect the model to re-read files and wander, the way Molinaro’s agent measured pixels. Tokens up, result flat. The tight budget is where the verifier eats the agent. Six tool calls, and each check costs one. I expect runs where the model spends its budget checking a broken draft and ends with budget_exhausted before it writes the fix. That is the configuration where the share of time spent in checks should be highest. What would change my mind: the verifier landing on cost only, or the planner landing on result, on more than one model. A single model will not settle either. Is the sample big enough? No. I promised myself I would say this plainly, so here it is. Eight tasks with three repetitions is 24 runs per configuration. A configuration that solves 12 of 24 has a 95% Wilson interval of roughly 31% to 69%. One that solves 15 of 24, a full 12.5 points better, has an interval of roughly 43% to 79%. Those overlap almost entirely. Pairing by task helps, but pairing does not create tasks: the unit of resampling is still eight tasks, and every single task is worth 12.5 points of pass rate. To detect a 10-point difference around a 50% pass rate, with the usual 95% confidence and 80% power, a simple unpaired comparison needs on the order of 390 runs per configuration. I am not going to get there with hand-written tasks on a laptop. So what can this rig actually say? Large result effects. If a piece turns a model that cannot get the code to compile into one that can, that shows up even at eight tasks. The size of cost effects. Tokens and seconds are measured, not estimated. A 3x token increase is a 3x token increase whether I have eight tasks or eight hundred. Not a strong “only cost.” This is the asymmetry I did not appreciate before building it. “This piece moved the cost” is easy to show. “This piece did not move the result” is a claim about the absence of an effect, and eight tasks cannot certify an absence. In my report, cost only really means "no task flipped on average, and the bill changed." That is weaker than the phrase sounds, which is why the unclear label exists. The Scaffold Effect authors said the same about their 50 tasks, where each task was worth 2 points. I have a quarter of their tasks. Anything I conclude from this rig on its own should be read as a direction to investigate, not as a finding. What I believe now I still think the harness is where most of the engineering is. I no longer think “the harness is the bottleneck” is a useful sentence on its own, because it hides the question that matters: bottleneck for what? For cost, the evidence is strong and consistent. Harness choice moved tokens per solve by around 40x in the Scaffold Effect paper while the model moved it by at most 1.3x. Khan’s system shipped 4 pieces out of 11. Molinaro’s agent spent most of its time measuring. If you care about the bill, the harness is the first place to look, and an ablation will tell you quickly which pieces are rent. For the result, the evidence is conditional. Swapping one reasonable harness for another on a capable model mostly lands inside the noise. Fitting a harness to a weaker model, or adding a piece that hands the model real information, can move it a lot. That is a narrower claim than the one I made a month ago, and I think it is the honest one. If you take one thing from this: whenever someone, including me, says a harness piece “made the agent better,” ask which axis moved and how many tasks it was measured on. If the answer is “the score went up” and “about ten,” read the transcripts before you believe it. Molinaro did, and found one page. Every file of the rig is in this post, with the remaining task files in the appendix below. Point it at whatever you run locally, and if one of my bets above is wrong on your model, I would genuinely like to hear which one. _order.AddFirst(node); value = node.Value.Value; return true; } value = default!; return false; } } 08-roman.task == prompt == Implement `Roman.ToRoman(int value)` in Solution.cs. items.summary_html:
I wrote two pieces arguing the harness is the bottleneck. This month the counter-evidence arrived, so I built a rig to test my own claim.

A few weeks ago I published “Harness Engineering Is the New Bottleneck, Not the Model.” A week later I followed it with a piece about running a harness eval loop on my own .NET agent. Both pieces leaned the same way: stop obsessing over which model is in the loop, look at what is wrapped around it.

I still think that was a useful correction at the time. But I wrote both pieces before reading the evidence I am going to walk through below, and some of it cuts against me. Not against “the harness matters” as a slogan, but against the way I let that slogan blur two different things together.

The two things are these. A harness piece can move the result: more tasks actually solved. Or it can move the cost: more tokens, more minutes, more money, for the same tasks solved. When I wrote “the harness is the bottleneck,” I was mostly thinking about the first. A lot of the new evidence says the second is far more common.

So this article does three things. It goes through the counter-evidence, carefully, with every number labeled by where it came from. It re-reads my own two pieces through that lens. And it builds an ablation rig in .NET, against a local model through Ollama or llama.cpp, where I can switch individual harness pieces off and see which ones move the result and which ones only move the bill.

The counter-evidence, as Jaroslaw Wasowski put it together

The piece that made me stop and re-read my own work was Jaroslaw Wasowski’s “Harness Engineering: When Agent Harness Moves the Result and When It Only Moves the Cost” on Level Up Coding. It is member-only, and I could read only the opening, so I went to his primary sources directly. Where my reading of a primary source differs from how his intro frames it, I say so.

His core move is simple and, I think, right: judge a harness on two axes, result and cost, and never infer one from the other. He also openly revises his own earlier view that the harness is a moat worth hiding behind. I appreciated that. It is easier to write the next article than to say the last one was partly wrong.

The METR note

METR published a research note in February 2026, “Measuring Time Horizon Using Claude Code and Codex.” The question was whether vendor harnesses beat METR’s own default scaffolds when measuring how long a task a model can complete. METR’s defaults are ReAct (a plain act and observe loop) and Triframe (advisor, actor and rater subagents choosing each action).

What the note reports, as I read it on METR’s site:

  • Opus 4.5 with Claude Code beat Opus 4.5 with ReAct in 50.7% of bootstrap samples. That is a coin flip.
  • GPT-5 with Codex beat GPT-5 with Triframe in only 14.5% of bootstrap samples. Not statistically significant either way.
  • Raising the Opus 4.5 token budget from 8M to 32M for the Claude Code runs barely moved the preliminary time horizon.

METR is careful to call it a research note, not a vetted publication. It covers two models. The vendor harnesses are built for interactive use with a human, and the evaluation was fully autonomous, which METR flags itself.

One discrepancy I want to be upfront about. Wasowski’s intro puts a token gap of up to 40x next to the METR finding. When I read the METR note, I could not find a 40x figure in it. The 40x I could trace comes from the next paper. His full text may attribute it precisely and I only saw the opening, so I am not calling it an error. I am telling you where I found the number.

The Scaffold Effect

“The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents: Harness Choice as a Hidden Variable in Coding-Agent Evaluation” by Naman Vats and Oleg Golev (Sentient Labs), arXiv 2607.22585, preliminary work under review at the DL4C workshop at ICML 2026. This one I read in full, and it is the cleanest experiment in this whole debate.

Setup: three harnesses (Goose, OpenCode, OpenHands-SDK), two models (Qwen 3.6 Plus and MiniMax M2.5, through OpenRouter), 50 tasks sampled from Terminal-Bench Pro across eight categories, 300 trials in total. Same sandbox, a 900 second wall-time cap.

Findings, from the paper:

  • Pass rates sat between 38% and 50%. Within one model, the spread across harnesses was 2 points for Qwen and 8 points for MiniMax. Most pairwise differences were not distinguishable from zero.
  • Tokens per solved task differed by roughly 40x between harnesses. Goose used around 28K (Qwen) and 37K (MiniMax) tokens per solve. OpenCode used around 1.15M and 1.55M.
  • Upgrading the model changed token cost by only 1.0x to 1.3x. The harness moved the bill far more than the model did.

That is the “0 to 8 point band” and the “40x” in one table. Same tasks, nearly the same outcomes, wildly different bills.

Two details in the paper matter more to me than the headline, though. First, the failure fingerprints were properties of the harness, consistent across both models: Goose tends to stop when stuck, OpenHands-SDK pushes toward closure and sometimes submits plausible wrong answers, OpenCode tends to run into the time cap. Second, on the IMPL category, OpenHands-SDK solved 69% against 38% for the other two. So the averaged band hides at least one place where the harness did move the result, on one kind of work.

The authors are honest about scale: with 50 tasks, every task is worth 2 points, and they read their pass-rate differences as descriptive. Keep that sentence in mind. It is going to come back to bite my own rig.

DeepSWE and the fixed harness

DeepSWE (Datacurve, arXiv 2607.07946) is a benchmark of 113 long-horizon tasks across 91 open-source repositories. The design choice relevant here: every model is evaluated inside the same mini-swe-agent harness, with the same bash tool and the same prompt, explicitly so the leaderboard reflects model capability rather than scaffolding. They acknowledge the trade: real developers use Codex CLI or Claude Code, not mini-swe-agent.

I find that choice telling. People who build benchmarks for a living decided the harness is enough of a confounder that it has to be pinned to a deliberately minimal one. That is not the same as “the harness does not matter.” It is “the harness matters enough that we have to hold it still to see anything else.”

Model-harness fit

Wasowski’s companion piece, “Harness Engineering: Model-Harness Fit: Why a Better Teacher Makes a Worse Agent,” summarizes a Salesforce preprint he cites as arXiv 2609.09134. I could not locate that preprint myself, so treat every number in this paragraph as secondhand, through his summary. As he describes it: a harness built around a weaker model lifted its success on seven agentic tasks from 29.2% to 78.0% without touching the weights. Fine-tuning the same model on a stronger expert’s full trajectories dropped it to 63.1%. Correcting single bad turns instead, one per failed rollout, brought it to 79.7%.

A separate ICML 2026 paper I could read, “The Interplay of Harness Design and Post-Training in LLM Agents” by Kyungmin Kim and co-authors, reaches a compatible conclusion on an ALFWorld-based benchmark: harness and post-training cannot be separated, a harness bolted on after training recovers little, and for the smaller model the harness was a prerequisite for post-training to help at all.

Put those two next to the Scaffold Effect and a picture forms that is more interesting than either camp. Swapping one reasonable harness for another, on a capable model, mostly moves cost. Building a harness that fits a specific, weaker model can move the result enormously. Those are different claims, and I had been making the second while citing evidence for the first.

Two practitioners who measured instead of arguing

Two pieces from the same weeks did something I respect more than any thread: they measured their own setup and reported where it disappointed them. Both are member-only, I could read only their introductions, and every figure below is author-reported from their own runs.

Fareed Khan, “Fixing Over-Engineering in LLM Coding Agents.” He built what he calls a proportional-code system around Qwen3.8–27B, aimed at agents that write far more code than a ticket needs. His opening example is a request that needed one database constraint and got 56 new lines, including a DELETE that silently removes members. His numbers: across 34 trap tickets, an unguided agent's passing answers added a median of 1.5x the reference code (the intro calls it "typical"). With his full system, on 25 held-out tickets, that dropped to 0.88x. The part I keep thinking about: of the 11 pieces he designed, only 4 shipped, and his first hypothesis, H1, missed.

Seven of eleven pieces did not earn their place. That is not a failure of his project. That is what an honest ablation looks like when you run one.

Pasquale Molinaro, “I Had a Free Qwen3.8–27B Agent Copy 10 Web Pages. It Spent 64% of Its Time Measuring Pixels.” Qwen3.8–27B at Q4_K_M on two free Kaggle T4s, rebuilding ten pages from the Design2Code benchmark under three conditions: a one-shot copy, a one-shot copy plus one revision, and an agent that starts from the one-shot page with a renderer and 20 minutes per page. He expected the agent, the only condition that could look at its own output, to win clearly. His numbers: the agent issued 237 measuring commands, and 64% of its 169 minutes went to measuring pixels. Most of the score gain traced back to a single page, through a change you cannot even see in a browser.

That second point is the one that scared me. An aggregate score went up, and the honest explanation was “one task, invisible change.” If he had stopped at the aggregate, he would have published a harness win.

Re-reading my own two pieces

So, what does this do to what I wrote?

In “Harness Engineering Is the New Bottleneck,” my strongest piece of evidence was LangChain moving a fixed model from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 by rebuilding the harness. I did flag that it was one receipt, not two. What I did not do was ask what kind of harness change it was. In light of the fit papers, that result reads less like “harnesses beat models” and more like “one team fitted a harness to one model and one benchmark.” Real, but narrower than the headline I hung on it.

In the eval loop piece, I actually had both axes in my own data and did not name them. The semantic search tool kept the pass rate flat and cut tokens by 41%. That was a pure cost move, and I kept it for exactly that reason. The self-review step moved the pass rate by 13 points and held at 68% on a rerun. That looked like a result move. But I scored 12 issues, I did not pair the comparison by issue, and with 12 issues each one is worth about 8 points. I would still bet the review step is real, because it gives the model information it did not have before (test output plus a fresh look at the diff). I would no longer state it as confidently as I did.

My revised position, before any new data: harness pieces reliably move cost and only conditionally move the result. My working guess about the condition is that a piece moves the result when it feeds the model a signal it could not get otherwise (a compiler error, a failing check, a rendered page), and mostly moves cost when it adds ceremony (a plan, another loop, more room to wander). That guess is testable, so I built something to test it.

The rig

I wanted the smallest thing that could tell the two axes apart. Here is what I settled on and why.

A local model. The fit evidence says harnesses matter most for weaker models, and both practitioners above ran a 27B local model. If harness pieces only move cost on a small local model, the strongest version of my original claim is in real trouble. Local also means I can run a few hundred configurations without watching a bill.

No SDK. The rig talks to any OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint with a plain HttpClient. Ollama exposes one at http://localhost:11434/v1, llama.cpp's llama-server at http://localhost:8080/v1. No NuGet packages at all, so between configurations the only thing that changes is the harness, not a library version.

Eight small tasks with traps. Each task is a C# function or class to implement. Each has visible checks the agent can run and hidden checks used only for scoring. The hidden checks target the edge cases a quick implementation misses: overflow, culture-sensitive lowercasing, SemVer pre-release ordering, a Turkish dotted capital I. A selftest command proves every reference solution passes all hidden checks and every starter fails them.

Four switchable pieces. A planner, a verifier tool, a harness-driven retry loop, and a tool budget.

Ten configurations. “Add one piece to bare” and “remove one piece from full.” I need both directions, because pieces overlap. If the verifier and the retry loop both feed check output back to the model, removing either one from the full harness might show nothing, while adding either one to the bare harness shows a lot. Only one direction would mislead me about which pieces are redundant.

Two cost metrics, not one. Tokens per run and tokens per solve, the metric the Scaffold Effect paper uses. Plus wall time, and the share of wall time spent in builds and checks, because Molinaro’s 64% made me want to know where the minutes go, not just how many there are.

Explicit outcomes. Dragos Bilaniuc’s “Reliability at the Core: Five Ground Rules for Building an Agent Loop” shaped the loop: every way a run can end is a named terminal (completed, budget_exhausted, turn_limit, model_error), the tool budget is checked before a tool fires rather than after, and a failed model call never leaves a half-written turn in the history.

Setting it up

You need the .NET 10 SDK and a local model server. On my Mac:

brew install --cask dotnet-sdk
brew install ollama

# The default context window has been small in the Ollama versions I have used.
# A long agent history gets truncated silently, and that hits "full" harder than "bare".
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=16384 ollama serve

In a second terminal:

ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b

If you prefer containers, the Docker route works too. On a Mac, Docker cannot use the GPU, so expect it to be much slower than native Ollama:

docker run -d --name ollama -p 11434:11434 -e OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=16384 \
  -v ollama:/root/.ollama ollama/ollama
docker exec ollama ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b

And the llama.cpp route, which is what I would use to match the GGUF and quantization exactly:

brew install llama.cpp
llama-server -hf Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-GGUF:Q4_K_M --jinja -c 16384 --port 8080

--jinja matters: without the chat template, tool calls come back as plain text and the rig counts them as fallback writes instead of tool calls.

Any model with tool calling works. A model without it makes Ollama reject the request, and those runs end as model_error, which the report excludes and lists.

HarnessConfig.cs: the switches
namespace Ablation;
/// 
/// One harness configuration. Every switch is one piece I can remove on its own.
/// 
/// Extra model call that writes a plan before the agent acts.
/// The agent may call run_checks (build + visible checks) itself.
/// After the agent stops, the harness runs the visible checks and, if they fail,
/// feeds the output back for up to this many more attempts.
/// Hard cap on tool calls for the whole run, checked before each call.
public sealed record HarnessConfig(string Name, bool Planner, bool VerifierTool, int Retries, int ToolBudget)
{
    public const int TightBudget = 6;
    public const int LooseBudget = 20;
    // "Add one piece to bare" and "remove one piece from full". Same tasks, same model, same seed.
    public static readonly IReadOnlyList All =
    [
        new("bare",           Planner: false, VerifierTool: false, Retries: 0, ToolBudget: TightBudget),
        new("+plan",          Planner: true,  VerifierTool: false, Retries: 0, ToolBudget: TightBudget),
        new("+verify",        Planner: false, VerifierTool: true,  Retries: 0, ToolBudget: TightBudget),
        new("+retry",         Planner: false, VerifierTool: false, Retries: 2, ToolBudget: TightBudget),
        new("+budget",        Planner: false, VerifierTool: false, Retries: 0, ToolBudget: LooseBudget),
        new("full",           Planner: true,  VerifierTool: true,  Retries: 2, ToolBudget: LooseBudget),
        new("full-no-plan",   Planner: false, VerifierTool: true,  Retries: 2, ToolBudget: LooseBudget),
        new("full-no-verify", Planner: true,  VerifierTool: false, Retries: 2, ToolBudget: LooseBudget),
        new("full-no-retry",  Planner: true,  VerifierTool: true,  Retries: 0, ToolBudget: LooseBudget),
        new("full-tight",     Planner: true,  VerifierTool: true,  Retries: 2, ToolBudget: TightBudget),
    ];
    public static HarnessConfig Get(string name) =>
        All.FirstOrDefault(c => c.Name.Equals(name, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
        ?? throw new ArgumentException($"Unknown config '{name}'. Known: {string.Join(", ", All.Select(c => c.Name))}");
}

The difference between the verifier and the retry is deliberate. With the verifier, the model decides when to look at the checks. With the retry, the harness decides, after the model says it is done. Those are different bets about who should own verification, and I wanted to price them separately.

A task file

Each task is one text file with five sections. Here is the one with my favorite trap. A naive baseDelay * Math.Pow(2, i) overflows TimeSpan well before attempt 100.

== prompt ==
Implement `Backoff.Delays(int attempts, TimeSpan baseDelay, TimeSpan max)` in Solution.cs.
Return one delay per retry attempt: attempt i (starting at 0) waits baseDelay * 2^i, but never more than max.
attempts == 0 returns an empty list. A negative attempts value throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
It must work for large attempt counts (for example 100) without overflowing; once the cap is reached,
every later delay equals max.
== starter ==
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
public static class Backoff
{
    public static IReadOnlyList Delays(int attempts, TimeSpan baseDelay, TimeSpan max)
    {
        throw new NotImplementedException();
    }
}
== visible ==
Check.Run("doubling", () => Check.Seq(new[] { 100.0, 200.0, 400.0 }, Backoff.Delays(3, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10)).Select(d => d.TotalMilliseconds)));
== hidden ==
Check.Run("cap", () => Check.Seq(new[] { 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.0 }, Backoff.Delays(4, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3)).Select(d => d.TotalSeconds)));
Check.Run("zero attempts", () => Check.Eq(0, Backoff.Delays(0, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3)).Count));
Check.Run("negative throws", () => Check.Throws(() => Backoff.Delays(-1, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3))));
Check.Run("no overflow", () => { var d = Backoff.Delays(100, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(250), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)); Check.True(d.Count == 100 && d.All(x => x > TimeSpan.Zero && x <= TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)) && d[^1] == TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)); });
== reference ==
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
public static class Backoff
{
    public static IReadOnlyList Delays(int attempts, TimeSpan baseDelay, TimeSpan max)
    {
        if (attempts < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(attempts));
        var list = new List(attempts);
        var current = baseDelay;
        for (int i = 0; i < attempts; i++)
        {
            list.Add(current < max ? current : max);
            if (current < max) current = current.Ticks > max.Ticks / 2 ? max : current + current;
        }
        return list;
    }
}

The other seven follow the same shape and are in the appendix at the end. If you write your own, keep the visible checks thin on purpose. The gap between visible and hidden is where a verifier can make the agent look better than it is, and that gap is exactly what I want to measure.

checklib/Check.cs: assertions without a test framework

Every check run compiles Solution.cs, this helper and a generated Main. No xUnit, no restore from a feed.

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
// Tiny assertion helper compiled into every check run. No test framework, no NuGet.
public static class Check
{
    private static int _passed, _failed;
    public static void Run(string name, Action body)
    {
        try
        {
            body();
            _passed++;
            Console.WriteLine($"PASS {name}");
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            _failed++;
            var msg = ex.Message.Length > 200 ? ex.Message[..200] + "..." : ex.Message;
            Console.WriteLine($"FAIL {name}: {ex.GetType().Name}: {msg}");
        }
    }
    public static void Eq(T expected, T actual)
    {
        if (!EqualityComparer.Default.Equals(expected, actual))
            throw new CheckFailed($"expected <{expected}> but got <{actual}>");
    }
    public static void Seq(IEnumerable expected, IEnumerable? actual)
    {
        var e = expected.ToList();
        var a = actual?.ToList() ?? throw new CheckFailed("got null");
        if (!e.SequenceEqual(a))
            throw new CheckFailed($"expected [{string.Join(", ", e)}] but got [{string.Join(", ", a)}]");
    }
    public static void True(bool condition, string? what = null)
    {
        if (!condition) throw new CheckFailed(what ?? "condition was false");
    }
    public static void Throws(Action action) where TEx : Exception
    {
        try { action(); }
        catch (TEx) { return; }
        catch (Exception ex) { throw new CheckFailed($"expected {typeof(TEx).Name} but got {ex.GetType().Name}"); }
        throw new CheckFailed($"expected {typeof(TEx).Name} but nothing was thrown");
    }
    public static int Done()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{_passed} passed, {_failed} failed");
        return _failed == 0 ? 0 : 1;
    }
}
public sealed class CheckFailed(string message) : Exception(message);
TaskSpec.cs: loading tasks and running checks
using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Text;
namespace Ablation;
/// A task file has five sections: prompt, starter, visible, hidden, reference.
public sealed record TaskSpec(string Id, string Prompt, string Starter, string Visible, string Hidden, string Reference)
{
    public static IReadOnlyList LoadAll(string dir, IEnumerable? only = null)
    {
        var filter = only?.ToHashSet(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
        return Directory.GetFiles(dir, "*.task")
            .OrderBy(f => f, StringComparer.Ordinal)
            .Select(Load)
            .Where(t => filter is null || filter.Any(f => t.Id.StartsWith(f, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)))
            .ToList();
    }
    public static TaskSpec Load(string path)
    {
        var sections = new Dictionary();
        StringBuilder? current = null;
        foreach (var line in File.ReadAllLines(path))
        {
            var t = line.Trim();
            if (t.StartsWith("== ") && t.EndsWith(" ==")) { current = sections[t[3..^3]] = new StringBuilder(); continue; }
            current?.AppendLine(line);
        }
        string S(string k) => sections.TryGetValue(k, out var sb) ? sb.ToString().Trim() : throw new InvalidDataException($"{path}: missing section '{k}'");
        return new(Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(path), S("prompt"), S("starter"), S("visible"), S("hidden"), S("reference"));
    }
}
public sealed record CheckResult(bool Passed, int ChecksPassed, int ChecksTotal, string Output, long ElapsedMs);
/// Builds a throwaway console project around Solution.cs and runs a set of checks against it.
public static class CheckRunner
{
    private static readonly string Tfm = $"net{Environment.Version.Major}.0";
    public static void WriteProject(string dir, string checkLines)
    {
        Directory.CreateDirectory(dir);
        File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(dir, "Checks.csproj"), $"""
            
              
                Exe
                {Tfm}
                enable
                disable
                $(NoWarn);CS8600;CS8601;CS8602;CS8603;CS8604;CS8618;CS8625;CS0168;CS0219
              
            
            """);
        File.Copy(Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, "checklib", "Check.cs"), Path.Combine(dir, "Check.cs"), overwrite: true);
        File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(dir, "Checks.cs"), $$"""
            using System;
            using System.Collections.Generic;
            using System.Linq;
            public static class Program
            {
                public static int Main()
                {
            {{checkLines}}
                    return Check.Done();
                }
            }
            """);
    }
    public static async Task RunAsync(string dir, TimeSpan timeout, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        var build = await Exec("dotnet", $"build \"{dir}\" -c Release -o \"{Path.Combine(dir, "out")}\" --nologo -v q -clp:NoSummary", timeout, ct);
        if (build.ExitCode != 0)
            return new(false, 0, 0, "BUILD FAILED\n" + Trim(Errors(build.Output)), sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
        var run = await Exec("dotnet", $"\"{Path.Combine(dir, "out", "Checks.dll")}\"", timeout, ct);
        var lines = run.Output.Split('\n');
        int passed = lines.Count(l => l.StartsWith("PASS ")), failed = lines.Count(l => l.StartsWith("FAIL "));
        var output = run.TimedOut ? "TIMED OUT (infinite loop?)\n" + run.Output : run.Output;
        return new(run.ExitCode == 0 && !run.TimedOut, passed, passed + failed, Trim(output), sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
    }
    // Compiler output repeats every error; keep the distinct error lines, which is what the model needs.
    private static string Errors(string output)
    {
        var errors = output.Split('\n').Where(l => l.Contains("error", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
            .Select(l => l.Trim()).Distinct().ToList();
        return errors.Count > 0 ? string.Join('\n', errors) : output;
    }
    private static string Trim(string s) => s.Length <= 3000 ? s.Trim() : s[..3000] + "\n...(truncated)";
    private sealed record ExecResult(int ExitCode, string Output, bool TimedOut);
    private static async Task Exec(string file, string args, TimeSpan timeout, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var psi = new ProcessStartInfo(file, args) { RedirectStandardOutput = true, RedirectStandardError = true };
        psi.Environment["DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT"] = "1";
        psi.Environment["DOTNET_NOLOGO"] = "1";
        psi.Environment["MSBUILDDISABLENODEREUSE"] = "1";
        using var p = Process.Start(psi)!;
        var stdout = p.StandardOutput.ReadToEndAsync(ct);
        var stderr = p.StandardError.ReadToEndAsync(ct);
        using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(ct);
        cts.CancelAfter(timeout);
        try { await p.WaitForExitAsync(cts.Token); }
        catch (OperationCanceledException) when (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            p.Kill(entireProcessTree: true);
            return new(-1, await stdout + await stderr, TimedOut: true);
        }
        return new(p.ExitCode, await stdout + await stderr, TimedOut: false);
    }
}

A build plus check run takes a couple of seconds, which is usually small next to a model call on a laptop GPU. That ratio is not universal. On a fast model server, the checks can become the dominant cost, which is exactly why the report shows the share of time spent in them.

ChatClient.cs: one HTTP call, no SDK
using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Text;
using System.Text.Json.Nodes;
namespace Ablation;
public sealed record ToolCall(string Id, string Name, JsonObject Arguments);
public sealed record ChatTurn(JsonObject AssistantMessage, string? Content, IReadOnlyList ToolCalls,
    int PromptTokens, int CompletionTokens, bool UsageMissing, long ElapsedMs);
/// 
/// Minimal client for any OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint:
/// Ollama (http://localhost:11434/v1) or llama.cpp's llama-server (http://localhost:8080/v1).
/// No SDK on purpose, so the only thing that changes between configurations is the harness.
/// 
public sealed class ChatClient(HttpClient http, string baseUrl, string model, double temperature, int seed)
{
    public string Model => model;
    public async Task CompleteAsync(JsonArray messages, JsonArray? tools, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var body = new JsonObject
        {
            ["model"] = model,
            ["messages"] = messages.DeepClone(),
            ["temperature"] = temperature,
            ["seed"] = seed,
            ["stream"] = false,
        };
        if (tools is { Count: > 0 }) body["tools"] = tools.DeepClone();
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        var json = await PostWithTransportRetryAsync(body.ToJsonString(), ct);
        var message = json["choices"]![0]!["message"]!.AsObject();
        var calls = new List();
        if (message["tool_calls"] is JsonArray arr)
        {
            foreach (var c in arr)
            {
                var fn = c!["function"]!;
                // Ollama and llama-server send arguments as a JSON string; some servers send an object.
                var rawArgs = fn["arguments"];
                var args = rawArgs switch
                {
                    JsonObject o => o,
                    JsonValue v when v.TryGetValue(out var s) && !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(s) => TryParseObject(s),
                    _ => new JsonObject(),
                };
                calls.Add(new(c["id"]?.GetValue() ?? Guid.NewGuid().ToString("n")[..8], fn["name"]!.GetValue(), args));
            }
        }
        var usage = json["usage"];
        int pt = usage?["prompt_tokens"]?.GetValue() ?? 0, ctok = usage?["completion_tokens"]?.GetValue() ?? 0;
        var assistant = new JsonObject { ["role"] = "assistant", ["content"] = message["content"]?.DeepClone() };
        if (message["tool_calls"] is JsonArray tc) assistant["tool_calls"] = tc.DeepClone();
        return new(assistant, message["content"]?.GetValue(), calls, pt, ctok, usage is null, sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
    }
    // Transport failures (dropped connection, reset) are retried twice. Nothing has been added to the
    // conversation yet, so a retry cannot duplicate a message. HTTP error statuses are not retried.
    private async Task PostWithTransportRetryAsync(string payload, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        for (int attempt = 0; ; attempt++)
        {
            try
            {
                // Buffered body with Content-Length. PostAsJsonAsync streams a chunked body,
                // which some local servers and proxies reject.
                using var content = new StringContent(payload, Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");
                using var resp = await http.PostAsync($"{baseUrl.TrimEnd('/')}/chat/completions", content, ct);
                var text = await resp.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(ct);
                if (!resp.IsSuccessStatusCode)
                    throw new InvalidOperationException($"HTTP {(int)resp.StatusCode}: {text[..Math.Min(text.Length, 500)]}");
                return JsonNode.Parse(text)!.AsObject();
            }
            catch (HttpRequestException) when (attempt < 2 && !ct.IsCancellationRequested)
            {
                TransportRetries++;
                await Task.Delay(500 * (attempt + 1), ct);
            }
        }
    }
    public int TransportRetries { get; private set; }
    private static JsonObject TryParseObject(string s)
    {
        try { return JsonNode.Parse(s) as JsonObject ?? new JsonObject(); }
        catch { return new JsonObject { ["_unparsed"] = s }; }
    }
}
