AgentRunner.cs: the loop

This is the part that matters. Every harness piece is an if on the config, so turning one off removes exactly that piece and nothing else.

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Text.Json.Nodes;
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
namespace Ablation;
public sealed record RunRecord(
    string Config, string Task, int Rep, string Model, DateTime StartedUtc,
    bool Passed, int HiddenChecksPassed, int HiddenChecksTotal, string Outcome,
    int PromptTokens, int CompletionTokens, int ModelCalls, int ToolCalls, int VerifierCalls,
    int RetriesUsed, int FallbackWrites, int UsageMissing,
    long ModelMs, long CheckMs, long TotalMs)
{
    public int Tokens => PromptTokens + CompletionTokens;
}
/// 
/// The agent loop. Outcomes are explicit terminals (completed, budget_exhausted, turn_limit, model_error),
/// never exceptions, so every run produces one record.
/// 
public sealed partial class AgentRunner(ChatClient chat, string runsRoot, TimeSpan checkTimeout)
{
    private const string SolutionFile = "Solution.cs";
    public async Task RunAsync(TaskSpec task, HarnessConfig cfg, int rep, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var started = DateTime.UtcNow;
        var total = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        var dir = Path.Combine(runsRoot, cfg.Name.Replace('+', 'p'), task.Id, $"rep{rep}");
        if (Directory.Exists(dir)) Directory.Delete(dir, recursive: true);
        var work = Path.Combine(dir, "work");      // the agent's workspace: visible checks only
        var hidden = Path.Combine(dir, "hidden");  // created after the agent stops; the agent never sees it
        CheckRunner.WriteProject(work, task.Visible);
        File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(work, SolutionFile), task.Starter);
        File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(work, "TASK.md"), task.Prompt);
        int pt = 0, ctok = 0, modelCalls = 0, toolCalls = 0, verifierCalls = 0, retriesUsed = 0, fallbacks = 0, usageMissing = 0;
        long modelMs = 0, checkMs = 0;
        string outcome = "completed";
        void Account(ChatTurn t) { pt += t.PromptTokens; ctok += t.CompletionTokens; modelMs += t.ElapsedMs; modelCalls++; if (t.UsageMissing) usageMissing++; }
        var messages = new JsonArray
        {
            Msg("system", SystemPrompt(cfg)),
            Msg("user", $"Task:\n{task.Prompt}\n\nCurrent {SolutionFile}:\n```csharp\n{task.Starter}\n```"),
        };
        var tools = Tools(cfg);
        try
        {
            if (cfg.Planner)
            {
                var plan = await chat.CompleteAsync(new JsonArray
                {
                    Msg("system", "You plan small C# coding tasks. Write a numbered plan of at most 6 steps, naming every edge case the implementation must handle. Do not write code."),
                    Msg("user", task.Prompt),
                }, null, ct);
                Account(plan);
                messages.Add(Msg("user", $"Plan to follow:\n{plan.Content}"));
            }
            for (int attempt = 0; attempt <= cfg.Retries; attempt++)
            {
                // Inner loop: model turns until the model stops calling tools or a limit is hit.
                int turns = 0;
                while (true)
                {
                    if (++turns > cfg.ToolBudget + 4) { outcome = "turn_limit"; break; }
                    var turn = await chat.CompleteAsync(messages, tools, ct);
                    Account(turn);
                    messages.Add(turn.AssistantMessage);
                    if (turn.ToolCalls.Count == 0)
                    {
                        // Small local models often answer with a code block instead of a tool call.
                        // Same lenient rule in every configuration, and it is counted.
                        if (ExtractCode(turn.Content) is { } code) { File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(work, SolutionFile), code); fallbacks++; }
                        break;
                    }
                    foreach (var call in turn.ToolCalls)
                    {
                        // Check the budget BEFORE firing the tool, not after.
                        if (toolCalls >= cfg.ToolBudget)
                        {
                            messages.Add(ToolMsg(call.Id, "Tool budget exhausted. Stop and reply without tool calls."));
                            outcome = "budget_exhausted";
                            continue;
                        }
                        toolCalls++;
                        var (result, ms, isVerifier) = await ExecuteToolAsync(call, work, ct);
                        checkMs += ms;
                        if (isVerifier) verifierCalls++;
                        messages.Add(ToolMsg(call.Id, result));
                    }
                    if (outcome == "budget_exhausted") break;
                }
                if (attempt == cfg.Retries || outcome is "budget_exhausted" or "turn_limit") break;
                // Harness-driven retry: the harness, not the model, decides to look at the visible checks.
                var visible = await CheckRunner.RunAsync(work, checkTimeout, ct);
                checkMs += visible.ElapsedMs;
                if (visible.Passed) break;
                retriesUsed++;
                messages.Add(Msg("user", $"The harness ran the visible checks and they failed:\n{visible.Output}\n\nFix {SolutionFile}."));
            }
        }
        catch (Exception ex) when (ex is HttpRequestException or TaskCanceledException or InvalidOperationException or NullReferenceException)
        {
            outcome = "model_error";
            Console.Error.WriteLine($"  [{cfg.Name} {task.Id} rep{rep}] model error: {ex.Message}");
        }
        total.Stop();
        // Scoring happens outside the measured time and outside the agent's workspace.
        CheckRunner.WriteProject(hidden, task.Visible + "\n" + task.Hidden);
        File.Copy(Path.Combine(work, SolutionFile), Path.Combine(hidden, SolutionFile), overwrite: true);
        var score = await CheckRunner.RunAsync(hidden, checkTimeout, ct);
        File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(dir, "transcript.json"), messages.ToJsonString(new() { WriteIndented = true }));
        File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(dir, "hidden-output.txt"), score.Output);
        return new(cfg.Name, task.Id, rep, chat.Model, started, score.Passed, score.ChecksPassed, score.ChecksTotal, outcome,
            pt, ctok, modelCalls, toolCalls, verifierCalls, retriesUsed, fallbacks, usageMissing,
            modelMs, checkMs, total.ElapsedMilliseconds);
    }
    private async Task<(string Result, long Ms, bool IsVerifier)> ExecuteToolAsync(ToolCall call, string work, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        switch (call.Name)
        {
            case "read_file":
            {
                var name = Path.GetFileName(call.Arguments["path"]?.GetValue() ?? SolutionFile);
                var path = Path.Combine(work, name);
                return (File.Exists(path) && name is SolutionFile or "TASK.md" or "Checks.cs" ? File.ReadAllText(path) : $"Cannot read '{name}'. Readable: {SolutionFile}, TASK.md, Checks.cs", 0, false);
            }
            case "write_file":
            {
                var content = call.Arguments["content"]?.GetValue();
                if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(content)) return ("write_file needs a non-empty 'content' with the full file.", 0, false);
                File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(work, SolutionFile), content);
                return ($"Wrote {SolutionFile} ({content.Length} chars).", 0, false);
            }
            case "run_checks":
            {
                var r = await CheckRunner.RunAsync(work, checkTimeout, ct);
                return ((r.Passed ? "ALL VISIBLE CHECKS PASSED\n" : "") + r.Output, r.ElapsedMs, true);
            }
            default:
                return ($"Unknown tool '{call.Name}'.", 0, false);
        }
    }
    private static string SystemPrompt(HarnessConfig cfg) =>
        "You are a careful C# developer working in a tiny workspace. " +
        $"{SolutionFile} is the only file you may change. Use write_file to save the COMPLETE new contents of {SolutionFile}. " +
        (cfg.VerifierTool ? "Use run_checks to compile the project and run the visible checks. " : "") +
        "When you are finished, reply with one short sentence and no tool call. Do not add features nobody asked for.";
    private static JsonArray Tools(HarnessConfig cfg)
    {
        var tools = new JsonArray
        {
            Tool("read_file", "Read a workspace file (Solution.cs, TASK.md or Checks.cs).",
                new JsonObject { ["path"] = new JsonObject { ["type"] = "string" } }, ["path"]),
            Tool("write_file", "Replace the full contents of Solution.cs.",
                new JsonObject { ["content"] = new JsonObject { ["type"] = "string", ["description"] = "Complete C# source of Solution.cs" } }, ["content"]),
        };
        if (cfg.VerifierTool)
            tools.Add(Tool("run_checks", "Build Solution.cs and run the visible checks. Returns compiler errors or PASS/FAIL lines.", new JsonObject(), []));
        return tools;
    }
    private static JsonObject Tool(string name, string description, JsonObject props, string[] required) => new()
    {
        ["type"] = "function",
        ["function"] = new JsonObject
        {
            ["name"] = name,
            ["description"] = description,
            ["parameters"] = new JsonObject
            {
                ["type"] = "object",
                ["properties"] = props,
                ["required"] = new JsonArray(required.Select(r => (JsonNode)JsonValue.Create(r)!).ToArray()),
            },
        },
    };
    private static JsonObject Msg(string role, string content) => new() { ["role"] = role, ["content"] = content };
    private static JsonObject ToolMsg(string id, string content) => new() { ["role"] = "tool", ["tool_call_id"] = id, ["content"] = content };
    [GeneratedRegex(@"```(?:csharp|cs|c#)?\s*\n(?[\s\S]*?)```", RegexOptions.IgnoreCase)]
    private static partial Regex CodeBlock();
    private static string? ExtractCode(string? content)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(content)) return null;
        var block = CodeBlock().Matches(content).Select(m => m.Groups["code"].Value)
            .LastOrDefault(c => c.Contains("class ", StringComparison.Ordinal));
        return block?.Trim();
    }
}

The decision I went back and forth on most is the fallback write. Small local models regularly answer “here is the code” in a fenced block instead of calling write_file. If I ignore that, I am measuring tool-calling discipline, not coding ability. If I accept it, I am adding a harness piece of my own. I accepted it, apply it identically in every configuration, and count it, so if one configuration leans on it far more than the others, the report shows that.

Report.cs: turning runs into verdicts
using System.Text;
using System.Text.Json;
namespace Ablation;
/// 
/// Turns run records into one ASCII table and a verdict per configuration:
///   result     the paired difference in pass rate vs the baseline has a 95% CI that excludes zero
///   unclear    the point estimate is a task's worth or more, but the CI touches zero
///   cost only  no detectable result change, but tokens or wall time moved by 25% or more
///   noise      neither
/// 
public static class Report
{
    public static string Build(IReadOnlyList allRuns, string baseline, int bootstrapSamples = 5000, int seed = 7)
    {
        // A model_error run is an infrastructure failure, not a harness result. Exclude it and say so.
        var errored = allRuns.Where(r => r.Outcome == "model_error").ToList();
        var runs = allRuns.Where(r => r.Outcome != "model_error").ToList();
        if (runs.Count == 0) return $"All {allRuns.Count} runs ended in model_error. Is the model server up?\n";
        var tasks = runs.Select(r => r.Task).Distinct().OrderBy(t => t).ToList();
        var configs = runs.Select(r => r.Config).Distinct()
            .OrderBy(c => HarnessConfig.All.Select(x => x.Name).ToList().IndexOf(c) is var i && i < 0 ? 999 : i).ToList();
        if (!configs.Contains(baseline)) throw new ArgumentException($"Baseline '{baseline}' has no runs.");
        double PassRate(string cfg, string task)
        {
            var rs = runs.Where(r => r.Config == cfg && r.Task == task).ToList();
            return rs.Count == 0 ? double.NaN : rs.Count(r => r.Passed) / (double)rs.Count;
        }
        var baseRuns = runs.Where(r => r.Config == baseline).ToList();
        double baseTokens = baseRuns.Average(r => (double)r.Tokens), baseSecs = baseRuns.Average(r => r.TotalMs / 1000.0);
        var sb = new StringBuilder();
        var header = $"| {"Config",-15} | {"Pass",-9} | {"95% CI",-9} | {"Tok/run",8} | {"Tok/solve",9} | {"s/run",6} | {"Chk%",4} | {"dPass vs base",-17} | {"Verdict",-9} |";
        var rule = "+" + string.Join("+", header.Split('|', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries).Select(c => new string('-', c.Length))) + "+";
        sb.AppendLine(rule).AppendLine(header).AppendLine(rule);
        foreach (var cfg in configs)
        {
            // Fresh seeded resampler per config: identical data must get an identical CI and verdict.
            var rng = new Random(seed);
            var rs = runs.Where(r => r.Config == cfg).ToList();
            int n = rs.Count, k = rs.Count(r => r.Passed);
            var (lo, hi) = Wilson(k, n);
            double tokRun = rs.Average(r => (double)r.Tokens);
            string tokSolve = k == 0 ? "n/a" : Short(rs.Sum(r => (double)r.Tokens) / k);
            double secs = rs.Average(r => r.TotalMs / 1000.0);
            double chk = rs.Sum(r => (double)r.CheckMs) / Math.Max(1, rs.Sum(r => (double)r.TotalMs));
            string delta = "-", verdict = "baseline";
            if (cfg != baseline)
            {
                // Pair by task: the unit of resampling is the task, not the run.
                var diffs = tasks.Select(t => PassRate(cfg, t) - PassRate(baseline, t)).Where(d => !double.IsNaN(d)).ToArray();
                double mean = diffs.Average();
                var boots = new double[bootstrapSamples];
                for (int b = 0; b < bootstrapSamples; b++)
                {
                    double s = 0;
                    for (int i = 0; i < diffs.Length; i++) s += diffs[rng.Next(diffs.Length)];
                    boots[b] = s / diffs.Length;
                }
                Array.Sort(boots);
                double bl = boots[(int)(0.025 * bootstrapSamples)], bh = boots[(int)(0.975 * bootstrapSamples) - 1];
                delta = $"{mean * 100,4:+0;-0;0} [{bl * 100:+0;-0;0},{bh * 100:+0;-0;0}]";
                double tokRatio = baseTokens > 0 ? tokRun / baseTokens : 1, timeRatio = baseSecs > 0 ? secs / baseSecs : 1;
                bool resultMoved = bl > 0 || bh < 0;
                bool costMoved = tokRatio >= 1.25 || tokRatio <= 0.8 || timeRatio >= 1.25 || timeRatio <= 0.8;
                // "cost only" is a claim that the result did NOT move. If the point estimate is a task's
                // worth or more but the CI still touches zero, that claim is not earned: say "unclear".
                bool bigButUnsure = !resultMoved && Math.Abs(mean) >= 1.0 / tasks.Count - 1e-9;
                verdict = resultMoved ? "result" : bigButUnsure ? "unclear" : costMoved ? "cost only" : "noise";
            }
            sb.AppendLine($"| {cfg,-15} | {$"{k}/{n} {100.0 * k / n:0}%",-9} | {$"{lo * 100:0}-{hi * 100:0}%",-9} | {Short(tokRun),8} | {tokSolve,9} | {secs,6:0.0} | {chk * 100,3:0}% | {delta,-17} | {verdict,-9} |");
        }
        sb.AppendLine(rule);
        int reps = runs.GroupBy(r => (r.Config, r.Task)).Max(g => g.Count());
        sb.AppendLine($"  {tasks.Count} tasks x {reps} reps per config. Model: {runs[0].Model}. Baseline: {baseline}.");
        sb.AppendLine($"  dPass is in percentage points, paired by task, 95% bootstrap CI over tasks.");
        sb.AppendLine($"  Chk% = share of wall time spent in builds and visible checks (verifier tool + harness retries).");
        if (tasks.Count < 30)
            sb.AppendLine($"  WARNING: with {tasks.Count} tasks each task moves a config's pass rate by {100.0 / tasks.Count:0.#} points. Read this as descriptive.");
        var outcomes = runs.GroupBy(r => (r.Config, r.Outcome)).Where(g => g.Key.Outcome != "completed")
            .Select(g => $"{g.Key.Config}:{g.Key.Outcome}={g.Count()}").ToList();
        if (outcomes.Count > 0) sb.AppendLine($"  Non-completed terminals: {string.Join(", ", outcomes)}");
        if (errored.Count > 0)
            sb.AppendLine($"  EXCLUDED {errored.Count} model_error runs: {string.Join(", ", errored.GroupBy(r => r.Config).Select(g => $"{g.Key}={g.Count()}"))}. Re-run them before trusting the table.");
        int missing = runs.Sum(r => r.UsageMissing), fallbacks = runs.Sum(r => r.FallbackWrites);
        if (missing > 0) sb.AppendLine($"  WARNING: {missing} model calls reported no token usage; token columns undercount.");
        if (fallbacks > 0) sb.AppendLine($"  Fallback writes (code block instead of a tool call): {fallbacks}.");
        return sb.ToString();
    }
    // Last record wins per (task, config, rep), so re-running errored runs replaces them.
    public static IReadOnlyList Load(string path) =>
        File.ReadAllLines(path).Where(l => l.Length > 0).Select(l => JsonSerializer.Deserialize(l)!)
            .GroupBy(r => (r.Task, r.Config, r.Rep)).Select(g => g.Last()).ToList();
    private static (double Lo, double Hi) Wilson(int k, int n, double z = 1.96)
    {
        if (n == 0) return (0, 0);
        double p = (double)k / n, d = 1 + z * z / n;
        double c = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / d, h = z * Math.Sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4.0 * n * n)) / d;
        return (Math.Max(0, c - h), Math.Min(1, c + h));
    }
    private static string Short(double v) => v >= 10_000 ? $"{v / 1000:0}k" : v >= 1000 ? $"{v / 1000:0.0}k" : $"{v:0}";
}

The verdict column is the whole point of the rig, so the rules are worth stating plainly. A configuration gets result only when the paired 95% interval for the pass-rate difference excludes zero. It gets cost only only when the pass rate did not move by even one task's worth and tokens or time moved by at least 25%. Anything in between is unclear, and I would rather read unclear ten times than have the table tell me a confident story it has not earned.

Program.cs: selftest, run, report
using System.Text.Json;
using Ablation;
// Usage:
//   dotnet run -- selftest
//   dotnet run -- run --base-url http://localhost:11434/v1 --model qwen2.5-coder:7b --reps 3 --out results/run.jsonl
//   dotnet run -- run ... --configs bare,+verify,full --tasks 01,04
//   dotnet run -- report results/run.jsonl [--baseline bare]
var opts = ParseArgs(args.Skip(1).ToArray());
string tasksDir = opts.GetValueOrDefault("tasks-dir", Path.Combine(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory(), "tasks"));
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
Console.CancelKeyPress += (_, e) => { e.Cancel = true; cts.Cancel(); };
switch (args.FirstOrDefault())
{
    case "selftest":
        return await SelfTest();
    case "run":
        return await Run();
    case "report":
        Console.Write(Report.Build(Report.Load(args[1]), opts.GetValueOrDefault("baseline", "bare")));
        return 0;
    default:
        Console.Error.WriteLine("Commands: selftest | run | report ");
        return 2;
}
// Proves the fixtures are fair: the reference passes every hidden check, the starter fails.
async Task SelfTest()
{
    var root = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "ablation-selftest");
    int bad = 0;
    foreach (var t in TaskSpec.LoadAll(tasksDir))
    {
        foreach (var (label, source, mustPass) in new[] { ("reference", t.Reference, true), ("starter", t.Starter, false) })
        {
            var dir = Path.Combine(root, t.Id, label);
            if (Directory.Exists(dir)) Directory.Delete(dir, true);
            CheckRunner.WriteProject(dir, t.Visible + "\n" + t.Hidden);
            File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(dir, "Solution.cs"), source);
            var r = await CheckRunner.RunAsync(dir, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2), cts.Token);
            bool ok = r.Passed == mustPass;
            if (!ok) bad++;
            Console.WriteLine($"{(ok ? "ok  " : "BAD ")} {t.Id,-14} {label,-9} {r.ChecksPassed}/{r.ChecksTotal} checks");
            if (!ok) Console.WriteLine(r.Output);
        }
    }
    return bad == 0 ? 0 : 1;
}
async Task Run()
{
    var baseUrl = opts.GetValueOrDefault("base-url", "http://localhost:11434/v1");
    var model = opts.GetValueOrDefault("model", "qwen2.5-coder:7b");
    int reps = int.Parse(opts.GetValueOrDefault("reps", "3"));
    int seed = int.Parse(opts.GetValueOrDefault("seed", "7"));
    double temperature = double.Parse(opts.GetValueOrDefault("temperature", "0.2"), System.Globalization.CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    var outPath = opts.GetValueOrDefault("out", Path.Combine("results", $"run-{DateTime.UtcNow:yyyyMMdd-HHmmss}.jsonl"));
    var configs = opts.TryGetValue("configs", out var cs) ? cs.Split(',').Select(HarnessConfig.Get).ToList() : HarnessConfig.All.ToList();
    var tasks = TaskSpec.LoadAll(tasksDir, opts.TryGetValue("tasks", out var ts) ? ts.Split(',') : null);
    Directory.CreateDirectory(Path.GetDirectoryName(Path.GetFullPath(outPath))!);
    using var http = new HttpClient { Timeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10) };
    var chat = new ChatClient(http, baseUrl, model, temperature, seed);
    var runner = new AgentRunner(chat, Path.Combine(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory(), "runs"), TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2));
    // Interleave configs in a seeded random order so a slow afternoon or a warm KV cache
    // does not land on one configuration.
    var plan = (from t in tasks from c in configs from r in Enumerable.Range(1, reps) select (t, c, r))
        .ToList();
    var rng = new Random(seed);
    plan = plan.OrderBy(_ => rng.Next()).ToList();
    // Resume: skip anything already in the output file, except runs that died on a model error.
    var done = File.Exists(outPath)
        ? Report.Load(outPath).Where(r => r.Outcome != "model_error").Select(r => (r.Task, r.Config, r.Rep)).ToHashSet()
        : [];
    int i = 0;
    foreach (var (t, c, r) in plan)
    {
        i++;
        if (done.Contains((t.Id, c.Name, r))) continue;
        if (cts.IsCancellationRequested) break;
        var rec = await runner.RunAsync(t, c, r, cts.Token);
        await File.AppendAllTextAsync(outPath, JsonSerializer.Serialize(rec) + "\n");
        Console.WriteLine($"[{i}/{plan.Count}] {c.Name,-15} {t.Id,-14} rep{r} {(rec.Passed ? "PASS" : "fail")} " +
                          $"{rec.HiddenChecksPassed}/{rec.HiddenChecksTotal} {rec.Tokens,7} tok {rec.TotalMs / 1000.0,6:0.0}s {rec.Outcome}");
    }
    Console.WriteLine();
    Console.Write(Report.Build(Report.Load(outPath), opts.GetValueOrDefault("baseline", "bare")));
    return 0;
}
static Dictionary ParseArgs(string[] a)
{
    var d = new Dictionary();
    for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++)
        if (a[i].StartsWith("--") && i + 1 < a.Length) d[a[i][2..]] = a[++i];
    return d;
}

What building the rig taught me before any model touched it

Before pointing the rig at a real model, I tested the plumbing against a tiny scripted fake server: a Python script that speaks the OpenAI format and behaves badly on purpose. One task always answers with a code block instead of a tool call, one re-reads the same file forever, a couple write a wrong first draft. It was meant to be a five-minute sanity check. It found four bugs, and every one of them would have quietly bent a real ablation.

Every request failed on the first try. HttpClient.PostAsJsonAsync streams the JSON body chunked, without a Content-Length header, and the fake server could not read it. Ollama and llama.cpp handle chunked bodies as far as I know, but a proxy in between might not. One StringContent later, it was fine.

A configuration where every run crashed was labeled “cost only.” With zero tokens recorded everywhere, my token ratio fell below 0.8 and the verdict logic happily called it a cost move. Infrastructure failures now get excluded from the statistics and listed loudly at the bottom of the report, instead of being scored as harness failures.

Dropped connections were scored as harness failures. The fake server closed every connection, and as far as I can tell .NET now and then reused one that was already dead. Real model servers do this under load too. Because a turn is only added to the history after a successful response, a transport retry cannot duplicate a message, which is exactly the property Bilaniuc’s rules ask for. Before that fix, those runs would have counted against whichever configuration made more calls, which is the full one. A harness with more model calls would have looked worse purely because it rolled the network dice more often.

Two configurations with identical results got different verdicts. Same pass counts, same tasks, one labeled result, the other one task short of it. The bootstrap shared one random stream across configurations, and with eight tasks the lower bound of the interval sat right on zero, so the resampler's luck decided the label. Each configuration now gets its own seeded resampler. But I want to say the uncomfortable part out loud: the fix made the verdict reproducible, not robust. At eight tasks, a verdict at the boundary is still a coin flip with a fixed seed.

None of this is about models or harnesses. All of it is about the measurement, and all of it would have shown up in a results table looking like a finding.

What I am betting on

I prefer to write down my expectations before looking at the table, for the same reason I set my noise threshold before looking in the eval loop piece: afterward, I will find a story for whatever comes out. These are my bets for a 7B coding model on these eight tasks, with the reasoning, so I can be wrong in public.

+-----------------+-------------------+-----------------+-------------------+----------------+
| Config          | Pass rate         | Tokens          | Wall time         | Expected label |
+-----------------+-------------------+-----------------+-------------------+----------------+
| bare            | baseline          | baseline        | baseline          | baseline       |
| +plan           | flat              | up, modest      | up, modest        | cost only      |
| +verify         | up                | up              | up, a lot         | result         |
| +retry          | up                | up on failures  | up                | result         |
| +budget         | flat              | up              | flat to up        | cost only      |
| full            | up, like +verify  | up the most     | up the most       | result         |
| full-no-plan    | same as full      | below full      | below full        | (vs full) cost |
| full-no-verify  | close to full     | below full      | below full        | (vs full) ?    |
| full-no-retry   | close to full     | below full      | below full        | (vs full) ?    |
| full-tight      | below full        | below full      | below full        | unclear        |
+-----------------+-------------------+-----------------+-------------------+----------------+

The reasoning, piece by piece:

The planner moves cost. These tasks are small enough that the prompt already is the plan. My guess is that a separate planning call costs one extra round trip and some prompt tokens and changes very little. If the planner earns a result verdict on a 7B model, that is the most interesting thing the rig could tell me, because it would mean smaller models need structure that larger ones do not, which is the fit papers' claim in miniature.

The verifier and the retry move the result. They are the only pieces that give the model information it cannot produce itself: the compiler’s opinion and the checks’ opinion. That matches the self-review result from my own eval loop and the one place the Scaffold Effect paper showed a harness moving outcomes. If either one comes back cost only, my revised position from earlier in this article is wrong too, not just the original one.

The verifier and the retry overlap. Removing one from the full harness should show much less than adding it to bare, because the other one covers for it. That is the reason for having both ablation directions.

More budget mostly buys more reading. With a looser budget, I expect the model to re-read files and wander, the way Molinaro’s agent measured pixels. Tokens up, result flat.

The tight budget is where the verifier eats the agent. Six tool calls, and each check costs one. I expect runs where the model spends its budget checking a broken draft and ends with budget_exhausted before it writes the fix. That is the configuration where the share of time spent in checks should be highest.

What would change my mind: the verifier landing on cost only, or the planner landing on result, on more than one model. A single model will not settle either.

Is the sample big enough? No.

I promised myself I would say this plainly, so here it is.

Eight tasks with three repetitions is 24 runs per configuration. A configuration that solves 12 of 24 has a 95% Wilson interval of roughly 31% to 69%. One that solves 15 of 24, a full 12.5 points better, has an interval of roughly 43% to 79%. Those overlap almost entirely. Pairing by task helps, but pairing does not create tasks: the unit of resampling is still eight tasks, and every single task is worth 12.5 points of pass rate.

To detect a 10-point difference around a 50% pass rate, with the usual 95% confidence and 80% power, a simple unpaired comparison needs on the order of 390 runs per configuration. I am not going to get there with hand-written tasks on a laptop.

So what can this rig actually say?

  • Large result effects. If a piece turns a model that cannot get the code to compile into one that can, that shows up even at eight tasks.
  • The size of cost effects. Tokens and seconds are measured, not estimated. A 3x token increase is a 3x token increase whether I have eight tasks or eight hundred.
  • Not a strong “only cost.” This is the asymmetry I did not appreciate before building it. “This piece moved the cost” is easy to show. “This piece did not move the result” is a claim about the absence of an effect, and eight tasks cannot certify an absence. In my report, cost only really means "no task flipped on average, and the bill changed." That is weaker than the phrase sounds, which is why the unclear label exists.

The Scaffold Effect authors said the same about their 50 tasks, where each task was worth 2 points. I have a quarter of their tasks. Anything I conclude from this rig on its own should be read as a direction to investigate, not as a finding.

What I believe now

I still think the harness is where most of the engineering is. I no longer think “the harness is the bottleneck” is a useful sentence on its own, because it hides the question that matters: bottleneck for what?

For cost, the evidence is strong and consistent. Harness choice moved tokens per solve by around 40x in the Scaffold Effect paper while the model moved it by at most 1.3x. Khan’s system shipped 4 pieces out of 11. Molinaro’s agent spent most of its time measuring. If you care about the bill, the harness is the first place to look, and an ablation will tell you quickly which pieces are rent.

For the result, the evidence is conditional. Swapping one reasonable harness for another on a capable model mostly lands inside the noise. Fitting a harness to a weaker model, or adding a piece that hands the model real information, can move it a lot. That is a narrower claim than the one I made a month ago, and I think it is the honest one.

If you take one thing from this: whenever someone, including me, says a harness piece “made the agent better,” ask which axis moved and how many tasks it was measured on. If the answer is “the score went up” and “about ten,” read the transcripts before you believe it. Molinaro did, and found one page.

Every file of the rig is in this post, with the remaining task files in the appendix below. Point it at whatever you run locally, and if one of my bets above is wrong on your model, I would genuinely like to hear which one.

using System;
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
public static class Durations
{
    private static readonly Regex Pattern =
        new(@"^(?:(\d+)h)?(?:(\d+)m)?(?:(\d+)s)?$", RegexOptions.IgnoreCase | RegexOptions.CultureInvariant);
    public static TimeSpan ParseDuration(string s)
    {
        var text = (s ?? "").Trim();
        var m = Pattern.Match(text);
        if (text.Length == 0 || !m.Success) throw new FormatException($"Invalid duration '{s}'.");
        long Part(int i) => m.Groups[i].Success ? long.Parse(m.Groups[i].Value) : 0;
        return TimeSpan.FromHours(Part(1)) + TimeSpan.FromMinutes(Part(2)) + TimeSpan.FromSeconds(Part(3));
    }
}

using System;
using System.Globalization;
using System.Text;
public static class Slugs
{
    public static string Slugify(string text)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(text)) return "";
        var sb = new StringBuilder();
        bool dash = false;
        foreach (var ch in text.Normalize(NormalizationForm.FormD))
        {
            if (CharUnicodeInfo.GetUnicodeCategory(ch) == UnicodeCategory.NonSpacingMark) continue;
            var c = char.ToLowerInvariant(ch);
            if ((c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') || (c >= '0' && c <= '9')) { sb.Append(c); dash = false; }
            else if (!dash && sb.Length > 0) { sb.Append('-'); dash = true; }
        }
        return sb.ToString().TrimEnd('-');
    }
}

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
public static class Intervals
{
    public static List<(int Start, int End)> Merge(IEnumerable<(int Start, int End)> items)
    {
        var result = new List<(int Start, int End)>();
        foreach (var (s, e) in items.OrderBy(i => i.Start))
        {
            if (result.Count > 0 && s <= result[^1].End)
                result[^1] = (result[^1].Start, Math.Max(result[^1].End, e));
            else
                result.Add((s, e));
        }
        return result;
    }
}

using System;
using System.Numerics;
public static class SemVer
{
    public static int Compare(string a, string b)
    {
        static (string Core, string? Pre) Split(string v)
        {
            v = v.Split('+')[0];
            var i = v.IndexOf('-');
            return i < 0 ? (v, null) : (v[..i], v[(i + 1)..]);
        }
        var (ca, pa) = Split(a);
        var (cb, pb) = Split(b);
        var xa = ca.Split('.'); var xb = cb.Split('.');
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
        {
            var c = BigInteger.Parse(xa[i]).CompareTo(BigInteger.Parse(xb[i]));
            if (c != 0) return Math.Sign(c);
        }
        if (pa == null && pb == null) return 0;
        if (pa == null) return 1;
        if (pb == null) return -1;
        var ia = pa.Split('.'); var ib = pb.Split('.');
        for (int i = 0; i < Math.Min(ia.Length, ib.Length); i++)
        {
            bool na = BigInteger.TryParse(ia[i], out var va), nb = BigInteger.TryParse(ib[i], out var vb);
            int c = (na, nb) switch
            {
                (true, true) => va.CompareTo(vb),
                (true, false) => -1,
                (false, true) => 1,
                _ => string.CompareOrdinal(ia[i], ib[i]),
            };
            if (c != 0) return Math.Sign(c);
        }
        return Math.Sign(ia.Length.CompareTo(ib.Length));
    }
}

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Text;
public static class Csv
{
    public static List SplitLine(string line)
    {
        var fields = new List();
        var sb = new StringBuilder();
        bool quoted = false;
        for (int i = 0; i < line.Length; i++)
        {
            char c = line[i];
            if (quoted)
            {
                if (c == '"' && i + 1 < line.Length && line[i + 1] == '"') { sb.Append('"'); i++; }
                else if (c == '"') quoted = false;
                else sb.Append(c);
            }
            else if (c == '"') quoted = true;
            else if (c == ',') { fields.Add(sb.ToString()); sb.Clear(); }
            else sb.Append(c);
        }
        fields.Add(sb.ToString());
        return fields;
    }
}
06-lru.task
== prompt ==
Implement the class `LruCache` in Solution.cs.

- Constructor `LruCache(int capacity)`; capacity must be at least 1, otherwise throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
- `void Put(TKey key, TValue value)` inserts or updates. Updating an existing key also makes it the most recently used.
- `bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue value)` returns the value and marks the key as most recently used.
- `int Count` is the number of stored entries.
- When a Put would exceed capacity, evict the least recently used entry.
Get and Put should be O(1).
== starter ==
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
public sealed class LruCache where TKey : notnull
{
    public LruCache(int capacity) => throw new NotImplementedException();
    public int Count => throw new NotImplementedException();
    public void Put(TKey key, TValue value) => throw new NotImplementedException();
    public bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue value) => throw new NotImplementedException();
}
== visible ==
Check.Run("put get", () => { var c = new LruCache(2); c.Put("a", 1); Check.True(c.TryGet("a", out var v) && v == 1); });
Check.Run("evicts oldest", () => { var c = new LruCache(2); c.Put("a", 1); c.Put("b", 2); c.Put("c", 3); Check.True(!c.TryGet("a", out _) && c.Count == 2); });
== hidden ==
Check.Run("get refreshes", () => { var c = new LruCache(2); c.Put("a", 1); c.Put("b", 2); c.TryGet("a", out _); c.Put("c", 3); Check.True(c.TryGet("a", out _) && !c.TryGet("b", out _)); });
Check.Run("update refreshes", () => { var c = new LruCache(2); c.Put("a", 1); c.Put("b", 2); c.Put("a", 10); c.Put("c", 3); Check.True(c.TryGet("a", out var v) && v == 10 && !c.TryGet("b", out _)); });
Check.Run("update keeps count", () => { var c = new LruCache(2); c.Put("a", 1); c.Put("a", 2); Check.Eq(1, c.Count); });
Check.Run("capacity one", () => { var c = new LruCache(1); c.Put(1, 1); c.Put(2, 2); Check.True(!c.TryGet(1, out _) && c.TryGet(2, out _)); });
Check.Run("zero capacity throws", () => Check.Throws(() => new LruCache(0)));
== reference ==
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
public sealed class LruCache where TKey : notnull
{
    private readonly int _capacity;
    private readonly Dictionary> _map = new();
    private readonly LinkedList<(TKey Key, TValue Value)> _order = new();
    public LruCache(int capacity)
    {
        if (capacity < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(capacity));
        _capacity = capacity;
    }
    public int Count => _map.Count;
    public void Put(TKey key, TValue value)
    {
        if (_map.TryGetValue(key, out var node)) { _order.Remove(node); _map.Remove(key); }
        else if (_map.Count == _capacity) { var last = _order.Last!; _order.RemoveLast(); _map.Remove(last.Value.Key); }
        _map[key] = _order.AddFirst((key, value));
    }
    public bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue value)
    {
        if (_map.TryGetValue(key, out var node))
        {
            _order.Remove(node); _order.AddFirst(node);
            value = node.Value.Value; return true;
        }
        value = default!; return false;
    }
}

== reference ==
using System;
using System.Text;
public static class Roman
{
    private static readonly (int Value, string Symbol)[] Table =
    {
        (1000, "M"), (900, "CM"), (500, "D"), (400, "CD"), (100, "C"), (90, "XC"),
        (50, "L"), (40, "XL"), (10, "X"), (9, "IX"), (5, "V"), (4, "IV"), (1, "I"),
    };
    public static string ToRoman(int value)
    {
        if (value is < 1 or > 3999) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(value));
        var sb = new StringBuilder();
        foreach (var (v, s) in Table)
            while (value >= v) { sb.Append(s); value -= v; }
        return sb.ToString();
    }
}

items.title: Why semantic layers will be essential for enterprise AI
items.summary: AI can find your data. It can’t read your mind. AI agents can already reach into your CRM, your warehouse, and your ERP, and with standards like MCP , that list keeps growing. Access is solved. Understanding is not. An agent can retrieve every record in your pipeline and still give your CRO the wrong answer, not because the data is bad, but because it doesn’t know what you mean by “pipeline.” Agents without semantics don’t fail loudly. They deliver confident answers to the wrong question. “Pipeline” means something different at every company Ask an executive, “How is pipeline looking this quarter?” and it sounds like a simple request. It isn’t. The answer depends on your sales stages, your forecasting methodology, your territory structure, and your qualification criteria, which are business rules that evolved over years, often without ever being written down. Two companies can use the same word and mean entirely different things. Businesses don’t run on raw data. They run on shared meaning, and humans carry that meaning around in their heads. For decades, employees logged into the CRM, the BI tool, or the ERP and supplied the judgment themselves, because they knew which dashboard to trust and which field was never quite right. Now they state intent, and an agent figures out the rest. The systems of record stay where they are, but a new layer sits between people and technology: a system of agency. In my experience, leaders spend a lot of time asking whether that layer can connect to everything and far less time asking whether it understands anything. If that layer doesn’t understand your business, nothing underneath it matters. Catalogs helped people find data. Semantic layers help AI understand it. For the last decade, we invested in governance, integration, quality, and catalogs, and those investments still matter because trusted data is the prerequisite. But a catalog tells people where the data lives. A semantic layer tells AI what it means. It captures what your best people carry in their heads: Business definitions, such as what counts as “pipeline,” “churn,” or “active customer” Policies that govern how data can be used Relationships between products, customers, contracts, and outcomes Rules that determine how decisions get made “A catalog tells people where the data lives. A semantic layer tells AI what it means.” Put that in a form both humans and machines can consume, and agents stop guessing. This isn’t a nice-to-have. It’s the difference between an agent that is technically capable and one that is operationally reliable. Relationships are where the value lives Definitions are only half the story, because business decisions rarely live in a single dataset. They depend on how concepts connect. Take an AI-powered quoting process, where the agent needs products, contracts, customer history, usage patterns, approval structures, and pricing rules all at once, and each lives in a different system. Retrieving them is the easy part. Reasoning across them is the hard part, and when the agent gets it wrong, it won’t throw an error. It will produce a plausible quote with the wrong discount and send it to a real customer. That’s where knowledge graphs and context graphs earn their place. They treat information as connected business knowledge rather than isolated facts, so instead of piecing together a customer’s story from scattered records, the agent gets a map of how your business fits together. Meaning is also an efficiency play Without encoded context, agents spend compute rediscovering relationships and re-inferring meaning your organization already understands, so every query becomes a small act of reconstruction. Define it once, and every agent reasons from the same source. That means more consistent answers, fewer contradictions between teams, and lower cost as usage scales. Consistency is underrated. If sales, finance, and operations each get a different answer to the same question from the same AI, you haven’t built intelligence. You’ve built an argument. Anyone can build now. Not everything should scale. Generative AI has finally delivered on the citizen developer promise. Employees can describe a workflow in plain language and get a working prototype back, which means good ideas can now come from anywhere. That’s the opportunity. “If sales, finance, and operations each get a different answer to the same question from the same AI, you haven’t built intelligence. You’ve built an argument.” The risk is that a tool that helps one person is a convenience, while the same tool deployed across departments is a liability if no one validated it, governed it, or owns it. Organizations need a path from experiment to enterprise asset. I think of it as a graduation factory: identify the promising prototypes, test them, apply governance, and promote the ones that earn it. Innovation should be easy to start and hard to scale carelessly. The same foundations apply here. Only 12% of organizations say their data is AI-ready , and only 31% can tie their AI initiatives to clear KPIs. Semantics and governance are how you close that gap. Where I’d start You don’t need a multi-year program to make progress. Start small and prove it: Pick the five terms your executives argue about most, and define them. Assign a business owner to each definition. Expose those definitions to your agents through a governed layer, then measure whether the answers improve. Meaning, like data, has to be managed. Someone has to own it. The bottom line Connecting AI to your data is table stakes. Everyone will do it, so it won’t differentiate you. Trusted data is the prerequisite. Shared meaning is the multiplier. Connect your agents to everything, and you’ve built access. Teach them how your business thinks, and you’ve built an advantage.
items.summary_html:
AI can find your data. It can’t read your mind. AI agents can already reach into your CRM, your warehouse, and your ERP, and with standards like MCP, that list keeps growing. Access is solved. Understanding is not. An agent can retrieve every record in your pipeline and still give your CRO the wrong answer, not because the data is bad, but because it doesn’t know what you mean by “pipeline.” Agents without semantics don’t fail loudly. They deliver confident answers to the wrong question.

“Pipeline” means something different at every company

Ask an executive, “How is pipeline looking this quarter?” and it sounds like a simple request. It isn’t. The answer depends on your sales stages, your forecasting methodology, your territory structure, and your qualification criteria, which are business rules that evolved over years, often without ever being written down. Two companies can use the same word and mean entirely different things. Businesses don’t run on raw data. They run on shared meaning, and humans carry that meaning around in their heads. Agents don’t have heads. They have whatever we give them.

From systems of record to systems of agency

That matters more as the way we work changes. For decades, employees logged into the CRM, the BI tool, or the ERP and supplied the judgment themselves, because they knew which dashboard to trust and which field was never quite right. Now they state intent, and an agent figures out the rest. 

The systems of record stay where they are, but a new layer sits between people and technology: a system of agency. In my experience, leaders spend a lot of time asking whether that layer can connect to everything and far less time asking whether it understands anything. If that layer doesn’t understand your business, nothing underneath it matters.

Catalogs helped people find data. Semantic layers help AI understand it.

For the last decade, we invested in governance, integration, quality, and catalogs, and those investments still matter because trusted data is the prerequisite. But a catalog tells people where the data lives. A semantic layer tells AI what it means. It captures what your best people carry in their heads:

  • Business definitions, such as what counts as “pipeline,” “churn,” or “active customer”
  • Policies that govern how data can be used
  • Relationships between products, customers, contracts, and outcomes
  • Rules that determine how decisions get made

“A catalog tells people where the data lives. A semantic layer tells AI what it means.”

Put that in a form both humans and machines can consume, and agents stop guessing. This isn’t a nice-to-have. It’s the difference between an agent that is technically capable and one that is operationally reliable.

Relationships are where the value lives

Definitions are only half the story, because business decisions rarely live in a single dataset. They depend on how concepts connect. Take an AI-powered quoting process, where the agent needs products, contracts, customer history, usage patterns, approval structures, and pricing rules all at once, and each lives in a different system. Retrieving them is the easy part. 

Reasoning across them is the hard part, and when the agent gets it wrong, it won’t throw an error. It will produce a plausible quote with the wrong discount and send it to a real customer. That’s where knowledge graphs and context graphs earn their place. They treat information as connected business knowledge rather than isolated facts, so instead of piecing together a customer’s story from scattered records, the agent gets a map of how your business fits together.

Meaning is also an efficiency play

Without encoded context, agents spend compute rediscovering relationships and re-inferring meaning your organization already understands, so every query becomes a small act of reconstruction. Define it once, and every agent reasons from the same source. That means more consistent answers, fewer contradictions between teams, and lower cost as usage scales. Consistency is underrated. If sales, finance, and operations each get a different answer to the same question from the same AI, you haven’t built intelligence. You’ve built an argument.

Anyone can build now. Not everything should scale.

Generative AI has finally delivered on the citizen developer promise. Employees can describe a workflow in plain language and get a working prototype back, which means good ideas can now come from anywhere. That’s the opportunity. 

“If sales, finance, and operations each get a different answer to the same question from the same AI, you haven’t built intelligence. You’ve built an argument.”

The risk is that a tool that helps one person is a convenience, while the same tool deployed across departments is a liability if no one validated it, governed it, or owns it. Organizations need a path from experiment to enterprise asset. I think of it as a graduation factory: identify the promising prototypes, test them, apply governance, and promote the ones that earn it. Innovation should be easy to start and hard to scale carelessly. 

The same foundations apply here. Only 12% of organizations say their data is AI-ready, and only 31% can tie their AI initiatives to clear KPIs. Semantics and governance are how you close that gap.

Where I’d start

You don’t need a multi-year program to make progress. Start small and prove it:

  1. Pick the five terms your executives argue about most, and define them.
  2. Assign a business owner to each definition.
  3. Expose those definitions to your agents through a governed layer, then measure whether the answers improve.

Meaning, like data, has to be managed. Someone has to own it.

The bottom line

Connecting AI to your data is table stakes. Everyone will do it, so it won’t differentiate you. Trusted data is the prerequisite. Shared meaning is the multiplier. Connect your agents to everything, and you’ve built access. Teach them how your business thinks, and you’ve built an advantage.

items.summary_html:
EvenUp cofounder and CEO Rami Karabibar.

EvenUp

  • EvenUp, a quiet giant of the legal tech space, has reached $150 million in contracted revenue.
  • The company sells AI software to personal injury law firms.
  • It's expanding into new products and reaching new customers as it also faces increased competition.

While Harvey and Legora battle for Big Law, another legal tech startup is carving out a sizable business in Small Law.

EvenUp, a seven-year-old company that sells AI software to plaintiff-side law firms, has grown to $150 million in recurring revenue under contract, Rami Karabibar, EvenUp's cofounder and chief executive, told Business Insider.

The milestone is a reminder that some of the biggest opportunities in legal AI lie beyond the white-shoe firms now adopting it.

For traditional law firms that bill by the hour, AI presents a dilemma. Software that makes lawyers more efficient could also eat into their revenue. But personal injury firms typically work on contingency, taking a cut of what their clients win. The faster they can move cases along, the sooner they get paid.

For much of its existence, EvenUp was something of a one-trick pony.

The company got its start automating demand letters, the detailed documents personal injury lawyers send to insurers making the case for a financial settlement. It's a valuable business, but one that competitors can imitate.

Over the past 18 months, EvenUp has expanded into AI software that helps lawyers manage cases from start to finish. Its newest offering goes a step further, combining AI agents with human case managers to handle much of the work that happens before a lawsuit is filed.

The expansion has transformed EvenUp's business. In early 2025, demand letters accounted for more than 90% of revenue, Karabibar said. Today, revenue is spread more evenly across its products, and demand letters represent less than a quarter of the business.

EvenUp now serves more than 2,000 personal injury firms and supports 20,000 cases each week. Law firms pay a fixed price per case and sign annual contracts committing to a certain volume of cases.

EvenUp may have barely scratched the surface. Most law firms still use only one of its products, Karabibar said. The company sees an opportunity to land customers with one offering, then expand into other parts of their business.

To make that happen, EvenUp has hired Stevie Case, the former chief revenue officer of Vanta, as president of field operations. She will oversee sales, marketing, and customer service as the company looks to win more law firms and sell additional products to existing customers.

Case and her team will still have to convince law firms to choose EvenUp over rivals.

Eve, founded a year after EvenUp, also targets plaintiff-side firms and says it now serves nearly 2,000, up from more than 1,400 in June.

Supio is gaining ground, too. The startup said it more than doubled its customer base in the first half of this year, though it declined to say how many customers it has. It appears the market for plaintiff-side legal tech is still up for grabs.

EvenUp investors, at least, appear to be doubling down.

The company raised $150 million in a Series E round led by existing investor Bessemer Venture Partners last year. Karabibar suggested the company has plenty of financial firepower left for the fight ahead.

"We haven't touched a dollar of that yet," he said.

items.title: Cloudflare Develops Public Certificate Authority for Post-Quantum Web Security
items.summary: Cloudflare is developing a public certificate authority for Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) to reduce the bandwidth overhead of post-quantum cryptography. A Chrome experiment served billions of MTCs to 50% of Chrome Beta 146 for selected domains, reporting 9% faster median performance. Wider deployment depends on browser support, transparency, and production-scale validation. By Leela Kumili

items.title: Real-time state has a cost your memory bill won’t show
items.summary: Real-time applications often combine tools with distinct roles. A typical setup might use Kafka to handle events, Flink to process them, Redis to serve the latest state, and a database to maintain the system of record. Applications that use vector search may add a vector store, too. This division of responsibilities offers flexibility and independent scaling. It also creates costs when data moves between components or when overlapping state is maintained in more than one place. “The copies to question are those maintained largely because processing happens in one system and applications read the results from another.” Some of those copies are necessary. Replicas protect against failures, checkpoints help systems recover, and durable event logs preserve history. They’re worth paying for. The copies to question are those maintained largely because processing happens in one system and applications read the results from another. Take a velocity counter tracking a payment card’s transactions over the past five minutes. Flink calculates the count and maintains keyed state to support that computation. But a fraud-scoring service also needs to retrieve the result. Flink’s internal state isn’t designed for general-purpose serving, and Flink deprecated its Queryable State feature in 1.18. A common solution is to publish the count to Redis. That gives applications a dedicated serving layer, with its own scaling and operational requirements. Flink’s working state and the Redis value may overlap but not be identical, and each published update involves serialization, network traffic, and processing before consumers see it. Where consistency gets complicated Keeping state synchronized gets more complicated when applications span availability zones. Consider a hypothetical payment system that serves reads from asynchronous replicas in several availability zones to reduce cross-zone traffic. A refund goes through, but the update is still making its way to one of those replicas. A service reading from it could see the transaction as not yet refunded and issue another refund, even though the first has already been processed. Without coordination between the refund paths, the customer could be paid twice. “Without coordination between the refund paths, the customer could be paid twice.” This is an application-design concern wherever decisions depend on asynchronously replicated state. Putting processing and storage on the same platform wouldn’t necessarily prevent it. The immediate issue is replica lag, combined with an application that decides without atomically checking and updating the state that authorizes the refund. If the refund calls an external payment service, that service also needs an idempotent request mechanism so retries cannot issue the same refund twice. A separate processing-and-serving design also introduces a publication delay: the processor may calculate an updated value before the serving store receives it. That’s export lag, distinct from replica lag within the serving store. During that lag, a burst of fraudulent transactions can be scored against an out-of-date count. Export lag and replica lag can leave applications reading stale data, but neither should be confused with the check-then-act race that could cause the duplicate refund. Hazelcast can avoid the separate publication step for workloads where computation runs directly against stored state. Its entry processors can atomically update individual map entries on the member holding the relevant key. That doesn’t make the system automatically strongly consistent during network partitions, though. Applications needing stronger coordination can use appropriately configured data structures in Hazelcast’s Raft-based CP subsystem . Using it does not turn an ordinary IMap into a strongly consistent map, or make a map update atomic with an external payment. Separate processing and storage systems can also use strongly consistent coordination. The cost of moving state Memory tends to dominate discussions of in-memory architectures, but CPU and networking costs can matter just as much. A 2025 paper from UC Berkeley and Databricks, Rethinking the Cost of Distributed Caches for Datacenter Services , examined caching economics using synthetic workloads, Meta traces, and production data from Databricks’ Unity Catalog. “Memory tends to dominate discussions of in-memory architectures, but CPU and networking costs can matter just as much.” Using the paper’s Google Cloud pricing assumptions of roughly $17 per vCPU-month and $2 per gigabyte-month of memory, the researchers found that adding in-memory caching cut operating costs by a factor of three to four. The CPU savings outweighed the cost of the additional RAM. That isn’t a comparison of Hazelcast against Flink and Redis; the study compares caching with no caching. Its remote-versus-linked-cache comparison supports the narrower argument that communication and serialization consume CPU. The paper also found that per-read version checks for stronger consistency could erase much of the cost benefit, so comparisons need equivalent consistency requirements. A 2019 paper by Google researchers, “Fast Key-Value Stores: An Idea Whose Time Has Come and Gone,” reported a 40% reduction in p99.9 latency for ProtoCache, a component of a Google application, after moving from a remote key-value store to an architecture that keeps application logic and in-memory state together . A separate, illustrative calculation shows the memory cost of maintaining two equivalent working sets. At the paper’s assumed memory price, 400 GB would represent about $800 a month in memory alone, before backups, checkpoints, and other infrastructure. Maintaining an equivalent amount in both processing and serving tiers would double that figure, although Flink’s intermediate state and the results published to Redis can differ substantially. Then there’s the work involved in keeping the systems synchronized. Each update must be serialized, transmitted, and processed, and both platforms require monitoring, scaling, and maintenance. One way to get a sense of this overhead is to count the steps involved in a single read-modify-write operation. With separate processing and serving systems, an event might be ingested, keyed state updated, the result serialized and published, then written to the serving store before an application reads it. That’s potentially four or five serialization or network steps for one update. Running the computation where the state is stored can reduce that to a single step. It’s not a precise measure of cost, but tracing the path of an update can help identify where CPU time and network resources are being spent. A fair total-cost comparison also needs node counts, instance types, licensing, discounts, and equivalent managed-versus-self-managed deployments. The $800 figure is memory arithmetic, not a total-cost estimate or measured Hazelcast saving. Bringing computation closer to the data Hazelcast provides one way to bring processing closer to stored data . Rather than sending information back and forth between separate systems, it distributes data across cluster members according to key and can run computations on the member that holds it. It keeps backup copies in case a member fails. Hazelcast offers two approaches, depending on the kind of processing involved. Hazelcast’s Jet engine can maintain internal state for windowed stream calculations and publish results to a distributed map that applications can read. That intermediate state and the result-publication step still exist on the same platform; processing, map writes, and backups may also involve traffic between members. Kafka can remain the durable event log in either design, and the database of record can remain in place. For applications that need to update stored values directly, Hazelcast also has entry processors . These run code against the map entry itself, rather than calculating a result elsewhere and then copying it across. Take the transaction counter discussed earlier. An entry processor could maintain per-minute transaction counts in a distributed map, and the application could sum the most recent five buckets to calculate the total. This avoids the need for a timer to remove expired transactions, though the result would be accurate to the minute rather than the second. The application would still need to account for late or duplicate events. Keep entry processors lightweight, since a long-running operation can block other work on the same partition. Network traffic still occurs between clients and the cluster, and Hazelcast still maintains backup copies. Serialization costs also depend on the map’s in-memory format : the default BINARY format stores serialized values, while OBJECT can reduce conversion work for entry processing. The difference is that, for workloads suited to this approach, there’s no separate processing tier that needs to keep publishing updates to the serving store. When separate systems make sense Keeping processing and storage apart has one significant advantage: each can scale independently. Consider an application running complex decision rules that produce little more than a yes-or-no answer. It might need substantial CPU capacity but very little storage. A separate processing tier allows teams to add compute resources without expanding the serving infrastructure. Other applications hold large amounts of state but do relatively little processing. Putting both workloads on one cluster may offer limited savings, particularly if CPU-intensive tasks compete with latency-sensitive reads. Separate platforms also allow independent deployments, workload isolation, and access to specialized processing features. Hazelcast can offer some of that flexibility within a single cluster, too. Its lite members handle compute tasks without storing data, allowing teams to dedicate regular members to storage and add compute capacity separately. For some workloads, keeping processing and storage on entirely separate platforms will still make sense. But when applications frequently read and update the same state, Hazelcast can reduce data movement between systems. What to measure before making the switch The starting point should be a profile of the existing deployment. How much CPU time goes into application logic, and how much is spent serializing data or communicating across the network? How much state is actually duplicated between processing and serving? Average response times won’t tell the whole story, either. A system might perform well most of the time but slow down considerably on certain requests. That’s why it’s worth checking p99 and p99.9 request latency, along with throughput and end-to-end latency: the time from an event arriving to its result being readable, including any export lag. Run the comparison with the same workload, the same end-to-end latency target, and the same durability guarantees. Failure testing matters as well: check recovery time, replay behavior, duplicate handling, and correctness during node failures and network partitions. Backup copies and recovery mechanisms add to the infrastructure bill. For some applications, independently scaling processing and storage will remain the better choice. Others may find they’re paying to move data between systems when they could do the same work directly against application-accessible state. Not every copy is unnecessary. Replicas protect against failures, checkpoints support recovery, and stream processors need intermediate state. The copies worth questioning are those maintained largely because processing and serving happen in different systems.

items.title: Nvidia’s Board Opens Investigation Tied to Jensen Huang: What Investors Should Watch
items.summary: Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation after reports that a foreign intelligence effort targeted CEO Jensen Huang, and the company at the center of the AI trade now faces questions about its leadership before it reports earnings on November 17. Nvidia shares fell roughly 5% to 6% in premarket trading on Monday. The drop extends a slide that began in early October. What the board is investigating The New York Times reported on October 29 that US intelligence officials concluded a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-center company and Nvidia customer, was passing information to Beijing, and that surveillance showed a close relationship between the executive and Huang. A November 6 follow-up said a Chinese spy agency had recruited the executive to collect information on Huang. Officials did not believe Huang knew when they first briefed President Donald Trump about a year ago, though the Times said it is unclear whether that view has changed and some senior officials doubt he could have been unaware. Everything here rests on anonymous sources describing classified intelligence, and authorities have charged no one. The Times could not determine which agencies monitored the executive. Nvidia says Megaspeed is a regional customer like any other, that it investigated and debunked the diversion claims last year, and that Huang’s contact with customer executives is routine. Trade records cited by the Times indicate a Malaysian sister company of Megaspeed bought at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026. Large purchases do not prove diversion, and Nvidia says it has found no evidence of smuggling. On November 4, the chairs of three US House committees (Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and Intelligence) asked Huang for a voluntary closed-door briefing on November 18 and requested a reply by November 11. Nvidia has not said whether he will attend. On Sunday the board announced a review overseen by independent directors with outside counsel. It said it has no reason to believe anyone compromised national security or Nvidia’s secrets, expressed confidence in Huang and his team, and set no end date. Huang emailed employees the same day. The Financial Times, which obtained the message, reported that he acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, wrote that there is “no excuse for what I did,” and promised full cooperation. As reported, the email did not directly address the intelligence allegations. A sell-off that started before the story The data suggests the Huang story did not start this slide. Nvidia lost 23.5% between October 7 and November 5, against 5.7% for the S&P 500, according to Trefis. On November 5 alone, Nvidia fell 9.26% to $181.60, AMD and Micron each dropped more than 17%, and the S&P 500 fell 4.4% in its worst session since April 2025. Coverage of that session pointed elsewhere: IBTimes reported that investors were questioning the pace, cost and financing of the AI boom, and Trefis cited post-election fears of a data-center slowdown and a weak Qualcomm outlook. Nvidia made no announcement that day, though the House letter surfaced the same day. Bloomberg reported that Nvidia’s Asian suppliers shrugged off Monday’s news. That pattern suggests investors treat the Huang matter as a governance risk at one company, not yet a threat to AI demand. The exposure reaches beyond Nvidia’s shareholders, because AP notes that a 1% move in Nvidia moves the S&P 500 more than a 1% move in almost any other US stock. What it means if Huang stays The board holds the power. Huang owns less than 4% of the company, and nine of the ten directors on the 2026 slate are independent, with Huang the only insider. The investigation therefore tests whether independent directors act as a check on a founder or as his advocates. Staying is the near-term base case. The board has expressed confidence in him and Trump has said he should keep the job. If the review finds no compromise, the stock goes back to trading on earnings and on guidance that already assumes no China data-center compute revenue. The remaining political risk sits in export compliance, where Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks asked Commerce in March to examine Huang’s 2025 statements on chip diversion. Staying also keeps the concentration that makes the stock sensitive to one person. Bloomberg reported in January that Nvidia lacks a clear successor, and a departure would be the most disruptive outcome. It looks unlikely on current signals, and Intel is an imperfect guide: CEO Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 over a relationship with an employee that violated company policy, while Nvidia’s board describes a foreign intelligence effort and sees no sign of compromise. What Huang needs to do to rebuild trust The apology covers only the personal part of this story, and it does not reach the part investors actually care about. The questions that matter are narrower: did the relationship influence any sales approval, customer decision or access to information, and did Nvidia’s controls work? Documents can answer those more convincingly than denials. First, Huang should ask the board to put a date on the review and publish a summary of its conclusions. Privilege will limit what the board can release, but a summary of scope, findings and remedies costs little against open-ended uncertainty. Second, he should accept the November 18 briefing unless his counsel advises otherwise, because declining would hand critics a story and appearing lets him answer on the record. While the review runs, he should step away from decisions involving Megaspeed and its affiliates. Third, the company needs to address oversight, since governance specialist Nell Minow criticized the board in 2024 for thin governance experience and unclear succession planning. A named succession process would show that Nvidia can withstand scrutiny of its founder without depending on him. What Musk’s and Trump’s support signals Trump told reporters on Sunday that Huang should remain CEO and that he had heard of no wrongdoing. On October 31 he had left open the possibility that his view could change if investigators find something new. Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire wrote on X that Huang ranks among the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation, and Elon Musk replied that he agreed. Both endorsers have ties to Nvidia. Nvidia holds a stake in xAI, and Huang has described hand-delivering the first DGX-1 system to Musk in 2016. The Times reported that Trump took no action on the findings a year ago and has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales and complicating trade relations with China. The support lowers the odds of an abrupt federal move against Nvidia. It does not bind the board, Congress or the intelligence agencies, and scrutiny crosses party lines: three House Republican committee chairs want the briefing, and Democratic Sen. Warren says Huang and the board owe Congress answers. The endorsements carry a cost: a board that investigates after the president has said Huang should stay must work harder to show independence. For the wider industry, the signals suggest a friendly White House keeps export relief plausible, while a compliance failure at Nvidia would give critics an argument for tighter limits on every chipmaker. Nvidia announced partnerships with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to set up financing platforms that aim to mobilize more than $500 billion of third-party capital for the buildout.
