items.summary_html:
Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation after reports that a foreign intelligence effort targeted CEO Jensen Huang, and the company at the center of the AI trade now faces questions about its leadership before it reports earnings on November 17. Nvidia shares fell roughly 5% to 6% in premarket trading on Monday. The drop extends a slide that began in early October.

What the board is investigating

The New York Times reported on October 29 that US intelligence officials concluded a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-center company and Nvidia customer, was passing information to Beijing, and that surveillance showed a close relationship between the executive and Huang. A November 6 follow-up said a Chinese spy agency had recruited the executive to collect information on Huang. Officials did not believe Huang knew when they first briefed President Donald Trump about a year ago, though the Times said it is unclear whether that view has changed and some senior officials doubt he could have been unaware.

Everything here rests on anonymous sources describing classified intelligence, and authorities have charged no one. The Times could not determine which agencies monitored the executive. Nvidia says Megaspeed is a regional customer like any other, that it investigated and debunked the diversion claims last year, and that Huang’s contact with customer executives is routine.

Trade records cited by the Times indicate a Malaysian sister company of Megaspeed bought at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026. Large purchases do not prove diversion, and Nvidia says it has found no evidence of smuggling. On November 4, the chairs of three US House committees (Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and Intelligence) asked Huang for a voluntary closed-door briefing on November 18 and requested a reply by November 11. Nvidia has not said whether he will attend.

On Sunday the board announced a review overseen by independent directors with outside counsel. It said it has no reason to believe anyone compromised national security or Nvidia’s secrets, expressed confidence in Huang and his team, and set no end date. Huang emailed employees the same day. The Financial Times, which obtained the message, reported that he acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, wrote that there is “no excuse for what I did,” and promised full cooperation. As reported, the email did not directly address the intelligence allegations.

A sell-off that started before the story

The data suggests the Huang story did not start this slide. Nvidia lost 23.5% between October 7 and November 5, against 5.7% for the S&P 500, according to Trefis. On November 5 alone, Nvidia fell 9.26% to $181.60, AMD and Micron each dropped more than 17%, and the S&P 500 fell 4.4% in its worst session since April 2025.

Coverage of that session pointed elsewhere: IBTimes reported that investors were questioning the pace, cost and financing of the AI boom, and Trefis cited post-election fears of a data-center slowdown and a weak Qualcomm outlook. Nvidia made no announcement that day, though the House letter surfaced the same day.

Bloomberg reported that Nvidia’s Asian suppliers shrugged off Monday’s news. That pattern suggests investors treat the Huang matter as a governance risk at one company, not yet a threat to AI demand. The exposure reaches beyond Nvidia’s shareholders, because AP notes that a 1% move in Nvidia moves the S&P 500 more than a 1% move in almost any other US stock.

What it means if Huang stays

The board holds the power. Huang owns less than 4% of the company, and nine of the ten directors on the 2026 slate are independent, with Huang the only insider. The investigation therefore tests whether independent directors act as a check on a founder or as his advocates.

Staying is the near-term base case. The board has expressed confidence in him and Trump has said he should keep the job. If the review finds no compromise, the stock goes back to trading on earnings and on guidance that already assumes no China data-center compute revenue. The remaining political risk sits in export compliance, where Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks asked Commerce in March to examine Huang’s 2025 statements on chip diversion.

Staying also keeps the concentration that makes the stock sensitive to one person. Bloomberg reported in January that Nvidia lacks a clear successor, and a departure would be the most disruptive outcome. It looks unlikely on current signals, and Intel is an imperfect guide: CEO Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 over a relationship with an employee that violated company policy, while Nvidia’s board describes a foreign intelligence effort and sees no sign of compromise.

What Huang needs to do to rebuild trust

The apology covers only the personal part of this story, and it does not reach the part investors actually care about. The questions that matter are narrower: did the relationship influence any sales approval, customer decision or access to information, and did Nvidia’s controls work? Documents can answer those more convincingly than denials.

First, Huang should ask the board to put a date on the review and publish a summary of its conclusions. Privilege will limit what the board can release, but a summary of scope, findings and remedies costs little against open-ended uncertainty. Second, he should accept the November 18 briefing unless his counsel advises otherwise, because declining would hand critics a story and appearing lets him answer on the record.

While the review runs, he should step away from decisions involving Megaspeed and its affiliates. Third, the company needs to address oversight, since governance specialist Nell Minow criticized the board in 2024 for thin governance experience and unclear succession planning. A named succession process would show that Nvidia can withstand scrutiny of its founder without depending on him.

What Musk’s and Trump’s support signals

Trump told reporters on Sunday that Huang should remain CEO and that he had heard of no wrongdoing. On October 31 he had left open the possibility that his view could change if investigators find something new. Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire wrote on X that Huang ranks among the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation, and Elon Musk replied that he agreed.

Both endorsers have ties to Nvidia. Nvidia holds a stake in xAI, and Huang has described hand-delivering the first DGX-1 system to Musk in 2016. The Times reported that Trump took no action on the findings a year ago and has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales and complicating trade relations with China.

The support lowers the odds of an abrupt federal move against Nvidia. It does not bind the board, Congress or the intelligence agencies, and scrutiny crosses party lines: three House Republican committee chairs want the briefing, and Democratic Sen. Warren says Huang and the board owe Congress answers. The endorsements carry a cost: a board that investigates after the president has said Huang should stay must work harder to show independence. For the wider industry, the signals suggest a friendly White House keeps export relief plausible, while a compliance failure at Nvidia would give critics an argument for tighter limits on every chipmaker.

The AI bubble question

Nothing in the evidence shows the Huang matter causing a bubble to burst or revealing one. The market was already fragile, and it reacted to news about its most important stock. Nvidia’s fundamentals remain strong: revenue for the quarter reported on August 26 reached $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, and the company guided to $108 billion for the current quarter without any China data-center compute revenue.

The bubble debate centers on financing. On November 2, Oracle filed to sell $10 billion of stock and $10 billion of senior notes to fund its AI buildout, and its shares fell more than 5%. Nvidia announced partnerships with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to set up financing platforms that aim to mobilize more than $500 billion of third-party capital for the buildout.

The Huang investigation works as a stress test and a possible catalyst. It measures how much confidence in AI infrastructure rests on one company and one executive, when investors already ask who pays for the buildout. If Nvidia holds its guidance on November 17 and the review finds no compromise, the episode probably fades from the price. If the review widens into export compliance or customer diligence, it could revive pressure for tighter controls and deepen doubts about builders that depend on outside capital.

Three dates that matter

Nvidia has until November 11 to answer the House request, reports earnings on November 17 and faces the proposed briefing on November 18. Those dates will show whether the guidance holds, whether Huang answers questions on the record and how much the board is willing to say. The investigation has no deadline, and the length of the board’s silence will carry its own signal.

What Is MLOps? Architecture, MLOps vs DevOps, and LLMOps

In this lesson, you will learn what MLOps is and why it is essential for scaling machine learning systems. We will explore how MLOps extends DevOps to manage not just code, but also data, models, and experiments, and compare the DevOps and MLOps lifecycles.

You will also get a high-level view of MLOps architecture, see how teams progress through maturity levels, and cover the MLOps tooling landscape from foundations to serving, deployment, and cloud platforms.

Along the way, we will include a short Linux basics primer (most modern MLOps/MLflow workflows run on Linux) to prepare readers for hands-on work in future lessons.

Finally, we will touch on LLMOps to understand what it is, how it relates to MLOps, and why it is becoming critical in the era of large language models.

This lesson is the 1st in a 3-part series on Machine Learning Operations (MLOps):

  1. What Is MLOps? Architecture, MLOps vs DevOps, and LLMOps (this tutorial)
  2. Lesson 2
  3. Lesson 3

To learn how to apply MLOps, including what it is, how it differs from DevOps, and where concepts such as MLOps architecture and LLMOps fit in, just keep reading.

Looking for the source code to this post? Jump Right To The Downloads Section
What Is MLOps?

At its core, MLOps (Machine Learning Operations) extends DevOps principles to the world of machine learning (ML). If DevOps is about managing the software lifecycle (from code to deployment), then MLOps is about managing the entire ML lifecycle: code, data, models, and experiments.

The key difference lies in what gets released. In traditional software, once you ship a binary, it stays the same until developers update the code. In machine learning, models are living artifacts. Their performance degrades as data distributions shift, and they require ongoing retraining or fine-tuning to stay useful.

Figure 1: Traditional software releases only code, while ML releases also depend on data and model parameters (source: image by the author)

But it is not just about the release. In ML systems, all 3 components (code, data, and models) evolve together.

  • New data arrives and may require relabeling.
  • Models must be retrained or replaced to keep up.
  • Code (algorithms, preprocessing, and infrastructure) adapts alongside them.
Figure 2: In ML applications, data, model, and code form a continuous feedback loop, with each change triggering updates to the others (source: https://ml-ops.org).

This makes MLOps far more than just “DevOps + ML.” It is a discipline designed to:

  • Version and track not only code, but also datasets and models.
  • Automate training, testing, and deployment pipelines.
  • Continuously monitor for drift and trigger retraining loops.
  • Ensure reproducibility across experiments and environments.

In short, MLOps is the glue that connects research notebooks to production systems. It helps turn fragile prototypes into reliable, scalable, and maintainable applications.

Why MLOps Matters for Production Machine Learning

It is easy to underestimate the gap between a great model in a Jupyter notebook and a robust system in production. Without MLOps, most teams hit the same pain points over and over:

  • “It works on my machine” syndrome: Running the same code on another machine gives different results because the data, libraries, or environment are not identical.
  • Model decay: Accuracy steadily drops after deployment as real-world data drifts away from training data.
  • Data chaos: No clear versioning or lineage for datasets. Teams cannot reproduce past experiments.
  • Wasted effort: Without experiment tracking, teams repeat trials that were already run but never logged.

The consequences are not academic. They are expensive.

  • Recommendation systems stop showing relevant items when customer behavior changes.
  • Fraud detection pipelines fail to keep up with new attack patterns.
  • Large language models require ongoing prompt updates and fine-tuning to remain useful.

MLOps addresses these problems head-on:

  • Reproducibility: lock down code, data, and models so results can be recreated exactly.
  • Reliability: models are deployed through pipelines, not copy-paste scripts.
  • Scalability: teams can retrain and redeploy with automation instead of manual handoffs.
  • Collaboration: data scientists, ML engineers, and DevOps teams work on a shared process.

When you adopt MLOps, models do not just “work once.” They keep working in production, evolving alongside the data they serve.

Core Principles of MLOps

MLOps is not just a set of tools. It is a set of principles that guide how machine learning systems are built, deployed, and maintained. A solid MLOps practice rests on the following 4 pillars.

1. Automation

The goal is to minimize manual handoffs. Data pipelines, training jobs, model packaging, and deployment should run automatically through continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. Automation reduces human error and shortens the time from experiment to production.

Example: Instead of a data scientist manually exporting a trained model, a pipeline retrains nightly and deploys the new version if it meets accuracy thresholds.

2. Reproducibility

Every model should be reproducible: same code, same data, same parameters → same result. This requires versioning not just of code, but also datasets, features, and model weights.

Example: MLflow or DVC can log experiments so you can revisit the exact conditions that produced a model months later.

3. Scalability

Prototypes often run on a laptop, but production models serve millions of predictions daily. MLOps ensures systems can scale horizontally (more replicas) and vertically (more compute), while pipelines handle larger datasets seamlessly.

Example: A fraud detection model that worked for thousands of transactions now needs to score millions. Kubernetes or serverless deployment can scale it without code changes.

4. Monitoring and Governance

Models cannot be “deploy once and forget.” Monitoring ensures that accuracy, latency, and drift are tracked continuously. Governance establishes controls and documentation that support compliance (fairness, privacy, and explainability) in regulated industries.

Example: A credit scoring model must flag if predictions start showing bias toward a subgroup, triggering retraining or human review.

Together, these pillars keep ML systems reliable, accountable, and future-proof. They also map directly to the MLOps lifecycle:

  • automation: powers the pipelines
  • reproducibility: secures experiments
  • scalability: supports deployment
  • monitoring and governance: closes the loop
MLOps vs DevOps: Key Lifecycle Differences

DevOps transformed how software teams build and ship applications. The process is well-defined: build → test → deploy → monitor. Once an application is shipped, it generally behaves the same until developers update the code.

Machine learning lifecycles look similar at a distance, but they introduce critical differences:

  • Data is first-class: The lifecycle does not start with “build.” It starts with data collection and preprocessing.
  • Validation goes beyond tests: Instead of just running unit tests, ML workflows validate against metrics such as accuracy, precision, or F1 score.
  • Models evolve: Monitoring is not just about uptime; it is about detecting drift. A healthy model may still lose accuracy as the real world changes.
  • Retraining closes the loop: Unlike software, where updates are developer-driven, ML requires automatic or scheduled retraining cycles.

A side-by-side comparison makes it clear (see Figure 3).

Figure 3: DevOps vs MLOps lifecycles. MLOps introduces data, validation, and retraining loops that traditional DevOps does not cover (source: https://www.databricks.com/blog/what-is-mlops).

Notice how MLOps extends DevOps with additional steps for data, validation, and retraining.

The extra loops (data, validation, and retraining) are why MLOps needs its own discipline. Traditional DevOps tooling does not fully capture these dynamics.

MLOps Architecture: How It All Fits Together

MLOps is not just a collection of tools. It is an architecture that ties together the entire machine learning lifecycle. The goal is to ensure that data, models, and code move seamlessly from experimentation to production while remaining reproducible, scalable, and reliable.

At the highest level, the MLOps lifecycle can be thought of in 3 interconnected stages (see Figure 4).

Figure 4: High-level MLOps lifecycle: Design → Model Development → Operations. Each of these stages expands into more detailed layers in a full MLOps architecture (source: MLOps Principles)
  • Design: requirements engineering, use case prioritization, data availability checks
  • Model Development: data engineering, model training, validation, iteration
  • Operations: deployment, CI/CD pipelines, monitoring, feedback loops

While this 3-stage view captures the essence, in practice each stage is supported by multiple layers and tools. A typical MLOps architecture looks like this:

Data Layer
  • Data ingestion (databases, APIs, streams)
  • Storage (data lakes, warehouses)
  • Versioning (DVC, lakeFS)
Experimentation and Training Layer
  • Prototyping (Jupyter, Colab, scripts)
  • Training pipelines (Kubeflow, Airflow, SageMaker)
  • Experiment tracking and model registry (MLflow, W&B)
Deployment Layer
  • Model packaging (Docker, ONNX, TorchServe)
  • Serving APIs (FastAPI, Flask, KServe, Lambda)
  • CI/CD pipelines for model delivery
Monitoring and Feedback Layer
  • Model performance metrics (accuracy, latency, drift detection)
  • Infrastructure monitoring (Prometheus, Grafana)
  • Feedback loops triggering retraining
Governance and Compliance Layer
  • Audit trails for data and models
  • Explainability and fairness checks
  • Security and access control

Together, these layers form a closed loop: data flows in, models are trained and deployed, predictions are monitored, and results feed back into retraining pipelines.

MLOps Maturity Levels

Not every team practices MLOps at the same depth. Just as DevOps adoption matures over time, MLOps also has levels of sophistication. Understanding these levels helps teams assess where they stand today and what is next on their roadmap.

Level 0: Manual and Ad Hoc
  • Experiments live in notebooks or scripts on individual machines.
  • Data is not versioned, and results cannot be reproduced.
  • Deployment might mean copying a .pkl file to a server.
  • Monitoring is manual, if it happens at all.

Risk: High chance of “it worked once, but we don’t know why.”

Level 1: Partial Automation
  • Some reproducibility through version control (Git) and basic experiment tracking (e.g., MLflow).
  • Pipelines exist but may be stitched together manually.
  • Deployment is more structured, but retraining cycles are still irregular.
  • Monitoring might check uptime, but drift detection is weak.

Benefit: Teams save time by reusing pipelines, but scaling is still painful.

Level 2: Full Automation
  • End-to-end pipelines handle data ingestion, training, validation, and deployment.
  • CI/CD is fully integrated, with automated testing of models.
  • Drift monitoring triggers retraining loops automatically.
  • Governance, audit trails, and compliance are built in.

Benefit: Models evolve smoothly with data, and the business can trust ML systems long-term.

Most organizations start at Level 0 or 1 and gradually build toward Level 2. The key is progress: every step toward automation and reproducibility reduces technical debt and unlocks scalability.

MLOps Tools for Data, Training, Deployment, and Monitoring

Talking about MLOps without mentioning tools would feel incomplete. But instead of diving deep into each one right now, let us zoom out and map the ecosystem. Think of this as a preview of what is coming in future lessons.

Figure 5: The MLOps tooling ecosystem spans data management, modeling, deployment, and end-to-end ML platforms (source: [Infographic] Data & Machine Learning Tools Landscape | DataCamp)

This ecosystem is huge, covering everything from managing datasets to serving models in production. To keep things practical, we will focus on a few core categories that we will explore in depth throughout the series.

Tools for Data Versioning and Experiment Tracking
  • Docker: containerizes ML applications for portability.
  • DVC (Data Version Control): versions datasets and pipelines.
  • MLflow / Weights & Biases (W&B): experiment tracking and model registry.
Model Training Frameworks and Feature Stores
  • PyTorch Lightning: structures training code for reproducibility.
  • TensorFlow, PyTorch, and XGBoost: are frameworks for training deep learning and classical ML models.
  • Feature Stores: manage and reuse features consistently across training and serving.
Model Serving, Deployment, and Monitoring Tools
  • FastAPI: is a lightweight API for serving ML models
  • TorchServe: is a production model serving framework for PyTorch
  • AWS SageMaker, ECS, and Lambda: are cloud-native deployment options
  • Model Monitoring: tools such as Evidently, Arize, or WhyLabs help detect accuracy and fairness issues in production
End-to-End Machine Learning Platforms
  • AWS SageMaker, Azure ML, Databricks, DataRobot: are end-to-end platforms that combine data, training, deployment, and monitoring into one managed environment.

The key takeaway: no team uses everything at once. The best tools are the ones that serve your workflow. As we move through this series, we will piece these building blocks together, showing how to combine them into an end-to-end MLOps practice.

What Is LLMOps? Operations for Large Language Models

As large language models (LLMs) such as GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer), LLaMA, and Mistral have moved from research into production, they have introduced new operational challenges. Traditional MLOps practices still apply, but the scale, complexity, and open-ended nature of LLMs demand their own extension: LLMOps.

At a high level, LLMOps is about applying the same principles of MLOps (automation, reproducibility, scalability, and monitoring) but adapting them to the unique requirements of LLMs:

  • Model Size and Serving: Unlike smaller ML models, LLMs often contain billions of parameters. Serving them requires distributed inference, quantization, or specialized GPU/TPU acceleration. Some companies even use hardware-aware optimizers (e.g., OctoML, Neural Magic) to squeeze efficiency out of large deployments.
  • Continuous Adaptation: Instead of retraining from scratch, teams often fine-tune with LoRA, adapters, or parameter-efficient training methods. On top of that, prompt engineering platforms (e.g., PromptLayer, Vellum) allow non-technical teams to manage prompts as first-class artifacts.
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): LLMs connected to external knowledge bases can stay up to date. This introduces new infrastructure needs such as vector databases (e.g., Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma) and data curation pipelines (e.g., Scale AI, Snorkel).
  • Evaluation and Safety: Unlike a classifier, which can be measured with accuracy or F1, LLMs produce open-ended text. Evaluating them requires new metrics (helpfulness, toxicity, hallucination rate), human feedback loops, and advanced monitoring/guardrails (e.g., Evidently, Arize, WhyLabs, Fiddler).
Figure 6: The emerging LLMOps tooling ecosystem spans everything from data annotation and vector databases for RAG to prompt engineering, deployment frameworks, and monitoring platforms, highlighting how this field is evolving beyond traditional MLOps (source: CB Insights LLM_Ops_market_landscape_6ac51baf56.png).

In short: LLMOps is MLOps, evolved for the LLM era. It builds on the same foundation but emphasizes scalable deployment, resource optimization, continuous adaptation, and safe usage at scale.

We will dive deeper into LLMOps in the advanced lessons of this series, where we will look at how to finetune and deploy LLMs, integrate retrieval pipelines, and set up monitoring for safety. For now, it is enough to recognize that just as MLOps became essential for productionizing ML, LLMOps is quickly becoming essential for productionizing LLMs.

LLMOps vs MLOps: Key Differences

MLOps and LLMOps share the same foundation i.e. bringing DevOps discipline to machine learning but the scale, complexity, and behavior of LLMs introduce new challenges that traditional MLOps does not fully address.

Table 1 compares MLOps and LLMOps.

Table 1: Comparing MLOps and LLMOps workflows

In other words, LLMOps extends MLOps by adding specialized workflows for:

  • handling massive models at inference time
  • updating models efficiently with lightweight fine-tuning
  • managing external retrieval pipelines
  • ensuring safe and aligned generation
Linux Basics for MLOps

If you are serious about MLOps, you need to be comfortable with Linux. Many ML workloads (whether it runs on a cloud VM, in a Docker container, or on a Kubernetes cluster) will run on a Linux server.

Even if you are training models on your laptop today, the moment you deploy to production, you will be SSH-ing into Linux boxes, tailing logs, and debugging file permissions. The earlier you build muscle memory, the smoother everything else becomes.

Why Linux Matters for MLOps Workflows
  • Servers Run Linux: AWS EC2, GCP, and Azure all default to Linux images.
  • Containers Use Linux: Docker and Kubernetes are built on Linux concepts (namespaces, cgroups).
  • Automation Assumes Linux: CI/CD pipelines, shell scripts, and cron jobs live in a Linux environment.

Learning Linux is not about memorizing 200 commands. It is about knowing the 20% of commands you will use 80% of the time.

Starter Commands for Everyday Use SSH (Secure Shell)

SSH is a protocol used to securely log onto remote systems. It is used most often in the command-line interface for Unix-like systems such as Linux. SSH provides a secure channel over an unsecured network in a client-server architecture. For instance, if you are at a computer in New York and need to manage a server located in Tokyo, you could use SSH to log into the server and run commands as if you were there in person.

Example:

ssh username@remotehost.com

The above command logs you into remotehost.com with the username username.

Vim

Vim is a highly configurable text editor built to enable efficient text editing. It is an improved version of the vi editor distributed with most UNIX systems. It has many commands and is known for its keyboard-centered operation, which lets users perform tasks efficiently without the use of a mouse.

Example:

vim filename.txt

This command opens the file filename.txt in Vim. If the file does not exist, it will be created.

htop

htop is an interactive system-monitoring tool for Unix-based systems. It provides a real-time, dynamic view of the processes running on a system. htop is much more interactive than the standard top command. It allows for scrolling vertically and horizontally to display processes and complete command lines.

Example:

htop

This command will run htop, displaying a real-time overview of system processes.

ps

The ps command in Unix and Linux is used to display information about active processes. It provides a snapshot of the current processes along with detailed information such as user identifier (ID), central processing unit (CPU) usage, memory usage, and command name.

Example:

ps -aux

The above command displays all processes from all users in a detailed format.

scp (Secure Copy)

The scp command is used to securely copy files and directories between 2 locations. Like SSH, scp uses the SSH protocol for data transfer.

Example:

scp /path/to/local/file username@remotehost:/path/to/remote/directory

The above command copies a local file to a remote directory.

rsync (Remote Sync)

rsync is a fast and versatile tool used for copying and synchronizing files both locally and remotely. rsync is great for maintaining backups and mirroring data because it only transfers the difference between source and destination.

Example:

rsync -avz /path/to/source/directory/ username@remotehost:/path/to/destination/directory/

This command syncs the contents of the source directory to the destination directory. The -avz flags enable archive mode (-a), verbose output (-v), and compression during transfer (-z).

tmux (Terminal Multiplexer)

tmux is a terminal multiplexer. It allows you to switch easily between several programs in one terminal, detach them (they keep running in the background), and reattach them to a different terminal.

Example:

tmux new -s train

This command starts a new tmux session. Within this session, you can create new windows (Ctrl+b c), switch between windows (Ctrl+b n for the next window), split windows into panes, and more.

Summary

In this lesson, we introduced MLOps and explained why it has become essential for scaling machine learning systems. We looked at how MLOps extends the principles of DevOps to manage not only code, but also the data, models, and experiments that make ML workflows unique. Along the way, we compared the DevOps and MLOps lifecycles, showing how additional practices (e.g., data validation, drift monitoring, and retraining) set MLOps apart.

We also explored the foundations of MLOps architecture, breaking it into stages and layers that connect data pipelines, training workflows, deployment systems, and monitoring. To make this practical, we discussed how teams progress through different maturity levels, from ad hoc scripts to fully automated pipelines that can retrain and redeploy models with minimal human intervention.

Another highlight was the MLOps tooling landscape. We mapped out the ecosystem from foundational tools (e.g., Docker, DVC, MLflow, and W&B) to deployment tools (e.g., FastAPI, TorchServe, and KServe) and cloud platforms (e.g., AWS SageMaker, Azure ML, and Databricks). To set the stage for hands-on work, we also included a short Linux basics primer. Since most modern MLOps and MLflow workflows run on Linux, learning essential commands now ensures you will be comfortable following along in future lessons.

items.title: Voters rejected data centers in dozens of communities, fueling the narrative that opposition to the AI infrastructure contributed to the 2026 blue wave
items.summary: A woman in New Port Richey, Fla., voices her opposition to the construction of AI data centers on July 18, 2026. Thomas Simonetti/AFP via Getty Images Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections. A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development. The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat , Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers. According to NBC exit poll data , 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%. Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure , housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use , higher utility bills and environmental degradation , outweigh the benefits. I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns. Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms. Data centers, like these near Social Circle, Ga., require enormous amounts of electricity. AP Photo/Mike Stewart Disrupting political polarization In contrast to many other issues , concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines. Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points. The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota , population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally. Allies and adversaries Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote , approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care , given their methodological limitations. These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away. The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance : environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests. William Lawrence, a Democrat who flipped a red House seat in Michigan in the 2026 midterm elections, speaks on the campaign trail. AP Photo/Paul Sancya Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers. Similar concerns killed the Senate version , a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change. Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements. Politics as usual As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers . President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.” Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president. It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built. What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform : “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day. As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring. items.summary_html:
A woman in New Port Richey, Fla., voices her opposition to the construction of AI data centers on July 18, 2026. Thomas Simonetti/AFP via Getty Images

Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections.

A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development.

The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers.

According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%.

Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits.

I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns.

Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms.

Data centers, like these near Social Circle, Ga., require enormous amounts of electricity. AP Photo/Mike Stewart Disrupting political polarization

In contrast to many other issues, concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines.

Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points.

The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally.

Allies and adversaries

Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care, given their methodological limitations.

These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away.

The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance: environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.

William Lawrence, a Democrat who flipped a red House seat in Michigan in the 2026 midterm elections, speaks on the campaign trail. AP Photo/Paul Sancya

Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers.

Similar concerns killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.

Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements.

Politics as usual

As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.”

Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president.

It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built.

What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day.

As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring.

items.summary_html:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Opinion: The climate case for AI has not been made 

—By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm

This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising. Read the full story.

Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests  

Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. 

The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. 

For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. 

Learn more about Dent, her work, and her impact on how we understand the role rainforests play in regulating our climate. 

—Matthew Ponsford

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Nvidia is investigating its own boss
Jensen Huang has admitted to intimacy with a suspected Chinese spy. (NYT $)
+ Shares in Nvidia were down 5% in pre-market trading. (CNBC)
+ Huang’s children are also employed by Nvidia. (WSJ $)

2 Democrats are planning a blitz of investigations into Big Tech
Reportedly starting with Apple, Meta, and Musk’s companies. (WP $)
+ They’re hoping to harness the data center backlash to rein in the AI sector. (Vox $)
+ Here’s why the midterms sparked an AI stock selloff. (BBC)

3 The UN annual climate meeting starts today
It’s the first to be held after confirmation the planet will exceed 1.5 °C warming. (Nature)
+ How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster. (MIT Technology Review)

4 Connecting fridges to the internet looks like a bad move now
We still don’t know who is behind recent hacks, or even if they’re connected. (The Atlantic $)
+ Experts say they should be a “wake up call” for the industry. (NPR)
+ Are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic? (The Guardian)
+ AI is already making online crimes easier. It could get much worse. (MIT Technology Review)

5 Tesla is axing the Cybertruck 
RIP, we hardly knew ye. (Wired $)

Ordinal Data: Ordinal data represents information with a clear order or ranking, but the differences between the values are not quantifiable. Discrete Data: Discrete data consists of separate values or categories you can measure. As you work with discrete data, you’ll often represent it as whole numbers, such as the number of employees in a company. Continuous Data: Continuous data embodies information that can assume any value within a defined range or interval. It’s typically measured on a continuous scale, such as time, temperature, or distance. Measures of Central Tendency : A measure of central tendency is a statistical measure that represents a central value for a dataset . It provides a summary of data by identifying a single value that is most representative of the dataset as a whole. Mean (Arithmetic Average) When to Use: Continuous or discrete numerical data with a symmetric distribution and no extreme values. Limitation: Highly sensitive to outliers and skewed data, which pull the mean away from the true center. 2. Median (Middle Value): When to Use: Skewed distributions (e.g., income, house prices) or ordinal data with potential outliers. Advanced Variants Weighted Mean: Assigns relative weights (w_i) to individual data points based on importance or frequency. While measures of central tendency (like mean, median, and mode) identify the center of the data, measures of dispersion quantify how far individual data points deviate from that center . High dispersion indicates a wide variation in data, while low dispersion indicates consistency and uniformity. Range: The simplest measure of variability is calculated as the difference between the highest and lowest values in a dataset. It provides a quick snapshot of how widely your data is spread out, though it is highly sensitive to extreme outliers. Formula + Example 2. A low variance indicates that the data points are close to the mean and to each other, while a high variance signifies that the data points are widely spread out from the mean. Population and Sample Variance # FAQ: Why is the variance of a population divided by N, while the sample variance is divided by n - 1? 3. Standard Deviation: The standard deviation is simply the positive square root of the variance . While variance measures the average squared distance from the mean, standard deviation brings that metric back to the original unit of measurement , making it much easier to interpret. When to Use: Finance & Investment: Measures portfolio risk and asset volatility (e.g., higher SD indicates greater price fluctuation). Quality Control & Manufacturing: Evaluates production consistency to ensure product dimensions or specs stay within acceptable tolerance limits (e.g., Six Sigma). Statistical Modeling & Testing: Serves as a core input for Z-scores, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and measuring standard error. Performance Evaluation: Compares standardized test scores or survey metrics across different populations relative to the average. Limitation: Because it relies on squared deviations from the mean, Standard Deviation is disproportionately sensitive to extreme outliers, making it misleading for heavily skewed distributions. 4. Formula: When to use: MAD can be used to understand how spread out a dataset is. MAD is commonly used to evaluate forecast errors, it is closely related to MAE ( Mean Absolute Error. Limitation: Sensitive to outliers: Extreme values can increase MAD significantly. MAD can be calculated around the mean or median. The interpretation changes depending on the chosen center. 5. Coefficient Of Variation(CV): Coefficient of Variation (CV) is a statistical measure that shows the relative variability or dispersion of data compared to its mean . In simple words: CV tells us how much variation exists relative to the average value. It is usually expressed as a percentage . Generally: Lower CV → Lower relative variability Higher CV → Higher relative variability This makes CV useful when comparing datasets with different means or different units/scales . Use Case: Finance: Compare risk relative to return between different investments. CV= Risk​ / Average Return 2. Scientific experiments: Compare consistency of measurements from different experiments or instruments. Limitation: Not suitable when the mean is zero or very close to zero Problematic with negative means: Interpretation becomes difficult when the mean is negative. Primarily useful for ratio-scale data: It is not appropriate for arbitrary scales such as temperature measured in Celsius. Shape of Data Skewness: Skewness is a statistical measure that tells us about the asymmetry of a distribution around its mean. In simple words: Skewness tells us whether the data is symmetrically distributed or has a longer tail on one side. Skewness measures the asymmetry or lack of symmetry in a dataset relative to its mean. Positive Skew (Right-skewed): Tail extends toward higher values on the right; Mean > Median > Mode Negative Skew (Left-skewed): Tail extends toward lower values on the left; Mean < Median < Mode Symmetric: Data is evenly distributed on both sides; Mean = Median = Mode Formulation: Interpretation: Skewness(Sk) = 0 then perfect Symmetric Skewness(Sk) > 0 then Positively / right skewed<0<0Small absolute valueApproximately symmetricLarge absolute valueStronger asymmetry Skewness(Sk) < 0 then Negatively / left skewed Small absolute value: approximately symmetric Large absolute value: strong asymmetry Use case: Understand the shape of the distribution Detect asymmetry Identify potential outliers Decide whether a transformation might be useful Understand assumptions behind some statistical models 2. Kurtosis: Kurtosis is a statistical measure that describes the shape of a distribution, particularly the behavior of its tails and the presence of extreme values . In simple words: Kurtosis tells us how prone a distribution is to producing extreme values compared with a normal distribution. A common misconception is that kurtosis only measures “peakedness.” In modern statistics, kurtosis is more closely associated with tail heaviness and extreme observations . Formulation: Type of Kurtosis: Mesokurtic → Kurtosis =3 Leptokurtic → Heavy tails → More extreme values → Kurtosis > 3 Platykurtic → Light tails → Fewer extreme values → Kurtosis < 3 Use Case: Kurtosis is particularly useful for studying financial returns . Outlier / Extreme-value analysis: High kurtosis does not automatically mean that the dataset contains an error or an outlier. Machine Learning / Data Science Limitation: Sensitive to extreme values Does not tell you which observation is an outlier Quantiles & Percentiles : Quantiles are cut-off points that divide a sorted dataset into equal-sized, continuous groups. A percentile is a specific type of quantile that divides data into 100 equal parts. It represents the value below which a certain percentage of data falls. Common Types of Quantiles: Quartiles (4 parts) : Cut data at 25%, 50%, and 75%. Quintiles (5 parts) : Cut data at 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%. Deciles (10 parts) : Cut data at 10%, 20%, …, 90%. percentile(100 Parts): Cut the data at 1%,2%,…99% 90th percentile Means: If your score is at the 90th percentile , it means approximately: 90% of the observations are at or below your score. It does not mean that you scored 90%. Formulation: Example: Use Case: Understand Data Distribution Outlier Detection Income Analysis Relative Scoring in Exam Limitation: Different calculation methods can give different results They don’t show the entire distribution Quantiles can be unstable with very small datasets IQR: One of the most important applications of quantiles is the Interquartile Range . How to Calculate the IQR Sort the data in ascending order from least to greatest. Find the median (Q₂(50%)) to split the dataset into lower and upper halves. Find the lower quartile (Q₁(25%)) by calculating the median of the lower half of the data. Find the upper quartile (Q₃(75%)) by calculating the median of the upper half of the data. Subtract Q₁ from Q₃ using the formula: IQR = Q₃ — Q₁. Use Case: Resistant to Outliers Outlier Detection 3. Boxplot: A Box Plot , also called a Box-and-Whisker Plot , is a graphical representation used to show the distribution, spread, center, and potential outliers of numerical data. Graph Of Univariate Analysis: Categorical Columns: For categorical columns, key metrics include frequency, percentages, mode, and cardinality. Frequency Table , Sales Chart , Bar Chart 2. Numerical Columns: For numerical columns, we first analyze basic numerical metrics such as Central Tendency (Mean, Median, Mode), Spread or Dispersion (Variance, Standard Deviation, IQR, CV), and the overall Distribution (Skewness, Kurtosis). To visualize the univariate distribution of numerical columns, we use histograms, box plots, KDE plots, and Q-Q plots. K(⋅) : The Kernel function — a symmetric, non-negative function that integrates to 1 (most commonly a standard normal/Gaussian bell curve). h : The Bandwidth (h > 0) — a smoothing parameter that controls the width of each individual bell curve. KDE Plot To build a KDE plot by hand or from scratch without a plotting library: Gussian functions as Kernel Choose a Kernel (K): Most implementations default to the Gaussian kernel. Select a Bandwidth (h): Pick a width for your individual curves (often estimated automatically using Silverman’s rule of thumb : Q-Q plot: A quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot is a graphical tool used in statistics to see if a set of data follows a specific theoretical distribution (like a normal distribution) or to compare two separate data samples. How It Works Ordering: The sample data is sorted from smallest to largest. Quantiles: These sorted values (sample quantiles) are plotted on the vertical (y) axis. Theoretical Values: Expected values from a reference distribution (such as a standard normal distribution) are plotted on the horizontal (x) axis. Reference Line: A straight diagonal line is drawn through the points. Q-Q Plot How to Interpret the Shape Straight line: If the points fall roughly along a straight diagonal line, the sample data matches the theoretical distribution. Curving at the ends (S-shape): If the tails curve away from the line, the data has heavy tails (more extreme values than a normal distribution would expect) or light tails . Bending upward or downward (Curves) An upward curve (concave up) usually signals right-skewed data. A downward curve (concave down) usually signals left-skewed data. Graph of Bivariate Analysis There are three main types of bivariate analysis: Here we only mention about the graphs which are useful but not discussion in depth, not any statistical methods for now. I will talk about this in an upcoming blog. Categorical vs. Categorical columns Visualizations: Grouped bar charts, stacked bar charts, and heatmaps (visualizing cross-tabulations). Statistical Methods: Cross-tabulation (contingency tables) and the Chi-Square test of independence. 2. Categorical vs. Numerical Visualizations: Side-by-side box plots, violin plots, overlapping histograms, and strip/swarm plots. Statistical Methods: Comparing group means/medians, Two-sample t-test, and ANOVA (Analysis of Variance). 3. Numerical vs. Numerical Visualizations: Scatter plots, line plots (especially for time-series data), and hexbin/2D density plots. Statistical Methods: Pearson correlation coefficient (linear relationship) and Spearman rank correlation (monotonic relationship). Conclusion Descriptive statistics serve as the foundational toolkit for raw data exploration, allowing us to summarize central tendencies, quantify variability, and understand data shapes before diving into complex modeling. While these metrics give us a clear snapshot of historical datasets, they only tell part of the story. To move beyond what the data looks like and begin making predictions, handling uncertainty, and testing hypotheses, we need to understand the underlying mechanics of randomness and risk. items.summary_html:
Descriptive statistics is the branch of statistics focused on summarizing, organizing, and presenting raw data so it becomes easy to understand. Instead of getting overwhelmed by thousands of unorganized data points, we use key metrics to reveal the story hidden inside the numbers.

This guide covers the core pillars of descriptive data analysis:

  • Population vs. Sample: Understanding who or what we are studying.
  • Types of Data: Categorical (nominal, ordinal) vs. numerical (discrete, continuous) data.
  • Measures of Central Tendency: Finding the center using mean, median, and mode.
  • Measures of Dispersion: Quantifying data spread using range, variance, standard deviation, MAD, and coefficient of variation.
  • Shape of Data: Checking symmetry and tail behavior using skewness and kurtosis.
  • Data Distribution & Visualization: Analyzing positions with quantiles, percentiles, IQR, box plots, KDE plots, and Q-Q plots.
What is Statistics?

Statistics is the branch of applied mathematics focused on the collection, analysis, interpretation, and presentation of data. It allows us to make sense of vast amounts of information by transforming raw numbers into meaningful insights, effectively acting as the science of extracting information in the face of uncertainty.

Descriptive Statistics vs Inferential Statistics
Greeks for Greeks image

Descriptive statistics describe the characteristics of a data set(like central tendency, spread, Data distribution, etc.), while inferential statistics use a sample of data to make predictions and conclusions about a larger population.

In this blog, we focus on essentials core founding concepts in Descriptive Statistics

Population Vs Sample

Population refers to the entire group that we want to study, such as the average income of the world’s population.

A sample is a subset of the population, which is taken from the population.

For example, we might randomly choose the incomes of 1,000 people from the Indian population.

Here 1000 peoples income is the sample, and the Indian Population is the Population.

Types of Data

Nominal data: Nominal data refers to categorical informaton that lacks inherent order or ranking.

Ordinal Data: Ordinal data represents information with a clear order or ranking, but the differences between the values are not quantifiable.

Discrete Data: Discrete data consists of separate values or categories you can measure. As you work with discrete data, you’ll often represent it as whole numbers, such as the number of employees in a company.

Continuous Data: Continuous data embodies information that can assume any value within a defined range or interval. It’s typically measured on a continuous scale, such as time, temperature, or distance.

Measures of Central Tendency :

A measure of central tendency is a statistical measure that represents a central value for a dataset. It provides a summary of data by identifying a single value that is most representative of the dataset as a whole.

  1. Mean (Arithmetic Average)
  • When to Use: Continuous or discrete numerical data with a symmetric distribution and no extreme values.
  • Limitation: Highly sensitive to outliers and skewed data, which pull the mean away from the true center.

2. Median (Middle Value):

  • When to Use: Skewed distributions (e.g., income, house prices) or ordinal data with potential outliers.
  • Limitation: Ignores the actual magnitude of data values outside the center; less mathematically tractable for statistical modeling.

3. Mode (Most Frequent Value)

  • When to Use: Categorical (nominal) data or identifying peak points in multimodal distributions.
  • Limitation: A dataset can have no mode, or multiple modes (bimodal/multimodal); uninformative for small-sample continuous data.

4. Advanced Variants

  • Weighted Mean: Assigns relative weights (w_i) to individual data points based on importance or frequency.
  • Trimmed Mean: Calculates the mean after removing a fixed percentage (e.g., 5\% or 10\%) of extreme values from both ends of the dataset to reduce outlier sensitivity while keeping most data.
Measure of Dispersion:

A measure of dispersion is a statistical value that indicates how spread out, scattered, or varied the data points are within a dataset. While measures of central tendency (like mean, median, and mode) identify the center of the data, measures of dispersion quantify how far individual data points deviate from that center. High dispersion indicates a wide variation in data, while low dispersion indicates consistency and uniformity.

  1. Range:

The simplest measure of variability is calculated as the difference between the highest and lowest values in a dataset. It provides a quick snapshot of how widely your data is spread out, though it is highly sensitive to extreme outliers.

Formula + Example

2. Variance:

Image by MATH MONKS

Variance is a statistical measure that quantifies the Spread of data points around their mean. It assesses how far each data point deviates from the average. A low variance indicates that the data points are close to the mean and to each other, while a high variance signifies that the data points are widely spread out from the mean.

Population and Sample Variance

# FAQ: Why is the variance of a population divided by N, while the sample variance is divided by n - 1?

3. Standard Deviation:

The standard deviation is simply the positive square root of the variance.

While variance measures the average squared distance from the mean, standard deviation brings that metric back to the original unit of measurement, making it much easier to interpret.

When to Use:

  • Finance & Investment: Measures portfolio risk and asset volatility (e.g., higher SD indicates greater price fluctuation).
  • Quality Control & Manufacturing: Evaluates production consistency to ensure product dimensions or specs stay within acceptable tolerance limits (e.g., Six Sigma).
  • Statistical Modeling & Testing: Serves as a core input for Z-scores, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and measuring standard error.
  • Performance Evaluation: Compares standardized test scores or survey metrics across different populations relative to the average.

Limitation: Because it relies on squared deviations from the mean, Standard Deviation is disproportionately sensitive to extreme outliers, making it misleading for heavily skewed distributions.

4. MAD:

Mean Absolute Deviation (MAD) is a measure of dispersion that tells us, on average, how far each data value is from the mean of the dataset.

MAD = Average distance of data points from the mean.

Formula:

When to use:

  1. MAD can be used to understand how spread out a dataset is.
  2. MAD is commonly used to evaluate forecast errors, it is closely related to MAE ( Mean Absolute Error.

Limitation:

  1. Sensitive to outliers: Extreme values can increase MAD significantly.
  2. MAD can be calculated around the mean or median. The interpretation changes depending on the chosen center.

5. Coefficient Of Variation(CV):

Coefficient of Variation (CV) is a statistical measure that shows the relative variability or dispersion of data compared to its mean.

In simple words:

CV tells us how much variation exists relative to the average value.

It is usually expressed as a percentage.

Generally:

  • Lower CV → Lower relative variability
  • Higher CV → Higher relative variability

This makes CV useful when comparing datasets with different means or different units/scales.

Use Case:

  1. Finance: Compare risk relative to return between different investments. CV= Risk​ / Average Return

2. Scientific experiments: Compare consistency of measurements from different experiments or instruments.

Limitation:

  1. Not suitable when the mean is zero or very close to zero
  2. Problematic with negative means: Interpretation becomes difficult when the mean is negative.
  3. Primarily useful for ratio-scale data: It is not appropriate for arbitrary scales such as temperature measured in Celsius.
Shape of Data
  1. Skewness:

Skewness is a statistical measure that tells us about the asymmetry of a distribution around its mean.

In simple words:

Skewness tells us whether the data is symmetrically distributed or has a longer tail on one side.

Skewness measures the asymmetry or lack of symmetry in a dataset relative to its mean.

  • Positive Skew (Right-skewed): Tail extends toward higher values on the right; Mean > Median > Mode
  • Negative Skew (Left-skewed): Tail extends toward lower values on the left; Mean < Median < Mode
  • Symmetric: Data is evenly distributed on both sides; Mean = Median = Mode

Formulation:

Interpretation:

  1. Skewness(Sk) = 0 then perfect Symmetric
  2. Skewness(Sk) > 0 then Positively / right skewed<0<0Small absolute valueApproximately symmetricLarge absolute valueStronger asymmetry
  3. Skewness(Sk) < 0 then Negatively / left skewed
  4. Small absolute value: approximately symmetric
  5. Large absolute value: strong asymmetry

Use case:

  1. Understand the shape of the distribution
  2. Detect asymmetry
  3. Identify potential outliers
  4. Decide whether a transformation might be useful
  5. Understand assumptions behind some statistical models

2. Kurtosis:

Kurtosis is a statistical measure that describes the shape of a distribution, particularly the behavior of its tails and the presence of extreme values.

In simple words:

Kurtosis tells us how prone a distribution is to producing extreme values compared with a normal distribution.

A common misconception is that kurtosis only measures “peakedness.” In modern statistics, kurtosis is more closely associated with tail heaviness and extreme observations.

Formulation:

Type of Kurtosis:

  1. Mesokurtic → Kurtosis =3
  2. Leptokurtic → Heavy tails → More extreme values → Kurtosis > 3
  3. Platykurtic → Light tails → Fewer extreme values → Kurtosis < 3

Use Case:

  1. Kurtosis is particularly useful for studying financial returns.
  2. Outlier / Extreme-value analysis: High kurtosis does not automatically mean that the dataset contains an error or an outlier.
  3. Machine Learning / Data Science

Limitation:

  1. Sensitive to extreme values
  2. Does not tell you which observation is an outlier
Quantiles & Percentiles :

Quantiles are cut-off points that divide a sorted dataset into equal-sized, continuous groups.

A percentile is a specific type of quantile that divides data into 100 equal parts. It represents the value below which a certain percentage of data falls.

Common Types of Quantiles:

  • Quartiles (4 parts): Cut data at 25%, 50%, and 75%.
  • Quintiles (5 parts): Cut data at 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%.
  • Deciles (10 parts): Cut data at 10%, 20%, …, 90%.
  • percentile(100 Parts): Cut the data at 1%,2%,…99%

90th percentile Means:

If your score is at the 90th percentile, it means approximately:

90% of the observations are at or below your score.

It does not mean that you scored 90%.

Formulation:

Example:

Use Case:

  1. Understand Data Distribution
  2. Outlier Detection
  3. Income Analysis
  4. Relative Scoring in Exam

Limitation:

  1. Different calculation methods can give different results
  2. They don’t show the entire distribution
  3. Quantiles can be unstable with very small datasets
IQR:

One of the most important applications of quantiles is the Interquartile Range.

How to Calculate the IQR

  1. Sort the data in ascending order from least to greatest.
  2. Find the median (Q₂(50%)) to split the dataset into lower and upper halves.
  3. Find the lower quartile (Q₁(25%)) by calculating the median of the lower half of the data.
  4. Find the upper quartile (Q₃(75%)) by calculating the median of the upper half of the data.
  5. Subtract Q₁ from Q₃ using the formula: IQR = Q₃ — Q₁.

Use Case:

  1. Resistant to Outliers
  2. Outlier Detection

3. Boxplot: A Box Plot, also called a Box-and-Whisker Plot, is a graphical representation used to show the distribution, spread, center, and potential outliers of numerical data.

Graph Of Univariate Analysis:
  1. Categorical Columns:

For categorical columns, key metrics include frequency, percentages, mode, and cardinality. These are the primary numerical values used to analyze categorical data.

For univariate visualization of categorical columns, we typically use bar charts, pie charts, and frequency tables.

2. Numerical Columns:

For numerical columns, we first analyze basic numerical metrics such as Central Tendency (Mean, Median, Mode), Spread or Dispersion (Variance, Standard Deviation, IQR, CV), and the overall Distribution (Skewness, Kurtosis).

To visualize the univariate distribution of numerical columns, we use histograms, box plots, KDE plots, and Q-Q plots.

A quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot is a graphical tool used in statistics to see if a set of data follows a specific theoretical distribution (like a normal distribution) or to compare two separate data samples.

How It Works

  1. Ordering: The sample data is sorted from smallest to largest.
  2. Quantiles: These sorted values (sample quantiles) are plotted on the vertical (y) axis.
  3. Theoretical Values: Expected values from a reference distribution (such as a standard normal distribution) are plotted on the horizontal (x) axis.

How to Interpret the Shape

  • Straight line: If the points fall roughly along a straight diagonal line, the sample data matches the theoretical distribution.
  • Curving at the ends (S-shape): If the tails curve away from the line, the data has heavy tails (more extreme values than a normal distribution would expect) or light tails.

Bending upward or downward (Curves)

  • An upward curve (concave up) usually signals right-skewed data.
  • A downward curve (concave down) usually signals left-skewed data.
Graph of Bivariate Analysis

There are three main types of bivariate analysis:

Here we only mention about the graphs which are useful but not discussion in depth, not any statistical methods for now. I will talk about this in an upcoming blog.

  1. Categorical vs. Categorical columns
  • Visualizations: Grouped bar charts, stacked bar charts, and heatmaps (visualizing cross-tabulations).
  • Statistical Methods: Cross-tabulation (contingency tables) and the Chi-Square test of independence.

2. Categorical vs. Numerical

  • Visualizations: Side-by-side box plots, violin plots, overlapping histograms, and strip/swarm plots.
  • Statistical Methods: Comparing group means/medians, Two-sample t-test, and ANOVA (Analysis of Variance).

3. Numerical vs. Numerical

  • Visualizations: Scatter plots, line plots (especially for time-series data), and hexbin/2D density plots.
  • Statistical Methods: Pearson correlation coefficient (linear relationship) and Spearman rank correlation (monotonic relationship).
Conclusion

Descriptive statistics serve as the foundational toolkit for raw data exploration, allowing us to summarize central tendencies, quantify variability, and understand data shapes before diving into complex modeling. While these metrics give us a clear snapshot of historical datasets, they only tell part of the story. To move beyond what the data looks like and begin making predictions, handling uncertainty, and testing hypotheses, we need to understand the underlying mechanics of randomness and risk.

What’s Next: Statistics in Data Science (Part 2): Probability Theory & Probability Distributions

In the next part of this series, we transition from describing data to modeling uncertainty:

  • Probability Theory Basics: Sample spaces, events, conditional probability, and Bayes’ Theorem.
  • Random Variables: Discrete vs. continuous random variables and expected value.
  • Probability Distributions: Deep dive into the Normal Distribution, Binomial, Poisson, and Bernoulli distributions.
  • Central Limit Theorem (CLT): Why the normal distribution is the backbone of statistical inference.

items.title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
items.summary: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands. Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys.
