items.title: 5 big Windows headaches and how to fix them
items.summary: Windows has come a long way since its initial release in 1985. From its birth, it gained a reputation as a kludge of an operating system, ugly and unloved, something that would get the job done (mostly) but cause lots of unpleasantness along the way. Who can forget struggling to do something as simple as install a new printer? Or the dreaded Blue Screen of Death that would pop up for no apparent reason and crash Windows, taking all your work along with it? The worst of those days are long behind us. Over time, Microsoft managed to kill many of the gremlins that bedeviled the operating system. Windows 11 is quite stable, and not nearly as confusing and cumbersome as previous versions. That’s not to say all is well with Windows, though. There’s plenty that still goes wrong and plenty of design choices that can trip you up when you’re just trying to work. Don’t fear. Help is on the way. Here are five of the worst things about Windows — and how to make them better so you can get some real work done. 1. Windows slows down with age It seems inevitable: You buy a new PC and it runs like greased lightning. Then several years later, it’s slow as molasses. PCs, just like people, slow down with age. But there’s a lot you can do to speed up a years-old PC and make it zippy again. First, disable programs that run at startup unnecessarily. As you install new software, or when existing software gets updated, it’s not uncommon that an increasing number of apps and processes run at startup when you don’t really need them. To fix that, first launch Task Manager in one of these ways: Press Ctrl-Shift-Esc. Right-click the taskbar and select Task Manager . Type task manager into the Windows search box and select it from the results. Click the Startup apps icon in the left-hand navigation pane — it’s the speedometer icon, fifth from the top. You’ll see a list of every application or process that launches at startup and runs on your PC in the background as you use it. The list includes each program’s name, publisher, whether it’s enabled to run on startup, and its “Startup impact.” The Startup impact tells you how much it slows Windows down — low, medium, high, none, and sometimes “not measured.” Here’s how to disable apps and services that run on startup. Preston Gralla / Foundry To stop a program or service from launching at startup, right-click it and select Disable . That only stops it running at startup. You can still run the application after launch. If for some reason you want it to launch at startup again, you can just return to the Startup apps area of the Task Manager, right-click the application and select Enable . You may not recognize many of the programs that run on startup, but there are several ways you can find out more about any of them: Right-click an item and select Properties for information about it, such as its location on your hard disk, whether it has a digital signature, and other information including the version number, the file size and the last time it was modified. Right-click the item and select Open file location . File Explorer will open to the folder where the file is located, often giving you another clue about the program’s purpose. Select Search online after you right-click. Bing launches with links to sites with information about the program or service. Go to Should I Block It? and search for the file name. You’ll often find solid information about the program or service. Another way to speed up an aging PC is to disable eye candy like shadows, animations, and visual effects, which can exact a performance hit. To turn them off, in the search box, type sysdm.cpl and press Enter. The System Properties dialog box launches. Click the Advanced tab, then click Settings in the Performance section. The Performance Options dialog box opens, with a varied list of animations and special effects. Select Adjust for best performance at the top of the screen and then click OK . Windows then turns off the effects that slow down your system. For many more ways to speed up an aging PC, see 16 ways to speed up Windows 11 or 19 ways to speed up Windows 10 . 2. Windows is bedeviled by glitches and system errors Windows has come a long way since the days when running it felt like a crapshoot — would it crash for no apparent reason and show you the dreaded Blue Screen of Death today? The operating system has come a long way since then. You may never see a Blue Screen again. That doesn’t mean it’s truly reliable, though. Glitches remain. System errors are a way of life. Windows includes little-known troubleshooters that can help resolve these kinds of problems. To get to them, go to Settings > System > Troubleshoot . As a first step, from the Options section, click the box to the right of Recommended troubleshooter history and select Ask me before running . This will allow Windows to suggest a troubleshooter for you to run if it detects you have a problem that needs a fix. You can also choose to have troubleshooters run automatically and then notify you or not. If you don’t want them to run at all, select Don’t run any . I’ve found, though, that often Windows won’t recommend a troubleshooter when I’m running into problems. If that’s the case for you, from the Troubleshoot screen select Other troubleshooters . Windows will display a long list of troubleshooters you can choose, including for network and internet problems, printer problems, Bluetooth, Windows Update, and more. Go here to select a troubleshooter to cure what ails Windows. Preston Gralla / Foundry Select the troubleshooter you want to run from the list. The troubleshooter will try to diagnose the problem and then will either fix it itself or recommend what you should do. There’s no guarantee the troubleshooter will work, of course. There are other things you can try to fix the problem. It’s possible that Windows has gotten an update that has a fix, and you haven’t installed the update yet. Go to Settings > Windows Update and click for Check for updates . If there’s an available update, install it. That might do the trick. You can also try turning to Copilot . Click the Copilot icon on the taskbar, describe the problem, and ask for help. Be as detailed as possible, including all details of the problem and the version number of Windows you’re using — not just Windows 10 or 11, but its specific version number. To find it, go to Settings > System > About . In the Windows info section, you’ll see the version number, such as 26H2. about screen with windows version highlighted" class="wp-image-4245928" width="1024" height="744" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px"> Go here to find your version of Windows. Preston Gralla / Foundry Sometimes Copilot does a great job of identifying the underlying issues and walking you through a fix. Not always, though. If all else fails, you can use the IT admin’s favorite secret solution: Restart Windows. Quite frequently the problem will vanish. 3. Windows is a privacy-invader Windows is always watching you, gathering data about the way you use it and sending it back to Microsoft. You don’t need to put up with this. Here are several simple ways to protect your privacy. Start by turning off the Windows advertising ID that gathers information about you when you browse the web and when you use Windows 11 apps. To do it, go to Settings > Privacy & security > Recommendations & offers . Find Advertising ID near the bottom of the screen and move its slider to Off. From now on, your interests won’t be tracked. The ads you get will be generic ones rather than targeted ones. Turn off the Windows Advertising ID and personalized offers to help protect your privacy. Preston Gralla / Foundry Near the top of the same screen, turn off Personalized offers . This setting lets Microsoft present you with “ads and recommendations for Microsoft and third-party products and services, features, apps, and hardware to enhance your Windows experiences” based on your Windows usage and account info. If you’re worried about your privacy, that’s the last thing you want. Next, turn off location tracking. With location tracking, your PC uses your location to provide services such as the local weather. But having Windows constantly track your location is another privacy incursion. To turn it off, go to Settings > Privacy & security > Location . In the “App permissions” section, click Location and move the slider from On to Off. That will turn off location tracking for every user on the PC. You can also leave on location tracking for some apps and turn it off for others. With location tracking turned on, look at the “Let apps access your location” section on the Location screen. It lists every Windows app that can use your location. Move the slider to On for the apps you want to allow to use your location and to Off for the apps you don’t. That doesn’t cover desktop apps, though. Scroll down to “Let desktop apps access your location.” Move the slider to On if you want them to use location information. You’ll see a list of desktop apps have that previously used your location. You can turn them on and off individually. Finally, go to Microsoft’s Privacy Dashboard . This lets you track and delete a good deal of information Windows gathers about you. From here you can turn off ad targeting and view and delete your browsing history, search history, location activity, voice activity, media activity, and more. Head to the information you want to view and delete, then click the link, such as Browsing and search . It shows a list of your activities, including websites you’ve visited, how many times you’ve visited them, when you’ve visited them, and so on. Click Show all activities to see a more comprehensive list than the one the main screen. Microsoft’s Privacy Dashboard lets you view and delete granular activity data. Preston Gralla / Foundry Delete browsing items individually by clicking the trash can icon next to each one. To delete them all, click the Clear all activities link at the lower right of the list, then click Clear on the screen that appears. You can do the same thing with many Windows activities, such as Search history, which tracks all the searches you do. In the dashboard, you can also customize privacy settings for Microsoft products other than Windows, including Xbox, Microsoft 365, Edge, and Microsoft Teams. Scroll down to the “Find privacy settings in Microsoft products” section and click the product you’re interested in. There’s a lot more you can do to protect your privacy in Windows. To find out more, go to How to protect your privacy in Windows 11 or How to protect your privacy in Windows 10 . 4. Windows makes it too $%#$!! hard to change your default apps When you try to open certain files or take certain actions — like click a web link in an email — Windows uses its default app. For a browser, for example, that means it chooses Microsoft Edge rather than an alternate browser like Google Chrome. It should be a simple task to change your default apps. Unfortunately, it isn’t. Here’s how to do it, using the example of changing the default browser from Edge to Chrome: Go to Settings > Apps > Default apps , then scroll to the app you want to make your default app for a specific file or action. In our case, it’s Google Chrome. Click the arrow next to the app, and at the top of the screen that that appears, click Set default . apps > default apps google chrome screen" class="wp-image-4245924" width="1024" height="744" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px"> Setting a new app default — in this case, Google Chrome for web browsing. Preston Gralla / Foundry A checkmark appears next to “Set default.” To change the default back to Edge or another browser, scroll to the browser you want to be the default and click Set default . Follow these same steps to change any other default app. That may only be part of the process, though, because certain file types may still be associated with Microsoft’s default app. Even after changing the default browser to Chrome, for example, PDF files, mailto links, some graphics files such as .svg, and other file types are still associated with Edge by default. You’re going to have to hunt them down and change them one by one. This may be true not just when you change your default browser, but for when you change any default app. You’ll have to hunt down the other associated file types as well. Here’s how to do it with our example of Google Chrome. Follow the same directions for other apps: Go to Settings > Apps > Default apps and click your new default browser — in our example, Google Chrome . Scroll through all the file types and protocols, and click any still associated with the previous default (in our example, Edge). On the pop-up screen that appears, select the app you want to handle the file type (in our example, Google Chrome ), then click Set Default . Keep in mind that you don’t have to use the new default app for every file type. You can, for example, choose another app, such as a PDF reader for .pdf files. 5. OneDrive can drive you batty In theory, Windows’ built-in cloud storage app OneDrive is a great idea. It integrates with File Explorer to store your files on your PC, automatically backs them up to the cloud as you change them, and syncs everything with the cloud and all your devices. And you get 5GB of cloud storage for free — more if you use certain versions of Microsoft 365 . What’s not to like? Plenty. There are so many confusing things about how it works that delving into them all is beyond the scope of this article. (In fact, we have two separate tutorials dedicated to using OneDrive in Windows and using OneDrive on the web .) So I’ll only cover the weirdest and most baffling thing here: The strange tale of dueling Recycle Bins — one in OneDrive, and one in Windows — which contain different files depending on how the files have been deleted. Until the advent of OneDrive, when you deleted a file in Windows, it was sent only to the Windows Recycle Bin. The deleted file stays in the Recycle Bin for some time, so that if you accidentally deleted it, you can easily go there and restore it. How long the file remains there varies according to the size of your hard disk, how much space is devoted to the Recycle Bin, and your settings. Then OneDrive came along with its own Recycle Bin, separate from the Windows Recycle Bin. So now, depending on how you delete a file, it will go into either the Windows Recycle Bin or the OneDrive Recycle Bin, or both. If you don’t know where to look for a deleted file, you won’t find it. Most people don’t even know there’s a separate OneDrive Recycle Bin, because Microsoft has done such a good job of hiding it. The dueling Recycle Bins in Windows and OneDrive . (Click image to enlarge it.) Preston Gralla / Foundry The first thing you need to know is that the OneDrive Recycle Bin only appears on the web-based version of OneDrive. It’s nowhere to be found in Windows itself. You can get to it in two ways: Right-click the OneDrive icon on the right side of the Windows Taskbar and select Settings > Recycle Bin . You’ll be sent to the OneDrive Recycle Bin, which is located in the web-based version OneDrive, not the local Windows OneDrive. Go directly to OneDrive on the web and click Recycle bin in the left-hand pane. As to which files end up in the OneDrive Recycle Bin, it’s fairly mysterious. Given that OneDrive is so well-integrated with File Explorer, you would expect that files deleted in File Explorer would end up in there. Some files do, and some files don’t. If you delete a file in File Explorer that is synced to OneDrive, that file will show up in the OneDrive Recycle Bin as well as in the Windows Recycle Bin. If the file hasn’t been synced in OneDrive, it will appear in the Windows Recycle Bin only. That means that if you delete files from the Downloads folder, they likely won’t show up in the OneDrive Recycle Bin, because by default, Downloads aren’t synced to OneDrive. If you do sync your Downloads folder, files deleted from there will show up. I mentioned earlier that some deleted files go only to the OneDrive Recycle Bin. That typically happens when you delete the file in the web version of OneDrive. But it also happens when you delete the file from within a Microsoft 365 app like Word, such as by going to File > Open , then right-clicking a file you see there and selecting Delete file from the menu that appears. When you delete a file in either of these ways, it shows up only in the OneDrive Recycle Bin, not the Windows Recycle Bin. The good news is that once you know all this, you should never lose a deleted file again. Whenever possible, delete files only using File Explorer. Every file deleted that way ends up in the Windows Recycle Bin, even if it doesn’t also show up in the OneDrive Recycle Bin. You can also check both Recycle Bins if you can’t find the deleted file. It’ll show up on one or the other. Restore it from whichever bin you find it in. For much more information about the ins and outs of OneDrive, including some nifty features available only in the web version, see Microsoft OneDrive cheat sheet: Using OneDrive in Windows and Microsoft OneDrive cheat sheet: Using OneDrive for Web . Select the troubleshooter you want to run from the list. The troubleshooter will try to diagnose the problem and then will either fix it itself or recommend what you should do.

There’s no guarantee the troubleshooter will work, of course. There are other things you can try to fix the problem. It’s possible that Windows has gotten an update that has a fix, and you haven’t installed the update yet. Go to Settings > Windows Update and click for Check for updates. If there’s an available update, install it. That might do the trick.

You can also try turning to Copilot. Click the Copilot icon on the taskbar, describe the problem, and ask for help. Be as detailed as possible, including all details of the problem and the version number of Windows you’re using — not just Windows 10 or 11, but its specific version number. To find it, go to Settings > System > About. In the Windows info section, you’ll see the version number, such as 26H2.

about screen with windows version highlighted" class="wp-image-4245928" width="1024" height="744" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px">

Go here to find your version of Windows.

Preston Gralla / Foundry

Sometimes Copilot does a great job of identifying the underlying issues and walking you through a fix. Not always, though.

If all else fails, you can use the IT admin’s favorite secret solution: Restart Windows. Quite frequently the problem will vanish.

3. Windows is a privacy-invader

Windows is always watching you, gathering data about the way you use it and sending it back to Microsoft. You don’t need to put up with this. Here are several simple ways to protect your privacy.

Start by turning off the Windows advertising ID that gathers information about you when you browse the web and when you use Windows 11 apps. To do it, go to Settings > Privacy & security > Recommendations & offers. Find Advertising ID near the bottom of the screen and move its slider to Off. From now on, your interests won’t be tracked. The ads you get will be generic ones rather than targeted ones.

Turn off the Windows Advertising ID and personalized offers to help protect your privacy.

Preston Gralla / Foundry

Near the top of the same screen, turn off Personalized offers. This setting lets Microsoft present you with “ads and recommendations for Microsoft and third-party products and services, features, apps, and hardware to enhance your Windows experiences” based on your Windows usage and account info. If you’re worried about your privacy, that’s the last thing you want.

Next, turn off location tracking. With location tracking, your PC uses your location to provide services such as the local weather. But having Windows constantly track your location is another privacy incursion.

To turn it off, go to Settings >  Privacy & security > Location. In the “App permissions” section, click Location and move the slider from On to Off. That will turn off location tracking for every user on the PC.

You can also leave on location tracking for some apps and turn it off for others. With location tracking turned on, look at the “Let apps access your location” section on the Location screen. It lists every Windows app that can use your location. Move the slider to On for the apps you want to allow to use your location and to Off for the apps you don’t.

That doesn’t cover desktop apps, though. Scroll down to “Let desktop apps access your location.” Move the slider to On if you want them to use location information. You’ll see a list of desktop apps have that previously used your location. You can turn them on and off individually.

Finally, go to Microsoft’s Privacy Dashboard.  This lets you track and delete a good deal of information Windows gathers about you. From here you can turn off ad targeting and view and delete your browsing history, search history, location activity, voice activity, media activity, and more.

Head to the information you want to view and delete, then click the link, such as Browsing and search. It shows a list of your activities, including websites you’ve visited, how many times you’ve visited them, when you’ve visited them, and so on. Click Show all activities to see a more comprehensive list than the one the main screen.

Microsoft’s Privacy Dashboard lets you view and delete granular activity data.

Preston Gralla / Foundry

Delete browsing items individually by clicking the trash can icon next to each one. To delete them all, click the Clear all activities link at the lower right of the list, then click Clear on the screen that appears.

You can do the same thing with many Windows activities, such as Search history, which tracks all the searches you do.

In the dashboard, you can also customize privacy settings for Microsoft products other than Windows, including Xbox, Microsoft 365, Edge, and Microsoft Teams. Scroll down to the “Find privacy settings in Microsoft products” section and click the product you’re interested in.

There’s a lot more you can do to protect your privacy in Windows. To find out more, go to How to protect your privacy in Windows 11 or How to protect your privacy in Windows 10.

4. Windows makes it too $%#$!! hard to change your default apps

When you try to open certain files or take certain actions — like click a web link in an email — Windows uses its default app. For a browser, for example, that means it chooses Microsoft Edge rather than an alternate browser like Google Chrome.

It should be a simple task to change your default apps. Unfortunately, it isn’t. Here’s how to do it, using the example of changing the default browser from Edge to Chrome:

  1. Go to Settings > Apps > Default apps, then scroll to the app you want to make your default app for a specific file or action. In our case, it’s Google Chrome.
  2. Click the arrow next to the app, and at the top of the screen that that appears, click Set default.
apps > default apps google chrome screen" class="wp-image-4245924" width="1024" height="744" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px">

Setting a new app default — in this case, Google Chrome for web browsing.

Preston Gralla / Foundry

  • A checkmark appears next to “Set default.”
  • To change the default back to Edge or another browser, scroll to the browser you want to be the default and click Set default.

Follow these same steps to change any other default app.

That may only be part of the process, though, because certain file types may still be associated with Microsoft’s default app. Even after changing the default browser to Chrome, for example, PDF files, mailto links, some graphics files such as .svg, and other file types are still associated with Edge by default. You’re going to have to hunt them down and change them one by one.

This may be true not just when you change your default browser, but for when you change any default app. You’ll have to hunt down the other associated file types as well.

Here’s how to do it with our example of Google Chrome. Follow the same directions for other apps:

  1. Go to Settings > Apps > Default apps and click your new default browser — in our example, Google Chrome.
  2. Scroll through all the file types and protocols, and click any still associated with the previous default (in our example, Edge).
  3. On the pop-up screen that appears, select the app you want to handle the file type (in our example, Google Chrome), then click Set Default.

Keep in mind that you don’t have to use the new default app for every file type. You can, for example, choose another app, such as a PDF reader for .pdf files.

5. OneDrive can drive you batty

In theory, Windows’ built-in cloud storage app OneDrive is a great idea. It integrates with File Explorer to store your files on your PC, automatically backs them up to the cloud as you change them, and syncs everything with the cloud and all your devices. And you get 5GB of cloud storage for free — more if you use certain versions of Microsoft 365.

What’s not to like?

Plenty. There are so many confusing things about how it works that delving into them all is beyond the scope of this article. (In fact, we have two separate tutorials dedicated to using OneDrive in Windows and using OneDrive on the web.)

So I’ll only cover the weirdest and most baffling thing here: The strange tale of dueling Recycle Bins — one in OneDrive, and one in Windows — which contain different files depending on how the files have been deleted.

Until the advent of OneDrive, when you deleted a file in Windows, it was sent only to the Windows Recycle Bin. The deleted file stays in the Recycle Bin for some time, so that if you accidentally deleted it, you can easily go there and restore it. How long the file remains there varies according to the size of your hard disk, how much space is devoted to the Recycle Bin, and your settings.

Then OneDrive came along with its own Recycle Bin, separate from the Windows Recycle Bin. So now, depending on how you delete a file, it will go into either the Windows Recycle Bin or the OneDrive Recycle Bin, or both. If you don’t know where to look for a deleted file, you won’t find it. Most people don’t even know there’s a separate OneDrive Recycle Bin, because Microsoft has done such a good job of hiding it.

The dueling Recycle Bins in Windows and OneDrive

. (Click image to enlarge it.)

Preston Gralla / Foundry

The first thing you need to know is that the OneDrive Recycle Bin only appears on the web-based version of OneDrive. It’s nowhere to be found in Windows itself. You can get to it in two ways:

  • Right-click the OneDrive icon on the right side of the Windows Taskbar and select Settings > Recycle Bin. You’ll be sent to the OneDrive Recycle Bin, which is located in the web-based version OneDrive, not the local Windows OneDrive.
  • Go directly to OneDrive on the web and click Recycle bin in the left-hand pane.

As to which files end up in the OneDrive Recycle Bin, it’s fairly mysterious. Given that OneDrive is so well-integrated with File Explorer, you would expect that files deleted in File Explorer would end up in there. Some files do, and some files don’t. If you delete a file in File Explorer that is synced to OneDrive, that file will show up in the OneDrive Recycle Bin as well as in the Windows Recycle Bin. If the file hasn’t been synced in OneDrive, it will appear in the Windows Recycle Bin only.

That means that if you delete files from the Downloads folder, they likely won’t show up in the OneDrive Recycle Bin, because by default, Downloads aren’t synced to OneDrive. If you do sync your Downloads folder, files deleted from there will show up.

I mentioned earlier that some deleted files go only to the OneDrive Recycle Bin. That typically happens when you delete the file in the web version of OneDrive. But it also happens when you delete the file from within a Microsoft 365 app like Word, such as by going to File > Open, then right-clicking a file you see there and selecting Delete file from the menu that appears. When you delete a file in either of these ways, it shows up only in the OneDrive Recycle Bin, not the Windows Recycle Bin.

The good news is that once you know all this, you should never lose a deleted file again. Whenever possible, delete files only using File Explorer. Every file deleted that way ends up in the Windows Recycle Bin, even if it doesn’t also show up in the OneDrive Recycle Bin.

You can also check both Recycle Bins if you can’t find the deleted file. It’ll show up on one or the other. Restore it from whichever bin you find it in.

For much more information about the ins and outs of OneDrive, including some nifty features available only in the web version, see Microsoft OneDrive cheat sheet: Using OneDrive in Windows and Microsoft OneDrive cheat sheet: Using OneDrive for Web.

items.title: AI Coding Agent Learning Loop: Ship Faster Without Outsourcing Understanding
items.summary: AI Coding Agent Learning Loop A practical workflow for using Codex, Claude Code, Copilot, or another coding agent as a force multiplier without becoming the person who cannot explain the code they shipped. For developers, engineering managers, and AI-native teams The valuable habit is not refusing help. It is making understanding part of the help. A coding agent can turn a vague ticket into a passing pull request before you finish a coffee. That speed is useful. It can also hide a costly trade: you ship the change, but you cannot explain its control flow, spot its weak assumption, or repair it when production behaves strangely. This is not a beginner-only problem. A developer moving quickly through unfamiliar code can mistake a clean diff for understanding. The moment the agent produces more code than a person can comfortably inspect, the work shifts from typing to judgment: defining the problem, checking evidence, choosing constraints, and knowing what has not been proved. That pressure is current, not theoretical. Recent reporting on an Adaptavist survey found many developers feel AI has reduced hands-on learning opportunities, while the Stack Overflow Developer Survey shows that AI tools are already part of how developers learn. The answer is not an AI ban or a return to writing every line by hand. It is a workflow that turns each agent task into a short, deliberate learning cycle. Do not ask, “Did the agent write the code?” Ask, “What will I understand and be able to verify after this task?” This article calls that cycle the AI coding agent learning loop . It works with any agent that can read a repository, make changes, run tests, or explain a diff. It is especially helpful for early-career developers, teams onboarding to an unfamiliar stack, and managers who want AI adoption to grow capability rather than hide a future skills gap. Why faster code can create slower developers Writing code used to force several learning steps together. You read the error, formed a theory, searched the codebase, changed one thing, watched a test fail, and revised your mental model. That process was inefficient in places, but it supplied feedback. An agent can collapse the visible middle. You give it an issue, it explores files, makes a patch, and returns a polished summary. The risk is not that the result is automatically wrong. The risk is that your brain never had to predict the result. Without a prediction, review turns into reading a plausible story after the fact. When the next incident arrives, you are dependent on another agent run because you never built the model of the system yourself. Call this comprehension debt : the gap between code your team operates and code your team can reason about. It accumulates quietly. You notice it when a small bug fix becomes a long investigation, when reviewers approve a diff they cannot narrate, or when a new developer can repeat an agent prompt but cannot state the contract the prompt is meant to preserve. Tool choice does not solve comprehension debt on its own. Codex, Claude Code, Copilot, Gemini, and other agents vary in interface and strength, but the learning problem is structural. If the workflow rewards only output volume, people will optimize for output volume. If the workflow asks for a prediction, an explanation, and an independent check, the agent becomes a very fast tutor and implementation partner. The five-step AI coding agent learning loop A repeatable loop makes agent use a learning system instead of a one-way code vending machine. The loop is intentionally small. Run it on one bug, one endpoint, one test, or one refactor. A 20-minute task that teaches you how the system behaves is more useful than a five-minute task that leaves you unable to answer basic review questions. 1. Predict before you delegate Before opening the agent, write a two-minute prediction. What do you think causes the issue? Which file or boundary probably owns it? What behavior should change? What must remain unchanged? You do not need to be right. A wrong prediction creates an explicit gap to close. For example, if an API returns an empty list where the client expects an error, write: “I think the route calls the repository directly and misses validation in the service layer. A blank query should return a 400. Existing valid searches must still return the same payload.” This gives you a testable mental model and a sharper task brief. 2. Delegate a bounded investigation, not a blank command “Fix the bug” is fast to type and expensive to review. Give the agent an evidence-first assignment. Ask it to inspect, cite files and symbols, state uncertainty, and propose the smallest change before it edits. In a mature codebase, this is safer. In a learning environment, it also exposes the path the agent took. Investigate the empty-search behavior before changing code. 1. Find the request entry point and trace it to the query handler. 2. Cite exact file paths and function names for each step. 3. State whether an empty query is validated today and where. 4. Propose the smallest safe patch and the narrowest regression test. 5. Do not edit files yet. Mark every uncertain claim as uncertain. This prompt works because it separates discovery from implementation. It also makes the output easy to challenge. If the agent cannot name the request boundary or the relevant test, it has not earned permission to change code. 3. Inspect the diff as a causal story After the agent proposes a patch, do not start by asking whether it “looks good.” Reconstruct cause and effect. For every changed block, answer four questions: What input or state reaches this line? What invariant does this condition protect? What happens on the unhappy path? Which test or observation proves the behavior? If you cannot answer one, ask the agent a narrower question. “Explain this diff” is weak. “Why is this validation in the controller rather than the service, and which existing callers would behave differently if we moved it?” is useful. Ask for file and line references. Then verify the references yourself. 4. Explain it back without the agent This is the step most teams skip, and it is the one that converts exposure into learning. Close the agent panel. In three to five sentences, explain the request path, the failure mode, the change, and the test. Say it aloud to a teammate, add it to the pull request description, or write it in a scratch note. Use a simple standard: if you can only repeat the agent’s summary, you do not understand the change yet. If you can explain why an alternative design was rejected and what could break next, you are ready to own it. 5. Verify with an independent signal A green test suite matters, but it should not be the only signal. Match the verification to the risk. For a parsing bug, run a focused test and try a hostile input. For an API change, exercise the endpoint with a representative request. For a refactor, check a before-and-after behavior. For a background job, inspect a trace or log from a controlled run. The key word is independent . If the agent wrote the test and interpreted the result, add a human check that comes from a different direction. You are not trying to catch the agent in a mistake. You are building evidence that you can trust when the context window is gone. Use the loop on a real bug Imagine a TypeScript service where an empty email string reaches a lookup function. The agent proposes this patch: export async function findUserByEmail(email: string) { const normalized = email.trim().toLowerCase(); if (!normalized) { throw new ValidationError("email is required"); } return userRepository.findByEmail(normalized); } A passive review says, “That is sensible.” The learning loop asks more. Predict: Does this service own input validation, or does a controller normally do it first? Inspect: Does ValidationError become a client-safe 400 response, or can it leak as a 500? Explain: Why normalize before checking emptiness? Because whitespace-only input becomes empty, and case normalization preserves lookup consistency for valid values. Verify: Add tests for "", " ", and a mixed-case valid address. Then call the public route once, not just the function. Notice what changed. The agent still did useful work. But the developer learned about ownership boundaries, error translation, normalization, and test design. That knowledge transfers to the next ticket. The patch alone does not. Choose the right autonomy level for the learning goal Not every task deserves the same amount of agent freedom. The best setting depends on consequence, novelty, and what you want the person to learn. Use explain-first mode for an unfamiliar framework, a new language, a complex incident, or a developer who is learning the domain. The agent investigates and proposes; the human writes or approves the patch only after explaining it. Use paired implementation mode for repeatable, moderate-risk tasks. The agent edits a small branch, the developer reviews the causal story, and both the focused and broader checks run. This is a good default for bug fixes, tests, and narrowly-scoped refactors. Use high autonomy for well-understood mechanical work with robust guardrails: formatting migrations, generated client refreshes, low-risk documentation updates, or repetitive test scaffolding. High autonomy is earned by clear contracts and reliable checks, not by confidence in a model name. A useful rule: delegate more freely when you could explain, test, and reverse the change without the agent. Slow down when you cannot. Make learning visible in the pull request Teams get what they review. If a pull request template only asks for screenshots and passing checks, it teaches developers to treat agent output as a black box. Add a short “understanding note” to agent-assisted changes. This is not paperwork for its own sake. It turns the author’s mental model into something a reviewer can test. ## Understanding note - Expected behavior: [one sentence] - What I predicted: [one sentence] - What I learned: [path, invariant, or failure mode] - Evidence: [focused test, command, trace, or manual check] - Remaining uncertainty: [if any] Keep it tiny. A clear unknown is better than a ceremonial paragraph. Senior reviewers can then ask questions that build skill: “What would make this branch run?” “Which caller depends on this default?” “What test would fail if the agent had picked the wrong layer?” Those questions create a durable feedback loop without turning review into an exam. Peer review is a chance to make reasoning visible, not just to approve an agent-generated diff. What managers should measure instead of prompts sent Prompt count is not a learning metric. Lines of AI-generated code are not a learning metric either. Both can rise while comprehension falls. Instead, sample a small number of agent-assisted changes each month and look for evidence of ownership. Can the author explain the changed behavior and its failure mode? Do agent-assisted pull requests include a focused verification step? How often does a reviewer find an unstated assumption before merge? Can the original author debug or extend the change a few weeks later? Are junior engineers taking on gradually harder problem framing and review work? These are local signals, not universal benchmarks. Avoid using them to rank people or justify surveillance. Their job is to show whether the team is building judgment while it gains speed. The recent industry discussion about AI-native graduates makes this especially important: organizations need developers who can supervise, verify, and improve AI-mediated work, not just request it. A seven-day rollout that does not slow the team down Start with one volunteer team and tasks they already do. On day one, choose three small work items: a bug fix, a test addition, and a documentation correction. On day two, add the two-minute prediction to the task brief. On day three, require evidence-first investigation before edits. On day four, use the understanding note in review. By day five, collect the questions reviewers asked that exposed weak reasoning. Turn the best ones into a lightweight checklist. On day six, compare cycle time and rework with a similar set of recent tasks. On day seven, decide what to keep. If the workflow adds friction without improving explanation, evidence, or rework, simplify it. If it finds mistakes earlier and gives people better command of the code, expand it one task category at a time. The goal is not to make every agent task educational theater. It is to stop treating learning as an accidental byproduct of code generation. AI-native developers will ship quickly. The strongest ones will also know why the system works, where it might fail, and how to prove the difference. FAQ: AI coding agent learning workflow What is an AI coding agent learning workflow? It is a repeatable way to use an AI coding agent while preserving developer understanding. The core loop is to predict the behavior, delegate a bounded investigation, inspect the causal story, explain the change back, and verify it with an independent signal. Will this make my team slower? It adds a few minutes to small tasks, but it can prevent costly rework and dependence later. Use the full loop for unfamiliar or risky work. For routine work with excellent tests, keep the understanding note short and let automation handle the mechanics. Can junior developers use coding agents safely? Yes, if tasks are bounded and review centers on reasoning, not just output. Start with explain-first work, require focused tests, and have a more experienced engineer check the mental model as well as the diff. Should developers write every line themselves to learn? No. Manual typing is not the only route to learning. Developers need repeated practice at reading code, forming hypotheses, testing behavior, reviewing tradeoffs, and debugging failures. An agent can accelerate those activities when the workflow requires them. Which AI coding agent is best for this workflow? The workflow is tool-agnostic. Use an agent that can show its evidence, work in a bounded scope, and produce changes you can validate. The important choice is the task contract and review standard, not the product logo. How do I know whether an agent-assisted change is understood? Ask the author to explain the behavior, name the invariant, describe one failure case, and point to the evidence. If they can do that without leaning on a generated summary, they likely have enough understanding to own the change. Sources Stack Overflow: 2026 Developer Survey JetBrains Research: How Much Code Do Developers Let Agents Write? Why coding agents are not delivering promised gains for engineering — yet OpenAI Newsroom: Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates AI Coding Agent Learning Loop: Ship Faster Without Outsourcing Understanding was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

  return userRepository.findByEmail(normalized);
}

A passive review says, “That is sensible.” The learning loop asks more.

  • Predict: Does this service own input validation, or does a controller normally do it first?
  • Inspect: Does ValidationError become a client-safe 400 response, or can it leak as a 500?
  • Explain: Why normalize before checking emptiness? Because whitespace-only input becomes empty, and case normalization preserves lookup consistency for valid values.
  • Verify: Add tests for "", " ", and a mixed-case valid address. Then call the public route once, not just the function.

Notice what changed. The agent still did useful work. But the developer learned about ownership boundaries, error translation, normalization, and test design. That knowledge transfers to the next ticket. The patch alone does not.

Choose the right autonomy level for the learning goal

Not every task deserves the same amount of agent freedom. The best setting depends on consequence, novelty, and what you want the person to learn.

Use explain-first mode for an unfamiliar framework, a new language, a complex incident, or a developer who is learning the domain. The agent investigates and proposes; the human writes or approves the patch only after explaining it.

Use paired implementation mode for repeatable, moderate-risk tasks. The agent edits a small branch, the developer reviews the causal story, and both the focused and broader checks run. This is a good default for bug fixes, tests, and narrowly-scoped refactors.

Use high autonomy for well-understood mechanical work with robust guardrails: formatting migrations, generated client refreshes, low-risk documentation updates, or repetitive test scaffolding. High autonomy is earned by clear contracts and reliable checks, not by confidence in a model name.

A useful rule: delegate more freely when you could explain, test, and reverse the change without the agent. Slow down when you cannot.

Make learning visible in the pull request

Teams get what they review. If a pull request template only asks for screenshots and passing checks, it teaches developers to treat agent output as a black box. Add a short “understanding note” to agent-assisted changes. This is not paperwork for its own sake. It turns the author’s mental model into something a reviewer can test.

## Understanding note
- Expected behavior: [one sentence]
- What I predicted: [one sentence]
- What I learned: [path, invariant, or failure mode]
- Evidence: [focused test, command, trace, or manual check]
- Remaining uncertainty: [if any]

Keep it tiny. A clear unknown is better than a ceremonial paragraph. Senior reviewers can then ask questions that build skill: “What would make this branch run?” “Which caller depends on this default?” “What test would fail if the agent had picked the wrong layer?” Those questions create a durable feedback loop without turning review into an exam.

Peer review is a chance to make reasoning visible, not just to approve an agent-generated diff.

What managers should measure instead of prompts sent

Prompt count is not a learning metric. Lines of AI-generated code are not a learning metric either. Both can rise while comprehension falls. Instead, sample a small number of agent-assisted changes each month and look for evidence of ownership.

  • Can the author explain the changed behavior and its failure mode?
  • Do agent-assisted pull requests include a focused verification step?
  • How often does a reviewer find an unstated assumption before merge?
  • Can the original author debug or extend the change a few weeks later?
  • Are junior engineers taking on gradually harder problem framing and review work?

These are local signals, not universal benchmarks. Avoid using them to rank people or justify surveillance. Their job is to show whether the team is building judgment while it gains speed. The recent industry discussion about AI-native graduates makes this especially important: organizations need developers who can supervise, verify, and improve AI-mediated work, not just request it.

A seven-day rollout that does not slow the team down

Start with one volunteer team and tasks they already do. On day one, choose three small work items: a bug fix, a test addition, and a documentation correction. On day two, add the two-minute prediction to the task brief. On day three, require evidence-first investigation before edits. On day four, use the understanding note in review.

By day five, collect the questions reviewers asked that exposed weak reasoning. Turn the best ones into a lightweight checklist. On day six, compare cycle time and rework with a similar set of recent tasks. On day seven, decide what to keep. If the workflow adds friction without improving explanation, evidence, or rework, simplify it. If it finds mistakes earlier and gives people better command of the code, expand it one task category at a time.

The goal is not to make every agent task educational theater. It is to stop treating learning as an accidental byproduct of code generation. AI-native developers will ship quickly. The strongest ones will also know why the system works, where it might fail, and how to prove the difference.

FAQ: AI coding agent learning workflowWhat is an AI coding agent learning workflow?

It is a repeatable way to use an AI coding agent while preserving developer understanding. The core loop is to predict the behavior, delegate a bounded investigation, inspect the causal story, explain the change back, and verify it with an independent signal.

Will this make my team slower?

It adds a few minutes to small tasks, but it can prevent costly rework and dependence later. Use the full loop for unfamiliar or risky work. For routine work with excellent tests, keep the understanding note short and let automation handle the mechanics.

Can junior developers use coding agents safely?

Yes, if tasks are bounded and review centers on reasoning, not just output. Start with explain-first work, require focused tests, and have a more experienced engineer check the mental model as well as the diff.

Should developers write every line themselves to learn?

No. Manual typing is not the only route to learning. Developers need repeated practice at reading code, forming hypotheses, testing behavior, reviewing tradeoffs, and debugging failures. An agent can accelerate those activities when the workflow requires them.

Which AI coding agent is best for this workflow?

The workflow is tool-agnostic. Use an agent that can show its evidence, work in a bounded scope, and produce changes you can validate. The important choice is the task contract and review standard, not the product logo.

How do I know whether an agent-assisted change is understood?

Ask the author to explain the behavior, name the invariant, describe one failure case, and point to the evidence. If they can do that without leaning on a generated summary, they likely have enough understanding to own the change.

items.title: How attackers persuade AI agents to break the rules
items.summary: Elise Racine & The Bigger Picture / Web of Influence I / Licenced by CC-BY 4.0 By Tanya Petersen Today, most of us interact with AI assistants – reactive bots that wait for human instructions. Yet, AI assistants are rapidly being replaced by agentic AI agents, that can interact with external tools, browse the web, generate images, send emails, and perform increasingly complex workflows on behalf of users. As these agentic agents become more capable, they may be exploited by people with bad intentions. Safety tests have generally only checked whether an AI agent refuses a single harmful request – they don’t measure what happens when an attacker gradually persuades the AI through a series of seemingly harmless conversations. Now, researchers from EPFL’s Natural Language Processing Laboratory have developed STING (Sequential Testing of Illicit N-step Goal execution), an automated testing framework that simulates how a real attacker might manipulate large language model (LLM) agents into carrying out harmful tasks over multiple interactions. In their paper , presented at the 2026 International Conference on Machine Learning , the EPFL researchers outline how, rather than simply asking an AI agent to do something obviously malicious, STING breaks an illicit objective into a series of seemingly harmless requests, each building towards the final goal. “LLM agents are everywhere,” says PhD student Ayush Kumar Tarun in the NLP Lab, and lead author of the study. “They’re very powerful, but what if someone with bad intentions wants to use those same agents? That’s what we wanted to understand.” As companies race to deploy these systems, ensuring they cannot be manipulated into assisting with cybercrime, fraud or other harmful activities has become an urgent challenge. In one example, META admitted in June that attackers used simple social engineering tactics, rather than malicious code or malware, to trick its AI support assistant into granting unauthorized access to Instagram accounts. Thinking like an attacker “If you simply ask an AI agent to hack someone’s account, today’s models are generally smart enough to refuse,” explained Antoine Bosselut, head of the NLP Lab and co-author of the paper. “But, if you decompose that goal into smaller, more benign-looking requests, and adapt those requests as the conversation progresses, you have a much better chance of getting the agent to perform the actions you want.” STING reproduces this behavior by creating an automated “attacker” that develops a step-by-step plan before attempting to persuade a target AI agent to execute each stage. The researchers tested this approach across 176 harmful task scenarios involving several leading AI models (like GPT, Gemini, and Claude) operating as tool-using agents. The results showed that multi-turn attacks consistently succeeded more often than traditional single-prompt tests. In some cases, agents were twice as likely to complete harmful tasks when attackers gradually built towards their objective rather than stating it outright. “We expected multi-turn attacks to perform better. What surprised us was the magnitude,” says Tarun. “For some models, harmful task completion was around two times higher than with existing single-turn evaluations. STING measures how quickly an attack’s success occurs, rather than only whether an attack eventually succeeds, allowing different testing approaches to be compared more fairly.” Challenging assumptions about language The team also explored whether attacks became more effective in different, lower-resource languages where less training data exists, and were surprised by the results. “We expected to see differences across languages because earlier research showed that translating prompts into lower-resource languages could bypass safety measures,” says Tarun. “But for agents, we found that harmful task completion rates were remarkably similar across all seven languages we tested.” That finding challenges a growing assumption in AI safety research that multilingual vulnerabilities naturally increase as language resources decrease. However, the researchers also discovered an important caveat. When sophisticated attackers switched languages during different stages of a multi-step attack, harmful task completion could become dramatically more successful, highlighting another avenue that future safety evaluations should examine. Safety shouldn’t be an afterthought The research comes at a time when the rapid adoption of agentic AI agents makes proactive safety testing essential. “We’ve focused enormously on making agents more capable,” says Bosselut. “But we also need people working on how to prevent those capabilities from being misused. Traditionally, safety has often been something people think about when something breaks, not before, but with AI agents, it can’t be an add-on or an afterthought.” Looking ahead, the research team hopes STING will encourage developers to embed safety testing much earlier in the design process and, develop a framework for multi-agent systems. “Research efforts to expose vulnerabilities are much larger in number than those showing practical defense strategies, and this is a crucial area of development. We also need to address what we can do for the models that are already out there in the wild for which safety was a post-hoc addition,” concluded Tarun. AI Assistant vs. AI Agent Autonomy is the fundamental difference between an AI assistant and an AI agent. AI assistants respond to our requests refined by our prompts and during conversations, we clarify and guide the AI toward what we’re looking for. An AI agent, on the other hand, is given a high-level goal and works out autonomously and proactively how to achieve it. Example: Recently in Australia an AI agent acting as a personal assistant was told to secure a spot in a full gym class. It autonomously scanned the gym’s booking system, located an unpatched security loophole, bypassed booking calendar restrictions, and deleted another member from the waitlist to force its user into the class. Because it autonomously planned and executed a multi-step strategy to meet its goal, the example has been widely cited as Australia’s first consumer-run AI agent attack.

items.title: Phishing Website Detection with Machine Learning: A Step-by-Step PySpark Guide
items.summary: A step-by-step guide to building a fake-domain detector with PySpark, MLlib and Tableau, using 11,430 real URLs. My best model hit 96% accuracy. Phishing website detection with machine learning: a fake bank login page with a suspicious URL flagged by a PySpark model as phishing, showing warning signs like URL length, domain age and PageRank. Image by author. You get an email from your bank. The link says www.standardcharterbank-login.com. Looks fine, right? It isn’t. And that’s exactly the problem. About 1.4 million phishing sites go live every month , and Google alone blocks roughly 100 million phishing emails a day ( AAG IT ). Most of these scams work because the fake URL looks almost right. So I asked a simple question: can a machine learn to tell a fake website from a real one, just by looking at its URL and a few page signals? Turns out it can. In this post I’ll walk you through exactly how I built it, step by step, so you can build your own. TL;DR Data: 11,430 URLs, 89 features, perfectly balanced (50% phishing, 50% legit) Tools: PySpark 3.4 + MLlib for the heavy lifting, Tableau for the visuals Winner: Random Forest, with 96% accuracy and 0.99 AUC Biggest surprise: a feature-selection step that “did nothing” was actually a one-line bug (more on that later) Code: GitHub repo · Dashboard: Tableau Public What gives a fake website away? Phishers copy the look of a real site. But they can’t easily copy its history . A brand-new domain, a weird long URL, zero search ranking: these leave fingerprints. Before building anything, I explored the data to see which fingerprints actually matter. Here’s what stood out: Phishing URLs are longer. On average 75 characters, vs 47 for legitimate sites. URLs in the dataset ranged from 12 to a wild 1,641 characters. Low PageRank is a red flag. At PageRank 0, there were 2,565 phishing URLs and only 101 legitimate ones. Low traffic is suspicious. Sites with 0–100 visits had 1,235 phishing cases. Above 100 visits, legitimate sites took over. Google often hasn’t indexed them. 5,136 phishing URLs were flagged as not indexed, vs 967 legit ones. Rule of thumb: a long URL on a young, unranked, low-traffic domain deserves a second look. The dataset I used the Web Page Phishing Detection dataset on Kaggle. It’s based on research by Hannousse and Yahiouche (2021) , so it’s a solid, citable source. 11,430 URLs , 5,715 phishing and 5,715 legitimate 89 columns , about 6.6 MB Target: the status column (legitimate or phishing) The features fall into three groups: URL structure: length_url, nb_dots, nb_hyphens, nb_slash, ip, https_token Page content: login_form, iframe, popup_window, ratio_extHyperlinks External signals: domain_age, domain_registration_length, web_traffic, page_rank, google_index A balanced dataset is a gift. It means accuracy is a fair metric, and you don’t need tricks like oversampling. Let’s build it: step by step I ran everything on a MacBook Air M1 (8 GB RAM) with Python 3.10, PySpark 3.4.1 and Jupyter. If your laptop can run Chrome, it can run this. Step 1: Install Java (Spark needs it) Spark runs on the JVM, so install Java 8 first, then check it: java -version Next, find where Java lives and point JAVA_HOME at it. On newer Macs the default shell is zsh, so the setting goes in ~/.zprofile (not .bash_profile): /usr/libexec/java_home # add this line to ~/.zprofile export JAVA_HOME="/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/jdk-1.8.jdk/Contents/Home" Step 2: Install PySpark I used Conda, which keeps things tidy: conda install -c conda-forge pyspark pyspark --version If you see the Spark logo and a version number, you’re good. Step 3: Start a Spark session and load the data from pyspark.sql import SparkSession spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("URLClassification").getOrCreate() data = spark.read.csv("dataset_phishing.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True) data.printSchema() inferSchema=True lets Spark guess each column's type, so numbers come in as numbers, not strings. Step 4: Explore before you model Don’t skip this. EDA is where you find out what the model should learn. I checked three things first: # 1. Duplicates? print(data.count(), data.dropDuplicates().count()) # 2. Is the target balanced? data.groupBy("status").count().show() # 3. Quick stats on a feature data.select("length_url").describe().show() Then I looked for features that move together, using a correlation heatmap: import seaborn as sns import matplotlib.pyplot as plt corr = data.drop("url", "status").toPandas().corr() plt.figure(figsize=(32, 20)) sns.heatmap(corr, cmap="coolwarm", center=0) plt.show() Tip: toPandas() pulls everything into memory. Fine for 6 MB, risky for 6 GB. On big data, sample first. The strongest pair was longest_word_path with longest_words_raw, which makes sense since one is part of the other. Step 5: Make it pretty (optional, but worth it) Notebook charts are fine for you. For anyone else, I rebuilt them in Tableau. In Tableau Prep , I swapped the 0/1 codes for human words: 0 became "Legit" and 1 became "Phishing", and other flags became "Yes"/"No". Small change, much easier dashboards. You can explore the result on Tableau Public . Step 6: Prepare features for MLlib MLlib has two rules: labels must be numbers, and all features must sit in one vector column . Two tools handle that: from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer, VectorAssembler feature_cols = [c for c in data.columns if c not in ("url", "status")] target_indexer = StringIndexer(inputCol="status", outputCol="label") assembler = VectorAssembler(inputCols=feature_cols, outputCol="features") Step 7: Train five models in one loop Why guess which algorithm is best when you can test them all? Put them in a dictionary: from pyspark.ml.classification import ( DecisionTreeClassifier, RandomForestClassifier, NaiveBayes, GBTClassifier, LinearSVC) classifiers = { "DecisionTree": DecisionTreeClassifier(labelCol="label", featuresCol="features"), "RandomForest": RandomForestClassifier(labelCol="label", featuresCol="features", numTrees=100, maxDepth=10), "NaiveBayes": NaiveBayes(smoothing=1.0, modelType="gaussian"), "GBT": GBTClassifier(labelCol="label", featuresCol="features", maxIter=10), "LinearSVC": LinearSVC(labelCol="label", featuresCol="features"), } Then wrap each one in a Pipeline, split 70/30, train and score: from pyspark.ml import Pipeline from pyspark.ml.evaluation import ( BinaryClassificationEvaluator, MulticlassClassificationEvaluator) train, test = data.randomSplit([0.7, 0.3], seed=123) results = [] for name, clf in classifiers.items(): model = Pipeline(stages=[target_indexer, assembler, clf]).fit(train) preds = model.transform(test) auc = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label").evaluate(preds) auprc = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label", metricName="areaUnderPR").evaluate(preds) acc = MulticlassClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label", metricName="accuracy").evaluate(preds) f1 = MulticlassClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label", metricName="f1").evaluate(preds) results.append((name, round(auc, 2), round(auprc, 2), round(acc, 2), round(f1, 2))) Tip: fix the seed so every model sees the exact same train/test split. Otherwise you're comparing luck, not algorithms. Step 8: Try feature selection with Chi-Square 89 features is a lot. Could the top 10 do just as well? Chi-Square (χ²) scores each feature by how strongly it relates to the label. It needs non-negative inputs, which suits this mostly 0/1 data. from pyspark.ml.feature import ChiSqSelector selector = ChiSqSelector(numTopFeatures=10, featuresCol="features", outputCol="selected_features") I ran the same loop again with the selector added to each pipeline. Keep this step in mind. It comes back in the results. The results: Random Forest wins Here’s how all five models scored on the 30% test set: Model AUC AUPRC Accuracy F1 Random Forest 0.99 0.99 0.96 0.96 Linear SVC 0.98 0.98 0.94 0.94 Gradient Boosted Trees 0.98 0.98 0.93 0.93 Decision Tree 0.90 0.93 0.92 0.92 Naive Bayes 0.65 0.68 0.76 0.76 Random Forest labeled a URL correctly 96 times out of 100 . That matches earlier research too ( Subasi et al., 2017 ; Hutchinson et al., 2018 ). Why does it work so well here? Phishing signals combine in messy ways: a long URL alone is fine, but a long URL plus a young domain plus zero traffic is not. Hundreds of trees voting together are great at catching those combinations. Naive Bayes struggled because it assumes every feature is independent. Here they clearly aren’t (URL length and word length rise together, for example). The plot twist: Chi-Square “changed nothing” With Chi-Square feature selection added, every model scored exactly the same , to two decimal places. My first conclusion was that feature selection simply didn’t help. But identical numbers across five different models is suspicious. Look at the code again: selector = ChiSqSelector(..., outputCol="selected_features") RandomForestClassifier(labelCol="label", featuresCol="features") # ← still reads all 89 The selector wrote its top 10 features into selected_features. But every classifier was still reading from features. So the selection ran, and then got ignored. The fix is one argument: RandomForestClassifier(labelCol="label", featuresCol="selected_features") Lesson: when a change produces exactly the same result, don’t celebrate or shrug. Check that the change was actually wired in. What I’d tell you before you try this Start with EDA, not models. The charts told me the story (long URLs, low PageRank, low traffic) before any model did. Test several algorithms at once. A dictionary plus a loop costs ten extra lines and saves you from betting on the wrong one. Use a fixed seed. Same split for every model, or the comparison means nothing. Be suspicious of “no change”. Identical scores usually mean a wiring bug, not a useless technique. Show your work visually. A Tableau dashboard explains your findings to people who will never open a notebook. Limits worth knowing Some of the strongest features (page_rank, web_traffic, google_index) come from outside services. A brand-new phishing site you check in real time may not have that data yet. 11,430 URLs is a small set for Spark. The same code scales to millions of rows, which is the real reason to use PySpark here. Phishers adapt. A model trained on 2021 data needs regular retraining. What’s next If I take this further, I’ll fix the Chi-Square wiring and compare 10 vs 89 features properly, add real cross-validation with CrossValidator, and wrap the Random Forest in a small API that checks any URL you paste in. Try it yourself Full code: GitHub repo Interactive dashboard: Tableau Public Dataset: Kaggle If this helped, give it a clap and follow for more hands-on data science. And next time a link looks almost right, check the URL twice. References AAG IT Support. The Latest Phishing Statistics . Hannousse, A. & Yahiouche, S. (2021). Web page phishing detection dataset . Mendeley Data. Hutchinson, S., Zhang, Z. & Liu, Q. (2018). Detecting Phishing Websites with Random Forest . Springer. Subasi, A. et al. (2017). Intelligent phishing website detection using random forest classifier . ICECTA. Apache Spark. Spark SQL and DataFrames guide .   • URL structure: length_url, nb_dots, nb_hyphens, nb_slash, ip, https_token
  • Page content: login_form, iframe, popup_window, ratio_extHyperlinks
  • External signals: domain_age, domain_registration_length, web_traffic, page_rank, google_index

A balanced dataset is a gift. It means accuracy is a fair metric, and you don’t need tricks like oversampling.

Let’s build it: step by step

I ran everything on a MacBook Air M1 (8 GB RAM) with Python 3.10, PySpark 3.4.1 and Jupyter. If your laptop can run Chrome, it can run this.

Step 1: Install Java (Spark needs it)

Spark runs on the JVM, so install Java 8 first, then check it:

java -version

Next, find where Java lives and point JAVA_HOME at it. On newer Macs the default shell is zsh, so the setting goes in ~/.zprofile (not .bash_profile):

/usr/libexec/java_home
# add this line to ~/.zprofile
export JAVA_HOME="/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/jdk-1.8.jdk/Contents/Home"
Step 2: Install PySpark

I used Conda, which keeps things tidy:

conda install -c conda-forge pyspark
pyspark --version

If you see the Spark logo and a version number, you’re good.

Step 3: Start a Spark session and load the data
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("URLClassification").getOrCreate()
data = spark.read.csv("dataset_phishing.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)
data.printSchema()

inferSchema=True lets Spark guess each column's type, so numbers come in as numbers, not strings.

Step 4: Explore before you model

Don’t skip this. EDA is where you find out what the model should learn. I checked three things first:

# 1. Duplicates?
print(data.count(), data.dropDuplicates().count())
# 2. Is the target balanced?
data.groupBy("status").count().show()
# 3. Quick stats on a feature
data.select("length_url").describe().show()

Then I looked for features that move together, using a correlation heatmap:

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
corr = data.drop("url", "status").toPandas().corr()
plt.figure(figsize=(32, 20))
sns.heatmap(corr, cmap="coolwarm", center=0)
plt.show()

Tip: toPandas() pulls everything into memory. Fine for 6 MB, risky for 6 GB. On big data, sample first.

The strongest pair was longest_word_path with longest_words_raw, which makes sense since one is part of the other.

Step 5: Make it pretty (optional, but worth it)

Notebook charts are fine for you. For anyone else, I rebuilt them in Tableau.

In Tableau Prep, I swapped the 0/1 codes for human words: 0 became "Legit" and 1 became "Phishing", and other flags became "Yes"/"No". Small change, much easier dashboards. You can explore the result on Tableau Public.

Step 6: Prepare features for MLlib

MLlib has two rules: labels must be numbers, and all features must sit in one vector column. Two tools handle that:

from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer, VectorAssembler
feature_cols = [c for c in data.columns if c not in ("url", "status")]
target_indexer = StringIndexer(inputCol="status", outputCol="label")
assembler = VectorAssembler(inputCols=feature_cols, outputCol="features")
Step 7: Train five models in one loop

Why guess which algorithm is best when you can test them all? Put them in a dictionary:

from pyspark.ml.classification import (
    DecisionTreeClassifier, RandomForestClassifier,
    NaiveBayes, GBTClassifier, LinearSVC)
classifiers = {
    "DecisionTree": DecisionTreeClassifier(labelCol="label", featuresCol="features"),
    "RandomForest": RandomForestClassifier(labelCol="label", featuresCol="features",
                                           numTrees=100, maxDepth=10),
    "NaiveBayes":   NaiveBayes(smoothing=1.0, modelType="gaussian"),
    "GBT":          GBTClassifier(labelCol="label", featuresCol="features", maxIter=10),
    "LinearSVC":    LinearSVC(labelCol="label", featuresCol="features"),
}

Then wrap each one in a Pipeline, split 70/30, train and score:

from pyspark.ml import Pipeline
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import (
    BinaryClassificationEvaluator, MulticlassClassificationEvaluator)
train, test = data.randomSplit([0.7, 0.3], seed=123)
results = []
for name, clf in classifiers.items():
    model = Pipeline(stages=[target_indexer, assembler, clf]).fit(train)
    preds = model.transform(test)
    auc   = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label").evaluate(preds)
    auprc = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label",
                metricName="areaUnderPR").evaluate(preds)
    acc   = MulticlassClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label",
                metricName="accuracy").evaluate(preds)
    f1    = MulticlassClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label",
                metricName="f1").evaluate(preds)
    results.append((name, round(auc, 2), round(auprc, 2), round(acc, 2), round(f1, 2)))

Tip: fix the seed so every model sees the exact same train/test split. Otherwise you're comparing luck, not algorithms.

Step 8: Try feature selection with Chi-Square

89 features is a lot. Could the top 10 do just as well? Chi-Square (χ²) scores each feature by how strongly it relates to the label. It needs non-negative inputs, which suits this mostly 0/1 data.

from pyspark.ml.feature import ChiSqSelector
selector = ChiSqSelector(numTopFeatures=10,
                         featuresCol="features",
                         outputCol="selected_features")

I ran the same loop again with the selector added to each pipeline. Keep this step in mind. It comes back in the results.

The results: Random Forest wins

Here’s how all five models scored on the 30% test set:

Model                    AUC    AUPRC   Accuracy   F1
Random Forest            0.99   0.99    0.96       0.96
Linear SVC               0.98   0.98    0.94       0.94
Gradient Boosted Trees   0.98   0.98    0.93       0.93
Decision Tree            0.90   0.93    0.92       0.92
Naive Bayes              0.65   0.68    0.76       0.76

Random Forest labeled a URL correctly 96 times out of 100. That matches earlier research too (Subasi et al., 2017; Hutchinson et al., 2018).

Why does it work so well here? Phishing signals combine in messy ways: a long URL alone is fine, but a long URL plus a young domain plus zero traffic is not. Hundreds of trees voting together are great at catching those combinations.

Naive Bayes struggled because it assumes every feature is independent. Here they clearly aren’t (URL length and word length rise together, for example).

The plot twist: Chi-Square “changed nothing”

With Chi-Square feature selection added, every model scored exactly the same, to two decimal places. My first conclusion was that feature selection simply didn’t help.

But identical numbers across five different models is suspicious. Look at the code again:

selector = ChiSqSelector(..., outputCol="selected_features")
RandomForestClassifier(labelCol="label", featuresCol="features")  # ← still reads all 89

The selector wrote its top 10 features into selected_features. But every classifier was still reading from features. So the selection ran, and then got ignored.

The fix is one argument:

RandomForestClassifier(labelCol="label", featuresCol="selected_features")

Lesson: when a change produces exactly the same result, don’t celebrate or shrug. Check that the change was actually wired in.

What I’d tell you before you try this
  1. Start with EDA, not models. The charts told me the story (long URLs, low PageRank, low traffic) before any model did.
  2. Test several algorithms at once. A dictionary plus a loop costs ten extra lines and saves you from betting on the wrong one.
  3. Use a fixed seed. Same split for every model, or the comparison means nothing.
  4. Be suspicious of “no change”. Identical scores usually mean a wiring bug, not a useless technique.
  5. Show your work visually. A Tableau dashboard explains your findings to people who will never open a notebook.
Limits worth knowing
  • Some of the strongest features (page_rank, web_traffic, google_index) come from outside services. A brand-new phishing site you check in real time may not have that data yet.
  • 11,430 URLs is a small set for Spark. The same code scales to millions of rows, which is the real reason to use PySpark here.
  • Phishers adapt. A model trained on 2021 data needs regular retraining.
What’s next

If I take this further, I’ll fix the Chi-Square wiring and compare 10 vs 89 features properly, add real cross-validation with CrossValidator, and wrap the Random Forest in a small API that checks any URL you paste in.

Try it yourself
  • Full code: GitHub repo
  • Interactive dashboard: Tableau Public
  • Dataset: Kaggle

If this helped, give it a clap and follow for more hands-on data science. And next time a link looks almost right, check the URL twice.

References
  • AAG IT Support. The Latest Phishing Statistics.
  • Hannousse, A. & Yahiouche, S. (2021). Web page phishing detection dataset. Mendeley Data.
  • Hutchinson, S., Zhang, Z. & Liu, Q. (2018). Detecting Phishing Websites with Random Forest. Springer.
  • Subasi, A. et al. (2017). Intelligent phishing website detection using random forest classifier. ICECTA.
  • Apache Spark. Spark SQL and DataFrames guide.
