items.title: Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut
items.summary: More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows. The numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales. Investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.) That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses. The low point for Series A funding in the past five years was 2023, with $23 billion invested in U.S.-based startups. Series A investment totals each year since have grown, doubling this year compared to 2023. At the same time, round counts have settled, averaging 1,200 companies funded at Series A at $1 million or more in 2023 through 2025. This year, the trend is holding, with round counts in that range, give or take 100 deals. “On the application side, it’s a bit harder, and that’s where I think there’s more of a Series A crunch,” according to Siddharth Ramakrishnan , a partner at Scale Venture Partners , which primarily leads Series A and B rounds. This dynamic — steady deal count despite much more money flowing — is also impacting how early-stage VCs invest. Go big and early — or wait Among investors, there’s more competition, especially at the early stage. In turn, VCs are increasingly pursuing one of two opposing strategies: either writing much larger checks much earlier, or holding back until later rounds, Ramakrishnan said. With the first strategy, check sizes are getting much bigger, he noted, with $10 million to $20 million seed deals not uncommon. “Instead of waiting till the Series A, where they have $4 million in revenue and growing, you’re going to do it when they have $500,000 in revenue, they have a pilot, the team is smart,” he said. Other investors are waiting to invest later. “ ‘I’m not getting any new information by the time they’re at $2 million in revenue from $500,000, so I’m just going to wait until they actually take off,’ and then you’re seeing a gap,” Ramakrishnan said, explaining the thinking behind this investment approach. “People are putting in a lot of money at the Series B, Series C onwards, because that’s when you get the signal that things are really working.” Scale expects there to be a bit more variance in this current fund. Its preference is to stay at Series A and B risk profile, by “potentially pulling a little bit earlier and a little bit later and recreating it in the aggregate,” he said. The firm’s most recent fund 8 is its largest to date at $900 million, up from its prior $600 million fund. “We still think that Series A is a great place to be if you can make it happen, because it’s at that point where you ideally have enough information to make an informed bet, but not enough that there’s still some of the growth investors that are scared to come in,” Ramakrishnan said, “and so you get great companies at great prices.” Deals sizes trend higher At each quartile, U.S. Series A rounds have trended up in size this year, Crunchbase data shows. So far in 2026, 10% of Series A rounds are $75 million and over, up from $50 million in 2025. Those much-larger checks are translating into hypergrowth for some companies. “Instead of going zero to $7 million, which in the old world would have been amazing numbers, now there’s people going zero to $20 million, or zero to $30 million,” Ramakrishnan said. Raising a large Series A For founders, securing those larger checks often hinges on turning a handful of early customers into a repeatable sales process. Many startups get stuck in that transition, even as investors compete to back those that break through. “If you have the ambition to build a world-class company, then you also need to raise a big Series A to expand and go abroad, take on different types of markets,” according to European seed investor Anke Huiskes of NP-Hard Ventures , whom I interviewed on-stage at the HumanX Amsterdam conference on AI earlier this year. “I think the whole messy phase is in this go-to-market phase where you don’t really know who your ideal customer profile is,” said Huiskes, who invests at the seed stage in product-focused founders. She’s seen startups get stuck when they have a few customers but aren’t growing fast enough. “A lot of the companies hang out here,” she said. But for the companies who build that repetitive sales cycle, VCs are eagerly reaching out, she said: “And then I get a text, ‘Can you please give me an intro?’ And all of a sudden, I have 10 term sheets. So it’s really black and white.” Related Crunchbase queries: US Series A Funding, 2026 US Series B Funding, 2026 Related reading: Series B Funding Is Up, But Fewer Deals Are Getting Done Jumbo Series A Rounds Hiding The Real Squeeze On Seed Startups More Money, Fewer Checks: These 3 Charts Show The Divide Behind VC’s Record Funding Year Illustration: Dom Guzman

The numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales.

Investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.)

That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses.

The low point for Series A funding in the past five years was 2023, with $23 billion invested in U.S.-based startups. Series A investment totals each year since have grown, doubling this year compared to 2023.

At the same time, round counts have settled, averaging 1,200 companies funded at Series A at $1 million or more in 2023 through 2025. This year, the trend is holding, with round counts in that range, give or take 100 deals.

“On the application side, it’s a bit harder, and that’s where I think there’s more of a Series A crunch,” according to Siddharth Ramakrishnan, a partner at Scale Venture Partners, which primarily leads Series A and B rounds.

This dynamic — steady deal count despite much more money flowing — is also impacting how early-stage VCs invest.

Go big and early — or wait

Among investors, there’s more competition, especially at the early stage. In turn, VCs are increasingly pursuing one of two opposing strategies: either writing much larger checks much earlier, or holding back until later rounds, Ramakrishnan said.

With the first strategy, check sizes are getting much bigger, he noted, with $10 million to $20 million seed deals not uncommon. “Instead of waiting till the Series A, where they have $4 million in revenue and growing, you’re going to do it when they have $500,000 in revenue, they have a pilot, the team is smart,” he said.

Other investors are waiting to invest later. “ ‘I’m not getting any new information by the time they’re at $2 million in revenue from $500,000, so I’m just going to wait until they actually take off,’ and then you’re seeing a gap,” Ramakrishnan said, explaining the thinking behind this investment approach. “People are putting in a lot of money at the Series B, Series C onwards, because that’s when you get the signal that things are really working.”

Scale expects there to be a bit more variance in this current fund. Its preference is to stay at Series A and B risk profile, by “potentially pulling a little bit earlier and a little bit later and recreating it in the aggregate,” he said.

The firm’s most recent fund 8 is its largest to date at $900 million, up from its prior $600 million fund.

“We still think that Series A is a great place to be if you can make it happen, because it’s at that point where you ideally have enough information to make an informed bet, but not enough that there’s still some of the growth investors that are scared to come in,” Ramakrishnan said, “and so you get great companies at great prices.”

Deals sizes trend higher

At each quartile, U.S. Series A rounds have trended up in size this year, Crunchbase data shows. So far in 2026, 10% of Series A rounds are $75 million and over, up from $50 million in 2025.

Those much-larger checks are translating into hypergrowth for some companies. “Instead of going zero to $7 million, which in the old world would have been amazing numbers, now there’s people going zero to $20 million, or zero to $30 million,” Ramakrishnan said.

Raising a large Series A

For founders, securing those larger checks often hinges on turning a handful of early customers into a repeatable sales process. Many startups get stuck in that transition, even as investors compete to back those that break through.

“If you have the ambition to build a world-class company, then you also need to raise a big Series A to expand and go abroad, take on different types of markets,” according to European seed investor Anke Huiskes of NP-Hard Ventures, whom I interviewed on-stage at the HumanX Amsterdam conference on AI earlier this year.

“I think the whole messy phase is in this go-to-market phase where you don’t really know who your ideal customer profile is,” said Huiskes, who invests at the seed stage in product-focused founders.

She’s seen startups get stuck when they have a few customers but aren’t growing fast enough. “A lot of the companies hang out here,” she said.

But for the companies who build that repetitive sales cycle, VCs are eagerly reaching out, she said: “And then I get a text, ‘Can you please give me an intro?’ And all of a sudden, I have 10 term sheets. So it’s really black and white.”

items.title: Paper Unicorns Are Cheap. Building A $1B Revenue AI Company Takes A Multimarket Cap Table
items.summary: By Ilman Shazhaev A $1 billion valuation still makes a startup a unicorn on paper. Yet when 250 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in the first half of 2026, the speed of wealth creation raised another question : How many of these businesses can keep their customers once the initial excitement fades? I would set a higher benchmark for unicorns with $1 billion in revenue sustained by customers who keep paying. I spent five years at Harbin Institute of Technology and Shanghai Jiao Tong University , where “fail fast, improve faster” shaped my approach to building technology. Having studied in China before building an AI company in Abu Dhabi, I have also seen how the same growth story can raise different questions among investors, eventually boiling down to: “What will customers keep paying for?” The revenue test investors should demand Ilman Shazhaev, founder and CEO of Dizzaract. Fast revenue deserves attention. Founders who turn pilots into paying deployments are solving a real problem, and strong sales can make the next round easier. An annualized run rate built from discounts, experimental budgets or generous compute subsidies, however, offers little assurance that customers will stay. Since 2023, the price of hitting a fixed level of AI performance has dropped thirteenfold every year. Startups that just resell model access now face brutal price competition. Look at OpenRouter and its $113 million Series B: developers can already swap between models through one shared interface. Businesses built around proprietary workflows face a different test. Software embedded in a company’s approvals, records and daily decisions can be far harder to replace than the model doing the underlying work. I would check whether customers renew at full price and expand their contracts. Then I would see whether margins stay healthy after inference costs. Why the cap table should cross borders Once founders know who keeps buying, they should raise across regions, because a local backer can double as market entry. Borders barely slow an AI product down. Enterprise sales still depend on local budgets, procurement procedures and relationships. A foreign investor becomes valuable when those connections turn a product demonstration into a paid contract. The $30 million Series A for London- and Gulf-based 1001 AI offers a useful example . U.S. venture firm Lux Capital led the financing, alongside Saudi PIF-backed Sanabil Investments . The deal cannot establish future retention by itself, but it shows how capital, talent and customers can sit on different maps, with engineers in London and customers in the Gulf. Ask every investor what they bring besides money. One warm introduction to the right buyer can beat a higher valuation if it turns into a contract you can actually deliver and renew. Different money, different obligations The choice between traditional venture funding and sovereign-backed money is often framed as a choice between fast and patient capital. I find the more practical distinction lies in the obligations attached to each check. In conversations with U.S. and European venture investors, I have often been asked how quickly we could turn product adoption into repeatable sales before competitors caught up. Venture firms need returns within their fund’s life. That puts commercial momentum and a sizable exit at the center of their investment decisions. The pressure can sharpen execution. It can also backfire when founders who chase fast expansion without counting delivery costs may fill their pipeline with discounted experiments instead of enduring enterprise relationships. Sovereign-backed investors usually ask me a very different set of questions. They want to know where user data gets processed and which technical capabilities stay in the country. Will local customers still be able to rely on the service years from now? Some funds carry an explicit domestic development mandate. For them, those concerns can count as investment criteria alongside financial returns. The upside is a partner who cares about local infrastructure and enterprise adoption. The price can be longer diligence and localization spending. Contract terms that make it harder to expand elsewhere can also cause a problem. Neither mandate is universal. Many sovereign-backed funds pursue conventional financial returns, while traditional VCs can support long enterprise sales cycles. Government-affiliated capital doesn’t guarantee procurement wins, either. Founders should read the fine print: governance rights, exclusivity requests, promised commercial introductions. Then judge whether the investor’s regional reach is worth the constraints. Fund what customers will keep The best capital strategy follows the customer’s path, from a working product to a renewal. Venture money speeds up development and sales once the business model works. Regional strategic investors earn their place when a new market’s infrastructure and procurement rules call for local expertise. I would rather show an investor a small cohort of customers renewing without discounts than a glossy revenue forecast that depends on the next funding round. The numbers to watch are net revenue retention, production deployments and margins after delivery costs. Market sentiment will keep minting and erasing paper unicorns every quarter. The founding teams that build $1 billion in lasting annual revenue will likely balance venture momentum with regional obligations. Their global cap tables will mirror the enterprise markets they serve. Ilman Shazhaev is the founder and CEO of Dizzaract , an AI and gaming infrastructure company headquartered in Abu Dhabi and the largest game development studio in the Middle East. His work focuses on distributed AI infrastructure, human behavioral data and the interactive environments in which AI systems are trained and tested. Shazhaev is a United Nations expert under the UNODC program, advising on how AI can help solve social problems in developing economies. He is also the author of 46 scientific articles, including published research on AI that reads a player’s psychological state from ordinary gaming hardware, and holds 10 registered invention patents. Illustration: Dom Guzman

The affair weakens Huang's lobbying efforts against stricter AI chip export controls, with a newly elected Democratic Congress poised to ramp up scrutiny of AI chip smuggling to China and push for tighter restrictions. items.title: Adobe’s CX Enterprise Coworker Gets Embedded Within Leading AI Platforms
items.summary: On November 6, Adobe announced that CX Enterprise Coworker, which serves as an agentic teammate for customer experience orchestration, will now be embedded in leading AI platforms including ChatGPT as a plugin, Claude, Databricks Genie, Gemini for business, and Microsoft Copilot. Availability is also expected in Amazon Quick, IBM and Snowflake soon. An end-to-end agentic AI system manages their customers’ lifecycle, ranging from acquiring clients to converting lifetime customer value. CX Enterprise Coworker is built on open and flexible standards, including model context protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A). Anjul Bhambhri, Senior Vice President of Engineering, Customer Experience Orchestration, Adobe, said, “CX Enterprise Coworker connects these tools and workflows using brand, customer and channel intelligence, helping teams drive better business outcomes.” Meanwhile, Rao Surapaneni, Vice President, Gemini Agent Governance, Cloud AI, Google Cloud, spoke on how integrating CX Enterprise into Gemini enables customer data to be securely harnessed. “This collaborative, agent-to-agent approach represents the next frontier of productivity and creative execution for the modern enterprise,” Surapaneni added. Moreover, Adobe introduced new connectors for CX Enterprise Coworker that provide pre-built MCP server integrations with ecosystem technology partners. These include Microsoft Work IQ, RainFocus, Snowflake Cortex AI, Amazon Ads, Databricks Genie, Demandbase, and more, enabling CX Enterprise Coworker to act within well-known AI tools. To optimise the customer experience from start to finish, marketers can link the partner systems they already use without doing any integration work. They can then use a single request to extract data and take action across multiple systems. Global Systems Integrators (GSIs) such as Accenture, Capgemini, Cognizant, Deloitte Digital, EY, IBM, Infosys, PwC, and TCS employ CX Enterprise Coworkers’ agentic solutions and apply them immediately to their respective industries. GSIs plug their tools into Adobe CX Enterprise Coworker to link Adobe with wider corporate tech stacks, smooth out customer workflows, and turn AI tests into real business results. Agencies such as Dentsu, Havas, Omnicom, Publicis, Stagwell and WPP are also personalising CX Enterprise Coworker with proprietary IP, agents, tools and industry expertise to deliver personalised customer experiences directly into agentic customer experiences for joint clients.

items.title: Sarvam AI Appoints Ex-Google Cloud India MD Sashikumar Sreedharan as President and CBO
items.summary: Sarvam AI has appointed former Google Cloud India Managing Director Sashikumar Sreedharan as its President and Chief Business Officer (CBO), as the Indian AI startup looks to strengthen its presence in the enterprise and government sectors. Sreedharan will lead Sarvam’s business across enterprises and government institutions, while overseeing its work with digital-native companies, developers, and partners. He will also be responsible for marketing, finance, forward-deployed engineering, service delivery, and commercial operations. He will join the company's board of directors. Sreedharan joins Sarvam from Google Cloud, where he most recently served as Managing Director for India. He brings over three decades of experience in the technology industry. Before Google, he led Microsoft India’s enterprise business as Managing Director for more than five years. The appointment comes as Sarvam expands its enterprise and government customer base. The company said more than 100 enterprises and government institutions are building with its full-stack AI offering. Commenting on his appointment, Sreedharan said, “India should be a maker of the intelligence the world runs on. For me, joining Sarvam is a commitment to that opportunity. I look forward to working with the team and our customers to build products that become part of how industries and governments operate.” Sarvam said its next phase of growth will focus on advancing its research, developing products for global markets and scaling its operations. The company is also positioning enterprise ownership of AI as a central part of its strategy. Its approach centres on keeping enterprise data, models, and agents within organisations, allowing them to retain control over their AI systems and the value they generate. Sarvam believes enterprise requirements will also feed into its research efforts, with industry demands driving research and research breakthroughs supporting the development of new industries.

items.title: EXL Acquires Aimpoint Digital, Adds 250 AI and Data Experts
items.summary: EXL has acquired data and AI consulting firm Aimpoint Digital to expand its forward-deployed AI engineering capabilities and help enterprises move AI projects from pilot stages to production. The acquisition adds around 250 AI engineers, platform architects, analytics consultants, decision scientists and AI strategists to EXL’s workforce. The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the transaction. The acquisition will strengthen EXL’s capabilities across the enterprise AI lifecycle, covering strategy, architecture, engineering, deployment, evaluation and managed operations. It will also expand the company’s expertise across AI and data platforms, including Anthropic, Databricks and Snowflake. “Clients require a partner who can take them from AI ambition to impact at enterprise scale,” said Rohit Kapoor, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of EXL. “Aimpoint Digital’s forward-deployed strategists and engineers bring the hands-on expertise to turn AI strategy into production reality on the platforms our clients trust most,” Kapoor added. The acquisition comes as enterprises increase spending on AI but continue to face challenges in moving projects beyond pilots and into production. By combining Aimpoint Digital’s engineering capabilities with EXL’s industry expertise, data foundations and agentic AI solutions, the companies intend to help clients integrate AI into business workflows. Aimpoint Digital will bring expertise in building enterprise data and AI platforms, along with engineers who work closely with client teams to develop and deploy AI systems. “Joining EXL lets us do more breakthrough work on a much larger scale,” said Ben Yopp, Chief Executive Officer and Co-founder of Aimpoint Digital. “We bring deep AI strategy and engineering talent and EXL brings industry expertise, global reach and the ability to run AI in operations. Together, we can take clients’ most important AI initiatives into production and keep them performing at the highest levels,” Yopp added. The combined offering will also give clients a single partner across the AI implementation process, from initial strategy discussions and architecture to production deployment and ongoing operations. EXL said this approach would reduce handoffs between teams and establish clearer accountability for business outcomes. The acquisition follows EXL’s purchase of AI model training and evaluation company iMerit. The iMerit acquisition expanded EXL’s capabilities in model training, evaluation and reinforcement learning. With Aimpoint Digital, EXL is looking to strengthen the engineering and deployment side of its AI business, complementing iMerit’s expertise in developing and improving AI models. Together, the two acquisitions expand EXL’s capabilities across the AI lifecycle, from model development and evaluation to enterprise deployment and managed AI operations.

items.title: Coforge Joins SpaceX Network to Develop Industry-Specific Grok Applications
items.summary: Indian IT services firm Coforge has joined SpaceX’s Super Intelligence Partner Network to develop enterprise applications using the Grok artificial intelligence portfolio. Coforge will participate as a Transformation Partner, developing industry-specific solutions and integrating them into clients’ existing systems and workflows. The company did not disclose the financial details of the partnership. Deployments will be handled through Momentuum blue, Coforge's specialised forward deployed engineering (FDE) unit. It embeds pods of senior FDEs, associate FDEs and AI agents within client environments. Coforge said these teams would be accountable for delivering business outcomes measured against agreed baselines. The partnership will also draw on its AI-led engineering and modernisation services, including Nuuron, its enterprise AI enablement suite. These capabilities form part of the company's AI-led engineering strategy . “From software modernisation and customer service to enterprise applications, we bring the industry context, engineering expertise and adoption capabilities to turn Grok's technology into solutions,” said Anup Nair, Executive Vice President and Chief AI Commercial Officer at Coforge. The Grok portfolio includes tools for chat, research, analysis, reasoning, software development, enterprise applications, conversational experiences, and image and video generation. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Infosys and LTM have also partnered with Anthropic to bring its Claude models into enterprise environments. These partnerships between Anthropic and Indian IT services firms offer another example of frontier AI developers working with established services providers to reach enterprise customers.

items.title: Week in AI Careers: Most Hirers Now Use AI to Screen Resumes
items.summary: The week’s clearest read on how AI is changing hiring came from a 38,000-person Northeastern University survey, which found that most people who make hiring decisions now use AI to screen resumes and that a quarter of them are taking on fewer entry-level workers. Fresh October labor data from CompTIA pointed the other way on volume, with tech-occupation unemployment at 2.8 percent and job postings tied to AI skills still climbing. Maryland’s comptroller launched a public dashboard to track where AI is adding and removing jobs across the state. Quick Hits cover Google’s new Africa skilling platform, a federal contractor’s workforce coalition with AWS, and a Yale core course built around AI, followed by the ODSC AI NYC summit. Surveys and research Northeastern survey finds AI screening most resumes and thinning entry-level hiring What happened: Northeastern University ’s Institute for Information, the Internet and Democracy published “AI in the Hiring Room” on November 1, drawn from its AI & Society Survey of 38,375 United States adults fielded June 21 to August 11, with analysis focused on 8,174 respondents who said they hire or significantly influence hiring. It found that 54 percent of hiring decision-makers use AI to screen resumes at least to some extent, rising to 83 percent in information and technology roles. Among those whose hiring has already shifted because of AI, 26 percent are taking on fewer entry-level workers and 7 percent are taking on more. On credentials, 38 percent said a college degree has become more valuable for entry-level hires since AI’s rise, 40 percent said about the same, and 16 percent said less valuable, per the NU Info Institute report and Northeastern Global News . Why it matters: The survey puts a large sample behind two shifts employers usually describe anecdotally, that AI screening now sits between most applicants and a human reader, and that the entry rung is thinning as routine junior tasks get automated. The split on degree value suggests employers are re-weighting credentials against demonstrated AI skill rather than dropping them. For anyone advising early-career candidates or designing graduate programs, the practical signal is that a resume has to clear an AI filter before it reaches a person, and that entry-level roles are getting harder to find even where overall tech hiring holds steady. Skills demand and the labor market CompTIA reports steady October tech hiring and rising AI-skill demand What happened: CompTIA reported on November 6 that the United States technology sector added about 7,200 jobs in October while technology occupations across all industries grew by roughly 26,000, holding the tech-occupation unemployment rate at 2.8 percent against a national rate of 4.1 percent. Active job postings tied to AI skills reached 366,322, up 6.2 percent from September, and demand for specialized AI roles rose 9.8 percent. Total active tech job postings stood at 629,876, up 18.5 percent from a year earlier, according to CompTIA’s Tech Jobs Report . Why it matters: The monthly read separates the tech labor market’s volume from the automation worry in the survey data, and for October the volume held up. A 2.8 percent unemployment rate for tech occupations points to continued scarcity of skilled workers even as individual companies trim headcount. AI-skill postings climbing faster than postings overall is the clearest sign that employers are converting AI interest into specific hiring, which rewards workers who can show applied skills rather than general familiarity. Geographic and sector spread Maryland launches a state dashboard to track AI’s effect on jobs What happened: Maryland Comptroller Brooke Lierman launched a public AI Economic Impact Tracker on November 5, a dashboard that combines government, university, and private data to show where AI is adding jobs in the state, where it could remove them, and how quickly Maryland businesses are adopting it. The tracker draws on Tufts University’s American AI Jobs Risk Index , which projects that Maryland could lose about 7.2 percent of its jobs to AI automation over the next several years under a median adoption scenario, the third-highest share among states, and on state figures showing about 3,600 Maryland job postings in 2026 sought skills to build or run AI systems. The Tufts index estimates roughly 9.3 million United States jobs at risk over two to five years, within a range of 2.7 million to 19.5 million, as the Southern Maryland Chronicle reported. Why it matters: A state finance office building a standing dashboard, rather than commissioning a one-off report, signals that AI’s labor effects are becoming a budgeting and planning concern for governments, not only a research topic. Framing the Tufts projections as risk rather than realized loss is the right caution, since the index does not count jobs AI may create and rests on adoption assumptions. For workers and employers in exposed states, a tool like this will prove useful only if it tracks actual hiring and separation flows over time, not just model-based risk scores. Quick hits Reskilling and upskilling Google launched Skilling Africa with Google on November 2, a free platform that bundles more than 15 training programs in digital and AI skills, runs offline and on low bandwidth, and aims to train 3 million people across the continent by 2030, building on more than 7 million young Africans trained so far; the company notes that over 90 percent of regional firms report too few AI-ready workers, per Google . CGI Federal, Amazon Web Services, and the University of Tennessee launched a workforce development coalition on November 5 to train and credential workers for AI and advanced engineering roles across the United States public sector, pairing cloud and AI curricula with employer demand, per CGI . Education and credentialing Yale School of Management added a required AI course to its core MBA curriculum, aimed at sending graduates into management roles able to apply AI tools rather than treat them as a specialty, per Yale SOM . items.title: Today’s AI won’t achieve superintelligence. But catastrophic risk is real | Sunita Verma
items.summary: The same technical limits that prevent superintelligence make these systems dangerous. But we know how to regulate them Many Silicon Valley leaders believe superintelligence is an imminent threat to society. The White House even published an accord about it. This isn’t enough. Geoffrey Hinton, the godfather of AI, estimates the risk of human extinction is at least 10% within the next few decades. The Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, argued that unchecked AI “could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems”. In response, 1,300 leaders and employees from many leading AI companies signed a letter calling to “deliberately pace” development.

items.title: Podcast: Distributed LLM Inference on Kubernetes with llm-d, Wasm, & TornadoVM
items.summary: In this episode, Edoardo Vacchi discusses the evolving landscape of WebAssembly on the backend, running Java workloads on GPUs using TornadoVM, and optimizing distributed AI inference using llm-d and vLLM on Kubernetes. Edoardo explains how llm-d manages cache locality (KV and prefix caches), request routing, and batch inference across Kubernetes clusters to maximize expensive GPU utilization. By Edoardo Vacchi

items.title: Beyond Hire-to-Rehire: How Workforce Data Can Turn HRTech From a Cost Centre
items.summary: Enterprises are moving toward a model where AI does more than automate individual tasks or answer queries. The next phase will see AI connect fragmented data across human resources, finance, sales, and operations to help business leaders understand risks, make decisions, and drive execution. As organisations accumulate more systems and data, the challenge is increasingly about connecting information across departments and translating it into measurable business outcomes. “The biggest change is that technology has moved from enabling the business to shaping the business,” Prasad Rajappan, Founder and MD of human capital management software provider ZingHR, tells AIM. “The question is no longer, ‘What can we automate?’ but ‘What can the business do now that it could not do before?’ AI is accelerating this shift. Its real value is not automation alone, but using intelligence to make better decisions, act faster and deliver better business outcomes.” This shift is also changing how enterprises evaluate AI investments . Rather than adding AI features to existing workflows, businesses increasingly need to identify where the technology can improve productivity, reduce costs, accelerate growth, or strengthen decision-making. “The difference is whether AI is being deployed to drive a business outcome or simply to automate an existing process,” Rajappan says. Systems of Intelligence One of the central challenges facing enterprises is that their data remains distributed across systems designed for different functions. AI could help bridge this gap by creating an intelligence layer across existing enterprise applications, allowing organisations to interpret information across functions rather than analyse each department in isolation. “Enterprise architecture is moving from application-centric to intelligence-centric,” he says. “This does not mean replacing ERP, HCM, or CRM systems . They will continue to manage transactions and processes. The shift is towards an intelligence layer that connects these systems, interprets what is happening and orchestrates action around business outcomes.” However, connecting enterprise data alone does not guarantee better decisions. The value will depend on whether organisations can integrate reliable information, establish business context, and translate AI-generated insights into actions with measurable outcomes. “Recommendations are only an intermediate stage,” Rajappan says. Rather than replacing every existing workflow with an autonomous system, the opportunity lies in coordinating decisions and actions across functions, while retaining appropriate human oversight. “The bigger opportunity is enterprise orchestration—bringing together signals from people, finance, sales, operations, and other systems to understand what is happening, identify what matters, and connect decisions to accountable execution,” he says. The transition, however, will require enterprises to determine which decisions can be delegated to AI, which require human approval, and how actions are monitored. Generating a recommendation is different from executing it safely across business-critical systems. GHROWTH.ai and ZingHR's Expanding Role Rajappan points to GHROWTH.ai as an attempt to bring this intelligence-led approach to business leadership. It is an AI-powered “strategic command centre” for boards and CXOs, connecting information across people, finance, sales, operations, and other functions. The objective is to help leaders move beyond reviewing historical performance to identifying what requires attention and where the business should act. ZingHR, meanwhile, is evolving from its workforce technology roots toward a broader proposition that connects employee and organisational data with business outcomes. “We started with workforce technology, giving us a deep understanding of people, organisations and workforce data. As technology evolved with cloud, APIs, connected data and AI, we saw the opportunity to connect that intelligence to the broader business,” he says. “Today, ZingHR is evolving from managing the hire-to-rehire lifecycle to connecting people, intelligence, and business outcomes—helping organisations move from information to decisions and, increasingly, from decisions to action,” he adds. The shift also points to a potential change in HR technology . Rather than limiting AI to recruitment automation, employee queries, or workforce reporting, organisations could use it to understand how hiring, retention, learning, and performance influence business productivity, costs, and growth. “The bigger shift will be when AI moves HR from managing activities to understanding their impact on business outcomes,” Rajappan says. “That is the real shift—from HR that reports workforce data to HR that helps the business make better decisions.”

items.title: Getting ready for Apple’s next big thing: MacBook Neo 2
items.summary: Apple is on track to sell eight million MacBook Neo systems by the end of the year, and it expects the next generation of the device to do even better when it arrives in spring. To achieve this, Apple needs to remain focused on what made the product such a success . There is no doubt it has been a success. At one point Apple was complaining that it was unable to churn these things out fast enough . Tom Boger, Apple’s Vice President of Mac and iPad Product Marketing, recently called the introduction of the MacBook Neo “ a huge momentum creator ,” adding, “We’re bringing more new-to-Mac customers than we ever have in the 42 years that the Mac has been around.” He called this “remarkable” for a product that has been around for so long. A hit in the hard ground It’s also remarkable given the current environment. Consumer electronic sales are taking a beating from the combined effects of war, political instability, and AI-flation. As prices climb, cash-strapped buyers, both consumer and IT purchasers, have become much more discerning when hunting for the best available deal. Apple seems to be thriving all the same. Even at its higher-than-launch price (the $599 MacBook Neo now costs $699), Neo has stayed in the top three laptops sold on Amazon US since launch. All three of Amazon’s top selling laptops are Macs at time of writing. While global PC sales fell 21%, Apple’s global market share reached almost 10% . One data point claims that the Neo grabbed 23% of Apple’s total notebook sales volume within just 21 days of its release, purloining market share from midrange Windows devices and Chromebooks. Where the MacBook Neo won Where has it excelled? Consumers have flocked to it, but it has seen particular success in the education and enterprise markets. In education, Apple recently announced a massive contract with the Philippines Department of Education for more than 170,000 Macs for teachers and students. Apple called this the largest Mac deployment in its history. It also shows the MacBook Neo as a highly credible Chromebook alternative. In business, IT teams have already learned the ROI and TCO benefits of Macs . They know support costs fall as Mac deployment climbs, and that IT can support many more Macs per person than Windows. Price, or at least the perception of price, was the challenge — MacBook Neo lowered it, and enterprise purchasers saw the opportunity. Telia was one of the earliest large corporations to deploy the device at scale and found it well suited to all kinds of information workers for ease of use, manageability, and comfort. Helios X also deployed the device, and UK-based IT consultancy nDuo identified that many smaller companies are replacing Windows systems with Neos. Demand for their use within low-cost hybrid fleets is so strong that at least one reseller now provisions Neos with Windows 11 VMs preinstalled . This is real momentum. Many silver linings come shrouded in cloud, however. In this case, that cloud may be iPad sales, which fell 27.5% this year . While it is true the entire tablet industry has slumped this year, Apple purchasers might have felt that when they could buy MacBook Neo for about the same price as a midrange Apple tablet, then the Mac was the better choice. Zooming out, of course, Apple remains king of tablet hill with over a third of the market, so it may thrive despite that tradeoff. What must happen to the MacBook Neo 2? If we assume that Apple keeps the current $699 base price, then the Neo 2 must push at areas where the Neo 1 has already excelled. The anticipated improvements to the system should achieve that. A19 Pro chip: While only slightly better computationally than the A18 Pro, the GPU performance of the new processor is likely to improve. Industry watcher Tim Culpan says this will be a binned A19 chip with a 5-core GPU rather than the 6 cores found in iPhones. More memory: Current speculation suggests that Apple plans to increase memory to 12GB, up from 8GB. Storage and Touch ID: One way Apple can justify maintaining the higher entry-level cost is to bump up base storage and put Touch ID across the range. New colors, no fan, same Liquid Retina display: Apple intends to use new colors, turning the devices into a new kind of tech collectible. I still want the yellow one. Otherwise, the song remains the same — a quiet, light, affordable Mac for all of us. Apple must hope these tweaks will be enough to maintain the momentum this Mac has already achieved. What could go wrong? Memory prices are impacting costs across the supply chain right now, and Apple will need to find some way to keep the Neo within the pricing window potential customers have become used to: every dollar higher in cost will dent momentum a little more. Analysts will want to be reassured that the 12GB of included memory doesn’t squeeze Apple’s product margins too much; contrarywise, customers want to continue their love affair with the affordable everyMac. A Digitimes report tells us Apple has booked manufacturing for 16 million MacBook Neo 2 units, twice as many as it shifted for the MacBook Neo 1. I take that claim with a pinch of salt, but it still makes me think Apple’s management does not want to dent this momentum — which hints that next year’s Mac story may see even higher market share, albeit at the risk of some cannibalization of iPad sales. The MacBook Neo worked because it delivered Macs at a price that education, enterprise, and first-time Mac users could easily accept. If the Neo 2 can protect and improve on that offer, then Apple has a shot at even higher market share for the Mac. Now please subscribe to my daily, human-curated Apple-related news headline feed at The Core , or follow me on BlueSky , LinkedIn , or Mastodon .

items.title: India’s Office Workforce to Reach 48 Mn by 2030 as AI Reshapes Demand: Report
items.summary: India's office-using workforce is projected to increase from around 38 million in 2025 to 48 million by 2030, as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes commercial office demand, according to a study by real estate consultancy Cushman & Wakefield. Under its baseline scenario, office-using employment is expected to increase by nearly 9 million between 2025 and 2030, adding around 1.8 million workers annually. The study attributed the projected growth to the expansion of office-based services and global capability centres (GCCs), alongside their transition towards higher-value activities. The report said GCCs would remain a key driver of office demand as their operations increasingly shift towards research and development, product engineering, and analytics. This transition is expected to increase demand for high-quality, well-located and adaptable office spaces. "AI will undoubtedly change the nature of work and the skills businesses require, but that does not necessarily translate into lower office demand," Anshul Jain, Chief Executive – India, SEA, MEA and APAC Office and Retail at Cushman & Wakefield, said. The projected increase in office employment could coincide with higher vacancy levels as new commercial office supply continues to enter the market. The study projected India's office vacancy rate to rise from 14.3% in 2025 to a peak of 16.2% in 2029, before easing to 15.5% in 2030 as new supply normalises. The report also said India's relative labour cost advantage could limit the immediate business case for AI adoption. Productivity gains are expected to become more visible later in the decade, primarily through IT services and GCCs. Jain said occupiers would increasingly prioritise quality and flexibility in their office requirements, requiring developers and investors to adapt to changing workplace needs.

items.title: Jensen Huang admits affair amid spy claims
items.summary: Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 9,830 new readers. A week ago, Nvidia was brushing off a report about an alleged spy plot involving its CEO as routine customer meetings. Now, Jensen Huang is publicly apologizing, and his own board is investigating. Few founders are as inseparable from what they built as Huang, and no company touches the entire global AI industry like Nvidia. So the fallout from his admitted affair could reach far beyond a single boardroom. In today’s AI rundown: Jensen Huang admits affair as Nvidia probes spy claims The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases Turn your X bookmarks into a personal research desk Anthropic’s Claude ‘dreams’ to fix its own memory LATEST DEVELOPMENTS NVIDIA 🕵️ Jensen Huang admits affair as Nvidia probes spy claims Image source: NetThunder on LinkedIn The Rundown: Nvidia’s board of directors just ordered an independent review of reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a “foreign intelligence effort,” with Huang admitting to an extramarital affair in a letter to staff and saying, “There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” The details: Sec. of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw a spring memo on Jensen and Alice Huang, an Nvidia customer exec it linked to China’s top spy agency. After calling their meetings “completely normal” last month, Jensen told staff, “I was unfaithful to my wife” and reportedly confirmed the relationship to the board. Reporting has yet to establish what, if anything, Ms. Huang (aka Huang Le, no relation to Jensen) learned from him, while China denies the spying claims. Outside lawyers and independent directors will run the review as Jensen stays CEO, with the board seeing “no reason to believe” any secrets were compromised. Jensen also has until Nov. 11 to answer a House GOP request for a private briefing, with more congressional investigations expected over the relationship. Why it matters: AI stocks are already reeling from the midterm election results. Now, a spy scandal around the CEO of one of the industry’s biggest companies is unlikely to help either. Nvidia touches nearly every aspect of the AI industry, and Huang is the frontman of it all, so all eyes will be on what the board finds and his future with Nvidia. TOGETHER WITH GARTNER 🔮 How can you predict IT workforce needs? The Rundown: AI is accelerating how fast skills become obsolete, making future workforce needs nearly impossible to predict. This Gartner webinar explores three planning traps and offers a framework for building a resilient IT workforce. In this webinar, you'll learn how to: Avoid common workforce planning traps Separate enduring from transient skills Align talent with long-term value Register today . THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE 💡 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives. Brooke, Community Lead: I'm on the customer side, not the engineering side. When something breaks, I usually find out when a customer writes in, and by then a bunch of people have already hit it. We had an error chart in our analytics tool, but I don't often remember to check that dashboard every day, and a basic “alert me over X errors” setup would go off constantly for things that aren't real problems. I built a Claude scheduled task that checks our error chart every morning, filters out the noise, and tells the whole team in Slack only when something's actually wrong. I set it up just by describing what I wanted in plain English. I gave Claude the rules on which error types are real problems and which aren't, and it only counts the ones that matter. Now, I hear about issues before customers have to tell me. I tested it over the past couple of weeks, and it flagged every day something really broke and stayed silent on a busy day that was all harmless errors. Jennifer, Tech & Robotics Writer: My preteen daughter has spent months debating whether or not to get bangs, mostly worried about the "total humiliation" if they went wrong. So we uploaded her photo to ChatGPT and asked for four versions of bangs: blunt, curtain, wispy, side-swept. She loved it and finally narrowed down her choice, and the appointment is booked for this weekend. It’s hardly a groundbreaking use case, but it’s a fun way to try on a decision before a stylist makes it permanent. AI TRAINING 🔖 Turn your X bookmarks into a personal research desk The Rundown: X moves quickly, and saving posts is easy. Finding the useful ideas again is harder. In this guide, you’ll connect Grok Bot to X, review a week of bookmarks, spot repeated themes, and turn one finding into a post draft. Step-by-step: Check the difference between free Grok chat and Grok Bot. Bot is included with Premium, Super, and Ultra on the X Subscription. X Chat is still rolling out Connect the official X plugin with the Grok Bot. Check that it is linked to the same account where you save posts Bookmark 8 to 12 useful posts about one topic. Choose examples, questions, and problems, not just launch announcements Message your Bot in X Chat and ask it to group the bookmarks into themes. Check the direct links and compare each claim with the original post Choose one supported theme and ask for an X post draft. Review the wording and sources yourself; leave publishing off Pro tip: A set of bookmarks can show what you have been reading, but it can’t prove what all of X thinks. Keep the source links with every theme. PRESENTED BY OPENART 💡 Create a launch video for your business The Rundown: Need a launch video for your business? Simply paste your website link, add your brand assets, and define your target audience. OpenArt's AI video agent will shape the story and messaging while handling the script, motion design, voiceover, and video editing. With OpenArt, you can: Turn your website, screenshots, or pitch deck into a launch video Create short promos or longer videos to showcase your business Refine scenes, voiceovers, or music by describing the changes Go beyond launches with product ads and UGC-style videos Create your launch video with OpenArt. ANTHROPIC 💤 Anthropic’s Claude ‘dreams’ to fix its own memory Image source: Anthropic The Rundown: Anthropic just published its own take on AI “dreaming,” sharing how Claude agents use downtime to fix and reorganize their memory, and what it’s learned about what an AI should actually bother remembering. The details: Memory refers to notes Claude saves as files and reads back in later sessions, so it can build on past work instead of starting from scratch each time. Unlike ChatGPT’s version, which previously built a profile of the user, Anthropic’s dreaming has Claude check its notes against logs of past work to catch errors. Anthropic said newer models have gotten much better at judging what to save, and that explaining to the AI why memory matters beats rules on what to write. In tests on Pokémon, Fable 5 earned four badges with only 10 memory files, while an older Sonnet 3.7 got just one using 413, and Opus 5.5 beat the game entirely. Why it matters: It feels like not too long ago that the early iterations of ‘memory’ in AI assistants were a comically simple scratchpad with bare-bones notes on the user. Now they can recall past chats in detail down to the most obscure reference, and the next step is agents that continuously remember the job and improve at it the longer they work. Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 9,830 new readers. A week ago, Nvidia was brushing off a report about an alleged spy plot involving its CEO as routine customer meetings. Now, Jensen Huang is publicly apologizing, and his own board is investigating.

Few founders are as inseparable from what they built as Huang, and no company touches the entire global AI industry like Nvidia. So the fallout from his admitted affair could reach far beyond a single boardroom.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Jensen Huang admits affair as Nvidia probes spy claims

  • The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

  • Turn your X bookmarks into a personal research desk

  • Anthropic’s Claude ‘dreams’ to fix its own memory

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

NVIDIA🕵️ Jensen Huang admits affair as Nvidia probes spy claims

Image source: NetThunder on LinkedIn

The Rundown: Nvidia’s board of directors just ordered an independent review of reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a “foreign intelligence effort,” with Huang admitting to an extramarital affair in a letter to staff and saying, “There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The details:

  • Sec. of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw a spring memo on Jensen and Alice Huang, an Nvidia customer exec it linked to China’s top spy agency.

  • After calling their meetings “completely normal” last month, Jensen told staff, “I was unfaithful to my wife” and reportedly confirmed the relationship to the board.

  • Reporting has yet to establish what, if anything, Ms. Huang (aka Huang Le, no relation to Jensen) learned from him, while China denies the spying claims.

  • Outside lawyers and independent directors will run the review as Jensen stays CEO, with the board seeing “no reason to believe” any secrets were compromised.

  • Jensen also has until Nov. 11 to answer a House GOP request for a private briefing, with more congressional investigations expected over the relationship.

Why it matters: AI stocks are already reeling from the midterm election results. Now, a spy scandal around the CEO of one of the industry’s biggest companies is unlikely to help either. Nvidia touches nearly every aspect of the AI industry, and Huang is the frontman of it all, so all eyes will be on what the board finds and his future with Nvidia.

TOGETHER WITH GARTNER🔮 How can you predict IT workforce needs? 

The Rundown: AI is accelerating how fast skills become obsolete, making future workforce needs nearly impossible to predict. This Gartner webinar explores three planning traps and offers a framework for building a resilient IT workforce.

In this webinar, you'll learn how to:

  • Avoid common workforce planning traps

  • Separate enduring from transient skills

  • Align talent with long-term value

Register today.

THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE💡 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.

Brooke, Community Lead: I'm on the customer side, not the engineering side. When something breaks, I usually find out when a customer writes in, and by then a bunch of people have already hit it. We had an error chart in our analytics tool, but I don't often remember to check that dashboard every day, and a basic “alert me over X errors” setup would go off constantly for things that aren't real problems.

I built a Claude scheduled task that checks our error chart every morning, filters out the noise, and tells the whole team in Slack only when something's actually wrong. I set it up just by describing what I wanted in plain English. I gave Claude the rules on which error types are real problems and which aren't, and it only counts the ones that matter.

Now, I hear about issues before customers have to tell me. I tested it over the past couple of weeks, and it flagged every day something really broke and stayed silent on a busy day that was all harmless errors.

Jennifer, Tech & Robotics Writer: My preteen daughter has spent months debating whether or not to get bangs, mostly worried about the "total humiliation" if they went wrong. So we uploaded her photo to ChatGPT and asked for four versions of bangs: blunt, curtain, wispy, side-swept.

She loved it and finally narrowed down her choice, and the appointment is booked for this weekend. It’s hardly a groundbreaking use case, but it’s a fun way to try on a decision before a stylist makes it permanent.

AI TRAINING🔖 Turn your X bookmarks into a personal research desk

The Rundown: X moves quickly, and saving posts is easy. Finding the useful ideas again is harder. In this guide, you’ll connect Grok Bot to X, review a week of bookmarks, spot repeated themes, and turn one finding into a post draft.

Step-by-step:

  1. Check the difference between free Grok chat and Grok Bot. Bot is included with Premium, Super, and Ultra on the X Subscription. X Chat is still rolling out

  2. Connect the official X plugin with the Grok Bot. Check that it is linked to the same account where you save posts

  3. Bookmark 8 to 12 useful posts about one topic. Choose examples, questions, and problems, not just launch announcements

  4. Message your Bot in X Chat and ask it to group the bookmarks into themes. Check the direct links and compare each claim with the original post

  5. Choose one supported theme and ask for an X post draft. Review the wording and sources yourself; leave publishing off

Pro tip: A set of bookmarks can show what you have been reading, but it can’t prove what all of X thinks. Keep the source links with every theme.

PRESENTED BY OPENART💡 Create a launch video for your business

The Rundown: Need a launch video for your business? Simply paste your website link, add your brand assets, and define your target audience. OpenArt's AI video agent will shape the story and messaging while handling the script, motion design, voiceover, and video editing.

With OpenArt, you can:

  • Turn your website, screenshots, or pitch deck into a launch video

  • Create short promos or longer videos to showcase your business

  • Refine scenes, voiceovers, or music by describing the changes

  • Go beyond launches with product ads and UGC-style videos

Create your launch video with OpenArt.

ANTHROPIC💤 Anthropic’s Claude ‘dreams’ to fix its own memory

Image source: Anthropic

The Rundown: Anthropic just published its own take on AI “dreaming,” sharing how Claude agents use downtime to fix and reorganize their memory, and what it’s learned about what an AI should actually bother remembering.

The details:

  • Memory refers to notes Claude saves as files and reads back in later sessions, so it can build on past work instead of starting from scratch each time.

  • Unlike ChatGPT’s version, which previously built a profile of the user, Anthropic’s dreaming has Claude check its notes against logs of past work to catch errors.

  • Anthropic said newer models have gotten much better at judging what to save, and that explaining to the AI why memory matters beats rules on what to write.

  • In tests on Pokémon, Fable 5 earned four badges with only 10 memory files, while an older Sonnet 3.7 got just one using 413, and Opus 5.5 beat the game entirely.

Why it matters: It feels like not too long ago that the early iterations of ‘memory’ in AI assistants were a comically simple scratchpad with bare-bones notes on the user. Now they can recall past chats in detail down to the most obscure reference, and the next step is agents that continuously remember the job and improve at it the longer they work.

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Kate built a custom camera feature for Facebook Live presentations

Today’s workflow comes from reader Kate MacGregor:

“I built a live camera bubble that floats over my slides during Facebook Live presentations. Because Facebook Live does not let me switch between my camera and a shared screen, I wanted my face to stay visible while I presented. This is useful for anyone who streams presentations to a Facebook Group and wants viewers to see them speaking.

Claude Code built the working app within about five minutes. I made one tweak to the camera bubble's shape, and it was then a finished, usable product.

When I'm ready to go live in the Facebook Group, I click the camera bubble app on my local desktop. It uses my laptop camera, and I can drag the bubble around the screen and choose the circle size that suits whatever I'm sharing. Before I go live, I select "share entire screen" in the Facebook Live settings. Viewers then see my slides or screen with my floating camera bubble, so they can see me speaking as I present.”

items.title: The climate case for AI has not been made
items.summary: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies. In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed , the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030. Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles. But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational? Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress. The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year. Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study. The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes. In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe , which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products. But few other alternative-protein companies had such a deeply integrated way of using AI in product development, the AI-assisted review suggests. Meanwhile, the sector seems to be facing more fundamental problems, including stubbornly slow mainstream consumer adoption and declining funding levels. Most notably, venture capital flowing into cultivated meat fell from a $989 million peak in 2021 to around $83 million last year. The transportation sector offers some hopeful examples of the type of AI integration necessary to achieve the study’s projections, particularly among battery manufacturers and ride-sharing platforms. CATL—which controls roughly 40% of the global market for electric-vehicle batteries—launched an AI system trained on more than 100,000 battery design cases and 600 terabytes of test data. It cut the time needed to screen candidate materials by two orders of magnitude, according to the company. Independent researchers also found that the ride-sharing platform Didi Chuxing was able cut per-trip emissions 16% on average by using AI-optimized routing to minimize detours. There’s another big problem in the climate case for AI, though: Oil and gas companies are also interested in these tools for many reasons, including the potential to increase production of fossil fuels . Technology firms that committed to sustainability goals in the past should answer questions about how their tools could be used to boost old, dirty energy as well as clean, renewable energy. Finally, it’s also worth noting that integrating AI is just the first step, and it remains unclear to what degree the technology can accelerate the sorts of improvements and innovations envisioned. AI also does little to shorten the standard paths to certifying, permitting, building, packaging, marketing, and selling any resulting products, facilities, or services. The findings of the analysis, carried out by Anthropic’s Claude Code, were reviewed against public documents and media accounts to ensure their accuracy. It is possible that some companies and utilities in these industries are pursuing AI-assisted applications that would fit into the initial study’s scenarios but haven’t yet been disclosed publicly. Greater and better-targeted AI integration and efficiency gains in these three sectors may well materialize, bringing the 2035 projections closer to reality. But it won’t happen without deliberate and sustained efforts to ensure that AI delivers more environmental benefits than harms. Notably, so far the rapid adoption of AI models and buildout of data centers has driven a huge increase in energy consumption and emissions, and this has led major tech companies like Microsoft, Google, and others to fall well off track in their corporate climate goals. At this point it would be surprising if the sector even manages to zero out its climate pollution: Emissions associated with global data centers (which may handle AI as well as non-AI computing tasks) could exceed 300 million tons annually in 2035, according to the IEA’s base forecast . Industry leaders must implement the technology in the ways that promise to do the most to drive down emissions. Corporate customers should select models with the lowest environmental impacts and opt to work with the AI developers doing the most to reduce their climate footprint. And states and regions need to do more to incentivize or require all these companies to operate in more responsible ways. The need has never been more apparent. Mary Nichols is distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board. Jeremy Tamanini is the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm.

items.title: NSE Launches Stock Discovery Platform, Adds AI Features
items.summary: The National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) has introduced new digital features across its website and mobile applications, including a beta version of NSE Market Lens , a stock discovery and screening platform designed to make market information more accessible to investors and trading members. “Technology has a vital role in simplifying India's capital markets and making them more accessible, inclusive and convenient for every Indian,” Viral Mody, Executive Director at NSE, said in a statement. Market Lens is available on both web and mobile platforms. The platform allows investors to explore popular stock screens, browse stocks by sector, and create customised screens using natural language queries. Its interface converts investor queries into editable screening filters, with results based on NSE market data. The exchange has also introduced a beta version of AI-assisted summaries of corporate announcements on its website. These summaries are available in text and audio formats to help investors access corporate disclosures. NSE has also added minute-wise updates for Option Greeks, including Delta, Gamma, Theta and Vega, which are used to assess options pricing and risk. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), NSE market data can also be accessed using compatible AI assistants, including ChatGPT and Claude , through natural language interactions, the exchange said. The redesigned NSE India mobile application includes personalised watchlists with sharing capabilities and price alerts. Investors can also track consolidated portfolios across asset classes, monitor family investments and nominations, access portfolio analytics, and view company announcements relevant to their holdings. NSE has also introduced a new Member Portal App for trading members. The application provides exchange-related analytics through Trade Pulse dashboards and Unique Client Code (UCC) metrics, including state-wise distribution. It also enables members to track upcoming regulatory compliances, submissions and connectivity compliance, alongside access to exchange circulars. The new features are part of NSE's efforts to use technology to simplify access to market information and improve digital engagement across India's capital markets ecosystem.

items.summary: The company's board claimed it found no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised and said Huang would cooperate with the inquiry into his affair with a woman U.S. intelligence identified as a spy for Beijing.

items.title: Reason Machines Open-Sources Aspen, a Git Server Built for AI Agents
items.summary:
Reason Machines has released Aspen , an open-source Git server for AI agent traffic. It targets repositories that hundreds of agents push to at once. Aspen independently implements the design OpenAI described for Pando. TL;DR Size: One Rust binary. Branches live in PostgreSQL (or SQLite), packs live in object storage. Runs on: A laptop ( aspen dev ), one host via Docker Compose, or Helm and Terraform clouds. Performance: Pushes to different branches never wait on each other, and fetches reuse stored packs. Best: 567 pushes per second sustained for 5 minutes on one 8-core server (self-reported). Worst: Landing on main runs at about 4 per second, and the project is pre-alpha. Bottom line: Best: per-branch writes remove the per-repository push ceiling. Worst: no releases, no web UI, and the 24-hour durability gate is not met. What is Aspen? Aspen is a self-hostable Git server from Reason Machines that scales writes per branch, not per repository. It speaks plain Git over HTTPS and SSH. Packs go to S3-compatible object storage; branch history goes to PostgreSQL. Why do classic Git servers struggle with AI agents? An agent pushes every few minutes, and CI fetches after each push. Per Reason Machines , a classic server queues every push to a repository together. It also builds a fresh pack for every fetch. Server work grows with clients, not with new code. OpenAI hit this wall and built Pando. It cut median push latency by nearly 5x and serves nearly a petabyte daily. How does Aspen work? Aspen follows Pando and drops 2 claims most Git servers keep. Per-branch compare-and-swap Each branch is a chain of versions in one Postgres row. A push uploads its pack, then moves the branch with one compare-and-swap. Pushes to different branches never wait for each other. If 2 pushes race on one branch, one wins. The other gets Git’s usual “fetch first” error. The cost: branches may be read at slightly different moments. Stored packs instead of per-client packs Aspen never unpacks a push. It checks the pack, completes missing bases and stores it as-is. A fetch streams stored packs the client lacks, recompressing nothing. Signed URLs can serve packs from a CDN. Trunk-only advertisement and compaction A push sees only the trunk branch, so negotiation stays small with a million branches. Background compaction merges packs 16 at a time, in levels like a log-structured merge tree. A client far behind gets a few dozen packs, not thousands. Depth-1 CI fetches get a tip pack built once and served to every job. Aspen Explainer

Aspen: 1 x 8-core server, S3 Standard, 4-core Postgres, git.git (~4,500 files, 75k commits), branch-scoped URL. Cursor: replicated cluster on its own monorepo. Setups differ; OpenAI published no Pando push rate.

Pre-alpha, no releases
Build from source. Storage formats may change. The 24-hour chaos run stopped after 11.59 clean hours.
Landing on main ~4/s
Separate landings run one at a time, limited by round trips. The merge queue rate is not measured yet.
Missing Git features
No partial clones, SHA-256 repositories, web UI or RSA SSH keys (Ed25519 and ECDSA only).
Force push needs -o force
Because a push only sees trunk, --force and --delete need an extra -o force, a lease or the branch URL.
Large monorepos
Each push still costs more as a repository grows, so very large monorepos see lower rates today.
Storage support conflict
The launch post lists Azure Blob; the README says Azure Blob is not supported yet and GCS works via its S3 API.

"> How fast is Aspen? The test used one 8-core server, S3 Standard and a 4-core Postgres. The target was a copy of git.git, about 4,500 files and 75,000 commits. Aspen sustained 567 pushes per second for 5 minutes with no errors. Each push reached S3 and Postgres before Git printed “ok.” Median push latency: 208 ms; 99th percentile: 314 ms. Another client saw each push 30 ms after acknowledgement, at the median. Depth-1 fetch storm: 1.029x the bytes of stock git upload-pack on git.git. Cursor reports up to 120 pushes per second for Origin on S3 Standard. On S3 Express One Zone it exceeds 300. That is a replicated cluster on Cursor’s monorepo, so setups differ. The README calls Aspen’s figures indicative, not performance claims. How does Aspen compare with other agent-scale Git backends? Feature Aspen Cursor Origin OpenAI Pando GitHub Spokes Availability Open source, self-hosted Commercial Cursor platform Internal to OpenAI Internal to GitHub License Apache 2.0 Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Push ordering Per branch (compare-and-swap) Per repository (write-ahead log in S3) Per branch Three-phase commit across replicas Ref storage PostgreSQL or SQLite WAL index in S3, no relational DB Metadata store Git repos on NVMe Fetch serving Stored packs, stitched or via URIs Local Git repo cache on NVMe Reused stored packs Git repo replicas Published push rate 567/s, S3 Standard, 1 server (self-reported) 120/s S3 Standard; 300+/s S3 Express Not disclosed Not disclosed Other published result p99 push 314 ms Linear read scaling to 100 replicas Median push latency cut nearly 5x Not disclosed How do you deploy Aspen? You build from source with Rust. aspen dev runs everything with SQLite and a local directory. Teams get Docker Compose with PostgreSQL and MinIO, plus a Helm chart. Terraform covers AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and Hetzner. Mirror mode fronts GitHub or GitLab, so you can trial it without migrating. The live demo is a 64 x 64 pixel canvas where each click is one pushed commit. Per the company, one Reason agent built Aspen from first commit to public in 4 days. That took 151 merged PRs. Key Takeaways Aspen is an Apache 2.0 Git server built for agent-scale push traffic. It is an independent, open implementation of OpenAI’s Pando design. Self-reported: 567 pushes per second on one 8-core server, p99 314 ms. Clients need no changes; stock git works over HTTPS and SSH. Check out the GitHub repo and the launch post .
