  • Best: 567 pushes per second sustained for 5 minutes on one 8-core server (self-reported).
  • Worst: Landing on main runs at about 4 per second, and the project is pre-alpha.
  • Bottom line: Best: per-branch writes remove the per-repository push ceiling. Worst: no releases, no web UI, and the 24-hour durability gate is not met.
What is Aspen?

Aspen is a self-hostable Git server from Reason Machines that scales writes per branch, not per repository. It speaks plain Git over HTTPS and SSH. Packs go to S3-compatible object storage; branch history goes to PostgreSQL.

Why do classic Git servers struggle with AI agents?

An agent pushes every few minutes, and CI fetches after each push. Per Reason Machines, a classic server queues every push to a repository together. It also builds a fresh pack for every fetch. Server work grows with clients, not with new code.

OpenAI hit this wall and built Pando. It cut median push latency by nearly 5x and serves nearly a petabyte daily.

How does Aspen work?

Aspen follows Pando and drops 2 claims most Git servers keep.

Per-branch compare-and-swap

Each branch is a chain of versions in one Postgres row. A push uploads its pack, then moves the branch with one compare-and-swap. Pushes to different branches never wait for each other. If 2 pushes race on one branch, one wins. The other gets Git’s usual “fetch first” error. The cost: branches may be read at slightly different moments.

Stored packs instead of per-client packs

Aspen never unpacks a push. It checks the pack, completes missing bases and stores it as-is. A fetch streams stored packs the client lacks, recompressing nothing. Signed URLs can serve packs from a CDN.

Trunk-only advertisement and compaction

A push sees only the trunk branch, so negotiation stays small with a million branches. Background compaction merges packs 16 at a time, in levels like a log-structured merge tree. A client far behind gets a few dozen packs, not thousands. Depth-1 CI fetches get a tip pack built once and served to every job.

How fast is Aspen?

The test used one 8-core server, S3 Standard and a 4-core Postgres. The target was a copy of git.git, about 4,500 files and 75,000 commits. Aspen sustained 567 pushes per second for 5 minutes with no errors. Each push reached S3 and Postgres before Git printed “ok.”

  • Median push latency: 208 ms; 99th percentile: 314 ms.
  • Another client saw each push 30 ms after acknowledgement, at the median.
  • Depth-1 fetch storm: 1.029x the bytes of stock git upload-pack on git.git.

Cursor reports up to 120 pushes per second for Origin on S3 Standard. On S3 Express One Zone it exceeds 300. That is a replicated cluster on Cursor’s monorepo, so setups differ. The README calls Aspen’s figures indicative, not performance claims.

You build from source with Rust. aspen dev runs everything with SQLite and a local directory. Teams get Docker Compose with PostgreSQL and MinIO, plus a Helm chart. Terraform covers AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and Hetzner. Mirror mode fronts GitHub or GitLab, so you can trial it without migrating.

The live demo is a 64 x 64 pixel canvas where each click is one pushed commit. Per the company, one Reason agent built Aspen from first commit to public in 4 days. That took 151 merged PRs.

Key Takeaways
  • Aspen is an Apache 2.0 Git server built for agent-scale push traffic.
  • It is an independent, open implementation of OpenAI’s Pando design.
  • Self-reported: 567 pushes per second on one 8-core server, p99 314 ms.
  • Clients need no changes; stock git works over HTTPS and SSH.

items.title: Salesforce Wants Indian SMBs to Ditch WhatsApp for Slack
items.summary: WhatsApp has become a convenient way for businesses to communicate with employees, customers, and partners. This is especially true for India, which boasts 550 million WhatsApp users and where 90% of consumers message at least one business on the platform weekly, per Rukam Capital. However, Salesforce believes that convenience comes with security concerns that could push enterprises towards dedicated workplace collaboration platforms such as Slack. Salesforce is also seeing growing Slack adoption among small and medium businesses (SMBs) in India. According to Gourav Ray, RVP, Slack and Service, Salesforce India, SMBs are among the segments contributing the most to the company’s revenue in the country. “Many enterprises are coming back to us because WhatsApp is not very secure. There have been a lot of personal data leaks. A large number of enterprises have given that as a major reason to move away from WhatsApp,” Ray tells AIM in an exclusive interview. There has been a recent spike in security incidents involving the messaging platform. In June, CERT-In warned about a malware campaign targeting WhatsApp Desktop and Web users, with attackers using compromised accounts to distribute malicious attachments disguised as financial documents. Once opened, these files could give attackers remote access to systems, steal credentials and exfiltrate data. In August, India’s cybercrime agency I4C warned companies about a related account-takeover campaign targeting corporate executives and finance teams. Attackers used compromised WhatsApp accounts to impersonate senior executives and issue fraudulent fund-transfer instructions. Operating System for Work Salesforce is positioning Slack as a workplace collaboration platform. After spinning out an AI-powered version of its automated assistant Slackbot earlier this year, the company wants Slack to become a central layer that connects employees, applications, enterprise data, and AI agents. On how Slackbot differs from ChatGPT or Claude, Ray explains that it draws on the context of conversations happening across an organisation, along with information from connected applications. “Every conversation we have brings in some value for the organisation. What organisations struggle with is that this is usually lost because people are not able to find this data or information anywhere,” Ray explains. According to him, Salesforce’s data layer and metadata provide the context required to make AI outputs deterministic, allowing enterprises to make business decisions and take action. Ray says conversations across Slack channels, emails, and other connected applications often contain useful information that businesses struggle to find later. Slackbot brings this information together. The platform has more than 2,600 native connectors, allowing employees to retrieve information across enterprise applications, including human resource management systems, customer relationship management platforms, and enterprise resource planning software. For instance, employees can search across customer data, HR information, Workday, and Concur without switching between multiple applications. Ray says digital-native businesses have been among the early adopters, partly because of Slack’s relatively intuitive interface and ease of deployment. Salesforce is also seeing interest across fintech, logistics, travel, and transportation, including trucking companies where drivers are using Slack. The Importance of SMBs for Slack SMBs are emerging as an important customer segment for Salesforce in India, contributing the most to the company's revenue in India. The company’s SMB Growth Kit, which it launched earlier this year, brings Agentforce Sales, Slack, and Tableau into a single platform. It aims to make Salesforce offerings easier for smaller businesses to adopt. Ray notes SMBs are unlikely to invest in expensive platforms that take three to four months to implement. He says the toolkit follows a plug-and-play approach, allowing smaller customers to purchase the application using credit cards and start using it without extensive partner support. Despite targeting smaller businesses, Ray acknowledges that Salesforce may not always be able to match the prices offered by smaller SaaS companies such as Zoho. “There are a lot of competitors in the market. The willingness to pay is largely dependent on what customers get in terms of value. We mostly drive value conversations with our customers rather than compete on price,” he says. AI Agents Build Sales Pipeline Salesforce is also using AI agents internally to improve sales productivity and generate revenue. Ray says the company uses Agentforce and Slackbot to prepare employees for sales meetings, coach them on their pitches, and evaluate their performance. Its AI coach assesses sales pitches against a predefined rubric, identifies missed points, and suggests improvements. It can also debrief employees after meetings and help frontline managers improve their teams' performance. Salesforce also uses intelligent dashboards to monitor sales pipelines, identify deals that need attention, and flag potential risks. Another application is Hunter, an agentic sales development representative that can reach out to prospects and conduct initial sales calls. The company also uses its Help Agent, internally referred to as KC, to handle inbound customer calls when sales teams are unavailable. The agent can answer queries, resolve issues, and record customer interactions. Ray says the Help Agent has handled more than 5 million customer conversations and resolved nearly 70% of them. For Salesforce, these deployments show how AI can help generate more revenue by reaching more customers, helping employees close sales and identifying business opportunities that might otherwise be missed.

items.title: Do AI agents have minds? A philosopher explains
items.summary: Teslariu Mihai / Unsplash In the past few months, partly autonomous or “agentic” artificial intelligence (AI) systems have racked up some astonishing feats, from hacking tech startups to solving some of the world’s most famous open mathematical questions . Agentic AI systems can work in “swarms” that communicate among themselves to complete tasks. The communications involved are often surprisingly human-like – which is spurring a debate over whether these systems are conscious. Researchers at the leading AI lab Anthropic believe their systems may well be conscious – but other experts, including the head of Microsoft AI, say this view is misguided . This question isn’t just an academic one. The future status of AI systems and their role in society – how they can be treated, whether they have rights, and more – may depend on it. How can we decide if AI systems are conscious? How do we even approach a question like this? One strategy is to look at existing theories of what consciousness is and see if agentic AI systems meet the criteria . However, existing theories of consciousness tend to start from the assumption that the agent has some kind of mental state. These theories are focused on the difference between having a state consciously or unconsciously. This is why they appeal to features such as higher-order thought, or a system that broadcasts thoughts to the rest of the mind. These are features that could distinguish between conscious control and states like sleepwalking. So when thinking about AI, we must not skip a crucial first question: do agentic AIs even have mental states? What is a mental state? In the 1870s, philosopher Franz Brentano developed an influential view: “intentionality is the mark of the mental”. What Brentano means by “intentionality” is how mental states are about something. They refer to something beyond themselves. So another way to put Brentano’s point is that all mental states are about something or other. What Brentano means by intentionality is not the same as the usual meaning of “intention” as aiming to do something. Yet intentionality and an intention to act significantly overlap, because having a perception or thought is something that we do . Whenever we perceive or think, we are trying to pick out some aspect of the world. Even our passive-seeming visual experiences are tasks the moment that we use the patterns striking our retinas to orient ourselves. So if a mental state is a task performed to achieve a goal, our question about AI minds turns on whether they have their own goals. Are agentic AI systems really agents? It is now common to refer to certain AI systems as “agents”. Yet this language is misleading. It implies the AI systems have agency, or the capacity to act towards their own goals. Humans use devices to achieve their aims, including their aims to refer to things, without those devices becoming agents in their own right. A thermostat regulates the temperature, but it does not have the goal of regulating the temperature. A book contains words that refer to things – but again, the book does not have the goal of referring to things. To attribute agency to a computer program, we must be convinced that no human is required to stand behind its goals. Its goal-directedness must be independent. We know that agentic AIs, when given a task, can develop complex and unexpected sub-goals on the way to achieving it. Yet the goals that ultimately drive their activity are set by the humans who program and instruct them. Any sub-goals generated by an AI are literally meaningless outside of these aims set by humans. Think of a game like football. A person might have the sub-goal of running past a defender, but it is literally meaningless without the larger goal of trying to score. And scoring a goal itself is simply making a ball cross a line without the larger goal of playing football. Without the larger goal, anything a player does on the field is merely activity. Why do agents have goals? A genuine agent has goals in order to promote things they care about – for example, you want to satisfy your hunger at lunchtime, so you go to a bakery and buy a sandwich. Agentic AI is unlikely to care about things in an independent way, because its activity is not connected to life in the same way minds are. What distinctively allows living beings to generate their own goals is that their mental activity develops out of the processes for constantly re-constituting their own bodies and keeping themselves alive . Goal-driven thinking builds up from simple signals for regulating nutrition and warmth to states like pain and pleasure and eventually to symbolic thought. Nothing like this is going on in agentic AI. There is a disconnect between its information-processing activities and the physical stuff on which it depends. Can AI ever be conscious? Agentic AI systems are not conscious. They don’t have mental states which could be conscious. Only living beings have conscious mental states because having a mental state requires a being to originate a certain kind of goal – the goal to mean something or to refer to something – and only living beings originate goals. This argument does not permanently rule out the possibility of AI consciousness. However, it does suggest that this could only arise in some artificial form of life. Until then, we have more reason to think that an ant is conscious than an agentic AI is. At least an ant seems to care about its own life. Of course, the fact agentic AIs are not really agents does not stop them from wreaking havoc by carrying out functions that their human originators do not properly supervise or understand. But we should be very clear on this: whatever an agentic AI does, that is a human or group of humans acting indirectly on the world, and those humans are responsible for the outcome. Why do agents have goals?

A genuine agent has goals in order to promote things they care about – for example, you want to satisfy your hunger at lunchtime, so you go to a bakery and buy a sandwich.

Agentic AI is unlikely to care about things in an independent way, because its activity is not connected to life in the same way minds are.

What distinctively allows living beings to generate their own goals is that their mental activity develops out of the processes for constantly re-constituting their own bodies and keeping themselves alive. Goal-driven thinking builds up from simple signals for regulating nutrition and warmth to states like pain and pleasure and eventually to symbolic thought.

Nothing like this is going on in agentic AI. There is a disconnect between its information-processing activities and the physical stuff on which it depends.

Can AI ever be conscious?

Agentic AI systems are not conscious. They don’t have mental states which could be conscious.

Only living beings have conscious mental states because having a mental state requires a being to originate a certain kind of goal – the goal to mean something or to refer to something – and only living beings originate goals.

This argument does not permanently rule out the possibility of AI consciousness. However, it does suggest that this could only arise in some artificial form of life.

Until then, we have more reason to think that an ant is conscious than an agentic AI is. At least an ant seems to care about its own life.

Of course, the fact agentic AIs are not really agents does not stop them from wreaking havoc by carrying out functions that their human originators do not properly supervise or understand. But we should be very clear on this: whatever an agentic AI does, that is a human or group of humans acting indirectly on the world, and those humans are responsible for the outcome.

items.summary_html:
If you manage a hotel, run a reputation-management tool or analyse a city's hotel market, Agoda is one of the review sources you can't skip in Asia. A single hotel page there mixes two review pools: reviews from Agoda's own guests and reviews from Booking.com guests that Agoda republishes. Each pool has its own score, its own review count and its own six sub-scores (cleanliness, facilities, location, room comfort, service, value for money).

Reading that by hand works for one property. For a competitive set of 20 hotels, checked every morning, it doesn't. This post pulls the reviews and scores into a CSV in Python and shows a daily "new reviews only" setup.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built Agoda API, an Agoda reviews scraper. It's a paid tool (prices below).

What each row holds

One row per review, from the hotel's public Agoda review page:

  • source (Agoda or Booking.com), rating out of 10, rating_text, title, text, and for Booking.com-style reviews positives and negatives.
  • language, plus original_title and original_text when Agoda shows an English translation, so you keep the guest's own words.
  • review_date (the date the page shows), stay_month, nights, room_type, traveller_type (couple, solo, family, group, business).
  • reviewer_name and reviewer_country as Agoda displays them, helpful_votes, photos.
  • owner_response, owner_response_date and responder_name when the hotel replied.
  • The hotel on every row: hotel_name, star_rating, address, city, country, agoda_score, agoda_review_count, agoda_sub_scores, agoda_score_distribution, booking_score, booking_review_count, booking_sub_scores.

Hotels can be given as Agoda links (any language version), Agoda hotel IDs, or a hotel name with its city.

A competitive set in one run 
pip install apify-client

import csv
import os
from collections import defaultdict

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/agoda-reviews-scraper").call(
    run_input={
        "hotels": [
            "https://www.agoda.com/the-peninsula-bangkok/hotel/bangkok-th.html",
            "Mandarin Oriental Bangkok",
            "Shangri-La Bangkok",
        ],
        "maxReviewsPerHotel": 300,
        "reviewsNewerThan": "90 days",
    }
)
reviews = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

fields = ["hotel_name", "source", "rating", "title", "text", "negatives", "traveller_type",
          "reviewer_country", "review_date", "owner_response"]
with open("reviews.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields, extrasaction="ignore")
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(reviews)

hotels = {}
by_type = defaultdict(list)
for r in reviews:
    hotels[r["hotel_name"]] = r
    by_type[(r["hotel_name"], r["traveller_type"])].append(r["rating"])

for name, h in hotels.items():
    subs = h["agoda_sub_scores"] or {}
    print(f"{name}: Agoda {h['agoda_score']} ({h['agoda_review_count']} ratings), "
          f"Booking.com {h['booking_score']}; cleanliness {subs.get('Cleanliness')}, "
          f"value {subs.get('Value for money')}")
for (name, kind), ratings in sorted(by_type.items()):
    if kind and len(ratings) >= 5:
        print(f"  {name} / {kind}: {sum(ratings) / len(ratings):.1f} over {len(ratings)} reviews")

The hotel name in the second line is matched through Agoda's own search box; the run's status message says which property each name matched, so check it once and switch to the link if it picked the wrong one.

Ideas for the same data:

  • Complaint mining: "maxRating": 6, "sortBy": "lowest" gives the unhappy reviews first; feed negatives and text to an LLM and ask for recurring themes per hotel.
  • Reply rate: count rows with owner_response per hotel. It's a quick read on how actively each competitor manages its reviews.
  • Who stays where: group by traveller_type and reviewer_country to see which segments each hotel attracts and how each segment rates it.
New reviews every morning 
run_input = {
    "hotels": ["https://www.agoda.com/the-peninsula-bangkok/hotel/bangkok-th.html", "..."],
    "maxReviewsPerHotel": 500,
    "onlyNewReviews": True,
    "trackingName": "my-compset-daily",
    "slackWebhookUrl": "https://hooks.slack.com/services/...",
}

With onlyNewReviews on, the first run returns the newest reviews up to your limit, and later runs with the same trackingName return only reviews newer than the ones you already have: reading newest first, each review source stops at the first review you already received. A daily run over 20 hotels takes seconds and bills $0.0003 per hotel plus the new reviews.   • $0.50 per 1,000 reviews ($0.40 on paid plans), cheaper than the leading tools.
  • Any number of hotels in one run, including by hotel name.
  • The original text next to the translation.
  • An only-new-reviews mode.
  • What it doesn't cover: room prices and availability.
Limits worth knowing
  • Rows exist only for written reviews. The review counts next to the scores include rating-only reviews, so they are higher than the number of rows.
  • Agoda's review service answers part of its requests with an empty page; the tool asks again before it decides a hotel has no more reviews, so long hotels take a little longer.
  • "Highest" and "lowest rated first" follow Agoda's own order page by page; sort the CSV if you need a strict order across both review sources.

items.title: The Physical Nightmare of On-Device AI: Why Your LLM Fails on a Custom PCB
items.summary: In 2026, the hottest buzzword in the tech world is undoubtedly "On-Device AI." From Apple Intelligence to the flood of AI PCs and AI smartphones hitting the market, the entire software industry is racing to cram large language models (LLMs) and vision models—previously running in the cloud—into portable devices weighing just a few dozen grams. As a software engineer, you might have fine-tuned models on a workstation with a dedicated GPU or run flawless inference in the cloud. But when your team moves to mass production and deploys the model onto a custom PCBA (Printed Circuit Board Assembly) you designed yourselves, the nightmare begins. The device gets burning hot, the battery drains in minutes, inference speed turns from silky smooth into a slideshow, and the system crashes and reboots repeatedly. I work at AnyPCBA, a manufacturer specializing in small-to-medium volume PCB and PCBA production. I frequently see software AI teams hit the wall of physical reality. Today, from the manufacturing perspective, let's dive deep into the three biggest "physical disasters" developers overlook when deploying on-device AI. 1. Peak Compute ≠ Sustained Compute (The Brutal Reality of Thermal Throttling) Software developers look at chip specs and fixate on TOPS (Trillions of Operations Per Second). For example, an edge NPU claims 20 TOPS, and you assume it's more than enough to run your lightweight model. But in the physical world, a chip cannot sustain its 20 TOPS peak indefinitely. When the NPU runs full-load LLM inference, it generates an astonishing heat flux density (reaching dozens of watts per square centimeter) on a few square millimeters of silicon. If your PCB design lacks large thermal copper pours, dense thermal via arrays, or external heatsinks, the chip temperature will skyrocket past 100°C within minutes. At this point, the chip's self-protection mechanism forces Thermal Throttling . Your model might run smoothly for the first 10 seconds, then drop to a slideshow, or simply reboot due to overheat protection. AnyPCBA's Solution: During DFM review, we recommend AI hardware teams use high-Tg materials and design large exposed thermal pads with dense via arrays directly beneath the NPU. Copper conducts heat 1,300 times faster than FR-4 substrate. Only through precise via plating processes can heat be rapidly conducted to the backside heatsink or liquid cooling module. Without proper physical thermal management, even the most powerful compute is meaningless. 2. Instantaneous Current Draw Leads to a "False OOM" (Voltage Droop) In the cloud, if you run out of memory, you hit an OOM (Out of Memory). On edge hardware, you'll encounter a similar crash— Voltage Droop . When an AI chip executes dense tensor operations, it draws tens of amps in microseconds from a low-power sleep state (extremely high di/dt). If your PCB's Power Delivery Network (PDN) can't respond fast enough—because decoupling capacitors are too far from the chip pins or trace parasitic inductance (ESL) is too high—the local supply voltage will collapse instantly. The result: logic gates fail, and the chip crashes and reboots. This "false OOM" cannot be fixed by changing code. AnyPCBA's Solution: PDN design for AI hardware is extremely demanding. We not only place 0201 or even 01005 decoupling capacitors as close as possible to the chip pins, but also use thinner dielectric layers to increase plane capacitance, pushing PDN impedance to extremely low levels—ensuring instant high current is delivered on demand. 3. The "Invisible Ceiling" of Memory Bandwidth and SI Disasters On a PC or server, you rarely worry about memory bandwidth. But on edge devices, it's a fatal bottleneck. LLM inference is a classic "memory-bound" task. No matter how powerful the compute, if memory can't feed it, everything is moot. Worse, data exchange between LPDDR memory and the main chip relies heavily on PCB traces. If length matching and impedance control are not precisely executed, data will experience phase skew and bit errors. From the software layer, the model suddenly outputs garbage or crashes. AnyPCBA's Solution: High-speed memory traces (such as LPDDR5/DDR5) must strictly meet 100Ω or 90Ω differential impedance requirements with precise length matching. Our engineering team uses TDR (Time Domain Reflectometry) testing before production to ensure signal integrity on the physical copper traces—so hardware weaknesses never drag down your algorithm. 4. The Limits of Physical Space: The Power Conflict That Can't "Pop Up" In software, if two threads compete for resources, the OS can schedule them. In hardware, the routing space for power and ground is physically fixed. The mainboards in AI phones or smart glasses are extremely compact. High-speed signals, high-current power lines, and sensitive analog sensors are forced into a few square centimeters. If layout is poor, the switching noise from high current will directly couple onto analog signal lines, causing sensor data to be completely corrupted. AnyPCBA's Solution: During layout, we strictly partition "Analog Ground (AGND)" and "Digital Ground (DGND)," adding proper shielding and isolation between power and ground planes. On the manufacturing side, we use blind/buried vias (HDI) with laser-drilled microvias to achieve more interconnections in limited space, avoiding signal interference. Conclusion: Bridging the Boundary Between Algorithm and Physics Deploying on-device AI is never purely a software problem. It's an ultimate battle between algorithms and thermodynamics, electronics, and materials science. At AnyPCBA, we frequently help edge AI teams with DFM (Design for Manufacturing) reviews. We don't just understand PCB manufacturing—we understand how to turn your algorithm into hardware that runs stably in a user's pocket. If you're developing AI PCs, smart wearables, or edge computing devices, and your model works great on a dev board but crashes on your custom PCB, contact us through our website. What's the most absurd thermal or crash issue you've encountered in edge AI hardware development? Share your experience in the comments.

items.title: Tokenization: BPE from Scratch, Vocab Size, and What Tokenizers Hide
items.summary: Tokenization: BPE from Scratch, Vocab Size, and What Tokenizers Hide Before a language model reads a single word, a tokenizer has already decided how that word gets cut up. The model never sees letters. It never sees words either. It sees token IDs, numbers drawn from a fixed list, and everything the model can and cannot do starts with that list. We built byte pair encoding from scratch, trained it on 83,159 real words from our own published articles, and measured it against OpenAI's real tokenizers. The headline numbers: the same sentence costs 16 tokens in English and 60 in Urdu, a vocabulary stops paying for itself after about 5,000 merges, and the number 2026 is two tokens because the tokenizer chops digits into groups of three. This is Deep Part 2 of the AI Engineer Deep series, and it goes one layer deeper than Part 3 of the original series, How LLMs Actually Work , where we first showed that tokens, not words, are what you pay for. The 30-second answer Tokenization turns text into a sequence of integer IDs using a fixed vocabulary built by byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from single characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until the vocabulary reaches its target size. Frequent words stay whole, rare words split into pieces, and any word at all can be represented because the vocabulary always contains single characters as a fallback. The size of that vocabulary is a real engineering tradeoff: a bigger vocabulary packs text into fewer tokens, which saves money and context, but every extra token adds a row to the embedding matrix, which costs parameters. And because the vocabulary is learned from data, it carries the biases of that data: English is cheap, Urdu is expensive, and a handful of tokens in every vocabulary were barely trained at all. Where BPE came from BPE started life as a compression algorithm. Philip Gage described it in 1994 as a way to squeeze data by repeatedly replacing the most frequent pair of bytes with a single unused byte. It sat in compression textbooks for twenty years until Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow, and Alexandra Birch adapted it for neural machine translation in their 2016 paper, Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units. Their problem was concrete: word-level translation models had fixed vocabularies, so rare words became an unknown token and the model had nothing to say about them. BPE fixed that by letting any word be spelled out as a sequence of frequent pieces. On the WMT 2015 English to German and English to Russian tasks, their subword models beat a word-level model with a back-off dictionary by up to 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU. That is a modest number on paper and a large idea in practice: the same greedy merge loop now sits at the front of every major language model, from GPT-2 to Llama 3. The experiment: BPE from scratch on the paper's own toy corpus We implemented the exact algorithm from the Sennrich paper in plain Python, no libraries, and ran it on the paper's own example dictionary: low (5 times), lowest (2), newer (6), wider (3), new (2). The algorithm counts every adjacent symbol pair weighted by word frequency, merges the most frequent pair everywhere, and repeats. Ten merges in, the vocabulary already looks like a real tokenizer in miniature. MergePair mergedResultCount 1e + rer9 2er + end of worder9 3n + ene8 4ne + wnew8 5l + olo7 6lo + wlow7 7new + ernewer6 8low + end of wordlow5 9w + iwi3 10wi + dwid3 After ten merges, the frequent words are whole tokens and the rare ones are pieces: low is one token, newer is one token, lowest splits into low plus e plus s plus t, and wider splits into wid plus er. That is the whole trick. Nothing in the algorithm knows English. It only knows frequency. The code is short enough to read in one sitting, and it is the same loop that builds production vocabularies, just with a smaller corpus and fewer merges. import collections def get_pair_stats ( vocab , freq ): pairs = collections . defaultdict ( int ) for word , symbols in vocab . items (): for i in range ( len ( symbols ) - 1 ): pairs [( symbols [ i ], symbols [ i + 1 ])] += freq [ word ] return pairs def merge_pair ( pair , vocab ): out = {} bigram = "" . join ( pair ) for word , symbols in vocab . items (): i , merged = 0 , [] while i " ] for w in corpus} for step in range(10): pairs = get_pair_stats(vocab, corpus) best = max(pairs, key=pairs.get) vocab = merge_pair(best, vocab) The experiment: training BPE on 83,159 real words A toy corpus proves the loop works. It says nothing about scale, so we trained the same code on every word in our own published articles: 83,159 words, 6,233 unique. Then we encoded a held out sentence the tokenizer had never seen, 25 words about tokenizers themselves, and measured how many tokens it took as the vocabulary grew. MergesVocabulary sizeTokens for the held out sentenceCharacters per token 0271390.99 100127692.00 500527433.21 2,0002,027304.60 5,0005,027255.52 10,0009,958255.52 Two things stand out. First, the early merges do almost all the work: the first 100 merges cut the token count in half, and 2,000 merges get you to 4.60 characters per token. Second, the curve flattens hard. Going from 5,000 merges to 10,000 merges bought exactly zero fewer tokens on held out text, because the extra merges memorized quirks of our training articles instead of learning general pieces. A bigger vocabulary is not automatically a better tokenizer. It is a bigger vocabulary that has to earn its keep on text it has never seen. At 2,000 merges, our little tokenizer split unseen words the way a real one would: tokenizer became tokeniz plus er, unbelievable became un plus be plus li plus ev plus able, and transformers became trans plus form plus ers. To see what production tokenizers actually do, we ran the same text through tiktoken, OpenAI's own BPE library, with three real encodings: r50k_base from GPT-2, cl100k_base from GPT-4, and o200k_base from GPT-4o. LanguageSame sentence, charactersTokens (cl100k_base)Characters per token English73164.56 German86263.31 Chinese19280.68 Urdu63601.05 The same meaning costs 16 tokens in English and 60 in Urdu, a 3.75x multiplier, and Chinese needs 28 tokens for a 19 character sentence because each character carries a whole syllable of meaning and still splits into more than one token. Every API call is billed per token, every context window is measured in tokens, and a user writing in Urdu pays nearly four times as much as a user writing the same thing in English, for the same model and the same answer. Published analyses of token pricing across languages have found gaps as large as 10x for some languages. Numbers: the tokenizer chops digits into groups of three Numbers get special treatment, and it explains a famous model weakness. Under cl100k_base, 123456789 becomes three tokens, 123 plus 456 plus 789. The year 2026 becomes two tokens, 202 plus 6. Pi to fourteen decimal places becomes seven tokens, 3 plus a dot plus 141 plus 592 plus 653 plus 589 plus 79. The model never sees a number as a number. It sees digit chunks of up to three, glued together by position. That is why a model can write a poem about arithmetic and still fumble a five digit addition: the digits it must add were never presented as a single unit. The same blindness shows up in spelling. Ask a model how many r letters are in strawberry, and remember that it never sees the word strawberry. It sees str plus aw plus berry, three tokens, and the letter r is smeared across token boundaries the model cannot inspect. The failure is not in the model's reasoning. It is in the input representation, and no amount of prompting fixes a representation problem. Vocab size: the tradeoff nobody prices Every token in the vocabulary costs parameters twice over: once in the input embedding matrix that turns IDs into vectors, and once in the output head that turns vectors back into probabilities over the vocabulary. For GPT-2 small, the embedding matrix is 50,257 tokens times 768 dimensions, about 38.6 million parameters, or 31.1 percent of the whole 124 million parameter model. For Llama 3 8B, the matrix is 128,256 tokens times 4,096 dimensions, about 525 million parameters, or 6.6 percent of the model. The share falls as models grow, but the absolute cost never goes away, and a vocabulary of 262,145 tokens like Gemma 3 pays for it in both matrices. This is the real reason vocabularies do not grow without limit. A bigger vocabulary compresses text better, which saves context and money on every request, but it also makes the model bigger, slower to load, and more expensive to train, and our sweep shows the compression gain flattens long before the parameter cost does. Picking a vocabulary size is picking a point on that curve, and most teams pick it once and live with it for the life of the model. What tokenizers hide Three things about tokenizers surprise working engineers, and all three follow from how BPE is actually built. First, tokenization happens before the model, and it happens in two steps: a regex first splits text into chunks, then BPE merges inside each chunk. The regex decides that a leading space belongs to the following word, which is why hello world is two tokens, hello and space plus world, and why tokenization with a leading space is two tokens, space plus token and ization. Change the space and you change the tokens, which is why the same word can tokenize differently at the start of a sentence and in the middle of one. Second, the tokenizer and the model are trained separately, on different data, and that gap creates glitch tokens. A string that was frequent in the tokenizer's training text earns its own token, but if it barely appears in the model's training text, its embedding never gets trained. The famous case is SolidGoldMagikarp, a Reddit username that appeared in so many counting threads that GPT-2's tokenizer gave it a token of its own, while the model itself almost never saw it in training. Asked to repeat it, GPT-2 era models produced evasions, insults, or unrelated text. We verified the fix with tiktoken: the old r50k_base encoding splits it into two tokens, Solid and GoldMagikarp, and both cl100k_base and o200k_base split it into five, Solid plus Gold plus Mag plus ik plus arp. A 2024 paper by Land and Bartolo, Fishing for Magikarp, showed these undertrained tokens are common across many open model families and can be found automatically. Third, tokenizers are frozen the day the model ships. You cannot add a token for your product name, your file format, or your language without retraining the model, so every prompt you write is at the mercy of merge decisions made months or years ago on someone else's corpus. Our opinionated take Most teams treat the tokenizer as plumbing and never look at it, and that is a mistake we think costs real money. If you build on top of language models, the tokenizer is the first thing you should measure, not the last. Count tokens before you count dollars: our paragraph of English cost 39 tokens, and one million tokens of English prose is roughly five megabytes of text, so a retrieval pipeline that stuffs whole documents into context is paying a token bill it never budgeted for. Test your prompts in the languages your users actually write, because a 3.75x token multiplier is a 3.75x cost multiplier and a 3.75x smaller effective context window, and no one will tell you that until the invoice arrives. And if you train anything yourself, do not chase the biggest vocabulary you can afford. Our sweep flattened at 5,000 merges on real text, and the production lesson is the same: the vocabulary that wins is the one trained on your data, sized to the point where the curve bends, not the biggest number on a spec sheet. The tokenizer is the cheapest part of the model to understand and the most expensive part to ignore. Before a language model reads a single word, a tokenizer has already decided how that word gets cut up. The model never sees letters. It never sees words either. The 30-second answer

Tokenization turns text into a sequence of integer IDs using a fixed vocabulary built by byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from single characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until the vocabulary reaches its target size. Frequent words stay whole, rare words split into pieces, and any word at all can be represented because the vocabulary always contains single characters as a fallback. The size of that vocabulary is a real engineering tradeoff: a bigger vocabulary packs text into fewer tokens, which saves money and context, but every extra token adds a row to the embedding matrix, which costs parameters. And because the vocabulary is learned from data, it carries the biases of that data: English is cheap, Urdu is expensive, and a handful of tokens in every vocabulary were barely trained at all.

Where BPE came from

BPE started life as a compression algorithm. Philip Gage described it in 1994 as a way to squeeze data by repeatedly replacing the most frequent pair of bytes with a single unused byte. It sat in compression textbooks for twenty years until Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow, and Alexandra Birch adapted it for neural machine translation in their 2016 paper, Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units. Their problem was concrete: word-level translation models had fixed vocabularies, so rare words became an unknown token and the model had nothing to say about them. items.title: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3: Open-Weight MoE Scores #2 on SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning, Beating Gemini and Grok
items.summary: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3: Open-Weight MoE Scores #2 on SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning, Beating Gemini and Grok TL;DR: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is a 180-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model from VIDRAFT that scored 73.68 on the SuperCLUE November 2026 math and science reasoning dimension — ranking #2 overall and #1 among open-weight models on an independently administered, non-public test. It activates only ~3B parameters per token, ships weights under a Qwen community license permitting commercial use, and has a 4-bit quantized variant that runs on a 32 GB RAM laptop without a GPU. What it is Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model built on top of Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as a base. Key facts from the source: Parameter count: 180B total, with roughly 3B activated per token at inference time Architecture lineage: Inherits the expert layers from Qwen3.8-Flash-Next — 512 experts per layer, with the bulk of world knowledge stored in those feed-forward network (FFN) blocks What changed vs. the base: Only the attention layers, linear-attention layers, and shared expert layers were retrained using a self-improvement process; the FFN expert blocks were kept intact License: Qwen community license, open-weight, commercial use permitted Edge variant: POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF — a 4-bit quantized GGUF version designed to run from SSD on a 32 GB RAM consumer laptop, no GPU required Developer: VIDRAFT (South Korean Pre-AGI AI startup) The model was independently evaluated by SuperCLUE on November 5, 2026. SuperCLUE is a Chinese LLM benchmark that evolved from the 2019 CLUE (Chinese Language Understanding Evaluation) project. It issues fresh, non-public test sets each month and scores models across five dimensions: agentic coding, math & science reasoning, hallucination suppression, precise instruction following, and long-context understanding. How it works The core idea behind Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is surgical retraining : instead of fine-tuning an entire large model, VIDRAFT preserved the FFN expert layers — which encode the model's factual and domain knowledge — and exclusively retrained the components most responsible for multi-step reasoning: the attention layers, linear-attention layers, and shared experts. The retraining mechanism is described in Korean media coverage as a self-improvement loop : the model generates its own problems, produces candidate answers, verifies those answers internally, and uses that feedback signal to update weights. This is conceptually similar to self-play or self-distillation approaches common in the reasoning research literature, applied specifically to the layers governing how the model attends to and routes information rather than what it knows . The practical consequence of this design choice: the same 512-expert FFN knowledge base as the parent model, but with reasoning-focused layers optimized through iterative self-generated supervision. Benchmarks & results All numbers below come directly from the SuperCLUE November 2026 leaderboard (published 2026-11-05) and are independently administered — not self-reported by VIDRAFT. Metric Score / Rank SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning 73.68 (2nd of 19 models) SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning — open-weight rank #1 SuperCLUE 5-dimension composite index 43.08 (9th of 19 models, 5th among open-weight) GPQA Diamond (Hugging Face leaderboard) 94.44 (ranked #1 at time of reporting) Score delta vs. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next base (math & science reasoning) +15.8 points Composite rank improvement vs. base +6 positions The model ranked above Google Gemini, xAI's Grok, and DeepSeek on the math & science reasoning dimension. The only model ahead of it was GPT-6.1-Sol at 76.32. Important context: SuperCLUE places non-Chinese models on the same table for reference but does not include them in its official ranking. The 73.68 score is from a held-out, non-public November test set — not a contamination-prone static benchmark. How to try it The source article confirms that model weights are publicly available. Based on the information reported: Weights: Released under the Qwen community license (commercial use allowed). Check the VIDRAFT organization page on Hugging Face for Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 . Edge/CPU variant: POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF (4-bit quantized) is designed for 32 GB RAM laptops running inference from SSD — no GPU required. Look for it on Hugging Face under VIDRAFT's model hub. The source does not publicly document a specific API endpoint, GitHub repository URL, or installation command for this release. Check VIDRAFT's official channels for the latest access instructions before deployment. FAQ Q: Why does the model score #2 on reasoning but only #9 overall on SuperCLUE? A: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 was specifically optimized for math and science reasoning. The five-dimension SuperCLUE composite also includes agentic coding, hallucination suppression, instruction following, and long-context tasks — areas where the model was not specifically retrained. The result is a narrow specialist that excels on its target dimension while sitting mid-table overall. Q: Is retraining only the attention layers a proven approach, or experimental? A: The approach is conceptually grounded in existing research showing that FFN layers store factual knowledge while attention layers govern reasoning and information routing. The +15.8-point gain on an independently scored, non-public benchmark is a concrete external data point, though a single benchmark result should always be interpreted alongside broader evaluation. Q: Can I run the full 180B model on consumer hardware? A: Not the full-precision model. The POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF 4-bit quantized variant is specifically designed for 32 GB RAM laptops running from SSD without a GPU, according to the source coverage. Q: Does the Qwen community license allow me to use this in a commercial product? A: The source states commercial use is permitted under the Qwen community license. Always review the full license text in the model repository before production deployment. Originally reported by 넷이즈 网易 (중국) (2026-11-07) — source article .

Darwin-180B-RSI-R3: Open-Weight MoE Scores #2 on SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning, Beating Gemini and Grok

TL;DR: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is a 180-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model from VIDRAFT that scored 73.68 on the SuperCLUE November 2026 math and science reasoning dimension — ranking #2 overall and #1 among open-weight models on an independently administered, non-public test. It activates only ~3B parameters per token, ships weights under a Qwen community license permitting commercial use, and has a 4-bit quantized variant that runs on a 32 GB RAM laptop without a GPU.

What it is

Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model built on top of Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as a base. Key facts from the source:

  • Parameter count: 180B total, with roughly 3B activated per token at inference time
  • Architecture lineage: Inherits the expert layers from Qwen3.8-Flash-Next — 512 experts per layer, with the bulk of world knowledge stored in those feed-forward network (FFN) blocks
  • What changed vs. the base: Only the attention layers, linear-attention layers, and shared expert layers were retrained using a self-improvement process; the FFN expert blocks were kept intact
  • License: Qwen community license, open-weight, commercial use permitted
  • Edge variant: POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF — a 4-bit quantized GGUF version designed to run from SSD on a 32 GB RAM consumer laptop, no GPU required
  • Developer: VIDRAFT (South Korean Pre-AGI AI startup)

The model was independently evaluated by SuperCLUE on November 5, 2026. SuperCLUE is a Chinese LLM benchmark that evolved from the 2019 CLUE (Chinese Language Understanding Evaluation) project. It issues fresh, non-public test sets each month and scores models across five dimensions: agentic coding, math & science reasoning, hallucination suppression, precise instruction following, and long-context understanding.

How it works

The core idea behind Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is surgical retraining: instead of fine-tuning an entire large model, VIDRAFT preserved the FFN expert layers — which encode the model's factual and domain knowledge — and exclusively retrained the components most responsible for multi-step reasoning: the attention layers, linear-attention layers, and shared experts.

The retraining mechanism is described in Korean media coverage as a self-improvement loop: the model generates its own problems, produces candidate answers, verifies those answers internally, and uses that feedback signal to update weights. This is conceptually similar to self-play or self-distillation approaches common in the reasoning research literature, applied specifically to the layers governing how the model attends to and routes information rather than what it knows.

The practical consequence of this design choice: the same 512-expert FFN knowledge base as the parent model, but with reasoning-focused layers optimized through iterative self-generated supervision.

Benchmarks & results

All numbers below come directly from the SuperCLUE November 2026 leaderboard (published 2026-11-05) and are independently administered — not self-reported by VIDRAFT.

Metric Score / Rank SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning 73.68 (2nd of 19 models) SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning — open-weight rank #1 SuperCLUE 5-dimension composite index 43.08 (9th of 19 models, 5th among open-weight) GPQA Diamond (Hugging Face leaderboard) 94.44 (ranked #1 at time of reporting) Score delta vs. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next base (math & science reasoning) +15.8 points Composite rank improvement vs. base +6 positions

The model ranked above Google Gemini, xAI's Grok, and DeepSeek on the math & science reasoning dimension. The only model ahead of it was GPT-6.1-Sol at 76.32.

Important context: SuperCLUE places non-Chinese models on the same table for reference but does not include them in its official ranking. The 73.68 score is from a held-out, non-public November test set — not a contamination-prone static benchmark.

How to try it

The source article confirms that model weights are publicly available. Based on the information reported:

  • Weights: Released under the Qwen community license (commercial use allowed). Check the VIDRAFT organization page on Hugging Face for Darwin-180B-RSI-R3.
  • Edge/CPU variant: POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF (4-bit quantized) is designed for 32 GB RAM laptops running inference from SSD — no GPU required. Look for it on Hugging Face under VIDRAFT's model hub.

The source does not publicly document a specific API endpoint, GitHub repository URL, or installation command for this release. Check VIDRAFT's official channels for the latest access instructions before deployment.

FAQ

Q: Why does the model score #2 on reasoning but only #9 overall on SuperCLUE?
A: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 was specifically optimized for math and science reasoning. The five-dimension SuperCLUE composite also includes agentic coding, hallucination suppression, instruction following, and long-context tasks — areas where the model was not specifically retrained. The result is a narrow specialist that excels on its target dimension while sitting mid-table overall.

Q: Is retraining only the attention layers a proven approach, or experimental?
A: The approach is conceptually grounded in existing research showing that FFN layers store factual knowledge while attention layers govern reasoning and information routing. The +15.8-point gain on an independently scored, non-public benchmark is a concrete external data point, though a single benchmark result should always be interpreted alongside broader evaluation.

Q: Can I run the full 180B model on consumer hardware?
A: Not the full-precision model. The POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF 4-bit quantized variant is specifically designed for 32 GB RAM laptops running from SSD without a GPU, according to the source coverage.

Q: Does the Qwen community license allow me to use this in a commercial product?
A: The source states commercial use is permitted under the Qwen community license. Always review the full license text in the model repository before production deployment.
