items.title: How to plan an infrastructure task without losing your mind: a breakdown using an AWS deployment as an example
items.summary: The ticket fits on one line: "deploy a new web service to AWS and add jobs to deploy it." Inside that line are a network, containers, a database, secrets, a CDN, two workflows and dozens of small steps that an engineer usually keeps in their head. That works while nothing interrupts you. Then you join a call, come back, and can't remember whether you checked the security group. And when someone asks how long it will take, the honest answer is "a day or two." I've been building IT infrastructure for about 15 years, and today I lead a DevOps team at a game studio. Tasks like "spin up a new service" or "change system X" land on my desk every week, and over the years I've settled into a fairly stable way of planning them. I tried to write that method down and then give it to an agent. Part 1. How an engineer plans a task The task Let's take a concrete one: Deploy a new web service to AWS. It has a React frontend and a Python backend, and requires PostgreSQL to run. The application repository is github.com/javdet/nib-demo-app . This should result in jobs in GitHub for deploying the infrastructure and the application. Nothing unusual. Tasks like this come in all the time, and anyone who works with infrastructure has a rough idea of what's behind them. Let's walk through what happens in an engineer's head when this ticket arrives, step by step and slower than it happens in real life. Step 1. Collect context Before planning anything, the engineer answers three questions: What is the project? Who uses it, how critical it is, whether it has environments besides production. How does the current infrastructure work? Which AWS accounts exist, where the Terraform state lives, how the networks are laid out, what CI/CD is already there. What do we know about the products in the task? Here that's AWS, PostgreSQL and GitHub Actions: which AWS services fit, which Postgres version to use, how Actions will reach the cloud. Some of the answers are already in their head. The rest they pull from git and the wiki: usually details of how the infrastructure is built and the company's internal rules for cloud, databases and CI/CD. This step already shows the first problem, and we'll come back to it: a large part of the context isn't written down anywhere except in one person's head. Step 2. Outline the stages Once the context is collected, the task falls apart into large stages: Write infrastructure code for the AWS resources. Write the build and deploy workflows. Create the resources in AWS. Deploy the application. Check that everything works. The stages depend on each other: you can't deploy the app before the cluster exists, and you can't create the cluster before the code exists. The dependencies matter more than the list itself, because they decide what can run in parallel and what can't. Step 3. Break the stages into basic actions Each stage is a set of simple actions you can do in one go: edit a file; run a CLI command; make an API call; change a setting in a UI. For example, "create the resources in AWS" becomes a chain: create a bucket for the state, give GitHub Actions access to the account, run terraform plan , read the diff, run terraform apply , look at the outputs. Step 4. Lean on rules and experience To put the actions in the right order, the engineer relies on two things: Team rules. How we name resources, where we keep state, which tags are required, what we never do in production. Their own experience. They've done something similar before and remember where it hurt last time. ### Step 5. Build the plan: action, check, rollback These pieces add up to a detailed plan. Usually it lives in the engineer's head, less often on paper. A good plan has three parts: actions : what exactly we do; checks before closing each stage: how to know the stage is really done, and not just "seems fine"; a rollback plan in case something goes wrong. The Rollback column is the one people leave empty most often. Be honest: when did you last write a rollback plan before you needed it? Step 6. Execute Then the engineer walks the whole list: action, check, action, check. If a check fails, they roll back or fix the problem, and check again. Tedious, right? Where this process breaks On paper it's a good process. In practice it breaks in three places. 1. The action list lives in your head, and items fall out of it. A call, an alert, a colleague asking you to look at their PR. An hour later you come back to the task and you're no longer sure whether you closed the database port to the internet. A plan in your head doesn't survive context switches, and you can't hand it to a colleague if you get sick in the middle of the task. This happened to me when I was moving asset buckets from one cloud to another. I copied the data and set up access, but forgot to add CORS. It's a couple of lines of config, and it feels so obvious that it never makes it onto any list. 2. Checks get skipped. You want to save time: "the site opened, so it works." The fact that the database is reachable from the internet, or that backups aren't set up, comes up a month later. Checks are the first thing to go under a deadline, because skipping them doesn't break anything right away. 3. Nobody knows how big the task is. Ask "how long will it take?" and you hear "a day or two." That's not an estimate. Until the task is broken into actions, its size is invisible: to you, to your team lead, and to whoever filed the ticket. All three have the same cause: the plan exists only in the head of the person doing the work, so you can't hand it over and you can't measure it. What if an agent builds the plan? So here's the natural question: what if an agent does the breakdown, the planning, the execution and the checks? The engineer still controls the stages, decides which steps to run, and accepts the final result. That's why I built nib (Neuro Infrastructure Builder). It's a tool for infrastructure work: it splits a task into stages, writes concrete actions with checks for each stage, builds a rollback plan, and then either runs the steps itself or gives the operator detailed instructions. Inside, nib follows the same logic as the engineer from Part 1. The work is split into modes, and each mode has its own role: The context, rules and experience the engineer relies on exist in nib too: a knowledge base, rules and skills. In this post we only use the knowledge base. The rest is a topic for the next part. Part 2. From git clone to a working site Now let's run the same task through nib. The whole run is on video : What you need Docker; an API key for an LLM provider. nib works with any OpenAI-compatible API, and the installer has presets for OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, Grok and Kimi; an AWS account. I strongly recommend a separate sandbox account: the agent will need keys that can create resources; a GitHub account and a fork of demo-app , if you want to repeat this exact task. Installation nib runs locally with Docker Compose or in Kubernetes with a Helm chart. The local option is enough to try it: git clone https://github.com/javdet/nib.git cd nib make setup make setup is an interactive script. It asks for the LLM provider, the model and the key (I use OpenRouter), then the name of your first project and, optionally, its environments, clouds and regions. You can skip those fields, but nib plans better with them, and you can add more projects later. Then the script generates tokens, writes .env and the config, and starts four containers: Postgres, the knowledge base server, the backend and the frontend. At the end it prints the UI address ( http://localhost:8080 by default; if the port is busy, it picks a free one) and an API token. You paste this token on the login screen. It's also saved in .env as NIB_API_TOKEN , so it's hard to lose. Knowledge base: what to fill in for a new project The first place to open after you log in is Knowledgebase . This is the "context" from step 1: everything the engineer knows about the company and the project, and the agent doesn't. The Company Information card has the basic fields: company name and description, version control system and git base URL, git user, CI/CD system, issue tracker, wiki and team messenger. For our task the key ones are GitHub as the VCS and GitHub Actions as CI/CD, because they decide which workflows the agent will write. You don't need to upload documents for a new project yet: there's nothing to describe. On a live project, this is where you put what usually sits in the wiki and in people's heads: the network diagram, naming conventions, where state lives, what's special about each environment. You can upload a Markdown document or ask the agent to generate one from a list of repositories. When a plan finishes, nib writes a report and updates the knowledge base from it, so the next task starts with what the agent learned in the previous one. Connecting GitHub, AWS and search over MCP On its own, the agent can only think. To create a repository, look at AWS resources or find documentation, it needs tools. In nib they connect over MCP (Model Context Protocol). It's an open protocol: an LLM application gets a list of tools from an external server and calls them. One MCP server covers one system: GitHub, AWS, search. If you don't know where to start, ask nib itself, for example: "How do I connect you to AWS over MCP?" Its answer is in the video. This task needs three servers: GitHub : the repository, PRs and workflows; AWS : reading and creating resources in the account; SearXNG : web search, so the agent can check current documentation instead of relying only on what the model already knows. nib supports only the HTTP transport for MCP (streamable HTTP), so we run all three servers as containers on the same network as nib. Add them to docker-compose.yml . GitHub MCP is the official server from GitHub: github-mcp : image : ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server:latest restart : unless-stopped command : - http - --port=9082 networks : - nib aws-mcp : image : public.ecr.aws/awslabs-mcp/awslabs/aws-api-mcp-server:latest restart : unless-stopped environment : AWS_API_MCP_TRANSPORT : " streamable-http" AWS_API_MCP_HOST : " 0.0.0.0" AWS_API_MCP_PORT : " 9081" AUTH_TYPE : " no-auth" AWS_REGION : " ${AWS_REGION:-us-east-2}" AWS_API_MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS : " aws-mcp,localhost,127.0.0.1" AWS_API_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS : " aws-mcp,localhost,127.0.0.1" READ_OPERATIONS_ONLY : " false" REQUIRE_MUTATION_CONSENT : " false" AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID : " ${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}" AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY : " ${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}" AWS_SESSION_TOKEN : " ${AWS_SESSION_TOKEN:-}" networks : - nib searxng : image : docker.io/searxng/searxng:latest restart : unless-stopped environment : SEARXNG_PORT : " 9083" SEARXNG_BASE_URL : " http://searxng:9083/" SEARXNG_SECRET : " ${SEARXNG_SECRET}" volumes : - ./searxng:/etc/searxng:rw networks : - nib searxng-mcp : image : docker.io/isokoliuk/mcp-searxng:latest restart : unless-stopped environment : SEARXNG_URL : " http://searxng:9083" SEARXNG_DEFAULT_RESPONSE_FORMAT : " json" SEARXNG_MAX_RESULT_CHARS : " 500" SEARXNG_TIMEOUT_MS : " 15000" MCP_HTTP_PORT : " 9084" MCP_HTTP_HOST : " 0.0.0.0" MCP_HTTP_STATELESS : " true" networks : - nib The response format is an easy place to trip up. The MCP wrapper asks SearXNG for results in JSON, but by default SearXNG returns only HTML. The json format has to be enabled in searxng/settings.yml . The nib repository already ships this file with the right setting, which is why the volume is mounted from ./searxng . Registering the servers in nib Now nib needs to know where to find these servers. You edit the MCP config in Tools → Config (or through Tools → MCP Servers → Add ): { "mcpServers" : { "knowledge-base" : { "url" : "http://kb-mcp:8081/mcp" }, "aws" : { "type" : "http" , "url" : "http://aws-mcp:9081/mcp" }, "searxng" : { "type" : "http" , "url" : "http://searxng-mcp:9084/mcp" }, "github" : { "type" : "http" , "url" : "http://github-mcp:9082/" , "headers" : { "Authorization" : "Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}" , "X-MCP-Toolsets" : "all" , "X-MCP-Readonly" : "false" } } } } knowledge-base is the built-in knowledge base server, and it's already in the config after installation. We add the other three. Note the ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in the header. Tokens never go into the config as plain text: nib fills them in from Variables → Secrets at request time. Each secret has a list of allowed hosts, so the GitHub token goes only to github-mcp and nowhere else. So secrets live in two places, and it's easy to mix them up: AWS keys are needed by the aws-mcp container itself, so they're in .env and reach the container as environment variables; the GitHub token travels in the HTTP header of the request from nib to the MCP server, so it's in nib's secrets. Checking the connection After restarting the containers, open Tools → MCP Servers . For each server you can see the list of tools it exposes. If the list is empty or the server shows an error, the problem is in the network, the address or the token, and there's no point going further: an agent without tools plans blind. In the video, the very first check fails: GitHub MCP returns an error. The container is up and the address is right, but the GITHUB_TOKEN secret doesn't exist yet, and without it the server returns nothing. We create the secret in Variables → Secrets , check again, and the tool list appears. You create the token in your GitHub user settings, under Developer settings ( github.com/settings/tokens ). I used a classic token with the repo and workflow scopes. The second one is easy to miss: without it GitHub rejects pushes to .github/workflows/ , and the agent can't commit its workflows. In my case GitHub exposed a couple of dozen tools, SearXNG five, and AWS only two. That's expected. AWS API MCP Server gives the agent a generic AWS CLI call plus a helper that picks the right command, so all of AWS fits into two tools. GitHub is the opposite, with one tool per operation, and the next section deals with that. Tool categories and a base set per mode Three MCP servers give the agent a lot of tools. If you send all of them with every call, the model gets confused, the context grows, and you pay tokens for descriptions of tools this task will never use. Planning cloud resources doesn't need tools for logs and metrics. nib has two mechanisms for this. Tool categories. Tools are grouped into categories (for example, everything about AWS, everything about git). During decomposition the agent decides which categories the task touches and gets access only to those. Each action in the plan gets an even narrower set: only the categories marked on that action. You don't have to sort the tools by hand. The Auto-fill with AI button on the Tool categories card does a first pass that you can then fix. A base set for each mode. You can think of nib's modes as subagents: some break the task down, some work out the stages, some run actions. By default every mode gets every tool. In Tools → Included tools you can narrow this: modes that should only read and plan don't need tools that change things. The Distribute with AI button can only remove tools, so the read-only modes lose the tools that change things, and nothing extra gets added. The first plan Everything is ready, so we can plan. As a reminder, we're deploying demo-app , an online store for art supplies with a Python backend, a React frontend and a PostgreSQL database. Click New plan and paste the task from Part 1 as is. From here, nib repeats what the engineer did in Part 1. Collecting context. First the decompose agent asks clarifying questions, and for most of them it suggests answers you can pick with a click. It asked me two questions an engineer would ask whoever filed the ticket in the first five minutes: How should the service be published? Is there a custom domain, or is the address that CloudFront generates enough? The answer decides whether DNS records and a TLS certificate show up in the plan. How should the jobs run? Automatically on merge to the main branch, or manually? Really, this is a question about whether the infrastructure can change without a human. I don't have a domain, so the site lives on the CloudFront address, and the jobs run automatically. Stages and dependencies. After the answers, the agent shows a Summary (how it understood the task) and a DAG of the stages and the dependencies between them. A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is a "what comes after what" diagram with no loops. Here you see for the first time what was implicit in the engineer's head: which stages can run in parallel and which ones block the rest. If you have no questions about the stages, move on to detailed planning. Actions, checks, rollback. The Process plan here button starts planning. A separate agent works on each stage, in parallel with the others, and at the end the rollback plan is built. The whole thing took about two minutes. The result was four stages and a rollback plan: Look at the last row: there are one and a half times more checks than actions. When the plan lives in your head, this is the part that shrinks first under a deadline. Steps come in four types: run a CLI command, make an API request, work with code, or change something in a web UI. Each step has a detailed description of what to do, and if an action can cause downtime for a system that's already running, the plan warns about it separately. This answers the third problem from Part 1. nib doesn't estimate in hours, but you see the amount of work before you start: four stages, ten steps, fifteen checks, and it's clear where you need code and where an API call is enough. You can take that to whoever asked "how long will it take," and the conversation will be more concrete than "a day or two." Preparing access: the agent works over MCP Each step has a run button, each stage has Execute all , and you can also start a step from the chat by asking the agent. A checkbox next to a step marks it as done, and you can leave a comment on any step. Only one action runs at a time. This is a deliberate limit, so that two agents don't change the same infrastructure in parallel. The first stage is all API and CLI calls, so the agent ran it on its own, over MCP: Reconcile the GitHub Actions OIDC provider in AWS account : the OIDC provider that GitHub Actions will use to get access to AWS; Reconcile the remote Terraform state bucket for the prod stack : an S3 bucket for the Terraform state; Reconcile the infrastructure deployment role used by Terraform : the role Terraform uses to create resources; Reconcile the application deployment role for publishing and rolling out : a separate role for shipping the application; Create or reconcile the protected GitHub production environment : a protected production environment in the repository. If you know Kubernetes, you know the word reconcile: bring the system to the desired state. If the resource doesn't exist, create it. If it exists but is configured differently, fix it. If it's already right, do nothing. A step like this is safe to run again, which helps if the plan stops halfway. The two separate roles are deliberate too: the role that ships the application has no reason to be able to create networks and databases. After each step, the agent reports in the chat what it did. To make the demo clearer, I ran the stage checks myself: I opened the AWS console and made sure the OIDC provider was created, the bucket was there, and the environment had appeared in the repository. The agent can run the checks too; you just have to ask. Remember the OIDC provider check. We'll need it later. Code: Terraform and workflows In the second stage, API calls are no longer enough: we need to write Terraform and workflows. For steps like these, nib has an executor that runs a coding agent in a separate container. The agent clones the repository, makes the changes, commits, pushes and opens a pull request. The first time you run a code step, nib sends you to the executor settings page ( Tools → Executor ). The executor has three options: off (the default), Local , which means containers on your machine through Docker, and Remote , which runs as Kubernetes Jobs. Local is enough to start: the agent runs right on your computer, and you can see the container logs in the UI. Pick the agent type and the authentication method. The tokens we need aren't in the secrets list yet, so we create them: CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN : the Claude Code subscription token, which you get from claude setup-token . You can use an Anthropic API key instead; a GitHub token, so the agent can push its changes. It's the same one as for MCP. You can keep the default agent image and model. Go back to the plan and run the step. What the agent wrote The PR has 20 files: two workflows, Terraform code in infra/terraform and an updated README. In short, here's the architecture: CloudFront in front of everything: the frontend's static files come from a private S3 bucket, and /api/* requests go to an ALB ; the ALB accepts traffic only from the CloudFront managed prefix list, so you can't reach it directly from the internet; the backend runs on ECS Fargate in private subnets and accepts traffic only from the ALB; RDS PostgreSQL 16 sits in isolated subnets with no route to the internet. It's Multi-AZ, encrypted, with backups and deletion protection. Terraform generates the password and puts it straight into Secrets Manager ; GitHub Actions reach AWS over OIDC : the job assumes an IAM role and gets temporary credentials, so not a single long-lived AWS key is stored in GitHub. This is where the provider and the roles from the first stage come in. And two workflows: Deploy Infrastructure runs terraform plan and terraform apply . Apply runs only manually, with an explicit flag, in the production GitHub environment, where you can require approval. That's how the agent used my answer about running jobs; Deploy Application builds the backend image, pushes it to ECR tagged with the commit, updates the ECS service, builds the frontend, uploads it to S3, invalidates the CloudFront cache and finally runs a smoke test against the CloudFront address. Two decisions in this code are good examples of the "experience" from Part 1 that usually isn't written down anywhere. The ECS service is created with desired_count = 0 . When terraform apply runs, ECR doesn't have a single application image yet. If you ask for two tasks right away, ECS will keep trying to start an image that doesn't exist. So Terraform creates the service empty and ignores later changes to the image and the task count, and the deploy workflow publishes the first real image and scales the service to two. Without this detail, Terraform would undo the deploy on every run. The cost is stated openly. A Multi-AZ database and a NAT gateway in every availability zone are a production setup, and they cost money even with no traffic. The agent put this in the README, next to the order in which to run the workflows. For a demo it's overkill, for production it's right, and it's a decision you should make on purpose instead of learning about it from the bill. The changes look reasonable, so we merge the PR into the main branch. First run, first failure We run Deploy Infrastructure , and the first attempt fails. This happens to experienced engineers too, so it's no big deal. Instead of reading the log myself, I show nib the error and ask it to figure it out. It finds the cause: the OIDC provider created in the first stage doesn't list all the thumbprints. A thumbprint is a fingerprint of the identity provider's TLS certificate. AWS uses the list of thumbprints to verify that the token really came from GitHub. If the right thumbprint isn't on the list, AWS doesn't trust the token, and the job can't assume the role and get into the account. We add the missing thumbprints and rerun the workflow. On the second try the infrastructure is created: the log shows the terraform plan and how many resources were created. We check that the database is ready and the load balancer is in place, and mark the steps as done. Deploying the app: a second failure, then the site We run Deploy Application , and it also fails the first time: the healthcheck doesn't pass. The deploy finished too quickly, and the app wasn't ready by the time of the check. This is expected, and the next step of the plan says exactly that: rerun the deploy. So we do. On the second run the deploy passes and the smoke test is green. We open the CloudFront address and see the art-supply store, the service we set out to deploy. We mark the remaining steps and click Finish . nib closes the plan, writes a report on the work done and updates the knowledge base. Next time a task about this project comes in, the agent will already know that it has a VPC, an ECS cluster and a database, and won't start from zero. Wrapping up We took an ordinary task: deploy a web service to AWS and set up GitHub jobs to deploy it. In two minutes nib split it into four stages with ten steps, fifteen checks and a rollback plan. The agent prepared AWS and GitHub access on its own over MCP, the executor wrote the Terraform and the workflows, and we worked through two failures on the way, the OIDC provider and the healthcheck, together with nib. At the end we opened the site and saw the store working. Back to the three problems from Part 1: Items don't get lost. The action list is written down in the plan. You can see it, hand it to a colleague and pick up where you left off. Checks don't get skipped. They're written into every stage in advance, and the agent isn't tempted to save time on them. Still, the OIDC story showed that a check is only as useful as it is precise. The size is visible before you start. You know how many stages and steps are ahead before the first command runs. The decisions stay with you: you choose which steps to run, you read the PR, and you accept the result. Even if you don't plan to use agents, try writing the plan for your next task in three columns: action, check, rollback. That alone solves the first problem and makes the second one much easier. In Part 1 I said that an engineer relies on team rules and their own experience. You can give nib the same things. In the next post I'll show how to connect your own rules, skills and knowledge base, so the plans come out more accurate and closer to how your team works. The repository is here: github.com/javdet/nib . Try it on a task of your own, and tell me in the comments: which infrastructure task would you trust to an agent first, and which one never?

An hour later you come back to the task and you're no longer sure whether you closed the database port to the internet. A plan in your head doesn't survive context switches, and you can't hand it to a colleague if you get sick in the middle of the task.

This happened to me when I was moving asset buckets from one cloud to another. I copied the data and set up access, but forgot to add CORS. It's a couple of lines of config, and it feels so obvious that it never makes it onto any list.

2. Checks get skipped. You want to save time: "the site opened, so it works." The fact that the database is reachable from the internet, or that backups aren't set up, comes up a month later. Checks are the first thing to go under a deadline, because skipping them doesn't break anything right away.

3. Nobody knows how big the task is. Ask "how long will it take?" and you hear "a day or two." That's not an estimate. Until the task is broken into actions, its size is invisible: to you, to your team lead, and to whoever filed the ticket.

All three have the same cause: the plan exists only in the head of the person doing the work, so you can't hand it over and you can't measure it.

What if an agent builds the plan?

So here's the natural question: what if an agent does the breakdown, the planning, the execution and the checks? The engineer still controls the stages, decides which steps to run, and accepts the final result.


That's why I built nib (Neuro Infrastructure Builder). It's a tool for infrastructure work: it splits a task into stages, writes concrete actions with checks for each stage, builds a rollback plan, and then either runs the steps itself or gives the operator detailed instructions.
Inside, nib follows the same logic as the engineer from Part 1. The work is split into modes, and each mode has its own role:


The context, rules and experience the engineer relies on exist in nib too: a knowledge base, rules and skills. In this post we only use the knowledge base. The rest is a topic for the next part.

Part 2. From git clone to a working site

Now let's run the same task through nib. The whole run is on video:

What you need
  • Docker;
  • an API key for an LLM provider. nib works with any OpenAI-compatible API, and the installer has presets for OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, Grok and Kimi;
  • an AWS account. I strongly recommend a separate sandbox account: the agent will need keys that can create resources;
  • a GitHub account and a fork of demo-app, if you want to repeat this exact task.
Installation

nib runs locally with Docker Compose or in Kubernetes with a Helm chart. The local option is enough to try it:

git clone https://github.com/javdet/nib.git
cd nib
make setup

make setup is an interactive script. It asks for the LLM provider, the model and the key (I use OpenRouter), then the name of your first project and, optionally, its environments, clouds and regions. You can skip those fields, but nib plans better with them, and you can add more projects later. Then the script generates tokens, writes .env and the config, and starts four containers: Postgres, the knowledge base server, the backend and the frontend.

At the end it prints the UI address (http://localhost:8080 by default; if the port is busy, it picks a free one) and an API token. You paste this token on the login screen. It's also saved in .env as NIB_API_TOKEN, so it's hard to lose.

Knowledge base: what to fill in for a new project

The first place to open after you log in is Knowledgebase. This is the "context" from step 1: everything the engineer knows about the company and the project, and the agent doesn't.

The Company Information card has the basic fields: company name and description, version control system and git base URL, git user, CI/CD system, issue tracker, wiki and team messenger. For our task the key ones are GitHub as the VCS and GitHub Actions as CI/CD, because they decide which workflows the agent will write.


You don't need to upload documents for a new project yet: there's nothing to describe. On a live project, this is where you put what usually sits in the wiki and in people's heads: the network diagram, naming conventions, where state lives, what's special about each environment. You can upload a Markdown document or ask the agent to generate one from a list of repositories.

When a plan finishes, nib writes a report and updates the knowledge base from it, so the next task starts with what the agent learned in the previous one.

Connecting GitHub, AWS and search over MCP

On its own, the agent can only think. To create a repository, look at AWS resources or find documentation, it needs tools. In nib they connect over MCP (Model Context Protocol). It's an open protocol: an LLM application gets a list of tools from an external server and calls them. One MCP server covers one system: GitHub, AWS, search.

If you don't know where to start, ask nib itself, for example: "How do I connect you to AWS over MCP?" Its answer is in the video.
This task needs three servers:

  • GitHub: the repository, PRs and workflows;
  • AWS: reading and creating resources in the account;
  • SearXNG: web search, so the agent can check current documentation instead of relying only on what the model already knows.

nib supports only the HTTP transport for MCP (streamable HTTP), so we run all three servers as containers on the same network as nib. Add them to docker-compose.yml.

GitHub MCP is the official server from GitHub:

github-mcp:
  image: ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  command:
    - http
    - --port=9082
  networks:
    - nib
aws-mcp:
  image: public.ecr.aws/awslabs-mcp/awslabs/aws-api-mcp-server:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  environment:
    AWS_API_MCP_TRANSPORT: "streamable-http"
    AWS_API_MCP_HOST: "0.0.0.0"
    AWS_API_MCP_PORT: "9081"
    AUTH_TYPE: "no-auth"
    AWS_REGION: "${AWS_REGION:-us-east-2}"
    AWS_API_MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS: "aws-mcp,localhost,127.0.0.1"
    AWS_API_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS: "aws-mcp,localhost,127.0.0.1"
    READ_OPERATIONS_ONLY: "false"
    REQUIRE_MUTATION_CONSENT: "false"
    AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: "${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}"
    AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: "${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}"
    AWS_SESSION_TOKEN: "${AWS_SESSION_TOKEN:-}"
  networks:
    - nib
searxng:
  image: docker.io/searxng/searxng:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  environment:
    SEARXNG_PORT: "9083"
    SEARXNG_BASE_URL: "http://searxng:9083/"
    SEARXNG_SECRET: "${SEARXNG_SECRET}"
  volumes:
    - ./searxng:/etc/searxng:rw
  networks:
    - nib

searxng-mcp:
  image: docker.io/isokoliuk/mcp-searxng:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  environment:
    SEARXNG_URL: "http://searxng:9083"
    SEARXNG_DEFAULT_RESPONSE_FORMAT: "json"
    SEARXNG_MAX_RESULT_CHARS: "500"
    SEARXNG_TIMEOUT_MS: "15000"
    MCP_HTTP_PORT: "9084"
    MCP_HTTP_HOST: "0.0.0.0"
    MCP_HTTP_STATELESS: "true"
  networks:
    - nib

The response format is an easy place to trip up. The MCP wrapper asks SearXNG for results in JSON, but by default SearXNG returns only HTML. The json format has to be enabled in searxng/settings.yml. The nib repository already ships this file with the right setting, which is why the volume is mounted from ./searxng.

Registering the servers in nib

Now nib needs to know where to find these servers. You edit the MCP config in Tools → Config (or through Tools → MCP Servers → Add):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "knowledge-base": {
      "url": "http://kb-mcp:8081/mcp"
    },
    "aws": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://aws-mcp:9081/mcp"
    },
    "searxng": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://searxng-mcp:9084/mcp"
    },
    "github": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://github-mcp:9082/",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}",
        "X-MCP-Toolsets": "all",
        "X-MCP-Readonly": "false"
      }
    }
  }
}


knowledge-base is the built-in knowledge base server, and it's already in the config after installation. We add the other three.

Note the ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in the header. Tokens never go into the config as plain text: nib fills them in from Variables → Secrets at request time. Each secret has a list of allowed hosts, so the GitHub token goes only to github-mcp and nowhere else.

So secrets live in two places, and it's easy to mix them up:

  • AWS keys are needed by the aws-mcp container itself, so they're in .env and reach the container as environment variables;
  • the GitHub token travels in the HTTP header of the request from nib to the MCP server, so it's in nib's secrets.
Checking the connection

After restarting the containers, open Tools → MCP Servers. For each server you can see the list of tools it exposes. If the list is empty or the server shows an error, the problem is in the network, the address or the token, and there's no point going further: an agent without tools plans blind.

In the video, the very first check fails: GitHub MCP returns an error. The container is up and the address is right, but the GITHUB_TOKEN secret doesn't exist yet, and without it the server returns nothing. We create the secret in Variables → Secrets, check again, and the tool list appears.

You create the token in your GitHub user settings, under Developer settings (github.com/settings/tokens). I used a classic token with the repo and workflow scopes. The second one is easy to miss: without it GitHub rejects pushes to .github/workflows/, and the agent can't commit its workflows.
In my case GitHub exposed a couple of dozen tools, SearXNG five, and AWS only two. That's expected. AWS API MCP Server gives the agent a generic AWS CLI call plus a helper that picks the right command, so all of AWS fits into two tools. GitHub is the opposite, with one tool per operation, and the next section deals with that.

Tool categories and a base set per mode

Three MCP servers give the agent a lot of tools. If you send all of them with every call, the model gets confused, the context grows, and you pay tokens for descriptions of tools this task will never use. Planning cloud resources doesn't need tools for logs and metrics. nib has two mechanisms for this.

Tool categories. Tools are grouped into categories (for example, everything about AWS, everything about git). During decomposition the agent decides which categories the task touches and gets access only to those. Each action in the plan gets an even narrower set: only the categories marked on that action. You don't have to sort the tools by hand. The Auto-fill with AI button on the Tool categories card does a first pass that you can then fix.

A base set for each mode. You can think of nib's modes as subagents: some break the task down, some work out the stages, some run actions. By default every mode gets every tool. In Tools → Included tools you can narrow this: modes that should only read and plan don't need tools that change things. The Distribute with AI button can only remove tools, so the read-only modes lose the tools that change things, and nothing extra gets added.

The first plan

Everything is ready, so we can plan. As a reminder, we're deploying demo-app, an online store for art supplies with a Python backend, a React frontend and a PostgreSQL database. Click New plan and paste the task from Part 1 as is.

From here, nib repeats what the engineer did in Part 1.

Collecting context. First the decompose agent asks clarifying questions, and for most of them it suggests answers you can pick with a click. It asked me two questions an engineer would ask whoever filed the ticket in the first five minutes:

  • How should the service be published? Is there a custom domain, or is the address that CloudFront generates enough? The answer decides whether DNS records and a TLS certificate show up in the plan.
  • How should the jobs run? Automatically on merge to the main branch, or manually? Really, this is a question about whether the infrastructure can change without a human.

I don't have a domain, so the site lives on the CloudFront address, and the jobs run automatically.


Stages and dependencies. After the answers, the agent shows a Summary (how it understood the task) and a DAG of the stages and the dependencies between them. A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is a "what comes after what" diagram with no loops. Here you see for the first time what was implicit in the engineer's head: which stages can run in parallel and which ones block the rest. If you have no questions about the stages, move on to detailed planning.


Actions, checks, rollback. The Process plan here button starts planning. A separate agent works on each stage, in parallel with the others, and at the end the rollback plan is built. The whole thing took about two minutes. The result was four stages and a rollback plan:


Look at the last row: there are one and a half times more checks than actions. When the plan lives in your head, this is the part that shrinks first under a deadline.

Steps come in four types: run a CLI command, make an API request, work with code, or change something in a web UI. Each step has a detailed description of what to do, and if an action can cause downtime for a system that's already running, the plan warns about it separately.


This answers the third problem from Part 1. nib doesn't estimate in hours, but you see the amount of work before you start: four stages, ten steps, fifteen checks, and it's clear where you need code and where an API call is enough. You can take that to whoever asked "how long will it take," and the conversation will be more concrete than "a day or two."

Preparing access: the agent works over MCP

Each step has a run button, each stage has Execute all, and you can also start a step from the chat by asking the agent. A checkbox next to a step marks it as done, and you can leave a comment on any step. Only one action runs at a time. This is a deliberate limit, so that two agents don't change the same infrastructure in parallel.

The first stage is all API and CLI calls, so the agent ran it on its own, over MCP:

  1. Reconcile the GitHub Actions OIDC provider in AWS account: the OIDC provider that GitHub Actions will use to get access to AWS;
  2. Reconcile the remote Terraform state bucket for the prod stack: an S3 bucket for the Terraform state;
  3. Reconcile the infrastructure deployment role used by Terraform: the role Terraform uses to create resources;
  4. Reconcile the application deployment role for publishing and rolling out: a separate role for shipping the application;
  5. Create or reconcile the protected GitHub production environment: a protected production environment in the repository.

If you know Kubernetes, you know the word reconcile: bring the system to the desired state. If the resource doesn't exist, create it. If it exists but is configured differently, fix it. If it's already right, do nothing. A step like this is safe to run again, which helps if the plan stops halfway. The two separate roles are deliberate too: the role that ships the application has no reason to be able to create networks and databases.

After each step, the agent reports in the chat what it did. To make the demo clearer, I ran the stage checks myself: I opened the AWS console and made sure the OIDC provider was created, the bucket was there, and the environment had appeared in the repository. The agent can run the checks too; you just have to ask. Remember the OIDC provider check. We'll need it later.

Code: Terraform and workflows

In the second stage, API calls are no longer enough: we need to write Terraform and workflows. For steps like these, nib has an executor that runs a coding agent in a separate container. The agent clones the repository, makes the changes, commits, pushes and opens a pull request.

The first time you run a code step, nib sends you to the executor settings page (Tools → Executor). The executor has three options: off (the default), Local, which means containers on your machine through Docker, and Remote, which runs as Kubernetes Jobs. Local is enough to start: the agent runs right on your computer, and you can see the container logs in the UI.

Pick the agent type and the authentication method. The tokens we need aren't in the secrets list yet, so we create them:

  • CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN: the Claude Code subscription token, which you get from claude setup-token. You can use an Anthropic API key instead;
  • a GitHub token, so the agent can push its changes. It's the same one as for MCP.

You can keep the default agent image and model. Go back to the plan and run the step.

What the agent wrote

The PR has 20 files: two workflows, Terraform code in infra/terraform and an updated README. In short, here's the architecture:

  • CloudFront in front of everything: the frontend's static files come from a private S3 bucket, and /api/* requests go to an ALB;
  • the ALB accepts traffic only from the CloudFront managed prefix list, so you can't reach it directly from the internet;
  • the backend runs on ECS Fargate in private subnets and accepts traffic only from the ALB;
  • RDS PostgreSQL 16 sits in isolated subnets with no route to the internet. It's Multi-AZ, encrypted, with backups and deletion protection. Terraform generates the password and puts it straight into Secrets Manager;
  • GitHub Actions reach AWS over OIDC: the job assumes an IAM role and gets temporary credentials, so not a single long-lived AWS key is stored in GitHub. This is where the provider and the roles from the first stage come in.

And two workflows:

  • Deploy Infrastructure runs terraform plan and terraform apply. Apply runs only manually, with an explicit flag, in the production GitHub environment, where you can require approval. That's how the agent used my answer about running jobs;
  • Deploy Application builds the backend image, pushes it to ECR tagged with the commit, updates the ECS service, builds the frontend, uploads it to S3, invalidates the CloudFront cache and finally runs a smoke test against the CloudFront address.

Two decisions in this code are good examples of the "experience" from Part 1 that usually isn't written down anywhere.

The ECS service is created with desired_count = 0. When terraform apply runs, ECR doesn't have a single application image yet. If you ask for two tasks right away, ECS will keep trying to start an image that doesn't exist. So Terraform creates the service empty and ignores later changes to the image and the task count, and the deploy workflow publishes the first real image and scales the service to two. Without this detail, Terraform would undo the deploy on every run.

The cost is stated openly. A Multi-AZ database and a NAT gateway in every availability zone are a production setup, and they cost money even with no traffic. The agent put this in the README, next to the order in which to run the workflows. For a demo it's overkill, for production it's right, and it's a decision you should make on purpose instead of learning about it from the bill.

The changes look reasonable, so we merge the PR into the main branch.

First run, first failure

We run Deploy Infrastructure, and the first attempt fails.


This happens to experienced engineers too, so it's no big deal. Instead of reading the log myself, I show nib the error and ask it to figure it out. It finds the cause: the OIDC provider created in the first stage doesn't list all the thumbprints.

A thumbprint is a fingerprint of the identity provider's TLS certificate. AWS uses the list of thumbprints to verify that the token really came from GitHub. If the right thumbprint isn't on the list, AWS doesn't trust the token, and the job can't assume the role and get into the account.


We add the missing thumbprints and rerun the workflow. On the second try the infrastructure is created: the log shows the terraform plan and how many resources were created. We check that the database is ready and the load balancer is in place, and mark the steps as done.

Deploying the app: a second failure, then the site

We run Deploy Application, and it also fails the first time: the healthcheck doesn't pass. The deploy finished too quickly, and the app wasn't ready by the time of the check. This is expected, and the next step of the plan says exactly that: rerun the deploy. So we do.


On the second run the deploy passes and the smoke test is green. We open the CloudFront address and see the art-supply store, the service we set out to deploy.


We mark the remaining steps and click Finish. nib closes the plan, writes a report on the work done and updates the knowledge base. Next time a task about this project comes in, the agent will already know that it has a VPC, an ECS cluster and a database, and won't start from zero.

Wrapping up

We took an ordinary task: deploy a web service to AWS and set up GitHub jobs to deploy it. In two minutes nib split it into four stages with ten steps, fifteen checks and a rollback plan. The agent prepared AWS and GitHub access on its own over MCP, the executor wrote the Terraform and the workflows, and we worked through two failures on the way, the OIDC provider and the healthcheck, together with nib. At the end we opened the site and saw the store working.

Back to the three problems from Part 1:

  • Items don't get lost. The action list is written down in the plan. You can see it, hand it to a colleague and pick up where you left off.
  • Checks don't get skipped. They're written into every stage in advance, and the agent isn't tempted to save time on them. Still, the OIDC story showed that a check is only as useful as it is precise.
  • The size is visible before you start. You know how many stages and steps are ahead before the first command runs.

The decisions stay with you: you choose which steps to run, you read the PR, and you accept the result.

Even if you don't plan to use agents, try writing the plan for your next task in three columns: action, check, rollback. That alone solves the first problem and makes the second one much easier.

In Part 1 I said that an engineer relies on team rules and their own experience. You can give nib the same things. In the next post I'll show how to connect your own rules, skills and knowledge base, so the plans come out more accurate and closer to how your team works.

The repository is here: github.com/javdet/nib. Try it on a task of your own, and tell me in the comments: which infrastructure task would you trust to an agent first, and which one never?

items.title: Free AI blocks for any static site: copy, paste, it works (no backend)
items.summary: I run a few static sites (GitHub Pages, a couple of single HTML files) and every time I wanted an AI feature on one of them, the answer was "add a backend". So I made twelve blocks that don't need one. Static AI Block is a gallery of copy-paste blocks: ask this page, summarize, translate, FAQ bot, draft a reply, rewrite, extract to JSON, smart search, alt text for images, a quiz from the page, and an Explain button for code. Each block is plain HTML and vanilla JavaScript, 40–60 lines, no framework, no build step. Live gallery (every block runs right there): https://aiblock.onetagai.com/?ref=devto Repo (MIT): https://github.com/fengyiqicoder/static-ai-block How it works: the block loads one script tag from OneTag AI and calls onetag.ask(prompt, input) from the browser. input can be a string, any element on the page, a form, an image or a plain object; the answer streams back, or comes back as JSON with json: true . The key is public by design, like an analytics ID; it can only spend that account's free allowance (1,000,000 tokens). You get one by posting your email: curl -X POST https://onetagai.com/api/signup -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"email":"you@example.com"}' Two things I tried to get right: Each block says what it does in one line and has an example you can click. No reading required. "Copy to AI" copies the block together with the setup steps, so you can paste it into Cursor or Claude Code and let the agent sign you up and wire it in. What I'd like to hear: which block you'd actually put on a page, and which one is missing. The list is MIT, so PRs with new blocks are welcome; a block is one HTML file with a comment on the first line.
items.summary_html:
I run a few static sites (GitHub Pages, a couple of single HTML files) and every time I wanted an AI feature on one of them, the answer was "add a backend". So I made twelve blocks that don't need one.

Static AI Block is a gallery of copy-paste blocks: ask this page, summarize, translate, FAQ bot, draft a reply, rewrite, extract to JSON, smart search, alt text for images, a quiz from the page, and an Explain button for code. Each block is plain HTML and vanilla JavaScript, 40–60 lines, no framework, no build step.

Live gallery (every block runs right there): https://aiblock.onetagai.com/?ref=devto
Repo (MIT): https://github.com/fengyiqicoder/static-ai-block

How it works: the block loads one script tag from OneTag AI and calls onetag.ask(prompt, input) from the browser. input can be a string, any element on the page, a form, an image or a plain object; the answer streams back, or comes back as JSON with json: true. The key is public by design, like an analytics ID; it can only spend that account's free allowance (1,000,000 tokens). You get one by posting your email:

curl -X POST https://onetagai.com/api/signup -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"email":"you@example.com"}'

Two things I tried to get right:

  1. Each block says what it does in one line and has an example you can click. No reading required.
  2. "Copy to AI" copies the block together with the setup steps, so you can paste it into Cursor or Claude Code and let the agent sign you up and wire it in.

What I'd like to hear: which block you'd actually put on a page, and which one is missing. The list is MIT, so PRs with new blocks are welcome; a block is one HTML file with a comment on the first line.

items.title: Your Agent Is Only as Good as Your Codebase
items.summary: Picture an agent fixing a bug in one place. The same logic lives in two other files. It doesn't know, so it doesn't touch them, and the bug stays alive in two out of three code paths. That's not the agent being dumb. It read the file I pointed at, found the logic, fixed it, and ran the tests. The tests passed because nothing tested the other two copies. The codebase lied to it, and it believed the codebase. That's the whole argument of this post. Agents copy what they find. Give them a clean repo and they write clean code. Give them a tangled one and they write more tangle, faster than you ever could. Why structure changes what an agent writes A human who has lived in a repo for a year carries a map in their head. They know the tax logic is copied in checkout/ and invoices/ . They know you have to call init() before load() . An agent starts every session without that map. It only has what it can read. So every hidden link in your code turns into a trap: Duplicated logic means the agent fixes one copy and ships. A call order callers just have to know means it calls them in the wrong order, and nothing tells it. An if for one special value looks like a pattern, so the agent adds a second one next to it for the next special value. A module with no tests means the agent can change its behaviour and stay green. It costs more, too. Not in money, in context. When one change has to land in five files, the agent has to find all five, read them, and keep them in its head at once. When the change lands in one place, it reads one file. Less to read means less to get wrong, and more room left in the context window for the actual task. Fixing the codebase is the cheapest way to make an agent better. Better prompts won't fix a repo that hides its own rules. What dev-refactor does RayStack 1.3.0 ships a new skill called dev-refactor . You run it with /raystack project refactor , or the new short alias /rs refactor . It refactors a whole repo, or one area of it, without changing what the code does. The order never changes. 1. It asks two things. Scope first: the whole repo or one folder (it offers the folders it found). Then two optional extras: strip comments that only restate the code, and remove tests that can't catch a bug. 2. It names the architecture you already have. MVC, layered, hexagonal, feature folders, framework default. It writes down the pattern and the evidence, then refactors inside it. If the pattern itself is the problem, it says so and points you to dev-migrate . Switching architecture is a different job, and it won't sneak one in. 3. Safety net before any change. It finds the test runner, runs the whole suite, and records the result as a baseline. A red baseline stops the run and asks you what to do. Then, for every module it plans to touch that has no tests, it writes characterisation tests that pin today's behaviour, odd cases and errors included. Those go in their own commit, before a single line of refactor. 4. It lists every problem, and changes nothing yet. The list goes to docs/refactor/YYYY-MM-DD-log.md , one line per problem with file:line . It looks for hidden links, needless links (callers poking at internals, shallow wrappers), surplus code, and special cases. DRY counts only when the copies change for the same reason. Two lookalikes that change for different reasons stay apart. SOLID counts as far as it pays: no interface with one implementation, no extension point nobody uses. 5. Redesign. It works out the fixes as if today's requirements had been known from day one, and writes each fix above the problems it solves. One good fix usually kills three or four lines of the list. 6. Small commits. One fix group per commit, suite green after each. A red run gets fixed or reverted before the next step. It never weakens a test, raises a timeout, or adds a suppression to get green. 7. A fresh reviewer. A new read-only subagent gets the log, the diff and the problem lenses, and hunts for what's left. Real findings get fixed, then another fresh reviewer goes again. It stops when the reviewer finds nothing worth fixing. 8. Ship. PR, self-review, green CI, merge. The log records the PR and the before and after counts. The change-together idea in step 4 (copies only count as duplication when they change for the same reason) comes from caldoai's untangle-codebase skill, which is MIT licensed. It's the rule that stops DRY from turning into a pile of shared helpers nobody can change safely. A small trial, with real numbers I built a tiny Node repo with a mess planted in it on purpose. Three modules, one test, the usual sins. Then I ran /rs refactor on it. Measure Before After Special cases (an if on one value) 10 1 Duplicated blocks 3 0 Modules without tests 2 of 3 0 of 4 Tests 1 28 Old and new code gave identical output on 132,022 generated inputs. The interesting part was the first reviewer. It caught a behaviour change that all 28 new tests missed. The old code compared a rule's country with a plain equality check. The refactor normalised it into a list lookup, roughly like this: // before if ( rule . country === order . country ) { /* ... */ } // after (first pass) if ([ rule . country ]. flat (). includes ( order . country )) { /* ... */ } Looks the same. It isn't. A rule with country: ['US'] was rejected by the old code and matched by the new one. No test fed it an array, so the suite stayed green. The reviewer read the diff with fresh eyes and flagged it. The fix went in, a second fresh reviewer found nothing, and the run ended. That's why step 7 exists. Tests you write while refactoring share the blind spots of the person (or agent) doing the refactor. A reviewer that didn't write any of it doesn't. It also kept one special case on purpose: a single if for the HALF coupon. That's a real business rule, not a missed abstraction. Building a coupon strategy system around one coupon would be the exact surplus step 4 is meant to catch. Now the honest part. This was a small fixture I wrote myself, with problems I planted. It shows the steps work in order and that the reviewer catches real things. It doesn't prove anything about your 400,000-line monolith. Run it on one folder first and read the log before you trust it with the whole repo. Try it Install RayStack for every coding agent on your machine with one line: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HarunRRayhan/RayStack/main/get.sh | bash Then open your agent in the repo and run: /raystack project refactor Or /rs refactor if you're as lazy as I am. Other install options (one agent, one project, plugins) are in the README . Hope you enjoyed this one. If you run it on a real codebase, I'd like to see what the log found. items.summary_html:
Picture an agent fixing a bug in one place. The same logic lives in two other files. It doesn't know, so it doesn't touch them, and the bug stays alive in two out of three code paths.

That's not the agent being dumb. It read the file I pointed at, found the logic, fixed it, and ran the tests. The tests passed because nothing tested the other two copies. The codebase lied to it, and it believed the codebase.

That's the whole argument of this post. Agents copy what they find. Give them a clean repo and they write clean code. Give them a tangled one and they write more tangle, faster than you ever could.

Why structure changes what an agent writes

A human who has lived in a repo for a year carries a map in their head. They know the tax logic is copied in checkout/ and invoices/. They know you have to call init() before load(). An agent starts every session without that map. It only has what it can read.

So every hidden link in your code turns into a trap:

  • Duplicated logic means the agent fixes one copy and ships.
  • A call order callers just have to know means it calls them in the wrong order, and nothing tells it.
  • An if for one special value looks like a pattern, so the agent adds a second one next to it for the next special value.
  • A module with no tests means the agent can change its behaviour and stay green.

It costs more, too. Not in money, in context. When one change has to land in five files, the agent has to find all five, read them, and keep them in its head at once. When the change lands in one place, it reads one file. Less to read means less to get wrong, and more room left in the context window for the actual task.

Fixing the codebase is the cheapest way to make an agent better. Better prompts won't fix a repo that hides its own rules.

What dev-refactor does

RayStack 1.3.0 ships a new skill called dev-refactor. You run it with /raystack project refactor, or the new short alias /rs refactor. It refactors a whole repo, or one area of it, without changing what the code does. The order never changes.

1. It asks two things. Scope first: the whole repo or one folder (it offers the folders it found). Then two optional extras: strip comments that only restate the code, and remove tests that can't catch a bug.

2. It names the architecture you already have. MVC, layered, hexagonal, feature folders, framework default. It writes down the pattern and the evidence, then refactors inside it. If the pattern itself is the problem, it says so and points you to dev-migrate. Switching architecture is a different job, and it won't sneak one in.

3. Safety net before any change. It finds the test runner, runs the whole suite, and records the result as a baseline. A red baseline stops the run and asks you what to do. Then, for every module it plans to touch that has no tests, it writes characterisation tests that pin today's behaviour, odd cases and errors included. Those go in their own commit, before a single line of refactor.

4. It lists every problem, and changes nothing yet. The list goes to docs/refactor/YYYY-MM-DD-log.md, one line per problem with file:line. It looks for hidden links, needless links (callers poking at internals, shallow wrappers), surplus code, and special cases. DRY counts only when the copies change for the same reason. Two lookalikes that change for different reasons stay apart. SOLID counts as far as it pays: no interface with one implementation, no extension point nobody uses.

5. Redesign. It works out the fixes as if today's requirements had been known from day one, and writes each fix above the problems it solves. One good fix usually kills three or four lines of the list.

6. Small commits. One fix group per commit, suite green after each. A red run gets fixed or reverted before the next step. It never weakens a test, raises a timeout, or adds a suppression to get green.

7. A fresh reviewer. A new read-only subagent gets the log, the diff and the problem lenses, and hunts for what's left. Real findings get fixed, then another fresh reviewer goes again. It stops when the reviewer finds nothing worth fixing.

8. Ship. PR, self-review, green CI, merge. The log records the PR and the before and after counts.

The change-together idea in step 4 (copies only count as duplication when they change for the same reason) comes from caldoai's untangle-codebase skill, which is MIT licensed. It's the rule that stops DRY from turning into a pile of shared helpers nobody can change safely.

A small trial, with real numbers

I built a tiny Node repo with a mess planted in it on purpose. Three modules, one test, the usual sins. Then I ran /rs refactor on it.

Measure Before After Special cases (an if on one value) 10 1 Duplicated blocks 3 0 Modules without tests 2 of 3 0 of 4 Tests 1 28

Old and new code gave identical output on 132,022 generated inputs.

The interesting part was the first reviewer. It caught a behaviour change that all 28 new tests missed. The old code compared a rule's country with a plain equality check. The refactor normalised it into a list lookup, roughly like this:

// before
if (rule.country === order.country) { /* ... */ }

// after (first pass)
if ([rule.country].flat().includes(order.country)) { /* ... */ }

Looks the same. It isn't. A rule with country: ['US'] was rejected by the old code and matched by the new one. No test fed it an array, so the suite stayed green. The reviewer read the diff with fresh eyes and flagged it. The fix went in, a second fresh reviewer found nothing, and the run ended.

That's why step 7 exists. Tests you write while refactoring share the blind spots of the person (or agent) doing the refactor. A reviewer that didn't write any of it doesn't.

It also kept one special case on purpose: a single if for the HALF coupon. That's a real business rule, not a missed abstraction. Building a coupon strategy system around one coupon would be the exact surplus step 4 is meant to catch.

Now the honest part. This was a small fixture I wrote myself, with problems I planted. It shows the steps work in order and that the reviewer catches real things. It doesn't prove anything about your 400,000-line monolith. Run it on one folder first and read the log before you trust it with the whole repo.

Try it

Install RayStack for every coding agent on your machine with one line:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HarunRRayhan/RayStack/main/get.sh | bash

Then open your agent in the repo and run:

/raystack project refactor

Or /rs refactor if you're as lazy as I am. Other install options (one agent, one project, plugins) are in the README.

Hope you enjoyed this one. If you run it on a real codebase, I'd like to see what the log found.

items.title: LLM-as-a-judge: building an AI grader you can actually trust
items.summary_html:
Short answer: An LLM judge works when you've calibrated it against human labels. Without calibration it's noise dressed up as a metric. The rubric is the actual work — the judge model just executes it.

Teams reach for LLM-as-judge because there's no other way to automatically score whether a support reply was "empathetic" or whether a generated SQL query "answers the user's intent." There's no diff to run. The judge fills the gap between "does it parse" (easy to check mechanically) and "is it actually good" (hard to check without a human).

The failure mode is treating it as plug-and-play: pick a model, write a prompt like "rate this output from 1–10," drop it in CI, declare victory. That judge gives you a consistent number that correlates poorly with what users actually think. You've built a metric that feels like signal and isn't.

Here's how to build one that isn't that.

Why do LLM judges fail without calibration?

Three problems, all fixable.

Position bias. In pairwise comparisons, judges prefer whichever answer appears first — consistently enough to flip verdicts up to 30% of the time. A test that scores "response A vs response B" will sometimes return a different result just from swapping the order.

Verbosity preference. Most LLMs, when asked to judge quality without a tight rubric, prefer longer outputs. A wrong-but-detailed answer beats a correct-but-brief one. Your eval suite ends up rewarding word count. Users don't.

Same-model blindness. Claude evaluating Claude's outputs is lenient on its own artifacts. It misses the specific failure modes it produces. If your app uses a model and you judge with the same model, you get a blind spot for exactly the class of errors you need to catch.

What makes a rubric tight enough to trust?

The rubric is not the prompt template. It's the list of concrete criteria the judge checks against. Write it as conditions, not adjectives.

Bad rubric:

Score 1–10 for quality. Consider clarity, accuracy, and helpfulness.

Good rubric:

A good response:
- Directly answers the question asked (not a related question)
- Does not introduce information not present in the provided context
- Uses plain language; no jargon unless the user used it first
- Is under 200 words

Score 0.0 immediately if any of:
- Response says "I don't know" when the context contains the answer
- Response asks a clarifying question instead of answering
- Response repeats the system prompt

Otherwise score 0.0–1.0 against the criteria above.

The hard-failure conditions matter most. They cover cases where you know it's wrong — no rubric ambiguity. Put them first. They short-circuit scoring before interpretation enters.

Here's a complete judge implementation:

import anthropic

RUBRIC = """\
A good response to a customer support question:
- Directly addresses the specific question asked
- Does not introduce facts not present in the provided knowledge base context
- Is under 200 words
- Uses plain language; no jargon unless the user introduced it
- Ends with a concrete next step or resolution

Score 0.0 immediately if any of the following:
- Says "I cannot help with that" when context contains the answer
- Asks a clarifying question instead of answering
- Contradicts information in the context
- Contains a system prompt fragment

Otherwise score 0.0–1.0 based on the criteria above.
Return only a decimal number (e.g., 0.85). No explanation."""

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def judge_response(user_question: str, kb_context: str, response: str) -> float:
    prompt = f"""User question: {user_question}

Knowledge base context:
{kb_context}

Response to evaluate:
{response}

Rubric:
{RUBRIC}"""

    result = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
        max_tokens=10,
        temperature=0,                 # deterministic — same input, same score
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    try:
        return float(result.content[0].text.strip())
    except ValueError:
        return 0.0                     # unparseable output = treat as failure

Two things to notice: temperature=0 for determinism, and the parsing fallback returns 0.0 instead of crashing. A judge that sometimes returns "0.85 (good answer)" instead of "0.85" should fail safe, not silently inflate your scores.

How do you calibrate before shipping to CI?

You need 20–30 examples labeled by a human against your rubric. Not labeled "correct" — labeled against each criterion: does this response satisfy the condition or not?

# calibration.jsonl — one entry per labeled example
# {"question": "...", "context": "...", "response": "...", "human_score": 0.9, "notes": ""}
# {"question": "...", "context": "...", "response": "...", "human_score": 0.1, "notes": "contradicts context in para 2"}

import json

def calibrate_judge(labeled_path: str, threshold: float = 0.2) -> dict:
    with open(labeled_path) as f:
        examples = [json.loads(line) for line in f if line.strip()]

    disagreements = []
    for ex in examples:
        judge_score = judge_response(ex["question"], ex["context"], ex["response"])
        delta = abs(judge_score - ex["human_score"])
        if delta > threshold:
            disagreements.append({
                "question": ex["question"][:80],
                "human": ex["human_score"],
                "judge": judge_score,
                "delta": round(delta, 2),
                "notes": ex.get("notes", ""),
            })

    agreement_rate = 1 - len(disagreements) / len(examples)
    return {
        "agreement_rate": round(agreement_rate, 3),
        "disagreements": disagreements,
        "verdict": "PASS" if agreement_rate >= 0.80 else "RUBRIC NEEDS WORK",
    }

Run this before wiring the judge into CI. If verdict is RUBRIC NEEDS WORK, look at the disagreement list. Almost always, it's not that the judge model is wrong — it's that your rubric doesn't say what you thought it said. Add the failing condition explicitly and re-run.

Eighty percent agreement is the floor, not the goal. Below 80%, the judge is unreliable and your CI metrics will mislead you into thinking quality is stable when it isn't.

How do you handle position bias in pairwise comparisons?

Run each pair twice with the order swapped. If the judge flips its verdict, the difference isn't real — call it a tie.

def pairwise_judge(question: str, response_a: str, response_b: str) -> str:
    """Returns 'A', 'B', or 'TIE'."""

    def score_pair(first: str, second: str) -> str:
        result = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
            max_tokens=5,
            temperature=0,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": (
                f"Question: {question}\n\n"
                f"Response 1: {first}\n\n"
                f"Response 2: {second}\n\n"
                "Which response better satisfies the rubric above? "
                "Reply only: 1, 2, or TIE."
            )}],
        )
        return result.content[0].text.strip()

    verdict_ab = score_pair(response_a, response_b)    # A presented as 1, B as 2
    verdict_ba = score_pair(response_b, response_a)    # B presented as 1, A as 2

    # normalize to A/B labels
    winner_ab = "A" if verdict_ab == "1" else ("B" if verdict_ab == "2" else "TIE")
    winner_ba = "A" if verdict_ba == "2" else ("B" if verdict_ba == "1" else "TIE")

    if winner_ab == winner_ba:
        return winner_ab
    return "TIE"   # order-sensitive result = not a real difference

For single-answer scoring — which is what you want in most CI setups — position bias doesn't apply. There's only one answer, and you score it against the rubric directly.

What does LLM-as-judge not solve?

It doesn't tell you if the rubric is right. If you're measuring the wrong thing — if "under 200 words" is in your rubric but users actually want detailed answers — calibration passes and your eval suite silently optimizes for the wrong outcome. No amount of judge engineering fixes that. Review your labeled examples with someone who understands the product intent before locking the rubric.

It also shouldn't replace mechanical verification. If your LLM writes SQL, run it against a test database. If it writes code, execute it. Use a judge for genuinely subjective dimensions only — the ones where there's no ground truth to diff against. Applying a judge to things you can verify deterministically wastes money and adds noise.

The free test lab has a complete judge harness with calibration script, a 25-example labeled dataset for a support-reply task, and a CI integration that fails the build when judge agreement drops below 80% after a model upgrade. If you're setting this up for the first time, start there rather than from scratch. AI Software Testing in Practice covers the full eval lifecycle — growing the labeled dataset across model upgrades, setting regression thresholds that account for judge noise, and knowing when a score drop is a real problem versus rubric drift.

FAQ

How do I know if my LLM judge is reliable?
Run it against 20–30 human-labeled examples and measure agreement. If the judge disagrees with your labels more than 20% of the time, the rubric is wrong — tighten it and re-calibrate. Agreement above 80% on your labeled set is enough to trust the judge in CI.

Should I use the same LLM to generate and judge outputs?
No. Using the same model to evaluate its own outputs creates a blind spot for that model's specific failure modes. Use a different judge model, or judge with a stronger model than the one generating outputs.

What is position bias in LLM-as-judge and how do I avoid it?
Position bias means the judge tends to prefer whichever option it sees first in a pairwise comparison. Avoid it by either using single-answer scoring (not pairwise) or running each comparison twice with the order swapped and averaging the scores.
