items.title: Stamping the downloader's email on every PDF page at download time in PHP
items.summary: When a contract leaks, the first question is: whose copy was it? In Warqa, a contract management platform for companies in Saudi Arabia, every PDF and image gets the downloader's email stamped on it at download time. The original file stays clean in storage. This post shows how we built it with FPDI and TCPDF, and what we learned. The rules we set Never change the stored original. Stamp a temporary copy for each download. The stamp names a person: the email of the logged-in user, or of the external recipient for a shared link. A failed stamp must never block work. If stamping throws, report the error and send the file. Every stamped copy gets its own tracking ID, written into the file and into the activity log. Pick the method by file type $extension = strtolower ( pathinfo ( $file , PATHINFO_EXTENSION )); if ( $extension === 'pdf' ) { try { return $this -> processPdf ( $file , $watermarkText , $title ); } catch ( Exception $e ) { report ( $e ); } } elseif ( in_array ( $extension , [ 'jpg' , 'jpeg' , 'png' ])) { try { return $this -> processImage ( $file , $watermarkText ); } catch ( Exception $e ) { report ( $e ); } } return $file ; // other types go out unchanged PDF and images cover almost all signed contracts and scanned documents. Word files are drafts, and a watermark in an editable file can simply be deleted. PDF: import each page, then draw on top FPDI imports pages of an existing PDF as templates. TCPDF then draws text over them: $pdf = new \setasign\Fpdi\Tcpdf\Fpdi (); $pageCount = $pdf -> setSourceFile ( $file ); for ( $pageNo = 1 ; $pageNo <= $pageCount ; $pageNo ++ ) { $templateId = $pdf -> importPage ( $pageNo ); $size = $pdf -> getTemplateSize ( $templateId ); $pdf -> AddPage ( $size [ 'orientation' ], [ $size [ 'width' ], $size [ 'height' ]]); $pdf -> useTemplate ( $templateId ); $this -> drawWatermark ( $pdf , $size [ 'width' ], $size [ 'height' ], $watermarkText ); } Keep the page size of each source page. Contracts often mix A4 portrait pages with landscape annex tables. The stamp itself is small diagonal text, repeated in a grid across the page. The text is gray at about 10% opacity, so the document stays readable when printed. A single large stamp in the middle is easy to crop out. A grid is not. The PDF that FPDI cannot open The free FPDI parser does not read every compression method in newer PDFs. When it fails, we rewrite the file with Ghostscript to an older PDF version, then try again. If that fails too, rule 3 applies: report the error and send the file unstamped. Images: GD is enough For JPEG and PNG we use PHP's GD extension: load the image, draw the same diagonal text grid, save to a new temp file. There is no need for Imagick for this job. A tracking ID per copy Each stamped copy gets a new ULID. We write it into the PDF metadata keywords as TID: and save it in the activity log next to the email, IP address and user agent. If a copy turns up somewhere, its ID points to one download event, even when the visible stamp was cut off. The download flow File :: put ( $tmpPath , $attachment -> getContent ()); $result = app ( LeakProtectionService :: class ) -> protect ( file : $tmpPath , watermarkText : $share -> recipient_email , title : pathinfo ( $attachment -> name , PATHINFO_FILENAME ), ); File :: delete ( $tmpPath ); $share -> recordDownload (); return response () -> download ( $result -> path ) -> deleteFileAfterSend (); Temp files are deleted after the response is sent. Nothing stamped stays on disk. Where the email comes from on shared links External recipients do not have accounts. A shared link opens only after the recipient enters a one-time code sent to their email. That verified email is the text we stamp. Without the code step, the stamp would only show the email of the person who created the link. What a watermark does not do A watermark does not stop a leak. It deters one and helps trace one. It works together with other controls: access permissions per folder, links that expire, and a log of who viewed or downloaded each file. ملخص بالعربية: يشرح هذا المقال كيف يضيف نظام إدارة العقود والمستندات علامة مائية تحمل البريد الإلكتروني للشخص الذي حمل الملف. وتضاف العلامة إلى ملفات PDF والصور لحظة التحميل، ويبقى الملف الأصلي دون تغيير. كما يتناول المقال رقم تتبع خاصًا بكل نسخة، يساعد على معرفة مصدر أي نسخة متسربة. Written by the engineering team at Renewable Systems in Riyadh, the makers of Warqa.
items.summary_html:
When a contract leaks, the first question is: whose copy was it? In Warqa, a contract management platform for companies in Saudi Arabia, every PDF and image gets the downloader's email stamped on it at download time. The original file stays clean in storage. This post shows how we built it with FPDI and TCPDF, and what we learned.

The rules we set
  1. Never change the stored original. Stamp a temporary copy for each download.
  2. The stamp names a person: the email of the logged-in user, or of the external recipient for a shared link.
  3. A failed stamp must never block work. If stamping throws, report the error and send the file.
  4. Every stamped copy gets its own tracking ID, written into the file and into the activity log.
Pick the method by file type 
$extension = strtolower(pathinfo($file, PATHINFO_EXTENSION));

if ($extension === 'pdf') {
    try { return $this->processPdf($file, $watermarkText, $title); }
    catch (Exception $e) { report($e); }
} elseif (in_array($extension, ['jpg', 'jpeg', 'png'])) {
    try { return $this->processImage($file, $watermarkText); }
    catch (Exception $e) { report($e); }
}

return $file; // other types go out unchanged

PDF and images cover almost all signed contracts and scanned documents. Word files are drafts, and a watermark in an editable file can simply be deleted.

PDF: import each page, then draw on top

FPDI imports pages of an existing PDF as templates. TCPDF then draws text over them:

$pdf = new \setasign\Fpdi\Tcpdf\Fpdi();
$pageCount = $pdf->setSourceFile($file);

for ($pageNo = 1; $pageNo <= $pageCount; $pageNo++) {
    $templateId = $pdf->importPage($pageNo);
    $size = $pdf->getTemplateSize($templateId);

    $pdf->AddPage($size['orientation'], [$size['width'], $size['height']]);
    $pdf->useTemplate($templateId);

    $this->drawWatermark($pdf, $size['width'], $size['height'], $watermarkText);
}

Keep the page size of each source page. Contracts often mix A4 portrait pages with landscape annex tables.

The stamp itself is small diagonal text, repeated in a grid across the page. The text is gray at about 10% opacity, so the document stays readable when printed. A single large stamp in the middle is easy to crop out. A grid is not.

The PDF that FPDI cannot open

The free FPDI parser does not read every compression method in newer PDFs. When it fails, we rewrite the file with Ghostscript to an older PDF version, then try again. If that fails too, rule 3 applies: report the error and send the file unstamped.

Images: GD is enough

For JPEG and PNG we use PHP's GD extension: load the image, draw the same diagonal text grid, save to a new temp file. There is no need for Imagick for this job.

A tracking ID per copy

Each stamped copy gets a new ULID. We write it into the PDF metadata keywords as TID: and save it in the activity log next to the email, IP address and user agent. If a copy turns up somewhere, its ID points to one download event, even when the visible stamp was cut off.

The download flow 
File::put($tmpPath, $attachment->getContent());

$result = app(LeakProtectionService::class)->protect(
    file: $tmpPath,
    watermarkText: $share->recipient_email,
    title: pathinfo($attachment->name, PATHINFO_FILENAME),
);

File::delete($tmpPath);
$share->recordDownload();

return response()->download($result->path)->deleteFileAfterSend();

Temp files are deleted after the response is sent. Nothing stamped stays on disk.

Where the email comes from on shared links

External recipients do not have accounts. A shared link opens only after the recipient enters a one-time code sent to their email. That verified email is the text we stamp. Without the code step, the stamp would only show the email of the person who created the link.

What a watermark does not do

A watermark does not stop a leak. It deters one and helps trace one. It works together with other controls: access permissions per folder, links that expire, and a log of who viewed or downloaded each file.

items.title: .NET: The Framework Formerly Known as Framework
items.summary: In our last installment, we explored some of C#'s more surprising behaviors. But C# is only part of a much bigger story. A story involving multiple programming languages, competing user interface frameworks, a rather complicated relationship with open source, and enough product renaming to keep an entire marketing department employed for decades. Welcome to .NET. Or .NET Framework. Or .NET Core. Or just .NET again. We'll get to that. 1. In the Beginning, There Was Windows When Microsoft launched .NET Framework in 2002, it represented an ambitious new direction for Windows development. At its heart was the Common Language Runtime (CLR), an execution environment providing garbage collection, memory management, exception handling, and other services that developers previously had to manage themselves. Instead of compiling directly to native machine code, supported languages generally compiled into Common Intermediate Language (CIL), which the runtime could then execute using just-in-time compilation. That was a pretty powerful idea. Multiple programming languages could share a runtime, a type system, and an extensive library ecosystem. A developer could write a library in one language and consume it from another. Naturally, Microsoft decided that one programming language wasn't enough. 2. C#, VB.NET, and F#: Three Languages Walk Into a Runtime C# was the obvious flagship. Modern syntax, strong typing, object-oriented programming, and enough familiarity with Java and C++ to make developers feel at home. But Microsoft had another a constituency to consider. Visual Basic developers. VB.NET: It's Visual Basic, Jim, but Not as We Know It Visual Basic had been wildly popular for Windows application development. Its selling point was accessibility. You could drag controls onto a form, write some event handlers, and have a functioning application without spending six months studying Windows internals. For a generation of developers, Visual Basic was how you built business applications, full stop. So Microsoft brought Visual Basic into .NET. Except VB.NET wasn't simply the old Visual Basic with a new runtime. It was substantially redesigned. The old VB6 world included COM-based components, default form instances, and a programming model that was quite different from the CLR's object-oriented architecture. VB.NET introduced a new type system, inheritance, structured exception handling, and the other capabilities required to participate in .NET. That was great for architectural consistency. Less great for developers discovering that their existing VB6 applications weren't going to migrate quite as effortlessly as they'd hoped. Today, Visual Basic still exists in modern .NET. But Microsoft has made its direction clear: VB will remain supported and stable, without aggressively expanding into new workloads or pursuing every new language feature introduced in C#. Which is a polite way of saying: "You are tolerated, former incumbent." F#: Wait, We Also Have a Functional Language? Then there's F#. While C# and VB.NET largely embraced object-oriented programming, F# arrived with a functional-first philosophy. Immutability by default. Pattern matching. Type inference. Functions as first-class citizens. And a syntax that looks refreshingly different from the sea of curly braces elsewhere in the ecosystem. What makes F# particularly interesting is that it isn't a separate runtime universe. It uses .NET too. An F# library can be consumed by C# code. Both can use much of the same underlying framework. That's convenient. You can write enterprise business logic in C#, functional transformations in F#, and maintain an application in VB.NET, all within the same general ecosystem. Although anyone who has actually maintained a multilingual solution will tell you that technically interoperable and pleasant to maintain are not necessarily synonyms. The fascinating part: .NET was designed to make programming languages less important than the runtime and libraries they shared. Twenty-four years later, C# overwhelmingly dominates the ecosystem, VB remains supported, and F# continues to serve developers who appreciate its different approach. One platform. Three officially supported languages. Three rather different philosophies. 3. Windows Forms: Just Drag the Button On Form1 Let's talk about building user interfaces. For many developers in the early .NET era, Windows Forms was one of the platform's most appealing features. Open Visual Studio. Create a form. Drag a button onto it. Double-click the button. Write some code. Keep the default icon. Congratulations. You have a Windows application. WinForms was wonderfully pragmatic. Its programming model was event-driven and closely tied to traditional Windows desktop controls. For business applications, internal tools, and database frontends, it was often exactly what developers needed. Of course, Microsoft eventually decided that Windows application development needed something more sophisticated. Enter WPF. 4. WPF and XAML: What if Buttons Were XML? In 2006, Microsoft introduced Windows Presentation Foundation as part of .NET Framework 3.0. WPF brought an entirely different approach to desktop UI development. Instead of primarily positioning controls in a visual designer and attaching event handlers, developers could describe interfaces declaratively using XAML. Extensible Application Markup Language. Because apparently XML hadn't yet appeared in enough places. To be fair, XAML enabled some powerful ideas. Data binding. Reusable styles and templates. Resolution-independent layouts. Rich graphics and animation. And better separation between the visual interface and application logic. WPF could produce interfaces that were dramatically more sophisticated than traditional WinForms applications. It also introduced concepts such as dependency properties, routed events, and elaborate binding mechanisms. Things that were pretty cool, right up until a binding silently failed and you spent the afternoon trying to understand why a button was disabled. Then came the familiar Microsoft ecosystem question: Which UI technology should you actually use? WinForms was still around. WPF was supposed to be the modern alternative. Someone at Microsoft said: "we're gonna need a bigger boat". SO they came up with Silverlight, UWP, WinUI, and eventually .NET MAUI. And here's an important distinction: XAML isn't itself a competing UI framework. It's a declarative markup language used by multiple frameworks, including WPF, WinUI, and .NET MAUI, with differences between their implementations. (And what about Xamarin? "THERE WAS NEVER A XAMARIN"). Today, WinForms and WPF remain supported on modern .NET. WinUI is Microsoft's primary recommendation for new general-purpose Windows desktop applications. And .NET MAUI targets multiple platforms, including Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS. Yes, a platform famous for introducing alternatives has managed to retain several of them simultaneously. The lesson: Microsoft rarely eliminates an old development technology simply because a newer one exists. Sometimes the future arrives, and the past just moves into the spare bedroom. Except for Xamarin. 5. Plot Twist: .NET Escapes Windows For much of its early history, Microsoft's official .NET Framework was closely associated with Windows. But an important part of this story happened outside Microsoft. The Mono project began developing an open-source, cross-platform implementation of .NET in the early 2000s. It demonstrated that .NET technology could live beyond Windows, including on Linux. This was a mic drop moment. Because the underlying .NET concepts were not inherently Windows-specific, even though many framework APIs and application technologies were. Years later, Microsoft began moving toward a much more open development strategy. It open-sourced major pieces of its developer tooling and runtime ecosystem. Then, in 2016, .NET Core 1.0 arrived. Open source. Cross-platform. Designed with modern server workloads, cloud deployment, and modularity in mind. A Microsoft development platform running naturally on Linux would once have seemed like a fairly elaborate practical joke. Now it was part of the official strategy. But there was a catch. .NET Core wasn't simply a cross-platform copy of everything in .NET Framework. It was a different implementation with different APIs and initially a smaller surface area. Some applications could migrate relatively easily. Others depended on Windows-specific technologies, legacy framework components, or third-party libraries that weren't available. And some simply couldn't be moved without significant rewrites. But the direction was clear. .NET was no longer synonymous with Windows. Or proprietary software. Which brings us to the naming department. 6. The Naming Department Has Entered the Chat Let's recap. We started with .NET Framework. Then Microsoft introduced .NET Core. Meanwhile, we had .NET Standard, which wasn't another runtime at all, but an API specification designed to help libraries work across different .NET implementations. Then, after .NET Core 3.1, Microsoft released... .NET 5. Not .NET Core 4. Not .NET Framework 5. Just .NET 5. Why skip four? Partly to avoid confusion with the existing .NET Framework 4.x product line. So Microsoft solved one naming conflict by skipping a number and dropping a word. There was probably a PowerPoint presentation involved. Since then, modern .NET has continued with annual version releases, reaching .NET 10 in November 2025. Meanwhile, the original .NET Framework continues to exist, with version 4.8.1 supported on Windows. And just to complete the picture, ASP.NET Core retains the word "Core" even though the main runtime dropped it. So today: .NET Framework means the original Windows-only implementation. .NET means the modern open-source, cross-platform implementation. .NET Standard describes a compatibility-oriented API specification, not a runtime. ASP.NET Core is the modern web framework, despite the runtime's naming change. .NET Core is the former name of what evolved into modern .NET. Now let's brace ourselves for .NET Copilot which is almost certainly cooking somewhere in Redmond. 7. And Then There's PowerShell Here's a part of the .NET ecosystem that doesn't always get enough attention. PowerShell. Most people think of it as a command-line shell and scripting language, particularly associated with Windows administration. Not wrong. But PowerShell is also deeply connected to .NET. Unlike traditional Unix shells, which primarily pass text between commands, PowerShell pipelines can pass structured objects. Actual objects, with properties and methods. Those objects are frequently .NET objects. Which means a PowerShell script can access parts of the .NET ecosystem directly. Want to work with filesystem APIs? Use .NET objects. Need regular expressions? They're available. Want to instantiate framework classes or call static methods? You can do that too. PowerShell is, in many ways, a .NET automation environment disguised as a shell. And naturally, it has its own version of the great .NET identity crisis. Windows PowerShell 5.1 runs on the original .NET Framework. Modern PowerShell 7 runs on modern .NET and supports Windows, Linux, and macOS. Both can exist on the same Windows machine. And they can behave differently when scripts depend on incompatible modules or framework APIs. So now we have two PowerShell families corresponding to two .NET families. At this point, the family tree needs a database. But underneath the confusing history lies something genuinely powerful: an administrator can write a script that manipulates rich runtime objects, while developers can expose functionality that PowerShell can consume without inventing an entirely separate scripting interface. It's one of .NET's more underappreciated achievements. 8. So What Exactly Is .NET? After all that, it's worth asking the obvious question. Is .NET a programming language? No. An operating system? Also no. A framework? Yes, but that answer is incomplete. A runtime? Yes, but still incomplete. .NET is better understood as an entire development platform. It includes runtimes, compilers, standard libraries, SDKs, development tools, and application frameworks. It supports different languages and workloads. You can build web APIs, desktop applications, cloud services, mobile applications, games, and command-line tools. The current platform is powerful. And the shift from the original Windows-centric .NET Framework to today's open-source implementation is one of Microsoft's most significant technological transformations. There is also a wonderfully ironic outcome. Microsoft spent years building an ecosystem closely associated with Windows development. Then it invested heavily in making that ecosystem work without Windows. Developers can now build a C# application on Linux, deploy it in a Linux container, run it in the cloud, and never touch a Windows desktop. Which would have sounded strange in 2002. Somehow, all those identities coexist. Not always elegantly. Not always compatibly. And certainly not under a naming scheme that anyone would describe as intuitive. But the result is impressive.
items.summary_html:
In our last installment, we explored some of C#'s more surprising behaviors.

But C# is only part of a much bigger story.

A story involving multiple programming languages, competing user interface frameworks, a rather complicated relationship with open source, and enough product renaming to keep an entire marketing department employed for decades.

Welcome to .NET.

Or .NET Framework.

Or .NET Core.

Or just .NET again.

We'll get to that.

1. In the Beginning, There Was Windows

When Microsoft launched .NET Framework in 2002, it represented an ambitious new direction for Windows development.

At its heart was the Common Language Runtime (CLR), an execution environment providing garbage collection, memory management, exception handling, and other services that developers previously had to manage themselves.

Instead of compiling directly to native machine code, supported languages generally compiled into Common Intermediate Language (CIL), which the runtime could then execute using just-in-time compilation.

That was a pretty powerful idea.

Multiple programming languages could share a runtime, a type system, and an extensive library ecosystem.

A developer could write a library in one language and consume it from another.

Naturally, Microsoft decided that one programming language wasn't enough.

2. C#, VB.NET, and F#: Three Languages Walk Into a Runtime

C# was the obvious flagship.

Modern syntax, strong typing, object-oriented programming, and enough familiarity with Java and C++ to make developers feel at home.

But Microsoft had another a constituency to consider.

Visual Basic developers.

VB.NET: It's Visual Basic, Jim, but Not as We Know It

Visual Basic had been wildly popular for Windows application development.

Its selling point was accessibility. You could drag controls onto a form, write some event handlers, and have a functioning application without spending six months studying Windows internals.

For a generation of developers, Visual Basic was how you built business applications, full stop.

So Microsoft brought Visual Basic into .NET.

Except VB.NET wasn't simply the old Visual Basic with a new runtime.

It was substantially redesigned.

The old VB6 world included COM-based components, default form instances, and a programming model that was quite different from the CLR's object-oriented architecture.

VB.NET introduced a new type system, inheritance, structured exception handling, and the other capabilities required to participate in .NET.

That was great for architectural consistency.

Less great for developers discovering that their existing VB6 applications weren't going to migrate quite as effortlessly as they'd hoped.

Today, Visual Basic still exists in modern .NET.

But Microsoft has made its direction clear: VB will remain supported and stable, without aggressively expanding into new workloads or pursuing every new language feature introduced in C#.

Which is a polite way of saying:

"You are tolerated, former incumbent."

F#: Wait, We Also Have a Functional Language?

Then there's F#.

While C# and VB.NET largely embraced object-oriented programming, F# arrived with a functional-first philosophy.

Immutability by default.

Pattern matching.

Type inference.

Functions as first-class citizens.

And a syntax that looks refreshingly different from the sea of curly braces elsewhere in the ecosystem.

What makes F# particularly interesting is that it isn't a separate runtime universe.

It uses .NET too.

An F# library can be consumed by C# code. Both can use much of the same underlying framework.

That's convenient.

You can write enterprise business logic in C#, functional transformations in F#, and maintain an application in VB.NET, all within the same general ecosystem.

Although anyone who has actually maintained a multilingual solution will tell you that technically interoperable and pleasant to maintain are not necessarily synonyms.

The fascinating part: .NET was designed to make programming languages less important than the runtime and libraries they shared.

Twenty-four years later, C# overwhelmingly dominates the ecosystem, VB remains supported, and F# continues to serve developers who appreciate its different approach.

One platform. Three officially supported languages. Three rather different philosophies.

3. Windows Forms: Just Drag the Button On Form1

Let's talk about building user interfaces.

For many developers in the early .NET era, Windows Forms was one of the platform's most appealing features.

Open Visual Studio.

Create a form.

Drag a button onto it.

Double-click the button.

Write some code.

Keep the default icon.

Congratulations. You have a Windows application.

WinForms was wonderfully pragmatic.

Its programming model was event-driven and closely tied to traditional Windows desktop controls.

For business applications, internal tools, and database frontends, it was often exactly what developers needed.

Of course, Microsoft eventually decided that Windows application development needed something more sophisticated.

Enter WPF.

4. WPF and XAML: What if Buttons Were XML?

In 2006, Microsoft introduced Windows Presentation Foundation as part of .NET Framework 3.0.

WPF brought an entirely different approach to desktop UI development.

Instead of primarily positioning controls in a visual designer and attaching event handlers, developers could describe interfaces declaratively using XAML.

Extensible Application Markup Language.

Because apparently XML hadn't yet appeared in enough places.

To be fair, XAML enabled some powerful ideas.

Data binding.

Reusable styles and templates.

Resolution-independent layouts.

Rich graphics and animation.

And better separation between the visual interface and application logic.

WPF could produce interfaces that were dramatically more sophisticated than traditional WinForms applications.

It also introduced concepts such as dependency properties, routed events, and elaborate binding mechanisms.

Things that were pretty cool, right up until a binding silently failed and you spent the afternoon trying to understand why a button was disabled.

Then came the familiar Microsoft ecosystem question:

Which UI technology should you actually use?

WinForms was still around.

WPF was supposed to be the modern alternative.

Someone at Microsoft said: "we're gonna need a bigger boat".

SO they came up with Silverlight, UWP, WinUI, and eventually .NET MAUI.

And here's an important distinction: XAML isn't itself a competing UI framework. It's a declarative markup language used by multiple frameworks, including WPF, WinUI, and .NET MAUI, with differences between their implementations.

(And what about Xamarin? "THERE WAS NEVER A XAMARIN").

Today, WinForms and WPF remain supported on modern .NET.

WinUI is Microsoft's primary recommendation for new general-purpose Windows desktop applications.

And .NET MAUI targets multiple platforms, including Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS.

Yes, a platform famous for introducing alternatives has managed to retain several of them simultaneously.

The lesson: Microsoft rarely eliminates an old development technology simply because a newer one exists. Sometimes the future arrives, and the past just moves into the spare bedroom. Except for Xamarin.

5. Plot Twist: .NET Escapes Windows

For much of its early history, Microsoft's official .NET Framework was closely associated with Windows.

But an important part of this story happened outside Microsoft.

The Mono project began developing an open-source, cross-platform implementation of .NET in the early 2000s.

It demonstrated that .NET technology could live beyond Windows, including on Linux.

This was a mic drop moment.

Because the underlying .NET concepts were not inherently Windows-specific, even though many framework APIs and application technologies were.

Years later, Microsoft began moving toward a much more open development strategy.

It open-sourced major pieces of its developer tooling and runtime ecosystem.

Then, in 2016, .NET Core 1.0 arrived.

Open source.

Cross-platform.

Designed with modern server workloads, cloud deployment, and modularity in mind.

A Microsoft development platform running naturally on Linux would once have seemed like a fairly elaborate practical joke.

Now it was part of the official strategy.

But there was a catch.

.NET Core wasn't simply a cross-platform copy of everything in .NET Framework.

It was a different implementation with different APIs and initially a smaller surface area.

Some applications could migrate relatively easily.

Others depended on Windows-specific technologies, legacy framework components, or third-party libraries that weren't available.

And some simply couldn't be moved without significant rewrites.

But the direction was clear.

.NET was no longer synonymous with Windows.

Or proprietary software.

Which brings us to the naming department.

6. The Naming Department Has Entered the Chat

Let's recap.

We started with .NET Framework.

Then Microsoft introduced .NET Core.

Meanwhile, we had .NET Standard, which wasn't another runtime at all, but an API specification designed to help libraries work across different .NET implementations.

Then, after .NET Core 3.1, Microsoft released...

.NET 5.

Not .NET Core 4.

Not .NET Framework 5.

Just .NET 5.

Why skip four?

Partly to avoid confusion with the existing .NET Framework 4.x product line.

So Microsoft solved one naming conflict by skipping a number and dropping a word.

There was probably a PowerPoint presentation involved.

Since then, modern .NET has continued with annual version releases, reaching .NET 10 in November 2025.

Meanwhile, the original .NET Framework continues to exist, with version 4.8.1 supported on Windows.

And just to complete the picture, ASP.NET Core retains the word "Core" even though the main runtime dropped it.

So today:

  • .NET Framework means the original Windows-only implementation.
  • .NET means the modern open-source, cross-platform implementation.
  • .NET Standard describes a compatibility-oriented API specification, not a runtime.
  • ASP.NET Core is the modern web framework, despite the runtime's naming change.
  • .NET Core is the former name of what evolved into modern .NET.

Now let's brace ourselves for .NET Copilot which is almost certainly cooking somewhere in Redmond.

7. And Then There's PowerShell

Here's a part of the .NET ecosystem that doesn't always get enough attention.

PowerShell.

Most people think of it as a command-line shell and scripting language, particularly associated with Windows administration.

Not wrong.

But PowerShell is also deeply connected to .NET.

Unlike traditional Unix shells, which primarily pass text between commands, PowerShell pipelines can pass structured objects.

Actual objects, with properties and methods.

Those objects are frequently .NET objects.

Which means a PowerShell script can access parts of the .NET ecosystem directly.

Want to work with filesystem APIs?

Use .NET objects.

Need regular expressions?

They're available.

Want to instantiate framework classes or call static methods?

You can do that too.

PowerShell is, in many ways, a .NET automation environment disguised as a shell.

And naturally, it has its own version of the great .NET identity crisis.

Windows PowerShell 5.1 runs on the original .NET Framework.

Modern PowerShell 7 runs on modern .NET and supports Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Both can exist on the same Windows machine.

And they can behave differently when scripts depend on incompatible modules or framework APIs.

So now we have two PowerShell families corresponding to two .NET families.

At this point, the family tree needs a database.

But underneath the confusing history lies something genuinely powerful: an administrator can write a script that manipulates rich runtime objects, while developers can expose functionality that PowerShell can consume without inventing an entirely separate scripting interface.

It's one of .NET's more underappreciated achievements.

8. So What Exactly Is .NET?

After all that, it's worth asking the obvious question.

Is .NET a programming language?

No.

An operating system?

Also no.

A framework?

Yes, but that answer is incomplete.

A runtime?

Yes, but still incomplete.

.NET is better understood as an entire development platform.

It includes runtimes, compilers, standard libraries, SDKs, development tools, and application frameworks.

It supports different languages and workloads.

You can build web APIs, desktop applications, cloud services, mobile applications, games, and command-line tools.

The current platform is powerful.

And the shift from the original Windows-centric .NET Framework to today's open-source implementation is one of Microsoft's most significant technological transformations.

There is also a wonderfully ironic outcome.

Microsoft spent years building an ecosystem closely associated with Windows development.

Then it invested heavily in making that ecosystem work without Windows.

Developers can now build a C# application on Linux, deploy it in a Linux container, run it in the cloud, and never touch a Windows desktop.

Which would have sounded strange in 2002.

Somehow, all those identities coexist.

Not always elegantly.

Not always compatibly.

And certainly not under a naming scheme that anyone would describe as intuitive.

But the result is impressive.

items.title: Who is Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive at the center of the Jensen Huang controversy
items.summary: Jensen Huang said in a note to staffers on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Sean Rayford/Getty Images Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a Sunday note that he had been unfaithful to his wife. A woman named Alice Huang is at the center of the resulting scrutiny. Here's what we know about Huang, who has been an executive at Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang's note to staff on Sunday, in which he acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, came as Nvidia opened an independent investigation into reports that he may have been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." At the center is Alice Huang, who has been an executive for Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. The New York Times reported in late October that US intelligence officials believe Huang, who developed a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO, was passing information to Beijing. Huang's role at Megaspeed Megaspeed first came under scrutiny after the Times reported last year that US authorities were examining whether the company and its Malaysian affiliate were helping Chinese businesses gain access to Nvidia's AI chips despite US export controls. It is unclear when Huang — who shares a last name with the CEO, but has no relation to him — first met the Nvidia chief. A 2024 LinkedIn post from the AI company NetThunder, shared during the Computex Taipei trade show, showed the pair at a bar with other technology executives. In May 2025, news footage from Taiwanese media showed them leaving a Taipei restaurant alongside other executives. However, beyond those public appearances, little is known about Huang. Singapore corporate filings identify her as Huang Le. Megaspeed International was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, before changing its name on March 7, 2023, according to Singapore corporate filings. A day earlier, Huang, a Chinese national, was appointed as both a director and managing director of the company, alongside another Chinese national, Cang Yang, who joined as a director. She resigned from both roles on November 10, the same day Cang also stepped down. When Huang assumed the role, corporate filings show that 7Road International HK Limited transferred all shares in the Singapore entity to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. That November, ownership was transferred again to Swiftdata, a Singapore company incorporated on October 31, 2023. Swiftdata remains Megaspeed’s sole shareholder. The Times reported that Megaspeed was formed after 7Road, a Chinese online gaming company, split off its Singaporean subsidiary. Before her time at Megaspeed, Huang worked as an executive director at a Shanghai investment fund that had backed 7Road and was connected to state-backed companies, per the Times. In an October response to a query from The Wall Street Journal, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said it had not investigated Huang over her alleged ties to Chinese intelligence or her relationship with Jensen Huang. It said, however, that the Singapore Police's investigation into Megaspeed is ongoing, and declined to comment further. Nvidia CEO's ties to Huang In response to The Times' initial reporting, Nvidia characterized Jensen Huang's interactions with Huang as routine business dealings. "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, told the Times in late October. The Nvidia CEO himself made similar comments to Bloomberg last week. "Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual," Huang said. On Sunday, Huang told Nvidia staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife. His note did not name Alice Huang or address the reported relationship directly. "Today's news will not slow Nvidia," a company spokesperson told Business Insider in a statement on Sunday. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." Read the original article on Business Insider

  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a Sunday note that he had been unfaithful to his wife.
  • A woman named Alice Huang is at the center of the resulting scrutiny.
  • Here's what we know about Huang, who has been an executive at Megaspeed International.

Jensen Huang's note to staff on Sunday, in which he acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, came as Nvidia opened an independent investigation into reports that he may have been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."

At the center is Alice Huang, who has been an executive for Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.

The New York Times reported in late October that US intelligence officials believe Huang, who developed a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO, was passing information to Beijing.

Huang's role at Megaspeed

Megaspeed first came under scrutiny after the Times reported last year that US authorities were examining whether the company and its Malaysian affiliate were helping Chinese businesses gain access to Nvidia's AI chips despite US export controls.

It is unclear when Huang — who shares a last name with the CEO, but has no relation to him — first met the Nvidia chief.

A 2024 LinkedIn post from the AI company NetThunder, shared during the Computex Taipei trade show, showed the pair at a bar with other technology executives.

In May 2025, news footage from Taiwanese media showed them leaving a Taipei restaurant alongside other executives.

However, beyond those public appearances, little is known about Huang. Singapore corporate filings identify her as Huang Le.

Megaspeed International was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, before changing its name on March 7, 2023, according to Singapore corporate filings.

A day earlier, Huang, a Chinese national, was appointed as both a director and managing director of the company, alongside another Chinese national, Cang Yang, who joined as a director. She resigned from both roles on November 10, the same day Cang also stepped down.

When Huang assumed the role, corporate filings show that 7Road International HK Limited transferred all shares in the Singapore entity to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company.

That November, ownership was transferred again to Swiftdata, a Singapore company incorporated on October 31, 2023. Swiftdata remains Megaspeed’s sole shareholder.

The Times reported that Megaspeed was formed after 7Road, a Chinese online gaming company, split off its Singaporean subsidiary.

Before her time at Megaspeed, Huang worked as an executive director at a Shanghai investment fund that had backed 7Road and was connected to state-backed companies, per the Times.

In an October response to a query from The Wall Street Journal, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said it had not investigated Huang over her alleged ties to Chinese intelligence or her relationship with Jensen Huang. It said, however, that the Singapore Police's investigation into Megaspeed is ongoing, and declined to comment further.

Nvidia CEO's ties to Huang

In response to The Times' initial reporting, Nvidia characterized Jensen Huang's interactions with Huang as routine business dealings.

"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, told the Times in late October.

The Nvidia CEO himself made similar comments to Bloomberg last week. "Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual," Huang said.

On Sunday, Huang told Nvidia staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife. His note did not name Alice Huang or address the reported relationship directly.

"Today's news will not slow Nvidia," a company spokesperson told Business Insider in a statement on Sunday. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption."

items.title: NVIDIA to Investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s Relationship with a ‘Chinese Spy’
items.summary: NVIDIA , the world’s most valuable US company with a $4.5 trillion valuation, launched an independent investigation into its Chief Executive Officer and billionaire Jensen Huang after he admitted to having a relationship outside marriage with a woman allegedly accused of working for Chinese intelligence. Huang acknowledged the relationship in an email to NVIDIA employees on November 8, apologising to his wife, family and colleagues. “I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it,” he said. The admission follows a NYT report that a Chinese executive, linked to a Singapore-based data centre company, has been funnelling information into Beijing. Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang came under scrutiny for allegedly exposing sensitive company information, raising national security concerns in the US. However, Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs Spokesperson Guo Jiakun denied any espionage charges. “The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China,” he said. Meanwhile, the company issued a statement saying a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. “The Board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” it said. “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” Huang has agreed to cooperate with the investigation. NVIDIA also expressed confidence in his leadership and said it would provide further updates as appropriate. Meanwhile, Republican lawmakers in the House of Representatives have called on Huang to testify before Congress about the relationship on November 18.

items.title: Here's what smart people are saying about Nvidia's investigation of CEO Jensen Huang
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a memo on Sunday that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife. Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images Nvidia's board of directors is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang. The company said it's investigating whether Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." Huang said he had been "unfaithful" to his wife in a memo to Nvidia employees. items.summary_html:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a memo on Sunday that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife.

Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images

  • Nvidia's board of directors is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang.
  • The company said it's investigating whether Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."
  • Huang said he had been "unfaithful" to his wife in a memo to Nvidia employees.

On Sunday, Nvidia said its board of directors opened an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang had been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."

Huang shared a memo with Nvidia employees earlier in the day in which he said he had been "unfaithful" to his wife.

In October, The New York Times reported that US officials believed that a Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang, had developed a relationship with the Nvidia CEO. Alice Huang has been an executive for Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.

As Nvidia teeters on the edge of a national security scandal, some business and tech leaders have weighed in. Here's what they're saying.

Bill Ackman, CEO of Pershing Square Capital Management

On Sunday, Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman suggested people should lead with empathy when it comes to Huang.

"An alert: @JensenHuang is human. And he is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes," Ackman said on X. "He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward."

Chris McGuire, senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations

Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the US Department of Commerce shared blame for the national security threat.

He said the department has enacted policies that make it easy for China to access Nvidia most advanced chips.

"@CommerceGov leadership knew that Jensen was sleeping with a Chinese spy and that Megaspeed was a Chinese cutout, but still actively opposed any policies to tighten export controls on Nvidia chips. Why?" he wrote in an X post on Sunday.

"Commerce could have blocked chip shipments to Megaspeed the moment it found out that it was run by a Chinese spy, but it did not. Commerce has also refused to enforce regulations—which ironically remain on the books—that would require exporters to apply for a license to ship large numbers of AI chips to untrusted entities in many countries, which would prevent China from using shell companies like Megaspeed to buy controlled chips," he added.

McGuire said it's important that Nvidia takes national security issues more seriously, but also called on the US Department of Commerce to "tighten up export controls."

Jason Calacanis, angel investor and "All-in" host

Jason Calacanis, an angel investor and host on the "All-In" podcast, said on Sunday that the US is in an urgent contest to lead the global AI industry and that Huang was central to that effort.

"We need to win, for the sake of democracy and humanity. We are all in this together: the left, the right and the center. There is no time for infighting," Calacanis wrote on X. "Jensen and NVIDIA's technology are a critical target, and we need to protect them both."

Calacanis called on the US to rally together against China and "go faster."

"Act accordingly," he wrote.

Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives

Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said on Sunday that the situation is a stain on Huang's reputation.

"This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang," Ives wrote.

Michael McCaul, House Rep.

Texas Rep. Michael McCaul said the US should "immediately pause" shipments of advanced AI chips to China until "we can get to the bottom of this incident and ensure our national security is not being undermined."

"This is a classic move from the CCP's playbook — and another example of why it can never be trusted," he wrote.

Shaun Maguire, partner at Sequoia Capital

Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire shared a few thoughts in an X post on Sunday. Maguire called Huang "one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation," who also did something "incredibly dumb."

He called the decision "bad for America" but doubted Huang had bad intentions.

"two mistakes don't make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership," Maguire said.

Ross Gerber, president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth and Investment Management

Ross Gerber also discussed the news in an X post on Sunday. Gerber is the president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management.

"Extremely disappointing to see the news regarding Jensen. A huge error of judgment and at a totally critical time for AI development. Not sure how this shakes out," he wrote.

Jason Calacanis, co-host of the 'All-In' podcast
Jason Calacanis said that the ban was "smart" because of the risk of terrorism.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Calacanis, a startup investor and co-host of the All-In podcast, urged an end to the infighting in the US about the security concerns.

"America is in a war with China and AI is the battlefield," Calacanis wrote on X on Sunday. "We need to win, for the sake of democracy and humanity." He said there was "no time for infighting" and called Huang and Nvidia's technology "a critical target" that needed protection.

Calacanis said the US must "win the race for super intelligence," describing the moment as "defcon 1."

Marc Lehman, independent trader

Lehman, an independent trader who posts market commentary on X, said the allegations could create an overhang for Nvidia's stock.

Lehman called the matter "a black eye moment for Jensen" that could prompt congressional inquiries. He said investors would focus on whether Huang would remain Nvidia's CEO.

Still, Lehman said Huang's position could depend on a board investigation, which poses a risk because he is so central to Nvidia's global strategy.

He added that the episode would increase scrutiny of Nvidia's chip sales to China, "which remains a key battleground issue in DC."

Stephanie Ruhle, MS NOW host and business analyst
Stephanie Ruhle said that AI stocks have already been unstable.

Charles Sykes/Bravo via Getty Images

Stephanie Ruhle, the host of MSNBC's "Money, Power, Politics" and the network's senior business analyst, said the allegations could destabilize the broader AI industry.

"AI stocks were already performing a high wire act," Ruhle wrote on X. She said the Nvidia situation "could be hugely problematic for the industry," from hyperscalers to CoreWeave.

Nvidia is "the tie that binds them all together and holds the ecosystem up," Ruhle wrote. She added that Huang's "clout & conviction are uniquely powerful."

items.title: I'm 22 and I bet $80,000 of my savings on an industrial AI startup. Now I'm dropping out of college to go all-in.
items.summary: At 22, Anderson Chen is building a Y Combinator-backed AI startup in an industry where he says competitors are often decades older. Anderson Chen Anderson Chen, 22, is planning to drop out of college to focus on his industrial AI startup, Operon. He says being a young founder in an industry dominated by older rivals has helped him attract clients. His startup has Y Combinator backing, and he says being young helps him attract interest from clients. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Anderson Chen, 22, the Taiwanese founder and CEO of San Francisco-based Operon Solutions, an industrial AI startup backed by Y Combinator. It has been edited for length and clarity. I'm taking my second gap year from Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, where I study chemical engineering and business. Now I'm planning not to return to college. During my first gap year, I started Operon, an industrial AI startup. We automate tasks that used to be run by human operators and specialists in heavy industries, including manufacturing, oil and gas, and construction. I initially thought I'd go back to school. But Operon grew exponentially toward the end of my first gap year, so I decided to take another year off. During that year, I realized that even if you graduate, it doesn't mean you'll figure things out. I was quite scared of dropping out, to be honest. Having a bachelor's degree is the Asian standard. My parents were also initially concerned because they thought I was doing badly at school. But my gap-year expenses were covered by a fellowship, so it was no risk for me. Now my parents are okay with my plans. They're like, "Okay, go for it." I think AI is changing the value of a college degree Another reason I'm planning not to return to college is that AI is moving so fast. OpenAI recently solved a version of the Navier–Stokes problem in fluid dynamics. I remember in my sophomore year, my professor in fluid dynamics told me it was unsolvable. I realized that if you know how to use AI effectively, you might even be able to outperform your own professor. I saw an opportunity to bring AI into heavy industries I started Operon after doing internships at manufacturing companies and connecting with manufacturers and founders in Taiwan. I saw engineers throwing engineering PDFs into ChatGPT and asking it to understand them and write engineering documentation. But frontier AI models couldn't understand those documents because they had never been trained on that confidential data. That was the moment I knew I had to start this company. In manufacturing, humans follow very rigorous standard operating procedures. But the data in heavy industries is too hard for AI to understand. It's too messy. So we're structuring everything together, building a context layer for them, and allowing these agentic workflows to actually happen. In May, we received funding from Y Combinator as part of a $700,000 pre-seed round that also included other investors. We closed the round in about three days. We have about 20 clients. Some of our projects are proofs of concept, while others are already full contracts. Anderson Chen's startup, Operon, works with heavy industries to automate tasks traditionally performed by human operators and specialists. Anderson Chen I put almost all my savings into my AI startup Before we raised funds, I put almost all my personal savings into Operon. It was around $80,000. I'm not paying myself a salary, although we're paying our employees. I made the money from businesses I started before Operon. When I was 14, I was selling sneakers and doing Amazon dropshipping. While I was in college, I built a tutoring agency connecting Malaysian students with parents of children attending international schools in Singapore. I did marketing for the tutors and hired a bunch of them. Being young in an old-economy industry has its advantages Our team has five people, all under 30. The oldest is 26, and the youngest is 16. I think there's skepticism because we're working in heavy industries, and the founders of our competitors are all in their 40s and 50s. But that's the best thing I could ever ask for. Skepticism brings exposure, and people will naturally be intrigued. They'll be thinking, "Oh my God, how are you able to break into this space? I have to check it out." items.summary_html:
At 22, Anderson Chen is building a Y Combinator-backed AI startup in an industry where he says competitors are often decades older.

Anderson Chen

  • Anderson Chen, 22, is planning to drop out of college to focus on his industrial AI startup, Operon.
  • He says being a young founder in an industry dominated by older rivals has helped him attract clients.
  • His startup has Y Combinator backing, and he says being young helps him attract interest from clients.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Anderson Chen, 22, the Taiwanese founder and CEO of San Francisco-based Operon Solutions, an industrial AI startup backed by Y Combinator. It has been edited for length and clarity.

I'm taking my second gap year from Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, where I study chemical engineering and business. Now I'm planning not to return to college.

During my first gap year, I started Operon, an industrial AI startup. We automate tasks that used to be run by human operators and specialists in heavy industries, including manufacturing, oil and gas, and construction.

I initially thought I'd go back to school. But Operon grew exponentially toward the end of my first gap year, so I decided to take another year off.

During that year, I realized that even if you graduate, it doesn't mean you'll figure things out.

I was quite scared of dropping out, to be honest. Having a bachelor's degree is the Asian standard.

My parents were also initially concerned because they thought I was doing badly at school. But my gap-year expenses were covered by a fellowship, so it was no risk for me.

Now my parents are okay with my plans. They're like, "Okay, go for it."

I think AI is changing the value of a college degree

Another reason I'm planning not to return to college is that AI is moving so fast.

OpenAI recently solved a version of the Navier–Stokes problem in fluid dynamics. I remember in my sophomore year, my professor in fluid dynamics told me it was unsolvable.

I realized that if you know how to use AI effectively, you might even be able to outperform your own professor.

I saw an opportunity to bring AI into heavy industries

I started Operon after doing internships at manufacturing companies and connecting with manufacturers and founders in Taiwan.

I saw engineers throwing engineering PDFs into ChatGPT and asking it to understand them and write engineering documentation.

But frontier AI models couldn't understand those documents because they had never been trained on that confidential data. That was the moment I knew I had to start this company.

In manufacturing, humans follow very rigorous standard operating procedures. But the data in heavy industries is too hard for AI to understand. It's too messy.

So we're structuring everything together, building a context layer for them, and allowing these agentic workflows to actually happen.

In May, we received funding from Y Combinator as part of a $700,000 pre-seed round that also included other investors. We closed the round in about three days.

We have about 20 clients. Some of our projects are proofs of concept, while others are already full contracts.

Anderson Chen's startup, Operon, works with heavy industries to automate tasks traditionally performed by human operators and specialists.

Anderson Chen

I put almost all my savings into my AI startup

Before we raised funds, I put almost all my personal savings into Operon. It was around $80,000. I'm not paying myself a salary, although we're paying our employees.

I made the money from businesses I started before Operon. When I was 14, I was selling sneakers and doing Amazon dropshipping.

While I was in college, I built a tutoring agency connecting Malaysian students with parents of children attending international schools in Singapore. I did marketing for the tutors and hired a bunch of them.

Being young in an old-economy industry has its advantages

Our team has five people, all under 30. The oldest is 26, and the youngest is 16.

I think there's skepticism because we're working in heavy industries, and the founders of our competitors are all in their 40s and 50s.

But that's the best thing I could ever ask for.

Skepticism brings exposure, and people will naturally be intrigued. They'll be thinking, "Oh my God, how are you able to break into this space? I have to check it out."

items.title: Forcing a Letter Suppresses Refusal: Mechanistic Evidence from WMDP
items.summary: Safety benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) commonly use multiple-choice question (MCQ) format. However, prior studies documented that MCQ format reduces refusal rates, which may significantly affect the safety behavior of the model. We provide a first mechanistic explanation of this effect on the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset across two models - Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B. First, we use the tuned lens technique to show that when processing MCQ the model commits to an answer-letter token very quickly, which is in contrast to the gradual refusal build-up in open-ended formats. Additionally, we observe that activations on the MCQ format lie roughly 3x further from the refusal direction, compared with their open-ended counterparts. Moreover, ablating the attention heads that carry the MCQ format answer increases the refusal, which is a direct evidence that the MCQ answer-selection competes with refusal. These findings indicate that MCQ safety scores primarily measure knowledge capabilities and do not assess the safety-mechanisms.

items.title: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
items.summary: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. Extraction must adapt without fragmenting shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules. Hand-authored persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost. Weight-free prompt optimization offers an alternative, but unconstrained evolution of a monolithic prompt can rewrite shared rules alongside persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review. We introduce FinEvolveKG, a KG-construction harness separating reusable general and persona-policy blocks and mechanically confining GEPA, a reflective prompt optimizer, to the designated block. During persona adaptation, the approved general block remains byte-stable and every optimizer edit is localized to a separately versioned persona policy. A dual objective balances generic temporal-KG quality with persona-relevant facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity. We evaluate five mutation scopes on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, with three seeds for the persona-conditioned arms (v3-v5) across three personas. On the three-seed mean, the complete two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) improves over the frozen prompt baseline (v1) by 19.4-30.9% and over the tested unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%, leading v5 on both objective components and winning all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona. Without further optimization, v4 also exceeds v5 across all evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. An SME audit supports using the generated triplets as ground truth; a blinded two-SME audit favors v4 over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments. These results show that mechanically attributable evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, without attributing the gains causally to the boundary.

items.title: Compression of Emotion in Language Model Representations
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been evaluated on their ability to identify emotions expressed in text and produce fluent emotional language. However, output predictions alone do not reveal how fine-grained emotion distinctions are organized internally. We study seven LLMs on GoEmotions, an English Reddit dataset annotated with 27 fine-grained emotion categories plus neutral. We compare model predictions and emotion-prompted final-token representations with the 28 GoEmotions categories and with coarser emotion-family and sentiment groupings. We find a consistent pattern of $\textit{overcompression}$ relative to the fine-grained GoEmotions taxonomy. Under the tested KMeans protocol, when we cluster their hidden representations without using emotion labels, the clearest split is into two groups that largely separate positive from negative emotion. Coarser emotion groupings are also recovered with fewer clusters than the full 28-category taxonomy. Yet linear probes retain substantial fine-grained predictive information. These results suggest that fine-grained emotion information remains accessible even though broader affective structure more strongly organizes the unsupervised geometry.

items.title: Contextuality and Contradictions: Exploring Real-World Identifications of AI-Generated Writing
items.summary: As AI-generated content spreads into nearly every domain of human interaction, practices and discourses of AI detection, both formal and informal, have become an everyday part of how people interact with text and with each other. In this paper, we explore the real-world practices and discourses of AI identification that have emerged in response to a shifting discursive landscape where the human provenance of a text can no longer be taken for granted. We pair qualitative coding with computational analysis of lexical change, grounded in linguistic anthropological perspectives on language and communication, to investigate AI identifications among English Wikipedia editors and students. We find that these identifications draw on a diversity of evidentiary types, from discrete textual features and judgments about content to circular sense-making claims and presumptions about the author's moral character, and that they are contradictory, dynamic, and contextually dependent. In practice, what often motivates an AI identification is not the presence of any specific textual element, but pragmatic infelicity: a perceived mismatch between the elements present and those deemed appropriate within the text's particular context. Consequently, real-world identifications of AI-generated writing do not merely neutrally point out the perceived presence of "AI-like" features, but can be leveraged as a discursive resource to maintain and define sociolinguistic norms: what can be said in a given context, what is appropriate, and, ultimately, what is human. Further, the design and implementation of systems and tools that treat AI-likeness as a context-free property of text may therefore inherit, and enforce at scale, the norms of whichever contexts they were trained on.

items.title: RL-ATTACK: A Generalized Black-Box Adversarial Attack on Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit vulnerabilities to adversarial perturbations that can induce unintended responses. These vulnerabilities can be identified via intentional attacks and subsequently used to improve model safety. In black-box settings where gradients are inaccessible, existing methods tend to guess adversarial transformations using external knowledge, ignoring the information provided by the target model. To mitigate this, we propose a trainable black-box framework based on reinforcement learning, which learns from the target model to generate tailored adversarial transformations. We demonstrate that our approach achieves lower post-attack accuracy, greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation on both natural language inference and generative Q&A tasks. On natural language inference, it drives post-attack accuracy to 2% within 20 queries. Against generative language models, our trained attacker consistently achieves lower post-attack accuracy than the untrained attacker and wins in 4 out of 6 settings when compared to a strong optimization-based baseline. We further experiment with multiple reward designs and training settings, and we find that no design or setting is consistently dominant. Our code is available at https://github.com/taikunudel/RL-ATTACK.

items.title: Structuring Survey Histories for LLM Digital Twins: A Controlled Study of Background, Decision Procedure, and Evaluation Profiles
items.summary: LLM-based digital twins aim to predict how individuals would respond in new settings from representations of their prior responses. Existing evidence that compression of survey histories need not reduce predictive accuracy suggests that representation structure, rather than information volume alone, may be an important design choice. We study BDE, a fixed representation that organizes each respondent's survey history into Background, Decision procedure, and Evaluation. We evaluate it on Twin-2K-500 (Toubia et al., 2025) by predicting each respondent's held-out answers on 17 tasks. In a paired evaluation with 100 respondents, a fully inferred BDE profile improves overall accuracy over the raw survey transcript by 1.27 percentage points (pp) on gpt-5.4-nano (p < 0.01) and 1.19 pp on gpt-5.4-mini (p < 0.001). Three analyses then examine the schema, extraction depth, and component composition. Against a length-matched free-form profile written from the same transcript by the same extractor, BDE improves pricing accuracy on both simulators (2.15 pp on nano, p < 0.01; 1.38 pp on mini, p < 0.05), while its overall advantage is significant only on nano (1.05 pp, p < 0.05). Allowing deeper inference during extraction yields no statistically significant gain on either simulator. By contrast, adding Evaluation to a Background--Decision procedure profile improves overall accuracy by 1.44 pp on nano (p < 0.001) and 1.22 pp on mini (p < 0.001). These results indicate that the advantage over raw transcripts is not explained by compression or length alone, and attribute it primarily to profile composition rather than deeper extraction.

items.title: Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS): A Formal Mathematical Framework
items.summary: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) operates on document pairs, returning a single scalar per comparison. In a multi-document setting where several sources may have contributed to one or more targets, pairwise STS cannot disentangle each source's marginal semantic contribution from their shared vocabulary. In this paper, Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS) is introduced as a conditional form of STS that computes similarity between two documents after eliminating semantic elements shared with a third via set-theoretic operations. SCS makes four contributions: 1) it introduces directionality, partitioning pairwise relations into lateral (inter-source) and vertical (source-to-target) classes; 2) conditioning induces role-dependent asymmetry by extending the comparison domain from unordered pairs to ordered, conditioned triples of a target, a reference, and a conditioning document; 3) SCS introduces inter-document conditioning by subtracting shared content from a third document, complementing the intra-document conditioning in recent C-STS work; and 4) the set-theoretic decomposition achieves threshold-free partitioning of shared and residual content, requiring no arbitrary similarity cutoff. Although developed for the $n \to 1$ configuration, the framework extends to $1 \to n$ via vertical role reversal and to $m \to n$ via independent composition of source- and target-side conditioning. With the established $1 \to 1$ case, these span the full spectrum of document cardinality. SCS scores should be interpreted ordinally, as rankings of marginal contributions rather than absolute measurements. The broader implication is that metric space axioms commonly assumed in similarity formalizations constrain expressiveness in role-differentiated multi-document settings, and that extending the domain to conditioned triples can recover information that pairwise-symmetric comparisons suppress.

items.title: Guardrail Erosion in Domain Fine-Tuned Large Language Models: A Paired Audit of Knowledge-Centric Abstention in Biomedical LLMs
items.summary: The number of domain fine-tuned models, particularly in the biomedical domain, is rapidly expanding. Fine-tuning promises high-performing models at a fraction of the cost of training a base model, but it can also produce unintended behavioral changes. Multiple studies have shown that safety guardrails can erode with fine-tuning, yet large-scale studies across model architectures, data mixtures, and fine-tuning methodologies remain limited. Where prior work in this space has studied value-centric refusal, this work focuses on knowledge-centric abstention. We audit 25 biomedical domain fine-tuned large language models against 11 paired base checkpoints on MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench to evaluate the impact of fine-tuning on knowledge-centric abstention. We find that defined appropriate abstention measured by these benchmarks, already low in base models (median 8.3% on MedAbstain), falls further after fine-tuning (median 4.2%, decreasing in 21 of 25 pairs on MedAbstain), and that the magnitude and direction of change are heterogeneous across pairs. These results motivate fine-tuning methods that improve domain-specific capability while preserving appropriate caution.

items.title: Richness Is Not Evenness: Ordered Renyi Crossings under Self-Training
items.summary: Recursive self-training of language models, a setting studied in model collapse, can reduce vocabulary while making frequent words, mostly function words, less dominant. We fine-tune English GPT-2 on its own output for nine generations, vary the training-data sampling temperature, and measure every model with one fixed sampler. As training temperature rises, Renyi entropy changes turn from loss to gain at distinct temperatures: min-entropy first, then collision entropy, Shannon entropy and observed richness. Between the outer crossings, word types fall while the most-common word becomes less dominant. Untruncated training at T = 1 lies in this interval: at 13,000 words, generation 9 has 24% fewer types than generation 0 yet collision entropy is 0.91 bits higher. The ordering persists with a finer grid, different measurement samplers, a fixed word budget and five fresh training seeds. Min-entropy again crosses before richness in four further settings (in Hindi only at interpolated roots) and in 12 of 13 distinct measurements under eight text representations. items.title: From Procedures to Permissions: Learning Precise Subagent Authorization from Agent Skills
items.summary: As language agents tackle increasingly complex tasks, they increasingly rely on multiple agents to coordinate specialized work, requiring decisions not only about what each subagent should do but also which tools and workspace resources it should access. Existing agent systems provide mechanisms for controlling tools and execution environments, but do not directly specify the resources required by each delegated subtask. Moreover, task outcomes and execution trajectories alone provide limited supervision for determining whether a subagent has received appropriate permissions. We observe that Agent Skills encode procedural knowledge describing the operations, tools, and files required at each step, providing a natural source of supervision for authorization. Building on this observation, we synthesize tasks and step-by-step procedures from Skills, execute them through subagent delegation in interactive environments, and use verified trajectories to construct training data for task execution and authorization. On ClawArena-Team, our method improves tool permission precision by 13.4 percentage points and workspace permission precision by 24.1 percentage points, while increasing overall task success by 11.6 percentage points for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench, our method remains competitive with existing agent data synthesis approaches. These results show that the procedural knowledge embedded in Agent Skills provides a source of supervision for precise subagent orchestration that task outcomes alone cannot provide.

items.title: On the Incompleteness of do-calculus for Universal Identifiability
items.summary: We study the problem of causal effect identification from an arbitrary set of observational and/or interventional distributions, which we call Universal Identifiability (uID). The uID problem generalizes existing classical identifiability (ID) and general identifiability (gID) problems, which considered the identification problem from either mere observational distributions or a specific type of interventional distributions. Prior research has established graphical criteria to determine when a causal effect is identifiable in ID and gID problems. Moreover, algorithms that leverage do-calculus and basic probability manipulations have been proposed to compute these effects. Consequently, it has been shown that do-calculus is both sound and complete in these problems. Despite these well-established results, a formal definition of what it means for the do-calculus to be complete does not exist. We propose a rigorous formalization for the completeness of the do-calculus and show that the completeness results in previous work remain valid. However, for more general problems, such as uID, the rules of do-calculus are no longer complete. This is perhaps the reason why the uID problem has remained open thus far.

items.title: Using an LLM to Tackle Difficult Cases in NER for Nepali Tweets
items.summary: Named entity recognition (NER) is challenging for social media data in a low-resource language. LLMs often lag behind pretrained language models (PLMs) in NER performance, but they show promise in handling cases that PLMs struggle with. Using a dataset of Nepali tweets, we split the test set into "easy" and "hard" cases using token probabilities from a fine-tuned pretrained language model (PLM). We then evaluate an LLM on the hard test cases using 16 different prompt configurations. We find that selecting examples based on semantic similarity and increasing the number of examples improves F1 score by almost 10 points from the baseline configuration. Although the LLM underperforms the PLM on the full and easy test sets, it surpasses the PLM on the hard test set, resulting in an improved score when the two models are combined.
